comments.author: RuixiangMa
comments.body:
@tong1heng Great work! The design  is clean and well-motivated. A few points I'd like to understand better:
1. submitFile splits at 16 MiB and batches at 128 entries, but GdsTransport::submitTransferTasks already does the same splitting (kMaxSliceSize) and batch checking (io_batch_depth_, user-configurable). If a user sets io_batch_depth=32, submitFile still batches 128 — only 32 get accepted per TENT batch. Is this intentional double-protection, and if so, should the batch limit be read from TENT config rather than hardcoded?
2. Main has added some TENT infrastructure since this RFC was written. Transport::tracksLocalBuffer() seems like a natural fit for GDS's cuFileBufRegister (local-only, shouldn't be advertised via desc.transports). Transport::quiesce() could settle cuFile I/O before buffer deregister. And the all-or-nothing submitTransferTasks contract means partial failure needs rollback of pushed params. Would it make sense to reference these in the RFC?
3. Main recently refactored lease (shared_ptr<Lease>, group-shared) and group eviction (GroupDomain, all-or-none). How do GDS-only objects interact — do they get an independent or group-shared lease? Could UnregisterGdsStorage stale cleanup break all-or-none eviction by removing one GDS replica from a group?
4. Preserve creates finalized=false entries that are never auto-cleaned. If finalize RPCs fail repeatedly (network jitter, master restart), the backing file could be exhausted silently. The Roadmap mentions eviction policy as future work — should the gap be acknowledged in the main body with a short-term mitigation (metric, max count, or TTL)?
5. storage_generation algorithm and collision risk aren't specified. The PR uses steady_clock XOR client_id — steady_clock resets on reboot, so if client_id is reused (e.g. vLLM config), a timestamp collision (low but non-zero) could cause stale descriptors to be accepted. Would it be worth specifying the algorithm and confirming generation=0 as an invalid sentinel?

comments.author: tong1heng
comments.body:
Thanks for the thoughtful review! These points identify several implementation gaps and areas where the RFC needs clarification.

1. The two layers serve different purposes: `submitFile` bounds store-level submissions and manages their futures, while `GdsTransport::submitTransferTasks` enforces cuFile limits. However, the hardcoded batch limit of 128 is inconsistent with the configurable `io_batch_depth`. One clarification: an over-capacity submission returns `TooManyRequests`; it does not accept only the first 32 entries. We will expose the effective GDS batch depth through TENT and use it in `submitFile`, counting capacity in terms of entries after splitting. We will also align the splitting limits and add tests for different batch depths and submissions spanning multiple batches.

2. Agreed. We will reference these interfaces in the RFC and adapt the implementation accordingly. GDS will implement `tracksLocalBuffer()` using its local registration registry and stop advertising cuFile registrations through `desc.transports`. We will implement `quiesce()` to stop new submissions and settle outstanding I/O before teardown releases buffers and batch resources. For the all-or-nothing submission contract, we will validate all requests before modifying the sub-batch and restore appended state on failure. We will also verify cuFile’s submission-failure semantics to ensure potentially accepted I/O cannot be treated as a clean rejection and retried through another transport.

3. The PR currently uses the older group-registration path and needs to be adapted to main’s `shared_ptr<Lease>` and `GroupDomain` implementation. GDS-only objects should follow the same semantics as other objects: ungrouped objects have an independent lease, while grouped objects share the group’s lease. The local GDS `ReadLease` separately protects an extent during an in-flight read. `UnregisterGdsStorage` removes matching GDS replicas and deletes an object only when no valid replica remains. We will preserve group bookkeeping through the common metadata-removal path and add mixed MEMORY/GDS group tests. We will also clarify that invalid-storage cleanup is distinct from policy-driven eviction; current main tests permit safe members to be evicted while unsafe members remain, so strict all-or-none wording needs qualification.

4. Yes, we will acknowledge this limitation explicitly in the main body. `Preserve()` retains an allocation because an RPC failure does not establish whether the master applied the operation, but these uncertain entries currently have no reconciliation or automatic reclamation path. The issue also includes entries committed locally before a finalize RPC fails, so tracking only `finalized=false` is insufficient. As a short-term mitigation, we will track uncertain-entry counts, bytes, age, and allocation failures, and introduce a configurable admission limit. A TTL may trigger reconciliation, but it must not directly reclaim an extent without confirming that the master no longer references it and that local I/O has completed.

5. Agreed. `steady_clock` XOR the client ID does not provide a reliable cross-restart uniqueness guarantee when the client ID is reused. We will replace it with a fresh, randomly generated nonzero 64-bit storage-incarnation token whenever the backing file is recreated, preserving the current wire format. The RFC will specify the algorithm and its probabilistic collision properties. `generation=0` is already invalid: initialization avoids it, and `RegisterGdsStorage()` rejects it. We will document this invariant and add tests for zero-generation rejection and stale descriptors after storage recreation with a reused client ID.

items.title: [Ascend Transport] Intermittent one-sided put failure (~2%): remote-buffer registration races transfer dispatch ("Can't find remoteBuffer", E19999 HcclBatchPut)
items.author: yeshouxiaobai
items.body_excerpt:
### Environment

- mooncake wheel: `mooncake-transfer-engine-npu 0.3.11.post1` (as shipped inside `quay.io/ascend/vllm-ascend:v0.30.0rc1-a3`)
- Hardware: 2× Atlas 800T A3 nodes, HCCS interconnect (16 NPU each)
- CANN 9.1.0, driver 26.0.rc1
- Use case: vLLM-Ascend PD disaggregation, AscendStore (mooncake backend) as an L2 KV pool — prefill workers put KV blocks into host-DRAM segments via `batch_put_from_multi_buffers`; 8 ranks per worker process, 32 segments total. Observed with both the shared global transfer engine and the store-independent TE path (`ASCEND_GLOBAL_RESOURCE_CONFIG` set); the P2P transfer engine (different connector, HBM-to-HBM one-sided reads) in the same process shows **zero** failures.

### Symptom

~2% of per-key puts fail with per-key error code `-1`. Engine-side log chain:

```text
E19999: Failed to invoke HcclBatchPut, hccl_result = 1 [comm_channel.cc:462]
  ... TransferSync ... remote_engine:192.168.x.x:20xxx, operation:write,
      op_descs size:22-24, timeout:30000 ms
client_service.cpp:1685] Transfer failed for key ...: TRANSFER_FAIL
client_service.cpp:1786] Successfully revoked failed put for key ...
(Worker) ERROR [mooncake_backend.py] Failed to put 1 keys out of 2. error_codes=[-1]
```

The real error is only visible in the CANN plog (`/root/ascend/log/debug/plog/`):

```text
[ERROR] HCCL(pid): [hccl_one_sided_conn.cc:364][GetTransInfo]
Can't find remoteBuffer by key[0x12e540000000][49152]
```

— i.e. the target host-DRAM buffer is not (yet) registered from the sender's perspective when the transfer dispatches. Same PID/thread, ~140µs before the E19999 line: directly causal.

### Evidence that this is an async-registration vs dispatch race

1. **Fails at zero concurrency**: first failure occurred during a single in-flight request (`Running: 0 reqs`) — not a load/resource-exhaustion issue.
2. **Uniform across targets**: failures spread evenly over all 32 remote segments (559–673 each over ~47 min) — not a port/binding/per-segment issue.
3. **Not idempotency/lease**: zero duplicate-key or lease errors; every failure is TRANSFER_FAIL.
4. **Small batches**: failing batches are 22–24 descriptors — not a descriptor overflow.
5. **Same-batch retries never recover; fresh dispatches do**: the transport's internal retry (same batch, ~300 ms apart, 3 attempts) fails every time; the next request that re-saves the same block (a fresh `batch_put_from_multi_buffers` call) succeeds. Consistent with the remote registration landing asynchronously *after* the raced dispatch.
6. **`ASCEND_THREAD_POOL_SIZE=1` makes it ~100% fatal** — the strongest signal. With the pool collapsed to a single thread, puts go from 98% success to near-total failure (only 2 keys stored; same key failing 6–7× back-to-back at 250 ms intervals): the blocking `TransferSync` starves the async registration task on the same `AscendThreadPool`. This strongly suggests remote-buffer registration is enqueued on the same pool that executes the sync transfer, and the two race under the default pool (~2% of the time).
7. Same remote address keeps failing in bursts over 18 minutes — a recurring race, not a one-shot boot-time problem.

### Attempted transport-level workarounds (both fail)

- `ASCEND_THREAD_POOL_SIZE=1` → livelock as above.
- `ASCEND_BUFFER_POOL=1` (adxl.BufferPool, would structurally bypass the per-allocation registration) → the *other* transfer engine in the same process (vLLM P2P connector via the global TE) then dies at boot: `adxl_engine_impl.cc:109 Failed to initialize AdxlEngine`. So BufferPool mode cannot be used when a P2P TE and a store TE coexist in one process.

### Current application-level mitigation

Re-issuing the failed key subset as a fresh `batch_put_from_multi_buffers` call (+50 ms / +200 ms) recovers the keys, which further confirms the async-registration model. We carry this as a patch on the vllm-ascend side (mooncake_backend.put re-issue loop) — but the race itself remains: the plog keeps logging `Can't find remoteBuffer` for every raced put.

### Ask

1. Make the one-sided put path self-consistent on Ascend: either resolve/register the remote buffer synchronously before dispatch, or have the in-batch retry re-resolve `remoteBuffer` instead of failing the whole task, or prioritize registration tasks over transfers on the shared pool.
2. Please document/consider making `ASCEND_BUFFER_POOL` coexist with a second (P2P) transfer engine in the same process — it looks like the intended structural fix but is unusable in mixed-TE deployments today.

Happy to share full logs (engine + plog), the repro workload, and the re-issue patch. Thanks!

items.title: unified_cache: MAMBA component nodes are pruned instead of downgraded on device eviction, breaking host-tier loadback
items.author: JustinTong0323
items.body_excerpt:
## Symptom

When the unified radix cache evicts a node whose model uses the MAMBA (hybrid-KDA) component, the node is pruned outright from the radix tree instead of being downgraded to host-resident. A subsequent request for the same prefix never even attempts H→D load-back and reports `cached_tokens_details=None` (no `host > 0` hit), even though the backup chain committed pages to the host tier correctly.

## Repro

1. Serve any hybrid-KDA model with:

```
--enable-hierarchical-cache --mamba-scheduler-strategy extra_buffer \
--enable-cache-report --max-total-tokens 14000
```

A small `max-total-tokens` is used only to force eviction with a few probes; the bug is independent of pool size.

2. Send a shared 4000-token prefix P followed by a distinct 3800-token suffix containing a unique word. Repeat for ~9 suffixes so the backup chain populates the host tier.

3. Send 3 fully unique ~7.8K prompts to force LRU device eviction of P.

4. Re-request P with a fresh suffix.

## Observed (TP4, extra_buffer, cache-report on)

- Hit-driven D→H backup triggers and commits fire on every P request (44× in the probe).
- On device eviction the node's Full-component value is tombstoned, but the node itself is dropped from the radix tree — not inserted into `evictable_host_leaves`.
- The re-request reports `cached_tokens_details=None` and no `load_back` is issued. Both device and host miss.

## Root cause

`python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/unified_cache/unified_tree_core.py` only considers the **Full** (KV) component when it decides whether a node can stay as an evictable-host leaf (`_evict_host_leaf` only checks `component_data[FULL].host_value`). `components/mamba_component.py` has the analogous `build_hicache_transfers` / commit path (line ~770 already writes `cd.host_value` for MAMBA on BACKUP_HOST), but the device's evict path checks only the Full component, so the node is detached wholesale even though both tiers' host data are present.

## Expected behavior

Same shape as the MLA tier case: node becomes a host-resident evictable leaf, a later request hits the host tier and issues `load_back`.

## Confirmed scope

- Only the unified controller path. The older `hi_mamba_radix_cache` (used for Qwen3-Next) does anchor the host side via `mamba_host_value`; the unified-tree KDA path does not.
- Reproduces on the hybrid-KDA Ling-3.0-flash model port (PR #33561) and also with vendor-side safe-gate tracking patches applied — the anchor logic itself is missing, this is not a KDA sidecar issue.

## Mitigation attempts

- Vendor-side safe-gate tracking patches (extend-tuple return, packed-decode kwargs) cover L3 storage-tier writes only; L2 behavior unchanged.
- #31474 (KDA prefix caching under mamba extra_buffer) addressed device-side tracking, not the host anchor.

## Direction

Happy to prepare a PR if maintainers want to assign this. The cleanest fix likely mirrors `component_data[FULL].host_value` for the MAMBA component at device-evict time so the node remains discoverable in the host LRU.

items.title: [Bug] Large HiCache UCX startup timeout on downstream build; not reproduced on v0.5.20
items.author: ByronHsu
items.body_excerpt:
### Result

**Not reproduced on the latest upstream image (v0.5.20).** A large HiCache pool triggered a UCX startup timeout on our earlier downstream build, but both HiCache and no-HiCache starts passed with the unmodified upstream image.

| Build | HiCache per rank | UCX initialization, all 8 ranks | Server ready |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Downstream `869abc0605`, NIXL 1.3.0 / UCX 1.21.0 | 234 GB | Six ranks explicitly timed out at 60s; none completed | No |
| Same downstream build, no HiCache | 0 | 3–4s | Yes |
| **Upstream v0.5.20, NIXL 1.4.1 / UCX 1.22.0** | **234 GB** | **~2s** | **234s after launch** |
| Same upstream image, no HiCache | 0 | ~2s | 62s after launch |

Each HiCache/control pair ran on the same eight-H200 node with fresh processes. The upstream pair used a different physical node from the downstream pair, and multiple software components changed: this does **not** identify a fix or prove the cause. Only startup was tested, with no inference requests. Both upstream runs registered all eight KV buffers, passed passive `/ready` checks for 30 seconds, and exited cleanly.

### Reproduction settings

8 H200s, approximately 2014 GiB host RAM; public `deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V2-Lite` real weights, revision `604d5664dddd88a0433dbae533b7fe9472482de0`.

Upstream image: `lmsysorg/sglang:latest` resolved to **v0.5.20**, source `94602c9c2b7cbdb8efd5c52802dac6a1c180089e`. Tested amd64 image digest:

```text
lmsysorg/sglang@sha256:b27fce60bc5494c118c4910702812bcfa8cee67abcdd1ff8b0902f21647552f4
```

No source overlay, serving patches, or dependency replacements. Download the model revision above into `$MODEL_DIR`, then run:

```bash
export SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_ENGINE_INIT_TIMEOUT=60
export SGLANG_NCCL_ALL_GATHER_IN_OVERLAP_SCHEDULER_SYNC_BATCH=1
export SGLANG_FORCE_STREAM_INTERVAL=1
export SGLANG_FORCE_CPU_IMAGE_PREPROCESSING=0

python -m sglang.launch_server \
  --model-path "$MODEL_DIR" --trust-remote-code \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 30000 \
  --tp-size 8 --dp-size 8 --ep-size 8 --enable-dp-attention \
  --disaggregation-mode prefill --disaggregation-transfer-backend nixl \
  --mem-fraction-static 0.7 --dtype bfloat16 --kv-cache-dtype bf16 \
  --page-size 64 --tokenizer-worker-num 4 \
  --context-length 150000 --max-running-requests 1024 \
  --skip-server-warmup --log-level debug --decode-attention-backend fa3 \
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --hicache-size 234 \
  --hicache-write-policy write_through \
  --hicache-mem-layout page_first --hicache-io-backend kernel
```

Remove the five HiCache options for the control. CUDA graphs stay enabled; NIXL is the PD transport, not L3 storage. Actual pool allocation: **234,001,612,800 bytes per rank**, about **1.872 TB total**. Size is per rank and requires sufficient host/cgroup headroom.

### Original failure

The downstream run failed **during UCX backend creation, before KV registration**:

```text
RuntimeError: NIXL create_backend('UCX', {'num_threads': '8'}) did not return within 60s
```

Five seconds before failure: **141.6 GiB host headroom**, **39.2–39.4 GiB free per GPU**, no host OOM-counter increase or CUDA OOM. Host memory pressure and compaction were high. No native stack inside UCX was captured. A later audit found rank 0 in a debugger tracing stop at 21:29:30 UTC, inside the 60-second UCX window, as well as earlier allocation-stage attachments. The retained samples do not establish total pause duration. Other ranks also timed out without a recorded tracing stop, but this run was not free of measurement interference. A telemetry gap further limits the evidence.

The upstream HiCache run kept at least **120 GiB host headroom**, logged no OOM, and completed UCX startup quickly. The underlying reason for the older failure remains unresolved.

<details>
<summary>Upstream runtime</summary>

Python 3.12.3; PyTorch 2.13.0+cu130; NIXL/nixl-cu13 1.4.1; bundled UCX 1.22.0; CUDA 13.0; driver 595.71.05; Linux 6.8.12; FlashInfer 0.6.18; Transformers 5.12.1. THP mode remains `madvise`. The 60-second UCX deadline and eight prefill backend threads were unchanged.

</details>

### Follow-up: the extra host memory is DC receive buffers

On one exclusive node, with the same upstream source/image and **232 GB/rank** HiCache, we compared fresh server processes:

| Native backend | DC interfaces | Receive-buffer chunks | Scheduler anonymous huge pages | UCX startup span |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| NIXL 1.4.1 / UCX 1.22 | 0 | 288 | 12.498 GiB | 2s |
| NIXL 1.3.0 / UCX 1.21 | 288 | 576 | 23.188 GiB | 4s |
| Same 1.3.0 package, only `UCX_TLS=^dc_mlx5` added | 0 | 288 | 12.502 GiB | 3s |

All three initialized all eight ranks, registered KV buffers, and held passive readiness for 30 seconds. No compaction stalls, THP fallbacks, or OOM occurred. No inference or PD transfers were tested. The third case is a diagnostic intervention, **not a verified timeout fix**.

UCX debug logs and per-scheduler memory maps identify the difference: **8 ranks × 9 workers × 4 ports = 288 DC interfaces**, each eagerly allocating a **38 MiB** receive buffer through `rc_recv_desc`. Those extra buffers account for **10.6875 GiB** of huge pages. Excluding only DC on the old package removes them and matches the newer package. Actual loaded UCX versions were verified in server logs.

The old binary includes DC; the new wheel omits it. [NIXL PR 1708](https://github.com/ai-dynamo/nixl/pull/1708) disables DC in the manylinux build. The v1.3.0 source tag also contains that flag despite the tested wheel including DC, so we report observed binary features rather than infer build history from tags.

During the **original failing UCX initialization window**, kernel counters rose by **10,496 compaction attempts, 10,492 failures, 3,407 THP fallbacks, and 3,668 direct-reclaim stalls**. They were flat just before UCX started. The examined SGLang NIXL startup and host-pool files are byte-identical between the downstream and upstream revisions.

This supports a host-memory compact

items.title: cumem allocator: double-free and stale error codes during sleep/wake cycles
items.author: markrogersjr
items.body_excerpt:
## Your current environment

vLLM v0.17.0 (also reproducible on main) with cumem allocator enabled, using sleep/wake cycles for colocated GRPO training.

## How would you like to use vllm

Colocated training where vLLM's GPU memory is released via `sleep()` during training steps and reclaimed via `wake_up()` for inference.

## Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] I have searched for [similar issues](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/issues).

## Description

Several bugs in the cumem allocator cause CUDA driver errors during sleep/wake cycles:

### 1. Double cuMemRelease on already-unmapped allocations

`sleep()` iterates all allocations and calls `unmap_and_release` unconditionally. If some allocations are already unmapped (e.g. from a previous partial sleep or external release), this causes a double `cuMemRelease`. Similarly, `wake_up()` calls `create_and_map` on already-mapped allocations. There is no per-allocation tracking of mapped state.

### 2. CUDA ops on freed memory during sleep

When the allocator is sleeping, PyTorch's garbage collector can trigger `my_free` on tensors whose backing memory was already released by `sleep()`. The C++ `my_free` then calls `unmap_and_release` on invalid handles, causing CUDA driver errors. Additionally, `gc.collect()` and `torch.cuda.empty_cache()` at the end of `sleep()` can trigger these frees while the allocator is in the sleeping state.

### 3. Stale global error_code propagation

`error_code` is a file-scope global in `cumem_allocator.cpp` that is not cleared between calls. A non-fatal error in one operation (e.g. `create_and_map`) can persist and cause a subsequent unrelated call (e.g. `unmap_and_release` or `my_free`) to take the wrong code path.

### 4. Size mismatch in my_free

`my_free` passes its `size` argument to `unmap_and_release` and `cuMemAddressFree`, but the correct size is `recv_size` returned from the Python callback. This can cause incorrect unmapping.

### 5. Flash Attention 4 rotary embedding import failure

`find_spec("flash_attn")` succeeds with FA4 installed, but `from flash_attn.ops.triton.rotary import apply_rotary` fails because FA4 restructured its module layout. This causes an unhandled `ImportError`.

## Fix

https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/36535

items.title: [Feature]: Request observer hook for the Rust frontend
items.author: questcollector
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

We run vLLM behind an API gateway and collect per-tenant usage records (prompt / cached / generated tokens) in an L7 proxy in front of it today. With the Rust frontend we would rather do this in process, as an out-of-tree module (a small crate that plugs into the frontend and writes usage records to our own store): the frontend knows the exact token counts without parsing responses, including for streams the client aborts before the final usage chunk is sent, which a proxy never sees. We don't want to patch vLLM for this, so upstream would only need a narrow, generic hook.

In the Python frontend this is possible out of tree: a stat logger plugin (`vllm.stat_logger_plugins`) receives per-request `FinishedRequestStats`, and `--middleware` can map the tenant by request id. The Rust frontend has no equivalent hook. (One gap on the Python side: requests aborted by the frontend, e.g. on client disconnect, are removed in `OutputProcessor.abort_requests` without finished stats, so they never reach stat loggers although they consumed tokens. The Rust frontend already records these aborts in Prometheus from `Drop`, so the hook below covers them.)

Today the terminal request data is computed in `RequestMetricsTracker::record_finished` and written straight to Prometheus, so nothing else can consume it. Prometheus is aggregated (no per-request or per-tenant data), and traces are sampled; the tracing plan in RFC #44757 also leaves client-initiated aborts out of the `llm_request` span, which is reasonable for tracing but means aborted streams, which still consume tokens, can't be metered from spans.

Proposal: two small, independent pieces.

**1. `vllm-llm`: a request-completion seam.** Both terminal points of `GenerateOutputStream` (`poll_next` on engine finish, `Drop` on frontend abort or stop-string match) produce one `FinishedRequest` (external / engine request id, model, LoRA, engine index, finish reason, token counts, lifecycle timestamps). The built-in Prometheus recording derives its latency breakdown from the same `FinishedRequestStats`, so metrics and other consumers cannot drift, which is the property RFC #44757 wants between metrics and the `llm_request` span. Registered observers are called synchronously, in registration order, at most once per request; panics are isolated. With no observer registered there is no extra allocation.

```rust
pub trait RequestObserver: Send + Sync + 'static {
    /// Called on the request path (possibly inside `Drop`); must not block.
    fn on_finished(&self, request: &Arc<FinishedRequest>);
    /// Called once after the engine client has shut down, e.g. to drain a queue.
    fn shutdown(&self) -> BoxFuture<'_, ()> { /* no-op */ }
}

impl Llm {
    pub fn with_request_observers(self, observers: RequestObservers) -> Self;
}
```

**2. `vllm-server`: register observers the same way as the router extension (#43774).** `ServeExtensions` (router extension + request observers) and `serve_with_extensions`; `serve` and `serve_with_router_extension` keep their behavior and delegate to it. Like
#43774, this is a composition hook for custom binaries, not a stable plugin API.

**Non-goals:** no engine protocol change, no new Prometheus metrics, no queueing or async adapter upstream (I/O-bound observers hand requests to their own task; the OTel SDK already batches spans), and no per-request attribute plumbing through the request types.

### Alternatives

- OTLP spans or logs as the metering source: spans are sampled and client aborts are left out (as planned in #44757), so they are not billing-grade. With this hook, a span emitter is just another observer.
- Scraping Prometheus: aggregated, no per-request or per-tenant data.
- Patching the frontend downstream: works, but every deployment re-patches `request_metrics.rs` / `output.rs`.

### Additional context

- Prototype: an out-of-tree crate on top of the two changes writes per-tenant usage records to a Redis Stream (the tenant is attached by a router-extension middleware keyed by request id, so no upstream change is needed for that). Verified with `vllm-mock-engine`: normal finish, client abort, Redis outage, and flush on SIGTERM.
- Both changes are small and additive: one new module plus wiring at the two terminal points in `vllm-llm`, and one new module plus entry-point wiring in `vllm-server`. Existing APIs keep their behavior; I have a working branch and would split it into two PRs.
- Related: RFC #44757 (this could serve as the base for the Phase 2 `llm_request` span; happy to coordinate with @tahsintunan), #47810, #43641 / #43774.
- #54144 and #57582 touch the same files; I would rebase onto them rather than race them.
- Disclosure: the prototype was developed with AI assistance (Claude Code). If this direction sounds reasonable, I'll open the PRs myself, having reviewed every change, and follow up on review feedback.

cc @BugenZhao

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Bug]: `--mamba-block-size` has no effect in any valid configuration after the removal of `mamba_cache_mode="all"`
items.author: fxhumble
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

<details>
<summary>Environment</summary>

```
vLLM 0.30.0 (behaviour also verified by reading main @ 28d76f3)
Model: Qwen3.8-27B (hybrid, Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration)
GPU: 1x NVIDIA H20 (96 GB), TP=1, dtype bfloat16
Args: --max-model-len 8192 --max-num-seqs 8 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.75
      --enable-chunked-prefill --enable-prefix-caching
      [--mamba-block-size N]
```

</details>

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`--mamba-block-size` is a documented, validated, user-facing flag, but on current
main there appears to be no configuration in which the user-supplied value
actually reaches the engine. It is silently replaced before it is ever read.

#### The flag's lifecycle on main @ `28d76f3`

1. The flag is registered and parsed — `vllm/engine/arg_utils.py:1383`.
2. `VllmConfig.validate_mamba_block_size` (`vllm/config/vllm.py:3360`) **raises**
   unless `--enable-prefix-caching` is also set:
   ```
   "--mamba-block-size can only be set with --enable-prefix-caching"
   ```
3. Enabling prefix caching forces `mamba_cache_mode = "align"` —
   `vllm/model_executor/models/config.py:687`.
4. `vllm/model_executor/models/config.py:700` only fills in a default
   (`if cache_config.mamba_block_size is None`), so a user value survives here.
5. `Platform._align_hybrid_block_size` (`vllm/platforms/interface.py:1105-1106`)
   then unconditionally discards it:
   ```python
   if cache_config.mamba_cache_mode == "align":
       cache_config.mamba_block_size = cache_config.block_size
   ```

Two changes seem to have closed the last escape hatches:

- `MambaCacheMode` is now `Literal["align", "none"]`
  (`vllm/config/cache.py:63`). `"all"` — the only mode where the user value fed
  into the derived block size — was removed in #58997.
- `user_specified_mamba_block_size` has been removed entirely, so there is no
  longer any state available to detect or warn about the override.

Net effect: the flag *requires* prefix caching, prefix caching *forces* align,
and align *discards* the value. `"none"` rejects the flag outright at step 2.

The docstring at `vllm/config/cache.py:177` still presents it as a tuning knob:

> Size of a contiguous cache block in number of tokens for mamba cache.
> Can be set only when prefix caching is enabled.
> Value must be a multiple of 8 to align with causal_conv1d kernel.

#### Reproduction

Four otherwise-identical servers, varying only `--mamba-block-size`, reading
`vllm:cache_config_info` from `/metrics` and replaying the same 24-turn
multi-turn chat trace against each:

| requested | resolved `block_size` | `kv_cache_size_tokens` | `kv_cache_max_concurrency` | aggregate hit rate |
|-----------|----------------------|------------------------|----------------------------|--------------------|
| 64        | 784                  | 181669                 | 22.18                      | 37.3%              |
| 128       | 784                  | 181669                 | 22.18                      | 37.3%              |
| 256       | 784                  | 181669                 | 22.18                      | 37.3%              |
| (unset)   | 784                  | 181669                 | 22.18                      | 37.3%              |

TTFT across the four runs differed by at most ~3 ms (P50 155.8–160.3 ms), i.e.
run-to-run noise. The flag is accepted and shows up in `non-default args`:

```
non-default args: {..., 'enable_prefix_caching': True, 'mamba_block_size': 64, ...}
```

and no `WARNING` is emitted about the override. The only hints are two `INFO`
lines that do not mention the user's value:

```
INFO [interface.py] Setting attention block size to 784 tokens to ensure that
     attention page size is >= mamba page size.
INFO [interface.py] Padding mamba page size by 0.13% to ensure that mamba page
     size and attention page size are exactly equal.
```

#### Why this is worth fixing

On hybrid models the derived block size can be large — 784 tokens here — and
prefix caching returns no hits at all until the shared prefix exceeds one block.
In the 24-turn trace above (prompt growing 63 → 998 tokens) the measured
per-turn hit rate was:

- turns 1–17 (prompt 63 → 811): **0 hits**, TTFT rising 87.6 → 397.3 ms
- turn 18 (prompt 836): shared prefix crosses 784, hit = exactly 784 tokens,
  TTFT drops to 80.1 ms
- turns 19–24: hit stays pinned at 784 while the prompt grows, so the hit *rate*
  decays from 93.8% to 78.6% until the next 1568-token boundary

Mean TTFT either side of that single boundary: 319.1 ms → 87.5 ms.

A user who measures this will quite reasonably reach for `--mamba-block-size` to
shrink the caching granularity. Today that silently does nothing, which costs
real debugging time — the flag exists, is documented, validates its input, and
errors if you pair it wrongly, so there is every reason to believe it works.

#### Possible directions

I did not want to guess at the intended design, so I have not opened a PR. Three
options I can see:

a. **Warn on override** — re-introduce tracking of whether the value was
   user-specified (or snapshot it before align) and emit a `WARNING`, mirroring
   the existing precedent in `vllm/platforms/cpu.py:250-266` for
   `user_specified_block_size`.
b. **Deprecate / remove the flag**, since no code path consumes the user value
   any more.
c. **Make align honour it** — likely infeasible given the hard constraint that
   attention page size must be >= mamba page size, which is what pins the value
   at 784 for this model.

Happy to send a PR for whichever direction you prefer.

Possibly related: #58997 (removal of `"all"`), #57278, #43624, #52895, #52898.

items.title: [Bug]: pythonic tool parsers stream wrong numbers in tool call arguments
items.author: u7k4rs6
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

vllm main (206e45d47). Reproduces on a live server and on CPU with just the parser.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

The pythonic-style tool parsers (`pythonic`, `llama4_pythonic`, `olmo3`, `lfm2`) can stream the wrong number in tool call args. Non-streaming is fine.

Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct with `--tool-call-parser pythonic`, asked to fetch a URL and then look up coordinates, temperature 0:

```
non-streaming: locate {"lat": 37.7749, "lon": -122.4194}
streaming:     locate {"lat": 37.0749, "lon": -122.0194}
```

The number gets streamed before it's done. When the text ends in `37.`, the parser closes it up, reads `37.` as `37.0` and sends that. Then it appends the rest of the real value by length, so you get `37.0749`. Exponents can even break the JSON (`1.5e3` streams as `1.00.0`).

It only hits calls after the first one. For the list-style parsers, an earlier call also needs an `=` inside a string (URLs with query strings, SQL...). olmo3 hits it on any second call.

Impact: wrong but valid-looking numbers (coordinates, prices, amounts), with no way for the client to notice.

items.title: [ROCm] torch.profiler stalls on ROCm 10 from a rocprofiler-sdk split lock
items.author: amd-mghanimi
items.body_excerpt:
On ROCm 10.0, `torch.profiler` makes each CUDA-graph replay idle after the 8th kernel.

With tensor parallelism this turns into a straggler rank. When profiling Kimi-K3 at TP8, whichever rank hits the stall reaches the next all-reduce late, and the other seven ranks wait for it, so every rank's step time grows. The single-GPU probe below shows the same per-replay stall without needing 8 GPUs.

`pool<signal_t>` is constructed in a `static_object` byte buffer with no `alignas(Tp)` ([ROCm/rocm-systems#9639](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-systems/issues/9639)). In the nightly wheel, `m_buffer` is at `0xba7514` (`mod 64 = 20`), so `m_reused` (`lock incq 0xe8`) starts at byte 60 of a cache line and bus-locks on signal reuse.

Seen on one MI350X, `HIP_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0`. Both images are the nightly built from vLLM `3f1bcfd82bb2e93fcd364fc7a5491718453a77e2`. ROCm 7.2.3 is `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly-3f1bcfd82bb2e93fcd364fc7a5491718453a77e2` (base `rocm/dev-ubuntu-22.04:7.2.3-complete`) and has no hole. ROCm 10 is `vllm/vllm-openai-rocm:nightly-rocm100-3f1bcfd82bb2e93fcd364fc7a5491718453a77e2`.

Idle after kernel 7 of each of two replays:

| N | ROCm 7.2.3 | ROCm 10 |
|---:|---|---|
| 256 | ~0 µs | 56 µs, 482 µs |
| 512 | ~0 µs | 517 µs, 591 µs |
| 2048 | ~0 µs | 540 µs, 523 µs |

Other gaps inside a replay stay near 1 ns. On 7.2.3 the only gaps above 5 µs are between the two replays (~25–34 µs).

One replay, median of 7. Wall time is `profiler off→on (+overhead)`. Idle share is shown as `7.2 / 10.0 / PR`; it is approximate because wall time and idle come from different replays.

| N | ROCm 7.2 wall (ms) | ROCm 10.0 wall (ms) | This PR wall (ms) | Idle share: 7.2 / 10.0 / PR |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 256 | 0.43→0.88 (+105%) | 0.43→1.43 (+233%) | 0.43→1.07 (+149%) | ~0 / 6–48% / 8% |
| 512 | 0.85→1.73 (+104%) | 0.86→2.27 (+164%) | 0.85→1.93 (+127%) | ~0 / 37–42% / 13–15% |
| 2048 | 3.36→6.87 (+104%) | 3.39→7.50 (+121%) | 3.37→7.09 (+110%) | ~0 / 13% / 4–5% |

Most profiler overhead is present on ROCm 7.2.3 too. At N=2048 the raw ROCm 10 idle is 13% of that overhead; after this PR it is 4–5%.

Solution: #61887 (cherry-pick [ROCm/rocm-systems#12089](https://github.com/ROCm/rocm-systems/pull/12089) into `Dockerfile.rock_base`).

<details>
<summary>Probe</summary>

Requires one visible GPU. Prints `(index, µs)` for gaps above 5 µs.

```python
import json

import torch
from torch.profiler import ProfilerActivity, profile


def sync() -> None:
    torch.cuda.synchronize()


def capture(n: int) -> torch.cuda.CUDAGraph:
    x = torch.zeros(1, device="cuda")
    graph = torch.cuda.CUDAGraph()
    stream = torch.cuda.Stream()
    stream.wait_stream(torch.cuda.current_stream())
    with torch.cuda.stream(stream):
        for _ in range(2):
            x.add_(1)
        sync()
        with torch.cuda.graph(graph):
            for _ in range(n):
                x.add_(1)
    torch.cuda.current_stream().wait_stream(stream)
    graph.replay()
    sync()
    return graph


def big_gaps(n: int) -> None:
    graph = capture(n)
    with profile(
        activities=[ProfilerActivity.CPU, ProfilerActivity.CUDA],
        record_shapes=False,
        with_stack=False,
    ) as prof:
        graph.replay()
        sync()
        graph.replay()
        sync()
    prof.export_chrome_trace("/tmp/t.json")
    events = json.load(open("/tmp/t.json"))["traceEvents"]
    kernels = [
        ev
        for ev in events
        if ev.get("ph") == "X" and "kernel" in str(ev.get("cat", "")).lower()
    ]
    kernels.sort(key=lambda ev: ev["ts"])
    gaps = [
        (i, kernels[i + 1]["ts"] - (kernels[i]["ts"] + kernels[i]["dur"]))
        for i in range(len(kernels) - 1)
    ]
    big = [(i, round(gap, 1)) for i, gap in gaps if gap > 5]
    print(f"N={n} kernels={len(kernels)} big={big}", flush=True)


def main() -> None:
    assert torch.cuda.device_count() == 1
    for n in (256, 512, 2048):
        big_gaps(n)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

</details>

items.title: [Bug][KV Connector] Load-failure report arriving after the owner was preempted: blocks stay cached, `fail` is not applied, stale output can be delivered
items.author: guanxingithub
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary
Follow-up to #61768 / #61769 (owner *aborted* before its failure report). The same orphaning happens when the owner is **preempted** between `schedule()` and `update_from_output()`: `_handle_invalid_blocks` scans `running` and the `WAITING_FOR_REMOTE_KVS` entries of `kv_holding_waiting`; a preempted request sits in `waiting` as `PREEMPTED` with its blocks already returned by `_free_request_blocks` (hashes kept). #61769 records block ids only in `_free_request`, so a preempted owner leaves nothing to scan. Tracked here so the work after #61769 has a home, as requested on #61768.

### Two ways to reach it (CPU scheduler probes, async scheduling, mock connector with a synchronous load; one of 8 blocks reported invalid)
| path | role | main `a97d19d7` | #61769 `7238ccdf` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **KV-pressure preemption** inside `schedule(N+1)` | top-level `kv_producer` (the deferred-free fence at `scheduler.py` L191 is consumer-only) | owner preempted; 7/8 blocks hashed; resumes on a 112-token hit (48 valid); under `fail` the owner is **not failed** | same |
| same | top-level `kv_consumer` / `kv_both` | fence holds the owner (`_request_blocks_can_be_freed` false) — not reachable | same |
| **`reset_prefix_cache(reset_running_requests=True)`** between `schedule(N)` and `update_from_output(N)` | `kv_consumer` | reset preempts the owner, then raises (deferred blocks still held); engine continues; 8/8 hashed; owner resumes on 112 | same |

Independent re-run of those probes (26.10 container, aarch64, CPU; main `0c2584929`, #61769 `7238ccdf`, and #61769 + a block-id record in `_preempt_request`); `H` = block still hashed:
| probe | main | #61769 | #61769 + record on preemption |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| pressure preempt, `kv_producer`, `fail` | preempted; `HHHHHHH-`; status `PREEMPTED` | same | **`HHH-----`**, status still `PREEMPTED` (not failed) |
| pressure preempt, `kv_producer`, `recompute` | `HHHHHHH-` | same | `HHH-----` |
| pressure preempt, `kv_consumer`, both | fence holds; `fail` → `HHH-----` + `FINISHED`; `recompute` → `RUNNING` | same | same |
| reset preempt, `kv_consumer`, both | reset raises; `HHHHHHHH`; `PREEMPTED` | same | **`HHH-----`**, still `PREEMPTED` |
| reset preempt, `kv_producer`, both | reset succeeds; `--------`; resume hit 0 | same | same |
| abort + reuse, `kv_producer`, `fail` / `recompute` | C fails / C rewound 128→64; `HHHH----` / `HHHHHHHH` | C fails / rewound; `---` / `-----HHH` | same as #61769 (allocation identity — #61905) |
So the record repairs eviction in both preempted-owner paths and nothing else: the `fail` disposition and stale-output items remain, as @Lewis-panda's follow-up addresses.
Real-connector reachability: scheduler-level so far; a connector that loads synchronously under a top-level producer role (MultiConnector children, LMCache depending on config) would reach the first path; the reset path needs only a consumer. Credit: probes by @ArijitDeb (inference-correctness-lab, followup-61768), reset path by @Lewis-panda.

### What a fix needs (from the discussion on #61768)
1. **Eviction**: keep the owner's ordered block ids across preemption (the #61769 record, created in `_preempt_request` before `_free_request_blocks`) — measured to evict blocks 3..7 in both paths, both policies.
2. **`fail` disposition**: a preempted owner whose load failed must still be failed via the existing error path, not silently recompute on resume.
3. **Stale output**: the sample from the failed-load step must not be delivered (pressure preemption without `requires_kv_delivery` can deliver it; reset already drops).
4. **Readmission**: wait for the outstanding outputs of a request whose in-flight step loaded external KV before readmitting it — the failure cannot be known until that output arrives (Arijit's position; Lewis's follow-up implements a drain).
@Lewis-panda has a local follow-up to #61769 covering 1–4 (18 new CPU regression cases, 485 standalone / 541 with #53298). Related: #61905 (late report attributed to an unrelated request after block-id reuse — the allocation-identity half, separate), #53298 (live-owner recovery), #42461 / RFC #35780 (request-level reporting would retire this path).

### Expected behaviour
Failed KV never produces a prefix hit until repaired; a `fail`-policy owner is failed whether or not it was preempted; no sample from the failed step is delivered; both policies, both scheduling modes.

items.title: [Bug]: pythonic and llama4_pythonic tool parsers break on a raw newline inside a string argument
items.author: shoichiromiyamoto
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

vLLM main @ d6f0b7a, CPU build on macOS arm64. The affected code is pure-Python parsing.

### 🐛 Describe the bug

`PythonicToolParser` and `Llama4PythonicToolParser` fail when a string argument contains a raw newline, such as multi-line code written with real line breaks inside `'...'`. Both parsers pass the text to `ast.parse` and `make_valid_python` unescaped, and a raw newline inside a quoted string is a syntax error.

```python
from transformers import AutoTokenizer
from tests.tool_parsers.utils import run_tool_extraction
from vllm.tool_parsers import ToolParserManager

tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("openai-community/gpt2")
out = "[write_file(content='a\nb'), get_time()]"
for name in ("pythonic", "llama4_pythonic"):
    for streaming in (False, True):
        parser = ToolParserManager.get_tool_parser(name)(tok)
        content, calls = run_tool_extraction(parser, out, streaming=streaming)
        print(name, streaming, [(c.function.name, c.function.arguments) for c in calls], repr(content))
```

Output on main:

```
pythonic False [] "[write_file(content='a\nb'), get_time()]"
pythonic True [('write_file', '{"content": "a')] None
llama4_pythonic False [] "[write_file(content='a\nb'), get_time()]"
llama4_pythonic True [('write_file', '{"content": "a')] None
```

Non-streaming returns the call list as plain content. Streaming cuts the first call's arguments off at the newline and drops the second call.

lfm2 (#48171) already escapes raw control characters with `escape_ctrl_chars_in_strings` before parsing, and #60436 does the same for olmo3. I plan to fix these two parsers the same way and will open a PR.

**Label**

`good first issue` — filing under [[Onboarding 2026] Good first issues](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/issues/3372).

**Summary**

`lmcache/storage_backend/serde/cachegen_basics.py` still builds five debug log messages with f-strings, so the strings are interpolated even when debug logging is disabled.

**Details**

All five call sites are in `CacheGenGPUEncoderOutput.debug_print_device()`:

```python
logger.debug(f"bytestream device: {self.data_chunks[0].bytestream.device}")
logger.debug(
    f"bytestream_lengths device: "
    f"{self.data_chunks[0].bytestream_lengths.device}"
)
logger.debug(f"cdf device: {self.cdf.device}")
logger.debug(f"max_tensors_key device: {self.max_tensors_key.device}")
logger.debug(f"max_tensors_value device: {self.max_tensors_value.device}")
```

Per @ApostaC's guidance in #3372, `%`-style is preferred so the arguments are formatted only when the record is actually emitted (ruff `G004`).

**Expected Outcome / Goal**

The five calls use `%s` placeholders, and `ruff check --select G004` reports no violations for this file. The rendered log text stays identical — f-string interpolation and `%s` both go through `str()`.

**Additional Context**

- Scope is this one file only, format style only, no behavior change. Whether the (currently uncalled) `debug_print_device` helper should exist at all is a separate question and out of scope here.
- Verification: `ruff check --select G004 <file>` and `pre-commit run --files <file>`.
- Repo-wide there are still 381 `G004` violations (271 under `lmcache/`), so this is one file out of a longer list.

Refs #3372

items.title: [Feature] Move shared cache transfer types out of hicache_storage.py
items.author: imReese
items.body_excerpt:
## Checklist

* [x] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
* [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

## Motivation

`PoolName`, `PoolTransfer`, `PoolHitPolicy`, and `PoolTransferResult` are currently defined in `hicache_storage.py`.

These types are no longer really HiCache-specific. They are also used by Unified Cache, `pool_host`, NIXL, HF3FS, and other cache/storage code.

This makes imports like this a bit confusing:

```python
from sglang.srt.mem_cache.hicache_storage import PoolName, PoolTransfer
```

Code that has nothing to do with HiCache still has to depend on a module named `hicache_storage`.

Would it make sense to move these shared types into a neutral module, for example:

```text
mem_cache/pool_transfer.py
```

and let `hicache_storage.py` import/re-export them for compatibility?

This should only be a code organization change, with no behavior change.

## Related resources

Current users include:

* `unified_cache/unified_cache_linker.py`
* `unified_cache/components/full_component.py`
* `pool_host/group.py`
* `storage/nixl/`
* `storage/hf3fs/`

items.title: [Bug]: ModelOpt Llama-4 Checkpoints Take 5+ minutes to load
items.author: robertgshaw2-redhat
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

In working on some MoE refactors, I discovered that L4 for ModelOpt takes 5+minutes to load weights even from CPU page cache. 
- https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-FP8

The root cause is basically this hack logic to load the state dict that ModelOpt uses
- https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/blob/main/vllm/model_executor/models/llama4.py#L439-L523 [modelopt is the fused case] 

What happens is that the CPU tensor (loaded weight) that we are going to load into the GPU tensor (param) becomes non-contiguous due to this logic. As a result, when we eventually call `_copy()` from CPU->GPU we are calling this on a non-contiguous cpu tensor which takes 3-4s per weight.

To hack around this for local R&D, I simply immediately move the loaded_weight to the GPU. This makes the gather happen on the GPU which accelerates things a lot. This isn't reasonable as an actual solution though

We should investigate where the logic in the weight loader can avoid creating non-contiguous CPU tensors


### Alternatives

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and asked the chatbot living at the bottom right corner of the [documentation page](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/), which can answer lots of frequently asked questions.

comments.body:
@robertgshaw2-redhat tested on H200 with `nvidia/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-FP8`:

| Approach | Load Time |
|----------|-----------|
| Original (buggy) | 78 sec |
| `.contiguous()` on CPU | 88 sec (slower - adds CPU alloc overhead) |

comments.author: robertgshaw2-redhat
comments.body:
> [@robertgshaw2-redhat](https://github.com/robertgshaw2-redhat) tested on H200 with `nvidia/Llama-4-Scout-17B-16E-Instruct-FP8`:
> 
> Approach	Load Time
> Original (buggy)	78 sec
> `.contiguous()` on CPU	88 sec (slower - adds CPU alloc overhead)
> **GPU-first** `.to('cuda').transpose()`	**37 sec (2.1x faster)**
> The GPU-first approach works well. You mentioned it's "not reasonable as an actual solution" - what are the specific concerns? Is it GPU memory during loading, or multi-GPU compatibility?
> 
> Happy to implement a different approach if preferred.

I thought it was a hack because we have:
- the param, which is loaded into gpu memory (empty tensor)
- the loaded_weight, which is coming from disk and is mapped into cpu memory

Right now, we have a simple trustworthy process where we never have a copy of `loaded_weight` in GPU ram. We simply call `._copy()` which copies the loaded wieight into the param. This guarantees that we do not have any straggling gpu memory from weight loading

If we move the loaded weight in to gpu memory, we have to be 100% certain that we put it back. This is kind of a can of worms IMO and I don't think we should do something like this to solve an edge case like a single model with a single quant framework (especially for a model that has limited usage like this)

So my preference would be to figure out if its possible to ensure that the cpu weights remain contiguous rather than moving them to the gpu unless we have a clean way to manage the lifecycle of the weight

comments.author: rohithputha
comments.body:
Hi, 
I have analyzed the possible causes for this issue. 
I have found some to be:
1. I believe there are two types of expert placement strategies: Linear and Round Robin. Linear is better for memory movement between CPU and GPU. I suspected that this problem might have been caused by the use of round-robin placement which causes multiple DMAs. But it turns out that the default is linear and mostly likely linear placement is being used.
2. One more root cause that I learnt might be that .transpose() in torch. PyTorch just Performs metadata remapping for transposing and hence this causes non contagious tensors and hence multiple DMA invokes.

These are some theories. I would like to test some solutions like performing indexing first, transferring to GPU and then performing transpose operations. 

I am new to contributing to vLLM and open source in general. If this approach works for you, I would like this to be assigned to me. Also, one note that I don't have Nvidia gpu to test and benchmark the changes. any leads or help or guidance regarding that would be appreciated.

Hey @rohithputha - thanks for your contribution. I think it will be tough to contribute to this type of feature without a GPU. There are many clouds you can rent them from. Otherwise, I would suggest looking into a different feature.

This does not have anything to do with linear vs round robin. The root cause of the issue is that the model opt checkpoints on disk are in a different "fused" format which require reshaping to get into the runtime format. The indexing associated with this casues the issue. The ideal solution here could be to figure out if its possible to avoid making things non-contiguous. It very well may not be possible and so we might have to hack around it by moving things to the gpu first, whihc as I said above is not ideal

comments.author: jadechip
comments.body:
Ran a few experiments against this issue and wanted to share the results in case they are useful.

- I was able to reproduce the slow post-warmup load: ~`495s` on 2x RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell.
- The trace supports the issue hypothesis: the hot path is CPU -> GPU copies from non-contiguous CPU tensors in the Llama-4/ModelOpt MoE loader.
- Tried two fixes but did **not** help:

1. Make routed expert source tensors contiguous before copy:

```text
measured load: 532.63s
routed_experts.copy: 4080 ms
make_contiguous: 609790 ms
```

This made the copy cheap but made total load time worse -_-

2. Slice the local TP shard first, move only that shard to GPU, transpose on GPU, and skip the later TP narrow:

```text
measured load: 494.73s
routed_experts.copy: 0 measured events
local shard -> device: 465178 ms
```

This removed the `routed_experts.copy` hotspot, but did not improve wall-clock time.

I guess the expensive part is repeatedly consuming these non-contiguous CPU views. The simple fixes above mostly move the cost around. A better fix probably needs to avoid creating those views, or load/reshape the checkpoint tensors in an order closer to the final parameter layout?

comments.author: ishrith-gowda
comments.body:
@guptapiyush16 @LeonxLJX heads up before you start, there are 3 open PRs against this issue already.

| PR | author | approach | file |
|---|---|---|---|
| #46766 | @pratheeknathani | `.contiguous()` before the copy | `models/llama4.py` |
| #50227 | @Dev-with-Mouzan | same, inline at the weight_loader call | `models/llama4.py` |
| #47580 | me | flip the strided side to the destination, no CPU gather | `layers/fused_moe/routed_experts.py` |

#46766 and #50227 are the same fix. `.contiguous()` is a no-op if already contiguous, so the conditional in #46766 and the unconditional call in #50227 do the same thing. #46766 was first, 2026-06-25.

That fix works but it makes the strided CPU gather explicit instead of removing it: `.contiguous()` still walks non-contiguous host memory element by element, then transfers the result densely. Same shape as #32081 (~68s to ~60s above), matches @jadechip's traces showing the cost moving, not disappearing.

#47580 removes the gather. Undoing the transpose recovers the contiguous on-disk slab for free, so the H2D transfer is dense with no CPU-side gather, and the layout change happens as a strided write on the device instead. No loaded weight ever sits in GPU memory, so it doesn't hit @robertgshaw2-redhat's lifecycle concern with GPU-first approaches. TP-narrowed slabs degrade to row-run memcpys instead of elementwise gathers.

Numbers: fp8 62.8ms to 4.0ms (15.8x), bf16 93.4ms to 7.5ms (12.4x) per copy on an A100-80G. End to end on a 24-layer truncation, 18.8s to 12.5s. @eric1932 then ran the full 48-layer model on 1x H200 with source-hash-verified builds and paired runs: 102.58s to 23.63s median, 4.34x, identical output tokens across all six runs. Thanks for that, it's exactly the full-model H200 datapoint this needed.

Two tradeoffs worth naming. It's in `routed_experts.py`, not `llama4.py`, so it covers any fused-MoE checkpoint that arrives transposed, not just Llama-4/ModelOpt. It's also bigger: +145/-3 vs +8/-0 and +5/-1, mostly a test file covering contiguous/transposed/TP-narrowed layouts across fp8/bf16/fp32; the fix itself is about 35 lines. If a maintainer wants the one-liner now and the general fix later, that's a fine call, I'd rather see this issue closed than fight for the merge.

Happy to rebase (it's ~2200 commits behind, still conflict-free) or split out the test file if that helps review.

items.title: [RFC]: CPU backend support for the vLLM connector + Mooncake Store L2 for multi-instance CPU serving
items.author: amd-lalithnc
items.body_excerpt:
## 1. Summary

This RFC proposes upstreaming two related contributions that enable **LMCache on the vLLM CPU backend** and make **cross-instance KV reuse** work for CPU serving:

1. **A CPU GPU-connector** (`VLLMCPUConnector`): a pure-torch gather/scatter path between vLLM's paged CPU KV cache and an LMCache `MemoryObj`, handling vLLM's 4D fused K/V CPU layout. This is the missing piece that lets LMCache run at all on `device=cpu`.
2. **Fixes to the Mooncake Store L2 connector** so it works on the CPU backend and shares KV **across instances** (fork-safe per-process client init, a correct `exists()`/lookup path, and a config-key alias).

Together these let multiple vLLM CPU instances behind a load balancer share one KV cache (SHM on a single box, or Mooncake Store over TCP across a cluster), instead of each instance recomputing the same prefixes.

Note that the CPU connector (contribution 1) is **backend-agnostic**: it is the shared foundation that unlocks the *entire* LMCache backend ecosystem on CPU (local DRAM L1, the shared SHM server, pickle, and remote L2s). Contribution 2 is one representative distributed L2 (Mooncake). We enable and validate **both** the default (SHM) and Mooncake paths because they target different deployment scopes (see §3.4).

We propose **two stacked PRs** (CPU connector, then Mooncake-on-CPU) plus this RFC to tie them together.

## 2. Motivation

- **CPU inference is growing** (cost, availability, disaggregated/CPU-tier deployments), and vLLM has a maturing CPU backend.
- **Multi-instance CPU serving needs *shared* KV.** vLLM's Automatic Prefix Caching (APC) is **per-instance**: behind a load balancer, instance B cannot reuse instance A's prefix KV, so shared system prompts / few-shot / documents are recomputed on every instance.
- **LMCache already solves cross-instance reuse**, but had **no CPU connector**, so it could not run on vLLM CPU at all; and the **Mooncake Store L2** path did not work on CPU or across instances (fork-safety + lookup bugs).
- **Measured impact** (Section 5): on a single-socket AMD EPYC, an external shared KV cache gives **+27-31% aggregate throughput at 3 instances** and **-28%/-34% p95/p99 tail latency** vs APC.

## 3. Design

### 3.1 Topology

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    LB[NGINX load balancer] --> V1[vLLM CPU inst 1]
    LB --> V2[vLLM CPU inst 2]
    LB --> V3[vLLM CPU inst 3]
    V1 <-->|store / load KV| L[(LMCache)]
    V2 <-->|store / load KV| L
    V3 <-->|store / load KV| L
    L <-->|put / get| S{{Shared KV: SHM  or  Mooncake Store L2 / TCP}}
```

### 3.2 CPU connector (`VLLMCPUConnector`)

**Why a CPU connector is needed.** Every existing GPU connector relies on CUDA custom ops (`c_ops`) and CUDA streams and assumes the GPU KV memory layout. None of that exists on CPU, so LMCache previously could not run on vLLM's CPU backend at all. `VLLMCPUConnector` fills that gap.

**What it implements.** The same connector interface, using **plain PyTorch tensor operations** (indexing + copy) with no CUDA kernels or streams:

- `from_gpu(...)` (**STORE / gather**): copy the KV for tokens `[start, end)` out of vLLM's paged CPU buffer into a contiguous `MemoryObj`.
- `to_gpu(...)` (**LOAD / scatter**): copy KV from a `MemoryObj` back into vLLM's paged buffer, placing each token's K/V into the slot given by vLLM's slot mapping.
- `batched_from_gpu(...)` / `batched_to_gpu(...)`: batched variants that handle several token ranges in one call.

**Handling vLLM's CPU KV layout.** vLLM's CPU backend stores each layer's cache as a single **4D fused K/V tensor** (K and V packed together), which is laid out differently from the GPU cache. For each layer the connector derives logical views shaped `[num_blocks, block_size, num_heads, head_size]` for K and for V (`_kv_token_views`), then uses the request's block/slot offsets to move exactly the right rows. This keeps gather/scatter correct without copying the whole buffer.

**Selection.** The connector is picked automatically when the device is CPU (`torch_device_type == "cpu"` in `CreateGPUConnector`), so no user config change is required.

**Plugging in as a `GPUConnectorInterface`.** So the CPU connector can subclass `GPUConnectorInterface` without importing the CUDA-heavy `gpu_connectors`/`utils` modules (which import `c_ops`, absent in NO_GPU_EXT builds), the interface ABC is extracted into a small `c_ops`-free `interface.py` that `gpu_connectors.py` re-exports. Existing GPU connectors are unaffected.

### 3.3 Mooncake Store L2 on CPU

The Mooncake client (Go runtime + multithreaded C++) is **not fork-safe**, and vLLM forks its scheduler/worker processes. Fixes:

- **Fork-safe, lazy per-process init**: the store/lookup client is created inside each process on first use (`_ensure_store()`), never inherited across a fork.
- **Correct lookup path**: `exists()`/`exists_sync()` now call `_ensure_store()` first (the contains/lookup path can run before any put/get on an instance) and compare `is_exist() == 1` (it returns `1/0/-1`) so an error never reads as a cache hit. Without this, cross-instance lookups were swallowed as misses and the instance recomputed.
- **Config-key alias**: accept `master_server_address` as an alias for `master_server_addr` in dict-based setup.

**Cross-instance key consistency (usage requirement, not connector code):** for a prefix computed on instance A to be found by instance B, the KV keys must hash identically across processes. Python's default randomized hashing breaks this; deployments must use a stable algorithm (e.g. `LMCACHE_PRE_CACHING_HASH_ALGORITHM=sha256` with `PYTHONHASHSEED=0`). This will be documented.

### 3.4 Why enable both paths (default SHM and Mooncake L2)

The CPU connector is transport/backend-agnostic, so a natural question is *why validate two L2 paths instead of one*. Because they are **complementary, not competing**: the right choice is dictated by deployment topology, and we want CPU users to be able to pick either without changing the connecto

items.title: LMCache MP GDS-L1 aborts in cuFileReadAsync with putStreamOp assertion during TP=4 hot retrieval
items.author: ekaynar
items.body_excerpt:
## Description

  LMCache MP native GDS-L1 crashes during the first hot KV-cache retrieval with TP=4 and DeepSeek V4 hybrid KV cache.

  The cold request successfully stores 8,192 tokens. Repeating the identical prompt finds all 32 GDS-L1 chunks, but the LMCache server aborts inside NVIDIA cuFile before completing the
  load.

  ## Error

  ```text
  [2026-08-16 07:32:46,757] LMCache INFO:
  Stored 8192 tokens in 0.642 seconds

  [2026-08-16 07:32:47,435] LMCache INFO:
  Prefetch request completed (L1+L2): 32/32 retained keys
  (32 L1, 0 L2) in 4.4 ms
  (external_request_id=chatcmpl-a1dc73801f7804a9-9b591ba6,
  prefetch_request_id=-1)

  [2026-08-16 07:32:47,451] LMCache INFO:
  AffinityThreadPool: affinity_key=-7117897118196929406 assigned to
  worker slot 0 of 1 (thread affinity-pool-0-0);
  2 distinct key(s) now bound

  [2026-08-16 07:32:47,451] LMCache WARNING:
  AffinityThreadPool: affinity_key=-7117897118196929406 wrapped onto
  worker slot 0 (only 1 workers), so it shares a thread with an earlier
  key and their tasks are serialized. Increase the worker count to give
  each client its own thread.

  [2026-08-16 07:32:47,452] LMCache INFO:
  AffinityThreadPool: affinity_key=-6742962413049701147 assigned to
  worker slot 0 of 1; 3 distinct key(s) now bound

  [2026-08-16 07:32:47,453] LMCache INFO:
  AffinityThreadPool: affinity_key=5784243743074828858 assigned to
  worker slot 0 of 1; 4 distinct key(s) now bound

  python3: cufile_async.h:107:
  void CUfileStream_s::putStreamOp(CUfileStreamInfo_t*):
  Assertion `tmp == sinfo' failed.
  ```

  This causes the LMCache process to abort rather than return a recoverable error.

  ## Secondary vLLM failure

  After the LMCache process aborts, vLLM enters the failed hybrid-cache-load path and exits with:

  ```text
  ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 1)

  File "vllm/v1/core/sched/scheduler.py", line 2293,
  in _update_requests_with_invalid_blocks

  (req_block_ids,) = self.kv_cache_manager.get_block_ids(req_id)
  ```

  This appears secondary to the LMCache/cuFile process abort.

  ## LMCache configuration

  ```bash
  CUFILE_ENV_PATH_JSON=/etc/cufile.json \
  LMCACHE_LOG_LEVEL=INFO \
  LMCACHE_USE_EXPERIMENTAL=True \
  lmcache server \
    --host 127.0.0.1 \
    --port 5560 \
    --http-host 127.0.0.1 \
    --http-port 18080 \
    --prometheus-port 19090 \
    --enable-extra-logging \
    --l1-size-gb 200 \
    --gds-l1-path /mnt \
    --gds-l1-use-direct-io \
    --eviction-policy LRU
  ```

 No CPU L1 or NIXL L2 is configured. All four GPUs register successfully before the request.

  ## Reproduction

  1. Start LMCache MP with the native GDS-L1 configuration above.
  2. Start vLLM with TP=4 and `LMCacheMPConnector`.
  3. Send an 8K-token prompt once to populate GDS-L1.
  4. Send the identical prompt again.
  5. LMCache finds all `32/32` L1 chunks and then aborts in `CUfileStream_s::putStreamOp()`.

  ## Environment

  - LMCache: `0.5.4rc3.dev1 (g0373a573)`
  - vLLM: `0.23.0`
  - Python: `3.12.3`
  - PyTorch: `2.11.0+cu130`
  - PyTorch CUDA: `13.0`

items.title: [Perf][SM103] sparse MLA decode: bf16-dense-KV ABI doubles KV bytes vs FlashMLA's packed pages; mid-batch q=6 verify regression (B=3–12)
items.author: brandonfzhang
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

On DeepSeek-V4.1 sparse MLA (top-k 512, real captured indexer selections),
FlashInfer's SM103 path requires a **bf16 dense KV cache**, while FlashMLA reads a
584-byte/token packed fp8 page — ~2x KV bytes per decode step for FI. On the
call-count-weighted view over 3,819 real selections FlashMLA comes out ~1.2x ahead
(FI wins the expensive full-length prefills and net device time, so the verdict is
genuinely split). Inside the decode family there is a clean, shape-local regression:
at the production verify width (q=6, table width 640), FI is **1.5–1.6x ahead at
batch 1–2, then 1.04–1.43x behind for batch 3–12**, then ahead again at 13+.
The serving integration also pays a per-step index repack feeding the FI call
(~8% of FI attention time), which the packed-page rivals do not need.

## Environment

- NVIDIA GB300 (SM103); CUDA 13.0; FlashInfer 0.7.1rc5; rival: FlashMLA (vLLM build)
- Timing: CUPTI, 20 interleaved rounds, SM clock locked 2070 MHz, fp64 gates
- Workloads: real indexer selections captured from live serving of the published
  DeepSeek-V4.1 GB300 recipes and replayed verbatim (grid-synthetic selection
  patterns overstate FI's cost ~2x, so only real selections are used)

## Exact call parameters

Sparse MLA decode: `num_q_heads=16`, `head_dim=512` (+64 RoPE), q_len 6 per
sequence (speculative verify), selection table width 640 (top-k 512 + sliding
window 128), real captured per-sequence KV lengths 31k-108k; FI reads a bf16
dense KV pool (its SM103 ABI), FlashMLA reads its packed 584 B/token fp8 pages —
same selections replayed for both.

## Measurements — q=6 verify decode, table width 640 (µs)

| batch | FlashMLA | FI (trtllm-gen) | verdict |
|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | 22.2 | 13.5 | FI 1.64x ahead |
| 2 | 22.2 | 15.2 | FI 1.46x ahead |
| 3 | 22.2 | 23.1 | FI 1.04x behind |
| 6 | 22.3 | 23.9 | FI 1.07x behind |
| 9 | 22.5 | 30.9 | FI 1.37x behind |
| 12 | 22.7 | 32.6 | FI 1.43x behind |
| 13 | 22.8 | 19.1 | FI 1.19x ahead |

FlashMLA is nearly flat in batch; FI's cost ramps from B=3 and drops back at B=13 —
it looks like a tiling/scheduling boundary. At the narrow table width (128) FI is
ahead across the board (the new `cake` backend takes several small-B classes).

## Ask

1. An fp8-packed KV page format for SM103 sparse MLA (it exists on SM120 only
   today) — the 2x KV-byte handicap is structural, and vLLM already defines a
   compatible 352-byte nvfp4 layout (#5716) and a 584-byte fp8 layout.
2. Fix the B=3–12 ramp at q=6/W=640 (the production verify regime: its weight is
   concentrated exactly at B=3–12 in our captures).

## Related

- #6301 (DSv4/4.1 sparse attention backend support, SM100/103/107)
- #5716 (nvfp4_ds_mla compressed KV layout)

items.title: [Bug] UnifiedRadixCache: L3 storage is never consulted when a prefix survives only as backuped stubs after host-tier eviction
items.author: todayim
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With HiCache enabled (UnifiedRadixCache + a storage backend), when a prefix's KV is evicted from both device (L1) and host (L2) tiers but its storage backup has completed, the prefix's tree nodes survive as backuped-only stubs. On re-sending the same prefix:

- the prefetch path treats the stub span as "already matched" and issues **no** storage query for it, and
- the load-back path rejects the span because stubs carry no host indices.

The request therefore recomputes the full prefix even though the data is present in L3. The same request **does** hit L3 after `flush_cache` or an engine restart (empty tree → root-anchored full-prefix prefetch works), proving the storage read path itself is functional — only the stub-anchored path is broken.

## Environment

- sglang v0.5.15.post1 (release image; code path also present in main @01e19ddf55)
- 1x NVIDIA L40S, CUDA 13, Python 3.12
- Storage backend: `file` (also reproduced with `mooncake`; the failure is tree-layer, backend-independent)

Server:

```bash
export SGLANG_ENABLE_UNIFIED_RADIX_TREE=1
export SGLANG_HICACHE_FILE_BACKEND_STORAGE_DIR=/data/hicache
python3 -m sglang.launch_server --model-path Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B --port 30000 \
  --tensor-parallel-size 1 --max-total-tokens 20000 --hicache-size 2 \
  --enable-hierarchical-cache --enable-metrics \
  --hicache-storage-backend file \
  --hicache-storage-prefetch-policy wait_complete \
  --hicache-io-backend direct --hicache-mem-layout page_first_direct
```

## Reproduction

```python
# prompt A must exceed hicache prefetch_threshold (default 256 tokens) — use 336 tokens
A = ("...336-token prompt...")

gen(A); gen(A)

# CRITICAL: wait until A's storage backup completes before flooding.
# If the flood evicts A's nodes before the backup finishes, the nodes die
# outright (evicted && !backuped) and the bug does NOT trigger — recall then
# works via the root-anchored path. The bug needs the steady-state ordering:
# backup completes first, eviction second.
while backuped_tokens_total() < 336:   # sglang:backuped_tokens_total
    sleep(2)

flood_until_evicted(target=45000)       # ~700 short requests, > device+host capacity

r = gen(A)   # after eviction
# ACTUAL:   r.cached_tokens == 0, latency ~0.05s,
#           sglang:prefetched_tokens_total UNCHANGED (no storage query issued)
#           sglang:storage_prefetch_unfulfilled_tokens_total unchanged
# EXPECTED: r.cached_tokens >= 335 (storage hit)

flush_cache()
r = gen(A)
# ACTUAL:   r.cached_tokens == 335, latency ~0.3s,
#           sglang:prefetched_tokens_total +335  ← same data, same process,
#                                                   works as soon as the tree is empty
```

Measured (v0.5.15.post1, file backend, 336-token prompt):

| step | cached_tokens | latency | prefetched_tokens_total |
|---|---|---|---|
| re-send after pressure eviction (stub path) | **0** | 0.047s | unchanged |
| re-send after flush_cache (root-anchored path) | **335** | 0.305s | +335 |

## Root cause (traced in main @01e19ddf55)

1. `unified_tree_core.py :: _match_prefix_helper` (~L787): the walk's only early-stop is `if child.evicted and not child.backuped: break` — nodes that are `evicted && backuped` (stubs) are **walked through** and their tokens accumulate into `full_kv_hit_length`.

2. `scheduler.py :: _prefetch_kvcache` (~L3051):
   ```python
   matched_len = len(req.prefix_indices) + req.host_hit_length   # == 335, stub span included
   new_input_tokens = req.full_untruncated_fill_ids[matched_len:match_end]  # == []
   ```
   → `prefetch_from_storage` receives an empty span → `prefetch_length (0) < prefetch_threshold (256)` → declined, **no storage query is issued for the stub span**.

3. `unified_radix_cache.py :: _load_back_transfers` (~L1520): load-back is host→device only; stubs have no host indices, so `kv_tokens == 0 < load_back_threshold (10)` → declined.

The stub span falls between the two paths: the prefetch path counts it as "matched, nothing new to fetch", the load-back path can't materialize it. No code path converts a matched backuped-stub span into an L3 fetch.

Also note the racy aspect (relevant for reproduction): if eviction outruns the async write-through, nodes die outright instead of becoming stubs, and recall then **works** via the root-anchored path. The bug therefore specifically hits the steady-state ordering — backup completes before eviction — which is the normal production case.

## Suggested fix directions

- **A.** In match/scheduler, distinguish stub-only matched spans and issue a storage hit-query/prefetch for that span (not just for new tokens).
- **B.** Extend load-back to source spans from storage (remote→device) when host indices are absent but the nodes are backuped.
- **C.** Don't count backuped-stub tokens into `host_hit_length`/matched_len (anchor at the last host/device-resident node), letting the stub span flow into the existing root-anchored prefetch path — which is proven to work (post-flush behavior).

## Impact

Any workload that re-sends a prefix after it has aged out of L1/L2 (long conversation cold-return, periodic repeated prompts) silently loses L3 recall and recomputes at full prefill cost, despite the tier being designed exactly for this case.

items.title: Agentic Cache Scheduling System Roadmap (Q4)
items.author: hzh0425
items.body_excerpt:
## 1. Agentic Cache Scheduling

- Supernode-wide KV Cache Sharing @hzh0425  @Shunkangz
	- Enable sharing of GPU-resident (L1) and host-resident (L2) KV caches across engines within the same super-node domain.
	- Add cache location awareness to the Router to coordinate request placement and KV transfers based on cache availability and engine load.
	- Extend HiCache linker integration to support GPU-to-GPU KV transfers over (NVLink @Shunkangz、AMD UALoE @TianDi101、SAIL's card-to-card interconnect @Vinsmoke86) and remote Grace DRAM access through EGM.
	- Optimize small KV-page transfers and NUMA placement; validate correctness, cache hit rate, and TTFT/TPOT on GB NVLink72、 AMD MI455X Helios Rack、and SAIL clusters.
- Build a KV cache orchestrator across the router and engine @ZhaiFeiyue @stmatengss 
	- Identify sessions, sub-agents, and tool calls, and expose `PREFETCH`, `DEMOTE`, and `PIN` hints for global cache scheduling. Align this work with the [[router roadmap](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/25760)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/issues/25760). 
	- Add session-aware scheduling to the router
- Enhance HiCache Linker Mode @hzh0425 @alphabetc1 @huangtingwei9988 
    - [[PR #40896](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40896)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/40896): Support fast failover and recovery.
    - [[PR #41343](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41343)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/41343): Extend support to hybrid models with Mamba and SWA.
    - Improve reliability and observability for production deployment.
    - Refactor `hybrid_pool_assembler.py`：Simplify pool assembly and improve extensibility across model architectures.
- Support a [[unified KV cache layout](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/33651)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/33651) for host cache and L3 storage: @Shunkangz @huangtingwei9988 
    - [[PR #39727](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39727)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39727): Add a page-unified host KV layout and topology-independent L3 keys.
    - [[PR #39726](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39726)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39726): Add a JIT kernel to load page-unified host KV back to the device one layer at a time.
    - [[PR #39815](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39815)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/39815): Integrate page-unified host pools and storage keys with the HiCache linker.
    - Add E2E Test For PD + PP/TP + UnifiedLayout @huangtingwei9988 

## 2. Decode Prefix Cache @jojoakm @HZY-Wade 

- Refactor the decode-side HiCache mixin to support L1-only, L1+L2, and L2-only cache configurations.
- Support an L2-only `DecodeRadixTree` to increase KV transfer batch sizes and reduce GPU memory pressure ([[PR #38292](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38292)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38292)).
- Extend the decode-side unified radix tree to fully support SWA, Mamba, and MTP.

## 3. Unified KV Cache Sharding for CP @Shunkangz @HZY-Wade 

- [[PR #38356](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38356)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38356): Add logical-page placement and a rotated allocator to distribute KV pages across shard ranks.
- [[PR #37615](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/37615)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/37615): Add sharded KV pools that store each rank’s owned pages and assemble the full prefix for prefill attention.
- [[PR #38468](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38468)](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/38468): Wire KV cache sharding into prefill scheduling and capacity checks.
- TODO: Optimize CPU Overhead and communication
- PR #42973: Extend CP KV cache sharding to GLM DSA and MTP, with P/D transfer and CPU HiCache support for both KV and indexer caches. @HZY-Wade 
- PR #43057: Fuse DSA indexer quantization with scratch/local writes and reuse raw FP8 latent staging, preserving fallbacks for unsupported layouts.  @HZY-Wade 
- Support unified kvcache layout for dcp.
   - TODO: Optimize FlashInfer Kernel

## 4. HiSparse @alphabetc1   @bingps  @Shunkangz 

- Develop HiSparse V2 to coordinate GPU and host memory as a larger decode cache, targeting up to **2× KV capacity** in GB deployments.
- Refactor HiSparse to support more sparse attention model variants through a common architecture.
- Optimize the HiSparse swap-in kernel by overlapping KV prefetch with computation to reduce the performance impact of cache I/O.
