items.title: [Performance]: FlashInfer NVFP4 KV cache causal prefill is ~1.7-1.8x slower than FP8 on SM120
items.author: lemonade1997
items.body_excerpt:
### Summary

On NVIDIA consumer Blackwell (SM120), FlashInfer attention with an NVFP4 KV cache shows a significant causal prefill regression compared with an FP8 KV cache.

In a matched profiler segment with the same 48 causal paged-prefill kernel calls, the NVFP4 path took about **145.8 ms**, while the FP8 path took about **84.0 ms**. This makes NVFP4 prefill approximately **1.74x slower** (about 1.7-1.8x across measurements).

The profiler indicates that the current SM120 path uses BF16 Q with packed NVFP4 KV:

```text
NVFP4:
BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheKernel<
  ...,
  __nv_bfloat16,      # Q
  __nv_fp4x2_e2m1,    # KV
  __nv_bfloat16,      # output
  ...
>

FP8:
BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheKernel<
  ...,
  __nv_bfloat16,      # Q
  __nv_fp8_e4m3,      # KV
  __nv_bfloat16,      # output
  ...
>
```

The regression appears to come from the existing SM120 NVFP4 software unpack/dequant path: packed FP4 KV values and their FP8 block scales must be unpacked, converted, and scaled before the BF16 QK/PV computation. Prefill is compute-heavy, so the KV bandwidth reduction does not compensate for this per-element conversion overhead.

### Environment

```text
GPU: NVIDIA RTX PRO 5000 Blackwell, compute capability 12.0 (SM120)
PyTorch: 2.10.0+cu129
CUDA: 12.9
FlashInfer: 0.6.15
Attention backend: FLASHINFER
KV cache layout: HND
Model dtype / Q dtype on this path: BF16
KV cache modes compared: nvfp4 and fp8_e4m3
```

The vLLM code includes the recently added NVFP4 KV cache path. The NVFP4 cache is represented as packed E2M1 data plus one FP8 block-scale value per 16 head-dimension elements.

### Kernel-level profile

A comparable trace segment was selected from each profile. Both segments contain exactly 48 causal prefill calls:

| Metric | NVFP4 KV | FP8 KV | NVFP4 / FP8 |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Causal paged-prefill calls | 48 | 48 | 1.00x |
| Causal paged-prefill total | 145.81 ms | 84.03 ms | 1.74x |
| Mean per call | 3.04 ms | 1.75 ms | 1.74x |
| CUTLASS GEMM total in the same segment | 93.61 ms | 96.69 ms | 0.97x |
| All GPU kernels in the segment | 297.73 ms | 238.45 ms | 1.25x |

The similar CUTLASS GEMM time suggests that the model's weight/MoE kernels are not the primary source of this difference. Most of the additional GPU time is inside `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheKernel`.

### Decode and KV append observations

The same profiles show that NVFP4 is beneficial for decode:

| Kernel | NVFP4 KV | FP8 KV |
|---|---:|---:|
| Single-token/decode paged attention | ~9.63 us/call | ~12.35 us/call |
| KV append/write | ~8.39 us/call | ~3.01 us/call |

NVFP4 decode is about 22% faster in this workload because decode is more bandwidth-bound. The NVFP4 append kernel is about 2.8x slower because it performs quantization, packing, block-scale generation, and slot mapping, but its cumulative cost is only around 7 ms and is not the end-to-end bottleneck.

### End-to-end capacity stress result

With 30 concurrent requests:

| KV dtype | Completed | Preemptions | Peak running | Peak cache | Wall time |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| NVFP4 | 30/30 | 0 | 30 | 68.6% | 102.3 s |
| FP8 | 30/30 | 6 | 24 | 97.6% | 65.4 s |

NVFP4 provides the expected capacity benefit and avoids preemption, but the causal-prefill regression dominates this particular workload.

### Expected behavior / proposal

On SM120, the packed NVFP4 KV representation matches the hardware block-scaled FP4 MMA layout well. An optimized path could:

1. quantize Q to per-16-block NVFP4 on the fly;
2. execute QK directly with SM120 block-scaled NVFP4 MMA;
3. avoid expanding K through the FP4 -> FP16/BF16 conversion chain before QK;
4. retain the existing dequantized P x V path where the V-scale axis does not match the MMA reduction axis.

This is similar to the A4Q approach demonstrated for SM120/SM121, where an opt-in FlashInfer kernel uses FP4 Q x FP4 K block-scaled MMA.

Would the vLLM maintainers be interested in tracking or integrating an optimized FlashInfer A4Q-style path for NVFP4 KV prefill on SM120? At minimum, it would be useful to document that the current NVFP4 KV path trades substantial prefill performance for capacity/decode benefits on this architecture.

### Additional notes

- The NVFP4 cache itself is correctly compact: packed FP4 data plus FP8 scales uses about 56.25% of FP8 KV storage, giving an expected capacity ratio of about 1.78x.
- The two profiler JSON files contain more than one non-contiguous capture interval, so the comparison above uses matched segments instead of comparing total trace file size or total event counts.
- Full profiler JSON files can be provided if useful.
- Related NVFP4 KV integration discussion: #49011 and #32220.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Searched existing and past issues for NVFP4/FP4 KV prefill performance and unpack/dequant regressions.

items.title: [Bug][CI] unit-tests-amd is not completing builds, and the one that did fails test_classification_matches_golden
items.author: aryangorde8
items.body_excerpt:
**Label**

`bug`, `ci`

**Describe the bug**

Three related problems in the `unit-tests-amd` Buildkite pipeline. The third is why the
first two went unnoticed.

### 1. `test_classification_matches_golden` fails on the ROCm agent

[Build #10714](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/unit-tests-amd/builds/10714) (ran
2026-08-14 17:40–17:51 UTC) stopped at 37%:

```
FAILED tests/v1/gpu_connector/test_kv_format_classification.py::test_classification_matches_golden
AssertionError: EngineKVFormat.NB_NL_TWO_BS_NH_HS: got (False, False, False, False), expected (True, False, False, False)
1 failed, 2125 passed, 79 skipped, 1 xpassed in 326.06s
```

On the commit that was built, the two sides of that assertion agree in source:

- `csrc/engine_kv_format.h` gives `NB_NL_TWO_BS_NH_HS` (enum value 0)
  `{.is_cross_layer = true}` in `format_facts`
- `EXPECTED` in `tests/v1/gpu_connector/test_kv_format_classification.py` says
  `(True, False, False, False)`

So the extension module loaded on the agent disagreed with the source it was built from.
Everything the golden table expects has exactly one `True`, and the observed value was
all-`False`, which is what a default-initialised `format_facts` entry would give.

The build did compile from source — `Built lmcache @ file:///var/lib/buildkite-agent/builds/ENC1-CLS01-SVR13-1/lmcache/unit-tests-amd`,
`Prepared 1 package in 4m 28s` — so this is not a missing build step.

I have not reproduced this off the ROCm agent; I do not have one. Two candidates worth
checking, in the order I would check them:

- a workspace left behind by an earlier build (see 3 below), so the editable install
  picked up objects compiled from different source
- `hipcc` and the `constexpr` designated-initialiser table in `format_facts` — the
  predicates are `LMC_KV_FORMAT_HD constexpr`, and an all-`False` table is consistent with
  that initialisation not surviving the HIP compile

### 2. The pipeline has not completed a build

Of the 61 most recent builds in `unit-tests-amd`, **none** finished: 32 are still
`scheduled` and 28 are `skipped`. Every recent `dev` build is `skipped`, so there is no
green baseline for this pipeline at all.

Build #10714 was queued on 2026-08-11 and only ran three days later. It happens to be the
only build in that window that executed, which is the sole reason the failure in (1) is
visible.

Because the check still reports to GitHub, every open PR currently carries a
`buildkite/unit-tests-amd` status that will never resolve.

### 3. A failing run never cleans up its workspace

In `.buildkite/pipeline.yml`, the cleanup is part of the same `command` block as `pytest`,
after it:

```yaml
LMCACHE_TRACK_USAGE="false" \
pytest --maxfail=1 --cov=lmcache ...

...

export TARGET="$PWD"
echo "Deleting current workspace $TARGET"
cd /
sudo rm -rf "$TARGET"
```

A non-zero `pytest` exit ends the block, so `rm -rf "$TARGET"` never runs and the next
build on that agent inherits the previous checkout. With the
`lmcache.c_ops` -> `lmcache.lmcache_native` rename in flight across several branches
(#4473, #4445), that is a direct route to the mismatch in (1).

A `pre-exit` hook, or splitting cleanup into its own step, would make it unconditional.

**To Reproduce**

1. Open any PR against `dev`
2. Wait for `buildkite/unit-tests-amd` — it stays `scheduled` indefinitely
3. If a build does get dequeued, it fails as above

**Expected behavior**

`unit-tests-amd` completes on `dev` and on PRs, and `test_classification_matches_golden`
passes on the ROCm agent as it does on the source it was built from.

**Additional context**

- Failing build: https://buildkite.com/lmcache/unit-tests-amd/builds/10714
- The golden values are unchanged on current `dev` — #4473 renamed
  `lmcache.c_ops` to `lmcache.lmcache_native` but did not touch `EXPECTED`, and the only
  change to `csrc/engine_kv_format.h` since is a comment — so `dev` should reproduce (1).
- `--maxfail=1` means one failure this early hides the rest of the suite. #10714 aborted
  at 37% and never reached `tests/v1/storage_backend/`.
- Noticed while looking into a red `unit-tests-amd` on #4484, which is unrelated to that
  PR's change.

items.title: NixlStoreL2Adapter reports negative pool usage for multi-page backing files
items.author: amd-ivaganev
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

The static NixlStoreL2Adapter can report a negative Pool used value when a NIXL backing file contains more than one allocation page. This is a status-reporting problem; it does not indicate that the allocator has over-allocated storage.

## Example

Configure the POSIX backend with two backing files, where each file holds four aligned pages. A new pool has eight free allocation slots.

Expected status: pool_size=8 and pool_free_slots=8, so the CLI displays 0 / 8 (0%).

Actual status: pool_size=2 and pool_free_slots=8, so the CLI calculates and displays -6 / 2 (-300%).

## Cause

For file-backed NIXL storage, NixlStorageAgent creates pool_size times pages_per_file allocation slots. However, NixlStoreL2Adapter.report_status() reports the configured backing-file count as pool_size, while it reports the free allocation-page count as pool_free_slots. The CLI correctly subtracts these fields, but the fields have different units.

Relevant paths:

- lmcache/v1/distributed/l2_adapters/nixl_store_l2_adapter.py
- lmcache/cli/commands/describe.py

## Expected behavior

Both status values should count allocation slots. The invariant should always hold:

0 <= pool_free_slots <= pool_size

The CLI should then show a non-negative used count and a percentage between 0% and 100%, without any clamping or backend-specific workarounds.

## Suggested fix

Expose total and free slot counts together from NixlObjPool through a public lock-protected method. Have report_status() use that method for pool_size and pool_free_slots. This also avoids accessing the pool private lock and mutable index list from the adapter.

## Acceptance criteria

- Report total and free allocation slots in the same unit.
- Add a regression test using a multi-page backing file.
- Confirm the invariant before, during, and after storage allocations.
- Preserve existing behavior for object backends and one-page-per-file configurations.

Validated against commit 4f96acf5.

items.title: LMCacheConnectorV1 (pd_role=sender): a request without transfer metadata crashes the producer engine ('NoneType' object has no attribute 'receiver_init_port')
items.author: binxuwang2002-lang
items.body_excerpt:
Hi — second report from the same 1p1d setup as the abort crash I just filed. This one is a smaller bug with the same blast radius: one badly-formed request kills the instance.

**Setup**

Identical to the other report: LMCache v0.5.5 (pip), vLLM 0.30.0; the two derefs are unchanged on current `dev` (`31272f68`). 1P1D per `examples/disagg_prefill/1p1d`, `LMCacheConnectorV1`, `pd_backend_mode: async`, producer with `pd_role: "sender"`.

**What happens**

A completion sent directly to the producer without `kv_transfer_params` is accepted and prefill runs normally — then the store path dies on it. In `batched_submit_put_task` (`lmcache/v1/storage_backend/pd_backend_async.py`) the transfer spec is dereferenced unguarded:

```python
receiver_init_port = transfer_spec.receiver_init_port[self.tp_rank]
receiver_alloc_port = transfer_spec.receiver_alloc_port[self.tp_rank]
```

For a request with no transfer metadata `transfer_spec` is `None`, so this raises `'NoneType' object has no attribute 'receiver_init_port'`. The immediate wrapper logs `batched_submit_put_task failed, ref counts rolled back: ...` and then the exception propagates out through `wait_for_save` into EngineCore, which dies with a fatal error. The request never returns anything; the process goes down.

Note that the coroutine this method submits already tolerates a missing spec — `_async_transfer_task` reads the request id as `getattr(transfer_spec, "req_id", "") if transfer_spec is not None else ""` (and `_send_proxy_notif` does the same). The two derefs above are the only place that assumption breaks.

**Steps to reproduce**

1. Start the producer/consumer as in the other report (only the producer matters here).
2. Send an ordinary completion to the producer with no `kv_transfer_params` — anything that skips the example proxy will do: a health-check style request, a retry from a client, a direct call:

```python
import json, urllib.request

body = json.dumps({"model": "<model>", "prompt": "word " * 512, "max_tokens": 2}).encode()
req = urllib.request.Request("http://localhost:8100/v1/completions", data=body,
                             headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
print(urllib.request.urlopen(req).read())
```

We used a 512-token prompt; the store triggers once prefill has at least one full chunk (chunk size 256 in the default config).

3. The engine dies during the store that follows prefill. On every attempt so far (n=1) — the deref is unguarded and `transfer_spec` is `None` for any request without transfer metadata, so we expect it to be deterministic.

**Traceback tail** (verbatim; the top frames are the usual engine step path):

```text
lmcache.v1.storage_backend.pd_backend_async: batched_submit_put_task failed, ref counts rolled back: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'receiver_init_port'
  File "/path/to/vllm/distributed/kv_transfer/kv_connector/v1/lmcache_connector.py", line 212, in wait_for_save
    self._lmcache_engine.wait_for_save()
  File "/path/to/lmcache/integration/vllm/vllm_v1_adapter.py", line 1219, in wait_for_save
    self.lmcache_engine.store(
  File "/path/to/lmcache/v1/cache_engine.py", line 564, in store
    ...
AttributeError: 'NoneType' object has no attribute 'receiver_init_port'
```

Happy to send the complete log if the tail isn't enough.

**Expected**

A request without transfer metadata is just a local request; the sender path should skip the transfer for it (or reject it with a clear 4xx before prefill burns the GPU). Crashing the engine on it is a rough trade for one request missing a field. Guarding those two derefs the way the request-id lookup is guarded would be enough.

Thanks for taking a look — we can test patches quickly if that helps.

items.title: Performance comparison for dense shared prefix + block-diagonal local mask: custom mask in BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper vs MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper
items.author: catnanami
items.body_excerpt: I am trying to evaluate the best way to implement an attention pattern with a dense shared/global prefix plus a local block-diagonal suffix. The mask pattern is shown below: I am considering two implementations: BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper with a custom mask MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper Questions: 1. For this pattern, is cascade attention expected to be faster than paged prefill with a custom mask? 2. Or is this pattern better handled by a custom kernel/backend? My use case is speculative decoding, where all verification tokens share the same prefix KV, but each local block should only attend to its own block.

comments.author: VectorPeak
comments.body:
For the mask in the image - a dense shared prefix on the left plus independent block-diagonal local regions on the right - `MultiLevelCascadeAttentionWrapper` is usually the better fit than `BatchPrefillWithPagedKVCacheWrapper` with one large custom mask.

The reason is that the custom-mask prefill path does not really exploit this structure as well: it still treats the problem like one masked attention problem over the full layout, so the block-diagonal sparsity mostly becomes masking overhead. Cascade attention lets you model this as:

- shared/global prefix KV: attended by all verification tokens
- local suffix KV: split into independent blocks/requests
- final result: merge prefix-attention state with each local block’s attention state

For speculative decoding, this is exactly the kind of case where cascade can help, especially when the shared prefix is large and the local verification blocks are relatively small. Each local block can be represented as a separate batch item sharing the same prefix. If the local part also needs causal masking inside each block, use the normal causal/local mask for that per-block suffix attention.

items.title: Feature Request: gguf-py: add numpy quantisation for Q1_0 and Q2_0
items.author: SomeNobody21112
items.body_excerpt:
### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

### Feature Description

Used gguf-py to dequantize weights from a gguf file with `Q1_0` or `Q2_0` in it. It errors: `NotImplementedError: Dequantization for Q1_0 is not yet implemented`, and same for `Q2_0`. Weird because gguf-py already handles 25 other formats (even new ones like `MXFP4`, `NVFP4`, `TQ2_0`). These 2 just got skipped when the C side added them in #21273 and #24448. `gguf.dequantize` (and `quantize`) should work for `Q1_0` and `Q2_0` like all the other formats. Seen on gguf 0.19.0 from pip, and latest master.

### Motivation

Real models use these formats: prism-ml's Bonsai models, `Bonsai-8B-Q1_0` / `Bonsai-1.7B-Q1_0` for `Q1_0` and `Ternary-Bonsai-8B-Q2_0` for `Q2_0`. Their tensors really are `Q1_0` / `Q2_0`, and lots of people download them. Transformers' GGUF loader calls `gguf.dequantize`, so transformers can't load these models right now, and that basically breaks any other python code reading these weights too. The C side keeps getting faster code for these formats but the Python side can't even read them, making these two not match properly.

### Possible Implementation

i have a fix of about 50 lines of code in `gguf-py/gguf/quants.py` and i have created two new classes `Q1_0` and `Q2_0`, written the same way as the existing `TQ2_0` class. Basically, `Q1_0` has blocks of 128, where scale = average of absolute values, then one sign bit per weight either + or - . `Q2_0` has blocks of 64, where scale = biggest absolute value and each weight is rounded to -1, 0, +1 or +2 times the scale, 2 bits each. I know this is right since, the repo's `gguf-py/tests/test_quants.py` compares python against the real C code byte for byte. I have built the C library and ran it and I can say with confidence that both the new types match exactly and the full run 66/66 checks across 27 types. I also added a small test with known values that run without the C library. In my checks i have found out this:  for `Q1_0`'s scale, C adds the 128 values one by one. np.sum adds in a different order, and float rounding then gave a different scale in 18 of 65,536 blocks. `np.cumsum` adds in order like C, 0 differences. I have also checked the PR #25681, it adds a separate pytorch module, my change basically fills the gap in the existing numpy code. I have used AI assistance for the runs and the code but i have reviewed and tested the same myself. Want me to open a PR?

items.title: [Regression]: draft-mtp decode ~10-13% slower on master vs a02c7f58c (RADV, RDNA3) — verify-step slowdown + cache-reuse-dependent acceptance instability
items.author: tczank
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

Paired A/B between `a02c7f58c` (Sep 26) and current master `2851b3bcb` on a
7900 XTX (RADV) shows the speculative `draft-mtp` path regressed ~10–13% while
the raw decode path did not:

- llama-bench, same commit pair: pp512 **+0.9%**, tg128 **−0.2%** (4/4
  counterbalanced pairs) — raw kernels unaffected.
- llama-server + `--spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2`: **−12.7%**
  paired mean (4/4 pairs), decomposing into two independent effects:
  - **(a) ~+10% verify-step time at identical work** — present with and
    without `--cache-reuse`.
  - **(b) within-session acceptance instability** — only with
    `--cache-reuse > 0`.

Not yet bisected. Two disjoint commit ranges are implicated (details below).

## Environment

- AMD RX 7900 XTX (NAVI31, RDNA3), headless (display on iGPU), 7800X3D, 32 GB RAM
- Arch Linux, Mesa RADV 26.2.4 (vulkan-radeon), loader 1.4.363
- Both builds: default CMake Release, Vulkan backend
  - A: `a02c7f58c`, llama-server md5 `1c810682934d0545ea8395b148baacc3`
  - B: `2851b3bcb` (clean tree), llama-server md5 `00e0d0dc645225203c8742c334169350`
- `GGML_VK_ALLOW_GRAPHICS_QUEUE=1` in both arms (constant; cancels in the
  comparison)
- Model: 27B dense, IQ3_S (3.4375 bpw) with MTP draft head, 11.28 GiB
- Flags: `-ngl 99 -c 131072 -np 1 --cache-reuse 256 -t 16 -fa on -ctk q4_0
  -ctv q4_0 --spec-type draft-mtp --spec-draft-n-max 2 --jinja`

## Method

4 counterbalanced pairs (AB|BA|AB|BA), fresh server per cycle, GPU edge-temp
gate ≤50 °C, discarded 300-token warmup per cycle, 3 × 300-token greedy
completions per cycle (identical 41-token prompt). Decode rate from
wall-clock; acceptance and exact target-decode counts ("steps") recovered
from server logs. Per-run md5/env/cmdline provenance.

## Results (production flags, --cache-reuse 256)

| pair | a02c tok/s | master tok/s | Δ | accept a02c/master | steps a02c/master |
|-----:|-----------:|-------------:|--------------:|-------------------:|------------------:|
| 1 | 82.77 | 75.42 | −8.9%  | 0.629 / 0.626 | 397.87 / 397.86 |
| 2 | 79.21 | 67.34 | −15.0% | 0.584 / 0.503 | 413.35 / 445.80 |
| 3 | 82.51 | 70.92 | −14.0% | 0.622 / 0.550 | 400.28 / 426.88 |
| 4 | 82.48 | 71.78 | −13.0% | 0.623 / 0.560 | 398.97 / 422.22 |

**Effect (a):** pair 1 ran the same number of target decodes with equal
acceptance (397.86 vs 397.87 steps; 0.626 vs 0.629) yet took 13.1 s vs 11.9 s
→ 32.9 vs 29.9 ms per decode step (+10%). Consistent in every master cycle
(32.5–32.9 ms vs 29.3–29.9 ms on a02c).

**Effect (b):** master acceptance within one server session is bimodal at rep
level (e.g. cycle 2 reps: 0.46 / 0.62 / 0.44) while a02c sessions stay uniform
(0.55–0.70). Degraded reps offer more drafts (draft_n 302–315 vs ~250–285)
with fewer accepted → steps inflate.

## Probe: --cache-reuse 0

| cycle | tok/s | accept | steps | per-rep accept |
|-------|------:|-------:|------:|----------------|
| master, cr0 (run 1) | 74.09 | 0.608 | 405.0 | 0.58 / 0.64 / 0.61 (uniform) |
| a02c, cr0           | 79.42 | 0.585 | 412.1 | — |
| master, cr0 (run 2) | 69.72 | 0.550 | 426.8 | 0.54 / 0.53 / 0.59 (uniform) |

- (b) disappears without reuse → tracks the KV-reuse / slot-state path.
- (a) persists: 32.6 vs 29.6 ms/step (+10.1%) → independent of reuse.
- cr0 is not a workaround (master still −9.4% at cr0).

## Candidate ranges (in a02c..2851b3bcb, not bisected)

- For (b): #30574 (save draft state in slot file), #30567 (slot preference /
  state overwrites).
- For (a): #29533 (matmul dispatch split), #29280 (descriptor-set reuse),
  #29877 (f16 FMA packing) — speculative-loop kernel/scheduling changes.
- Also in range, unexamined: #30049, #27703, #30580.

## Notes

- Between-session acceptance variance exists on both builds (a02c 0.584–0.629)
  — baseline run-to-run (GPU non-determinism under greedy); the distinctive
  master failure is the within-session swing with reuse on.
- Happy to run a bisect or collect more reps on request.

---
*Disclosure: measurement harness, analysis and this report were prepared with
AI assistance; all benchmark runs were performed and verified locally by me.*

items.title: [Bug]: HA snapshot recovery does not update applied sequence metric
items.author: Icedcoco
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

### Summary

When an HA standby starts from a batch OpLog snapshot, the snapshot state and recovery cursor are restored successfully, but the exported `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` metric remains at its initial value. This makes the metric disagree with the standby's actual recovery position.

### Reproduction

The issue is reproducible with a snapshot whose recovered sequence is `117` and which has no incremental OpLog entries to apply after the snapshot:

1. Create and publish a valid batch OpLog snapshot covering sequence `117`.
2. Start an HA standby with snapshot bootstrap enabled.
3. Allow snapshot recovery to complete and the standby to enter `WATCHING`.
4. Read the standby metrics and synchronization status.

Observed result:

```text
recovery log:          snapshot/applied = 117
OpLogApplier expected:  118
snapshot applied batch: 51
standby state:          WATCHING
sync status applied:    117
ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id: 0
```

The standby's internal cursor and synchronization status show that sequence `117` has been recovered, while the exported applied-sequence gauge still reports `0`.

### Root cause

`OpLogApplier::Recover(last_applied_sequence_id)` updates only `expected_sequence_id` to `last_applied_sequence_id + 1`. It does not update the HA applied-sequence gauge.

The gauge is currently updated when an individual `ApplyOpLogEntry` succeeds. The snapshot bootstrap path installs the recovered baseline through `HotStandbyService::LoadBatchOpLogSnapshotBaselineLocked` and updates the standby's internal `applied_seq_id_`, but does not update `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id`. Therefore, a snapshot with an empty incremental tail leaves the exported gauge at its initial value.

### Impact

- Monitoring reports an incorrect applied sequence immediately after snapshot recovery.
- Any alert, readiness check, or recovery validation based on `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` or derived lag can report a false failure or an incorrect recovery state.
- Operators cannot distinguish a metric reporting error from an actual OpLog replay failure using the exported metrics alone.

This is an observability and recovery-validation defect. The current evidence does not indicate data loss or incorrect recovered object metadata; the internal recovery cursor is correct.

### Expected behavior

After a successful snapshot recovery, `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` must equal the latest sequence represented by the recovered baseline, even when no incremental OpLog entries follow it:

```text
snapshot_applied_sequence = 117
ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id = 117
expected_sequence_id = 118
```

When incremental entries are subsequently applied, the metric must continue advancing to the latest successfully applied sequence.

### Scope of the fix

Synchronize the applied-sequence gauge with the recovered baseline during snapshot/bootstrap installation. Check all recovery paths that establish a baseline, including batch snapshot recovery, ordinary snapshot recovery, and local warm restart, so that the metric does not depend on at least one later OpLog entry being replayed.

Do not change the recovered cursor or treat the metric as the source of truth; the metric should reflect the already recovered cursor.

### Acceptance criteria

Add regression coverage for:

1. Snapshot recovery with no incremental OpLog tail.
2. Snapshot recovery followed by incremental entries.
3. A baseline at sequence `0`.
4. Consistency between the applied sequence, expected sequence, snapshot batch, and lag metrics.

The tests should verify both the internal synchronization status and the exported `ha_oplog_applied_sequence_id` metric.

### Additional context

The metric is defined as the "Latest OpLog sequence ID applied by Standby". A successful snapshot recovery already reports the recovered sequence in recovery logs and synchronization status, so the exported metric should expose the same value rather than remain at its process-start default.

items.title: [Bug]: TENT never releases per-peer state of departed peers (RDMA endpoints, 32 MiB pinned each, and idle RPC client connections)
items.author: xiaodouzi666
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

**What happens**

A TENT engine keeps per-peer state keyed by the peer's segment name (`ip:port` in P2P mode). When a peer goes away and is never contacted again — it exits, or restarts and comes back under a new `ip:port` (`rpc_server_port=0` picks a random port) — that state is not released. Line numbers below are as of `342c8aee`.

1. **RDMA endpoints.** Each local NIC has one `SIEVEEndpointStore` (`src/transport/rdma/context.cpp:320`), and an `RdmaEndPoint` is created lazily for every (local NIC, peer NIC) pair that carries traffic or that the peer bootstraps. Every endpoint's `construct()` allocates and registers two notification buffers of `kNotifyBufferSize` (64 KiB) × `kNotifyMaxPendingSends` (256) = 16 MiB each (`include/tent/transport/rdma/endpoint.h:303-304`, `src/transport/rdma/endpoint.cpp:187-210`): 32 MiB of pinned memory per endpoint, plus `1 + num_lanes` QPs, whether or not notifications are ever used. `closeSegment()` only drops the segment handle mapping (`src/runtime/transfer_engine_impl.cpp:735-738` → `SegmentManager::closeRemote`, `src/runtime/segment_manager.cpp:62`); no transport is told. An endpoint is retired only on a QP error or fatal event on it (`workers.cpp:671-677`, `rdma_transport.cpp:1130-1131`), a local port event (`context.cpp:520`), a new bootstrap from the same NIC path (`rdma_transport.cpp:860-866`; the comment there reads "Endpoints are never reset"), engine shutdown, or capacity eviction, which runs only when a new key is inserted after a successful `construct()` (`endpoint_store.cpp:263`) with a cap of `endpoint_store_cap` = 65536 per local NIC (`params.h:55`). An idle endpoint of a peer that left under a name that never comes back hits none of these.
2. **RPC client connections.** `CoroRpcAgent` keeps one `ClientPool` per server address (`include/tent/rpc/rpc.h:126`). A client goes back to the pool after every successful call (`src/rpc/rpc.cpp:104`), so the pool keeps as many idle connections as the peak concurrency towards that peer; it is cleared only when a later call to the same address fails or on `stop()` (`rpc.cpp:167-168`). A departed peer is never called again, so its connections stay open in `CLOSE-WAIT`.

**Measured** (two hosts, 4 RoCE NICs each; one long-lived engine serving 400 short sessions, each from a freshly started peer engine on a new `ip:port`):

- pinned memory grows by ~181 MiB per departed peer (≈ 5.7 endpoints × 32 MiB): 70.6 GiB after 400 peers;
- descriptors grow by ~6.6 per peer (2666 after 400). Classified after 20 peers: +140 TCP sockets, all `CLOSE-WAIT` outbound connections to the departed peers' RPC ports (7 per peer), and ~15 more each of eventpoll/timerfd/eventfd; the uverbs descriptors stay constant;
- with a finite `RLIMIT_MEMLOCK`, once the limit is reached new peers are refused (`Cannot allocate endpoint`; the notification-buffer `ibv_reg_mr` fails with `ENOMEM`), and capacity eviction does not help because it only runs after a successful `construct()`;
- exiting the long-lived process then takes ~30 ms per departed peer (~12 s after 400) to release the registrations.

**Why it matters**

Any long-running TENT process whose peers churn — prefill/decode workers restarted by an orchestrator, P2P segments with `rpc_server_port=0` — accumulates pinned memory and descriptors until `RLIMIT_MEMLOCK`, memory or `RLIMIT_NOFILE` runs out. Lowering `MC_MAX_EP_PER_CTX` / `endpoint_store_cap` bounds the endpoint part today, at the cost of also evicting live endpoints; nothing bounds the RPC pools.

**Possible directions**

Give the transports and the RPC agent a hook when a segment is closed or when the control plane learns that a peer is gone, then retire that peer's endpoints with the existing `RdmaEndPoint::resetConnection()` (`endpoint.cpp:700`, already used by `Workers::disableEndpoint` and by the notify path's `RetireEndpoint`) and drop its `ClientPool`; or an idle-time eviction in the endpoint store and the RPC pools, independent of the capacity cap; or allocate the notification buffers lazily, on the first notification. Happy to help with a patch if one of these is the preferred shape.

**Reproduction**

Engine A stays up; in a loop, start engine B (P2P, `rpc_server_port=0`), `openSegment(A)`, WRITE one buffer to A and send A one notification, exit. Watch `VmPin` in `/proc/<A>/status` and `ss -tnp` for A. We measured it with the diagnostics tool we are preparing for #2864 (on top of #4154); its reports can be attached.

**Environment**: commit `342c8aee` (first seen on an earlier main, `e4229791f3`); Linux x86_64 hosts with 400 Gb/s mlx5 RoCE v2 NICs; no GPU involved.

items.title: [Bug]: [Store] L4 (LOCAL_DISK offload) can serve another object's bytes: offload reports are matched by key alone
items.author: Juhyun-Kim-Memphis
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

#### Summary

With SSD offload enabled (`enable_offload`, `FileStorage` with a bucket backend), a `Get` that is served from a LOCAL_DISK replica can return the bytes of a different object than the one currently stored under the key. No master restart is needed: it happens under ordinary remove / re-put churn. A master restart (or a store re-registering its disk tier for any other reason) makes it much more frequent.

All three root causes below have the same shape: the master registers a LOCAL_DISK replica from a report that does not say which offload it is the report of. `NotifyOffloadSuccess` carries only `(tenant, key, size)`, so the master matches it against whatever offload task the key has *now*, or, when the key has no task, creates the object or attaches the replica anyway.

#### Environment

- Unit tests: Mooncake `main` `1d97a1df`, Linux x86_64, gcc 13.3, Release, `-DBUILD_UNIT_TESTS=ON -DUSE_CUDA=OFF -DUSE_ETCD=OFF`.
- Load test numbers below: `main` as of `245e7106` with an unrelated change to the master's restart path. The offload report handling involved behaves the same on current `main` (#4562 moved the offload task onto the object record without changing how reports are matched).

#### Observed

Load test: one standalone `mooncake_master`, four CPU-only stores with L4 on a bucket backend, TCP, a churn load (put / get / remove / re-put of the same keys with the same sizes) whose reader checks every byte against an oracle, and a static key set larger than memory so that eviction and offload run all the time.

| phase | wrong reads |
| -- | -- |
| no restart (control) | about 2 per 1M gets |
| after a master restart in which every store re-registers its files | 33,209 in the first minutes |

Every wrong read was traced back (per-key history rebuilt from the load's seeded draws) to one of the three causes below; none was left unexplained.

#### Root causes

1. **A late offload completion brings a removed key back, or completes the task of a newer object.** A store takes an offload item (`OffloadObjectHeartbeat`), copies the bytes and reports `NotifyOffloadSuccess`. If the key was removed while the store was copying, the report arrives for a key without an object: `NotifyOffloadSuccess` falls through to `AddReplicaForRetainedClient`, which *creates* the object from the disk replica. The removed key is readable again with its old bytes, and the next `Put` of the key fails as already existing. If the key was re-put in the meantime, the new object has its own offload task and the late report is accepted as that task's completion: reads of the new object that fall back to L4 get the old object's bytes.

2. **A store's rescan re-registers old files.** On start, and after the master answers `SEGMENT_NOT_FOUND` (master restart, client expiry), the store calls `ScanMeta` and reports every file it holds through `NotifyOffloadSuccess`. `Remove` never deletes the store's file, so such a file can hold the bytes of a removed key or of an earlier object of the key. The master creates the removed keys again and attaches the old files to the current objects (and to their offload tasks when they have one). This is the dominant cause after a restart.

3. **The copy source can change during the copy.** The store copies from the first readable memory replica of the key in its own segments, looked up when the bucket is built; nothing keeps that replica alive while the bucket is written. If the key is removed (or the replica evicted) during the copy, the buffer can be freed and reused by another object before the bytes are read, and the file holds that object's bytes. The report is then registered through (1).

Promotion-on-hit has the same weakness: promotion calls are matched by key, so a late `Success` can publish a staged buffer that a newer promotion of the key is still writing into, and a late `Failure` can free it.

#### Reproduction on main

Unit tests that fail on `main` (`1d97a1df`) with only the test files changed (test-only patch, no production change):

- `MasterServiceSSDTest.LateCompletionDoesNotRecreateARemovedKey` (cause 1): put, the store drains the offload item, `Remove(force)`, then the completion arrives. On main the key exists again and a new `PutStart` of it fails.
- `MasterServiceSSDTest.ReRegistrationNeverRegistersADiskReplica` (cause 2): two keys are offloaded and removed, one is re-put with new bytes of the same size, then the store's rescan entries for both files arrive. On main the re-put object gets the old file as a LOCAL_DISK replica and the removed key is recreated.
- `FileStorageTest.OffloadWhoseSourceChangesDuringTheCopyIsNotRegistered` (cause 3, through the real `FileStorage` offload path and an in-process master): the key is removed and re-put (same size, other bytes) after the bucket is written and before it is reported. On main the new object gets a LOCAL_DISK replica that holds the old object's bytes.

```
master_service_ssd_test.cpp: Failure  (removed key exists again; PutStart refused)
[  FAILED  ] MasterServiceSSDTest.LateCompletionDoesNotRecreateARemovedKey
master_service_ssd_test.cpp: Failure  (re-put object has 2 replicas, expected 1)
[  FAILED  ] MasterServiceSSDTest.ReRegistrationNeverRegistersADiskReplica
file_storage_test.cpp: Failure        (new object has 1 LOCAL_DISK replica, expected 0)
[  FAILED  ] FileStorageTest.OffloadWhoseSourceChangesDuringTheCopyIsNotRegistered
```

All three pass with the fix.

#### Related issues

- #4487 reports the stale-rescan half of cause 2 (a re-put object can get the old file on rescan) and proposes carrying an object incarnation through the offload task. The fix below covers that half and the late completion / NACK cases listed there. It does not fix the other half of #4487 (a re-put key is never offloaded again while the backend still holds the old entry).

items.title: [Feature] Unified JIT / Precompilation Cache Directory
items.author: whybeyoung
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [ ] If this is not a feature request but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [ ] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Motivation


## Summary

**Request:** Unify all JIT and precompilation cache paths under a single configurable root so that users and operators can manage cache location, size, and persistence in one place. The current situation is fragmented across multiple env vars and default paths (including `/tmp`), which makes it hard to reason about where compiled artifacts live and to reuse caches across runs or machines.

## Current State (Fragmented)

### 1. Triton JIT cache

| What | Env var / source | Default / behavior |
|------|------------------|--------------------|
| Direct `@triton.jit` (e.g. allocator, MoE kernels) | `TRITON_CACHE_DIR` (Triton runtime) | Triton default: `~/.triton/cache`; often overwritten by Inductor to a path under `/tmp/torchinductor_*` |
| SGLang override | `SGLANG_TRITON_CACHE_DIR` (if implemented) | e.g. `~/.triton/cache` or `~/.cache/triton` |

- Set only in some entry paths (engine, gRPC launcher, scheduler process); custom/PD launchers may not set it.
- When PyTorch Inductor runs first, it can set `TRITON_CACHE_DIR` to its own subdir, so later Triton JIT (including allocator) writes under `/tmp`.

### 2. PyTorch Inductor (torch.compile)

| What | Env var / source | Default / behavior |
|------|------------------|--------------------|
| Inductor cache | `TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` (PyTorch) | `/tmp/torchinductor_<user>` (or similar) |
| SGLang override | `SGLANG_TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` (if implemented) | e.g. `~/.cache/sglang/inductor` |

- Default lives in `/tmp`, so cache is often non-persistent and can conflict with other users on shared nodes.

### 3. DeepGEMM JIT cache

| What | Env var / source | Default / behavior |
|------|------------------|--------------------|
| DeepGEMM cache | `SGLANG_DG_CACHE_DIR` / `DG_JIT_CACHE_DIR` | `~/.cache/deep_gemm` |

- Set in `layers/deep_gemm_wrapper/compile_utils.py`; separate from Triton/Inductor.
- 
## Problems

1. **No single root:** Triton, Inductor, SGLang torch_compile, and DeepGEMM each have their own env or default; some write to `/tmp`, others to `~/.cache/...`.

## Proposal

### 1. Introduce a single JIT cache root

- **New env var:** `SGLANG_JIT_CACHE_ROOT` (or `SGLANG_CACHE_ROOT` if we want to align with existing `SGLANG_CACHE_ROOT` in custom_all_reduce_utils).
- **Default:** `~/.cache/sglang` (or `$XDG_CACHE_HOME/sglang` when set).
- **Semantics:** All JIT/precompilation caches that SGLang controls should live under this root in fixed subdirs.

### 2. Standard layout under the root

Suggested subdirs (all under `SGLANG_JIT_CACHE_ROOT`):

| Subdir | Purpose | Maps from |
|--------|---------|-----------|
| `triton/` | Triton JIT (direct `@triton.jit` and, when possible, Triton used by Inductor) | `TRITON_CACHE_DIR` |
| `inductor/` | PyTorch Inductor (torch.compile) | `TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR` |
| `torch_compile/` | SGLang torch.compile cache (hash-based, when using SGLangBackend) | `SGLANG_CACHE_DIR` + `torch_compile_cache` |
| `deep_gemm/` | DeepGEMM JIT | `SGLANG_DG_CACHE_DIR` / `DG_JIT_CACHE_DIR` |

- If we keep backward compatibility, existing env vars (`SGLANG_TRITON_CACHE_DIR`, `SGLANG_TORCHINDUCTOR_CACHE_DIR`, `SGLANG_CACHE_DIR`, `SGLANG_DG_CACHE_DIR`) could override the default subdir path when set; otherwise they are derived as `{SGLANG_JIT_CACHE_ROOT}/{subdir}`.

CC @Fridge003 @hnyls2002

_No response_

items.title: [Bug] HiCache staged write-back: the 128 KiB batch path passes registered host VAs to cudaMemcpyBatchAsync and faults where CanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem == 0
items.author: Edwardssss
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

HiCache backup copies device KV into the host pool through the JIT kernel `python/sglang/kernels/jit/csrc/kvcacheio/staged_write_back.cuh`. The kernel has two D2H strategies and picks between them by copy granularity: per-page `cudaMemcpyAsync` for small copies, and one `cudaMemcpyBatchAsync` for `src_ptrs.size() * num_pages` descriptors once `first_page_bytes = page_size * src_stride(0) * item_size >= kLargeCopyThresholdBytes` (128 KiB, defined at `:106`, branch at `:154`, call at `:170`, call sites `:274` MLA and `:279` MHA).

For the batch call the kernel passes **the raw host virtual addresses** of the host pool as the destination pointers (`dst_ptrs[t].data_ptr() + dst_indices[...] * stride * elem`). On a platform where `cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem` is **0** — i.e. registered host memory is
*not* accessible at the same virtual address on the device — those addresses are not valid device-space addresses, and the copy fails with an **asynchronous `cudaErrorIllegalAddress`**. The fallback path in the same kernel uses `cudaMemcpyAsync` over the *same* addresses and works,
because that API translates host pointers for you.

**Minimal demonstration.** One program, one descriptor, 128 KiB; only the destination form varies:

| `dst` passed to `cudaMemcpyBatchAsync` | submission | sync | bytes |
|---|---|---|---|
| host VA of `mmap()` + `cudaHostRegister()` — **what the kernel does today** | `no error` | **`an illegal memory access was encountered`** | not copied |
| `cudaHostGetDevicePointer()` alias of the *same* buffer | `no error` | `no error` | correct |
| `cudaHostAlloc()` buffer | `no error` | `no error` | correct |
| host VA of plain pageable `mmap()` (never registered) | `no error` | `no error` | correct |
| per-copy `cudaMemcpyAsync()` into the registered buffer | — | `no error` | correct |

Observed on the machine described under *Environment*:

```
$ ./repro_host_va_vs_alias va
cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem = 0
mode=va      dst=0x72be8c02b000
  submission -> no error
  sync       -> an illegal memory access was encountered
  host[0]    = 0x00 (expected 0x11)

$ ./repro_host_va_vs_alias alias
cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem = 0
host VA = 0x74371c101000, device alias = 0x204c00000 (same=NO)
mode=alias   dst=0x204c00000
  submission -> no error
  sync       -> no error
  host[0]    = 0x11 (expected 0x11)
```

The same holds at the kernel's real geometry (2 host tensors x 4 pages = 8 descriptors, 128 KiB each): host VAs -> illegal memory access; the two aliases -> success with `k=0x11`, `v=0x22` verified at both the first and the last byte of both buffers.

 `cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem` is documented as "Device can access host registered memory at the same virtual address as the CPU". On this machine it is `0`, and it is consistent with what the runtime reports for the two host-memory flavors:

```
mmap + cudaHostRegister : host VA 0x74371c101000 != device alias 0x204c00000   (same = NO)
cudaHostAlloc          : host VA == device alias                              (same = YES)
```

On typical native Linux x86_64 with UVA the attribute is `1`, so a host VA *is* a valid device address and the raw-address usage happens to be correct. That is consistent with #21631's benchmark (~48 GiB/s through this same API) and with the absence of earlier reports. Note that
sglang already encodes this exact concept for ROCm — `_resolve_device_accessible_ptr_fn()` in `python/sglang/srt/mem_cache/pool_host/common.py` documents that "on HIP they differ" and `get_device_accessible_ptr` exists to translate; the batch destination is the one place where the translation is not applied.

The two conditions are the default combination in production: the default host pool is `mmap`-backed and registered (`ALLOC_MEMORY_FUNCS` defaults to `alloc_with_host_register`, which calls `cudart.cudaHostRegister(ptr, size, 0)`, on buffers from `HostTensorAllocator.allocate -> alloc_mmap`; only `npu`/`musa` use `alloc_with_pin_memory`), and essentially any real checkpoint exceeds 128 KiB per page (e.g. `page_size=64`, 32 layers, 8 KV heads x 128 dim, bf16 -> 4 MiB). So the batch path is the *default* path, and whether a deployment survives depends on a device attribute that differs by platform/driver — including WSL2, which is where I hit it.

The batch call returns `cudaSuccess`; the error is asynchronous and sticky, so it is only observed at the next synchronization point. In our runs the first symptom was a stream query inside the HiCache ready-count logic:

```
torch.AcceleratorError: CUDA error: an illegal memory access was encountered
  unified_radix_cache.py:3069 _count_ready_acks -> torch/cuda/streams.py query()
  reached via _produce_buffer_l3 -> _buffer_backup_and_wait -> _pump_hicache_until
           -> check_hicache_events -> _sync_hicache_ready_counts
```

The frame in that traceback is not the faulting call, and under `retry()` the test retries until the budget is exhausted, so it presents as a flaky test rather than a broken D2H.

End-to-end confirmation at the sglang level (same test, same geometry, only the host pool backing changed):

| configuration (`test_buffer_only_load_back_drops_on_sibling_published_span`, page_size=32, num_layers=16) | result |
|---|---|
| default: host pool = `mmap` + `cudaHostRegister` | **FAIL** — illegal memory access |
| host pool = `cudaHostAlloc` (`torch.empty(..., pin_memory=True)`) | **PASS** |
| default, with `cudaMemcpyBatchAsync` forced

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Read the kernel on current main and the report holds exactly as written: the batch path builds every destination from `dst_ptrs[tensor_id].data_ptr()` (staged_write_back.cuh:147-150) and hands it to `cudaMemcpyBatchAsync` (:170), while the fallback `copy_page_first_pages_fallback` walks the same addresses through per-page `cudaMemcpyAsync` and works because that API translates host pointers. So the one place the device-accessibility translation is missing is the batch destination, matching your `cudaHostGetDevicePointer` control row.

On the fix shape, two kernel-local options, no wheel/op dependency either way:

1. Query `cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem` once (static cache) inside the batch helper and return false when it is 0. The caller then takes the existing fallback, which you already proved passes. Smallest possible diff, bulletproof, and the only cost is the batch fast path being unused on affected platforms.
2. Translate each batch destination through `cudaHostGetDevicePointer(..., 0)` and fall back to option 1's path if the alias call errors. Keeps the batch API on WSL2-class platforms at the price of a little more branching.

I would send option 1 as the safe default and mention 2 as a follow-up refinement; the per-page path is not the hot case on platforms where the attribute is 0 anyway.

One honest caveat: I do not have an attribute-0 platform (or any CUDA box) at hand, so my verification is code-level only and CI on UVA hardware can only prove no regression, not the fix itself. Your standalone repro is the right acceptance test for whoever lands it.

Happy to write the PR along these lines if you and the maintainers are good with the direction.

Sent #40571 with the option-1 shape from my earlier comment: the batch helper queries `cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem` per call and returns false (existing per-page fallback) whenever the device does not report support, or when the query itself errors. The alias-translation variant is noted in the PR as a possible follow-up refinement rather than part of this change.

Same caveat as before, repeated for honesty: I have no CUDA host here, so this is verified at code level only — CI plus your standalone repro are the real acceptance runs.

comments.author: Edwardssss
comments.body:
Thanks @he-yufeng — I worked through your reading line by line before replying, and it holds exactly as you wrote it:

- the destination is built from `dst_ptrs[tensor_id].data_ptr()` at `staged_write_back.cuh:147-150` and handed to the batch call at `:167-177`, while `copy_page_first_pages_fallback` (`:64-89`) walks the same addresses through `cudaMemcpyAsync` — checked in the file, not from memory;
- "no wheel/op dependency either way" also holds for the option-2 shape: the JIT-side `runtime.cuh` calls `cudaHostGetDevicePointer` directly rather than going through the AOT op, and the box behind this report has `sglang-kernel` 0.4.7, which has no `get_device_accessible_ptr` at all, yet the option-2 build runs.

You flagged that you have no CUDA host, so the part you could not run is the part I ran. I applied #40571 verbatim on top of `main` at `76f9213a41` and used the same configuration as in the report (`CacheConfig(page_size=32, num_layers=16)`, one subprocess per configuration, since an illegal access aborts the process):

| build | result |
| --- | --- |
| `main`, unpatched | FAIL — `err=2`, "an illegal memory access was encountered", exit 134 |
| `main` + #40571 applied as-is | PASS, exit 0 |
| #40233 (option 2) | PASS, exit 0 |

`cudaDevAttrCanUseHostPointerForRegisteredMem` is 0 on this machine, so in your build the gate returns false by construction and the existing fallback is what carries the run — exactly the outcome you predicted, and worth confirming on hardware given you flagged you had none.

Two observations, both about breadth rather than correctness:

1. The attribute query sits ahead of the `kLargeCopyThresholdBytes` check, so every staged write-back pays a `cudaDeviceGetAttribute` call — including copies that stay on the per-page path and platforms that were never affected. Your comment said "once (static cache)" while the PR body says per call; probably worth picking one and matching the other.
2. The attribute describes the device, not the memory. On an attribute-0 host it also retires the batch path for `cudaHostAlloc` / `pin_memory` pools, whose host VA is identity-mapped and was never the problem. That is the safe direction of error, just a wider brush than the defect needs.

On option 1 vs option 2, one piece of data you may not have had: option 2 is already implemented in #40233, so the "follow-up refinement" is code-complete rather than hypothetical. I put a temporary print in the batch helper to see which D2H path actually runs, and on this same attribute-0 box the batch call itself succeeds once the destination is the alias:

```
[probe] BATCH OK n=8 dst0=0x204e00000 host_va0=0x7cd2a813f000 alias_differs=1
```

So option 2 keeps the batch path on precisely the platforms where option 1 gives it up. Two smaller differences, stated plainly in both directions: the diff is 15 lines against 158; and #40233 carries a registered-host-pool regression test while #40571 has none — although, to be fair to your caveat, that test would pass on UVA CI with or without either fix, so it is a guard on affected hardware rather than a CI regression detector.

One clarification on your option 2, since it differs slightly from what #40233 does: for host memory that was never registered, `cudaHostGetDevicePointer` errors, and the helper there returns the host VA instead of falling back to per-page. That is deliberate — pageable host memory has no separate device address and the copy APIs expect the host VA, which is the combination that already worked in the report's table. Both behaviours are needed at one call site.

Suggestion for landing, maintainers' call and I am happy either way:

- if the smaller, assumption-free change is preferred, I will close #40233 and move its registered test into #40571, so the fallback path is at least covered by a test;
- if keeping the batch path on attribute-0 platforms is preferred, #40233 is ready, and #40571 folds in as an extra guard only if you want the belt-and-braces version —

items.title: RFC: Plugin Extension Points Needed for MetaX GPU Support
items.author: yangxin-mx
items.body_excerpt:
# Proposal: Generalize SGLang Hardware Plugin Interfaces for MetaX GPU Support

> Discussion draft based on a SGLang 0.5.19-derived codebase. The names below are proposed API shapes, not claims that they already exist on the latest `main` branch. If an equivalent upstream seam already exists, we would prefer to use or extend it. This is an umbrella discussion that can be split into smaller PRs.

SGLang already has useful foundations: hardware-platform entry points, `SRTPlatform.init_backend()`, an explicit OOT forward registry for fused ops, and MoE runner/fused-function registration. See the [plugin documentation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/docs/hardware-platforms/plugin.mdx) and [expert-parallelism documentation](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/main/docs/docs/advanced_features/expert_parallelism.mdx). When adapting another CUDA-compatible GPU, however, we still encounter framework call sites that select a built-in class, import a vendor implementation, or call a kernel through a module-level symbol before a platform plugin can participate.

Our goal is to make required hardware behavior expressible through platform methods and explicit, typed registries. We do **not** propose replacing module globals or monkey-patching framework functions. A missing optional platform implementation should preserve the current built-in behavior; a selected but unsupported implementation should fail with a clear capability error rather than silently run an incompatible kernel. The plugin owns its vendor kernels and package dependencies. The framework owns common algorithms, selection rules, lifecycle, and validation.

The Python snippets below illustrate **proposed interfaces and call sites, not complete, runnable code already present in the repository**. `ExampleGpuPlatform` and `vendor_ops` stand for any vendor plugin. Exact parameters should be settled against existing types and call paths in the corresponding PRs. Each section shows both where the framework would connect the extension point and how a plugin would use it.

## 1. JIT toolchain and cache identity

### Adaptation problem

In the 0.5.19-derived tree, JIT compilation derives the device compiler, architecture and flags through CUDA/ROCm-oriented paths in `kernels/jit/utils/compile/toolchain.py`. The build path (`ninja.py`) and cache path (`cache.py`) must agree on these values. A plugin cannot safely supply a different device compiler by changing only one path: the cache may reuse a binary built for another SDK or architecture.

### Plugin-oriented proposal

- Add an optional `SRTPlatform.get_jit_toolchain() -> JitToolchainSpec | None`. The immutable spec should include the host/device compilers, toolkit root, target architecture, include/link paths and flags, plus an explicit SDK/ABI cache identity.
- Resolve the spec lazily when compilation starts, and pass the **same resolved spec** to command generation and cache-key generation. `None` keeps the existing built-in toolchain logic.
- Let the vendor plugin package its AOT extensions itself. The common AOT setup need not import or name each vendor SDK.

On the framework side, add the optional method in `srt/platforms/interface.py` and have `kernels/jit/utils/compile/{toolchain,ninja,cache}.py` consume the same spec:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class JitToolchainSpec:
    host_compiler: str
    device_compiler: str
    toolkit_root: str
    target_arch: str
    device_flags: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    include_dirs: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    link_flags: tuple[str, ...] = ()
    cache_identity: str = ""  # SDK/ABI version

class SRTPlatform(DeviceMixin):
    def get_jit_toolchain(self) -> JitToolchainSpec | None:
        return None

def compile_extension(source, **kwargs):
    spec = resolve_jit_toolchain(get_platform().get_jit_toolchain())
    cache_key = make_cache_key(source, spec=spec, **kwargs)
    return build_with_ninja(source, spec=spec, cache_key=cache_key, **kwargs)
```

The plugin only describes its own SDK; it does not modify global `CUDA_HOME` or framework compiler symbols:

```python
class ExampleGpuPlatform(SRTPlatform):
    def get_jit_toolchain(self) -> JitToolchainSpec:
        return JitToolchainSpec(
            host_compiler="/opt/example/bin/c++",
            device_compiler="/opt/example/bin/device-cc",
            toolkit_root="/opt/example",
            target_arch="example-arch",
            cache_identity="example-sdk-1:abi-1",
        )
```

## 2. Device properties and per-operator Triton tuning

### Adaptation problem

Several launch paths infer hardware behavior from CUDA properties or NVIDIA/AMD architecture names, while `num_stages`, warps, tile sizes and shared-memory limits are selected locally. A plugin may expose a CUDA-compatible device but still need different launch parameters; pretending to be a particular SM is not a sound capability contract.

### Plugin-oriented proposal

- Expose a read-only `DeviceKernelProfile` through the active platform, with architecture identifier, warp size, maximum shared-memory bytes and relevant device capabilities.
- Add an optional `tune_triton_launch(op, shape, dtype, default) -> TritonLaunchConfig`. Each caller first computes its present default, then asks the active platform for a per-operator override and validates it before launch. There should be no global change to Triton's defaults.
- Start with launch sites where hardware differences actually affect correctness or feasibility (MoE, quantization and attention), keeping other paths unchanged.

The framework could define device facts in `srt/platforms/device_mixin.py`/`interface.py` and consume the policy immediately before each Triton launch, keeping hardware facts separate from per-operator tuning:

```python
@dataclass(frozen=True)
class DeviceKernelProfile:
    arch: str
    warp_size: int
    max_shared_memory_bytes: int

### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

In PD disaggregation with the NIXL backend, aborting a request after its KV transfer handles have been submitted does not cancel or bound the prefill transfer worker's wait for a handle that remains healthy but non-terminal (`PROC`).

The wait policy in `python/sglang/srt/disaggregation/nixl/conn.py` is:

```python
deadline = time.time() + NIXL_ERR_SETTLE_TIMEOUT_S if failure_seen else None
while True:
    ...
    if all_settled:
        return True, any_failed
    if not any_failed:
        time.sleep(0)
        continue
```

Thus, a batch is bounded only after an `ERR` is observed. If every handle remains `PROC`, the deadline stays `None`.

The prefill worker calls this with `failure_seen=False` after submitting handles:

```python
settled, any_failed = self._await_handles(handles, failure_seen=False)
```

An externally triggered decode-to-prefill abort notification then runs:

```python
self.record_failure(room_to_be_aborted, ...)
self.update_status(room_to_be_aborted, KVPoll.Failed)
...
self._handle_deferred_abort_ack(notification)
```

This changes the room status and registers a deferred ACK target, but it does not cancel the submitted NIXL handles and does not interrupt a worker already inside `_await_handles()`.

The room was counted before this wait:

```python
if not kv_chunk.staging_counted:
    self._staging_outstanding[room] += 1
    kv_chunk.staging_counted = True
```

The count is decremented and the deferred ACK is sent only after the handles reach a terminal state. Consequently, a healthy but permanently non-terminal handle leaves:

- one transfer worker alive but blocked;
- `_staging_outstanding[room] == 1`;
- the deferred abort ACK unsent.

The default worker count is four:

```python
SGLANG_DISAGGREGATION_QUEUE_SIZE = EnvInt(4)
```

Four aborted rooms with non-terminal handles can therefore consume all default prefill transfer workers.

This is not a claim that every ordinary abort leaks memory or KV blocks. Prefill scheduler failure paths can release request resources independently. The specific defect is that abort does not terminate the transfer-worker lifetime, room staging accounting, or deferred ACK lifecycle when the underlying NIXL handle remains `PROC`.


### Reproduction

The following deterministic reproduction exercises the production abort-notification handling and `_await_handles()` with a fake NIXL agent whose submitted handle remains healthy but non-terminal. It does not depend on GPU RDMA and does not modify live services.

```python
from collections import defaultdict
from threading import Event, Thread
from time import sleep
from types import SimpleNamespace

from sglang.srt.disaggregation.base.conn import KVPoll
from sglang.srt.disaggregation.common.conn import AbortNotification
from sglang.srt.disaggregation.nixl.conn import NixlKVManager

ROOM = 90210
HANDLE = object()


class FakeAgent:
    def __init__(self):
        self.state = "PROC"
        self.reads = 0

    def check_xfer_state(self, handle):
        self.reads += 1
        return self.state


def make_manager(agent):
    manager = NixlKVManager.__new__(NixlKVManager)
    manager.agent = agent
    manager.request_status = {ROOM: KVPoll.WaitingForInput}
    manager.req_to_decode_prefix_len = {}
    manager.transfer_infos = {}
    manager.exceptions = {}
    manager._staging_outstanding = defaultdict(int)
    manager._deferred_ack_targets = {}
    manager._deferred_ack_poisoned_rooms = set()
    manager.enable_deferred_decode_kv_release = True
    manager.enable_staging = False
    manager._staging_ctx = None
    manager.failure_events = []
    manager.sent_acks = []
    manager.update_status = lambda room, status: manager.request_status.__setitem__(room, status)
    manager.record_failure = lambda room, reason: manager.failure_events.append((room, reason))
    manager._send_abort_ack = lambda room, target: manager.sent_acks.append((room, target))
    manager._reload_invalidated_peers = lambda infos: None
    manager._staging_outstanding[ROOM] = 1
    return manager


agent = FakeAgent()
manager = make_manager(agent)
entered = Event()
returned = Event()
result = {}


def wait_for_handle():
    entered.set()
    result["value"] = manager._await_handles([HANDLE], failure_seen=False)
    returned.set()


thread = Thread(target=wait_for_handle, daemon=True)
thread.start()
assert entered.wait(1)
sleep(0.1)
reads_before_abort = agent.reads

abort_message = AbortNotification(
    room=ROOM,
    decode_ip="127.0.0.1",
    decode_port=54321,
    generation=7,
).to_zmq()
assert manager._handle_abort_notification(abort_message)
assert manager.request_status[ROOM] == KVPoll.Failed

sleep(0.2)
print({
    "state_after_abort": agent.state,
    "waiter_alive_after_abort": thread.is_alive(),
    "reads_before_abort": reads_before_abort,
    "reads_after_abort": agent.reads,
    "outstanding_after_abort": manager._staging_outstanding[ROOM],
    "abort_ack_sent_after_abort": bool(manager.sent_acks),
})

# Control: a terminal state immediately wakes this direct waiter.
agent.state = "DONE"
# This direct helper call does not itself perform worker accounting; the full
# transfer_worker() cleanup is covered by the four-worker result below.
assert returned.wait(3)
thread.join(1)
print({
    "control_state": agent.state,
    "control_return": result["value"],
    "direct_helper_outstanding": manager._staging_outstanding[ROOM],
    "direct_helper_ack_sent": bool(manager.sent_acks),
})
```

items.title: KernelLens: Deploying Triton Kernels to C++ Inference Engines (TensorRT & ONNX)
items.author: Just1truc
items.body_excerpt:
# Deploying OpenAI Triton Kernels to C++ Inference Runtimes (ONNX Runtime & TensorRT) with KernelLens

Hey Triton Community!

If you write custom `@triton.jit` kernels in Python for LLM operators (FlashAttention, Fused RMSNorm, SwiGLU, Selective Scans), you’ve probably hit the deployment bottleneck: How do you run your Python Triton kernels inside production C++ inference engines like NVIDIA TensorRT or Microsoft ONNX Runtime?

Traditionally, developers had two frustrating choices:
1. **Stay in Python PyTorch Eager/Dynamo**: Forfeiting TensorRT/ORT global graph optimizations across standard model layers.
2. **Manual C++/CUDA Rewrites**: Throw away Python Triton code and manually rewrite kernels in CUDA C++ (`__global__`) while authoring hundreds of lines of `OrtCustomOp` / `nvinfer1::IPluginV2DynamicExt` boilerplate.

To solve this, we created [**KernelLens**](https://github.com/Just1truc/kernel_lens), an open-source compiler framework from [Galiad Research](https://galiad-research.com) that automatically compiles PyTorch models containing Python `@triton.jit` kernels into native C++ plugins for ONNX Runtime and TensorRT in **1 line of Python**.

---

## Step-by-Step Guide to Run the Working Example

Follow these 3 simple steps to test KernelLens on any CUDA-enabled GPU machine:

### Step 1: Install Dependencies
```bash
pip install torch triton kernel-lens
```

### Step 2: Save the Python Script (`example.py`)
Save the following code into a file named `example.py`:

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import triton
import triton.language as tl
import kernel_lens as kl

# 1. Define a standard OpenAI Triton Kernel
@triton.jit
def add_kernel(x_ptr, y_ptr, out_ptr, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE: tl.constexpr):
    pid = tl.program_id(axis=0)
    block_start = pid * BLOCK_SIZE
    offsets = block_start + tl.arange(0, BLOCK_SIZE)
    mask = offsets < n_elements
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    y = tl.load(y_ptr + offsets, mask=mask)
    output = x + y
    tl.store(out_ptr + offsets, output, mask=mask)

# 2. Wrap the Triton Kernel inside a PyTorch Module
class VectorAddModule(nn.Module):
    def forward(self, x: torch.Tensor, y: torch.Tensor):
        out = torch.empty_like(x)
        n_elements = x.numel()
        grid = lambda meta: (triton.cdiv(n_elements, meta['BLOCK_SIZE']),)
        add_kernel[grid](<x, y, out, n_elements, BLOCK_SIZE=1024>)
        return out

if __name__ == '__main__':
    device = 'cuda' if torch.cuda.is_available() else 'cpu'
    x = torch.randn(4096, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    y = torch.randn(4096, device=device, dtype=torch.float32)
    model = VectorAddModule().to(device)

    print("Compiling PyTorch + Triton Model with KernelLens...")
    
    # 3. Compile Model to C++ Plugins in 1 Line
    compiled_model = kl.compile(
        model, 
        (x, y), 
        name="simple_vector_add", 
        backends=["onnx", "tensorrt"]
    )
    
    print("Executing Zero-Copy Inference in ONNX Runtime...")
    ort_output = compiled_model.run((x, y), backend="onnx")
    
    print("Executing Zero-Copy Inference in TensorRT...")
    trt_output = compiled_model.run((x, y), backend="tensorrt")

    # 4. Verify Numerical Parity against PyTorch Result
    torch_expected = x + y
    max_diff_ort = (ort_output - torch_expected).abs().max().item()
    max_diff_trt = (trt_output - torch_expected).abs().max().item()

    print("Verification Complete!")
    print(f"ORT Max Floating-Point Difference: {max_diff_ort:.6e}")
    print(f"TRT Max Floating-Point Difference: {max_diff_trt:.6e}")
    print(f"Exact Numerical Match (ORT): {torch.allclose(ort_output, torch_expected)}")
    print(f"Exact Numerical Match (TRT): {torch.allclose(trt_output, torch_expected)}")
```

### Step 3: Execute the Test
```bash
python3 example.py
```

### Expected Terminal Output
```text
Compiling PyTorch + Triton Model with KernelLens...
Executing Zero-Copy Inference in ONNX Runtime...
Executing Zero-Copy Inference in TensorRT...
Verification Complete!
ORT Max Floating-Point Difference: 0.000000e+00
TRT Max Floating-Point Difference: 0.000000e+00
Exact Numerical Match (ORT): True
Exact Numerical Match (TRT): True
```

---

## How it Works Under the Hood 🛠️

1. **PTX & Metadata Extraction**: KernelLens intercepts `@triton.jit` launches, extracting compiled PTX assembly strings, dynamic shared memory bytes, and parameter bitwidths directly from Triton’s compiler cache.
2. **SymPy Grid Transpilation**: Triton grid functions (e.g., `grid = lambda META: (triton.cdiv(M, BLOCK_SIZE),)`) are parsed via AST inspection into pure C++ integer arithmetic, evaluated dynamically at inference time with $< 0.5 \ \mu\text{s}$ CPU overhead.
3. **C++/CUDA Plugin Synthesis**: Synthesizes production-ready C++ source files implementing `Ort::CustomOp` and `nvinfer1::IPluginV2DynamicExt`, executing the PTX assembly via CUDA Driver API (`cuModuleLoadData` & `cuLaunchKernel`).
4. **Zero-Copy VRAM Binding**: Directly maps PyTorch VRAM pointers (`data_ptr()`) to ONNX Runtime `IOBinding` and TensorRT `setTensorAddress()`.
5. **Hardware Hardening**: Automatically injects dynamic 16-byte address checks to prevent misaligned vector load crashes (`ld.global.v4.b32`), and applies PTX ISA version clamping (`.version 9.0`) for NVIDIA Blackwell (`sm_120a`) GPU driver compatibility.

---

## Benchmarks & Numerical Parity

Across LLaMA 3, Mistral, Qwen 2.5, and Liger-Kernel operators, KernelLens achieves **$3.4\times$ to $7.0\times$ speedups** over eager PyTorch execution while maintaining exact floating-point numerical parity ($\text{MaxDiff} = 0.00\text{e}+00$).

---

## Links & Resources

* 💻 **GitHub**: [Just1truc/kernel_lens](https://github.com/Just1truc/kernel_lens)
* 📦 **PyPI**: `pip install kernel-lens`
* 📄 **Technical Report (DOI)**: [10.5281/zenodo.23194523](https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo

items.title: [Gluon] async_load accepts a pointer whose element type differs from the shared memory buffer
items.author: shuyilinn
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

Gluon's `async_copy.async_load` (and `async_copy_global_to_local` in general) does not check that the pointer element type matches the shared memory element type. Copying from an fp32 pointer into an fp16 buffer compiles and copies raw bytes, and the reverse faults with a misaligned address. `smem.store` rejects the same mismatch at compile time.

```python
import torch
from triton.experimental import gluon
from triton.experimental.gluon import language as gl
from triton.experimental.gluon.language.nvidia.ampere import async_copy


@gluon.jit
def kernel(inp, out, SMEM_DTYPE: gl.constexpr, N: gl.constexpr):
    L: gl.constexpr = gl.BlockedLayout([4], [32], [4], [0])
    offs = gl.arange(0, N, L)
    smem = gl.allocate_shared_memory(SMEM_DTYPE, [N], gl.SwizzledSharedLayout(1, 1, 1, [0]))
    async_copy.async_load(smem, inp + offs)
    async_copy.commit_group()
    async_copy.wait_group(0)
    gl.store(out + offs, smem.load(L))


N = 512
inp = torch.arange(N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32) + 0.5
out = torch.zeros(N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
kernel[(1, )](inp, out, gl.float16, N)  # fp32 pointer -> fp16 smem: compiles, wrong values
print(out[:8].tolist())

inp = torch.arange(N, device="cuda").to(torch.float16)
out = torch.zeros(N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
kernel[(1, )](inp, out, gl.float32, N)  # fp16 pointer -> fp32 smem
torch.cuda.synchronize()                # RuntimeError: CUDA error: misaligned address
```

```
[0.0, 1.75, 0.0, 1.9375, 0.0, 2.28125, 0.0, 2.34375]
RuntimeError: CUDA error: misaligned address
```

The first kernel should print `[0.5, 1.5, 2.5, ...]`; instead each 8-byte copy moves the raw bytes of two fp32 values into four fp16 slots.

Expected: a compile-time error for both, like `smem.store` gives for a value whose dtype does not match the buffer.

The frontend (`python/triton/experimental/gluon/language/nvidia/ampere/async_copy.py`, and the AMD `cdna4`/`cdna5` versions) only checks the shapes, and `AsyncCopyGlobalToLocalOp::verify` only checks that the destination is mutable. The lowering sizes each copy by the shared memory element type, so a mismatch reads with the wrong stride.

### Environment details

Triton: main @ 41846bc965
GPU: NVIDIA RTX 4090 (sm_89), driver 570 / CUDA 12.8

items.title: [Bug]: Prefix caching is ineffective on Mamba-2/GDN hybrid (Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration)
items.author: semil007
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

vLLM 0.26.0
GPU: GB10 / sm_121a
Not re-verified on current main
Found with an AI assistant (Claude Code)

### 🐛 Describe the bug

Summary:
On Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (architecture: Qwen3_5MoeForConditionalGeneration — a Mamba-2/GDN hybrid), enabling prefix caching (--enable-prefix-caching) results in 0% prefix-cache hits even for requests that share a long, identical prefix. The model's recurrent conversational + SSM state is not stored in the APC (which tracks attention KV blocks), so no prefix-cache entries are created. As a result, prefix caching is effectively a silent no-op.

Reproduction / measurement:
1. Start vLLM with: --enable-prefix-caching --max-num-batched-tokens 4096
2. Send request A: a ~561-token prompt (as token IDs) with max_tokens=1.
3. Wait ~2 seconds (staggered, not concurrent).
4. Send request B: the exact same token IDs as A followed by a short suffix.
5. Inspect /metrics. Example observed values:

vllm:prefix_cache_queries_total  1131
vllm:prefix_cache_hits_total     0

The staggered timing rules out a race where the cache hasn't populated; instead the hybrid recurrent state simply has no APC entry.

Expected behavior / ask:
Is this a known limitation? Preferably either:
- vLLM should warn that --enable-prefix-caching is ineffective for hybrid SSM/Mamba models, or
- vLLM should be extended to support caching the recurrent conv+SSM state so shared-prefix prefill reuse works for these hybrids.

Notes:
Observed on vLLM 0.26.0 (GB10 / sm_121a). Not re-verified on main.
