items.title: Upgrade to Transformers v5
items.author: hmellor
items.body_excerpt:
## What is this issue?

This issue serves as a living tracker for the current issues preventing us from upgrading vLLM to Transformers v5.

We will use sub-issues to track individual failures and PRs should be made against these sub-issues.

The solutions to these issues may need to be applied to either:

- Transformers in the form of:
  - Adding missing backward compatibility (usually for custom code models)
  - General bug fixes/improvements to new features of v5
- vLLM in the form of:
  - Forward compatibility with how something is now done in v5
  - Edge case handling for issues that v4 ignored (such as config validation)

Sometimes, the issue is simply with the model checkpoint itself, for example if it:

- Contains a malformed `config.json` that cannot be used to instantiate the newly input validated `PreTrainedConfig` class
- Custom code* uses deprecated/removed APIs

In these situations, the best solution will likely be to skip these tests in vLLM and open a PR to Transformers to contribute this model. This will be faster and more sustainable than waiting for the model vendor to fix their custom model code, sometimes they nevert do.

Contributing the new model should be done using the new [Modular Transformers](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/main/en/modular_transformers) so that the implementation is easy to maintain and will remain maintained by the Transformers team.

_*particularly in the parts of the model implementation that vLLM tries to directly reuse, such as config/tokenizer/multimodal processor_

items.title: [Performance] Measure Transformers backend startup time vs native
items.author: hmellor
items.body_excerpt:
This comes from an old comment and was never backed by measurements, so the first
task is to establish whether the effect is real at all. It may not be.

Runtime throughput was brought in line with native implementations in #47187, but
nobody has measured startup time either before or since.

### Step 1: is there a difference?

Time engine init for a model that has both implementations, e.g.:

    vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --model-impl transformers
    vllm serve Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B --model-impl vllm

Compare time-to-ready across a few runs and a couple of model sizes. Warm vs cold
HF cache matters, so control for it.

If there is no meaningful difference, say so and close this issue. That is a
perfectly good outcome and still worth having measured.

### Step 2: only if a delta shows up

The backend does some work at load time that native implementations do not, so
these are plausible starting points rather than known causes:

- `fuser.py` — `get_fuser` traces each module class with `fx` to match it against
  the available fusers. Cached per class, but tracing is not free.
- `base.py` — `recursive_replace` walks the module tree applying fusers per instance.
- Config resolution and `auto_map` handling for remote-code models.

A profile of init (py-spy or cProfile) will be more informative than guessing from
this list.

### Done when

Either the startup delta is quantified and explained, or it is shown that there
isn't a meaningful one and this is closed.

items.title: Starting a localization (l10n) effort for LMCache
items.author: quaid
items.body_excerpt:
I'd like to propose we start building a localization community around LMCache, beginning with blog posts and expanding to documentation and other parts of the website over time.

tl;dr – 
- localizing content and software is valuable to all of us;
- we can automate the toil of translation but we need human editors who can review the translations and make sure they are properly localized;
- localization means words and phrases are fixed so the final product makes more sense to a native reader;
- we can use RHLF to improve this process and reduce toil over time.

## What is the problem

We already receive blog posts written natively in Mandarin and English. This is a good thing.

But we also need to localize this content without putting a burden on people. Fortunately this content has completed a technical review before being translated, so the focus can be on fixing idioms and grammar for better understanding by the widest audience.

## Why this matters

Ultimately this is about attracting more users to LMCache, some of whom will become intentional contributors over time.

Twenty-five years ago, localization (l10n) projects were one of the main ways Linux distributions and communities like the Fedora Project made headway into new parts of the world. It usually wasn't a corporate initiative. It was people who were enthusiastic about bringing free and open source software to their fellow country members, and who put in the effort to translate strings and make the software make sense locally. That work produced translations AND collaborations. It grew contributors, built regional communities, and carried the free software and open source ethos into places it hadn't reached before.

LMCache has users and watchers all over the world, and there are almost certainly people already adjacent to this project who could help bring information and education about the software to their local communities.

## What I'm proposing

We form loosely as `l10n-sig` out of anyone who wants to be an editor and approver for one or more languages. Languages get added when someone steps forward to take one. Rather than announcing a target list and hoping it fills in, we start with whoever volunteers.

I'm volunteering to be an editor and reviewer for anything translated to English, and I'd love more help with that role. I'm confident we can get Mandarin covered right away. But what else and how?

Japanese and Korean are the obvious early candidates given where our users are, but the principle is that a language becomes active when a person is willing to own it.

It only takes one person to get things started and be the gravity to bring another language.

As I said above, this isn't only English needing localizing. I currently have an original blog post written in Mandarin that I want to bring into English through this same process. I'd like to stop doing one at a time reviews by asking around in Slack to see who might need a break from creating features or fixing bugs. I'd rather offer the opportunity to people who aren't or can't create features or fix bugs.

Therefore, posts written originally in any language are welcome, and translation should flow in whatever direction it needs to.

## This is not a request for volunteer translation labor

LLM translation is pretty good now, and we should lean on it for the first pass. What we need is a human review step, and there are two kinds of people who can do that well.

The first is someone capable in both the source and target language, who can read the machine translation and confirm the meaning carried over and the tone is right. Not necessarily final-polish copy editing — a human or AI copy edit can always be applied later — just confirmation that it makes sense and reads naturally.

The second, and possibly just as valuable, is someone technical who knows their own language well and doesn't necessarily read the source language at all. Because the models are good enough now, a domain expert can look at a translated technical passage and say "ah, I see what this was trying to say" and correct the terminology so it's actually right in their language. Technical accuracy matters as much as idiomatic flow, and that person is well placed to catch it.

So the ask is much closer to "read this and tell us if it sounds right" than "translate three thousand words."

## How the workflow might look

Initially all of this can be manual, while we work out which models produce the best tone for technical writing in each language and we develop any necessary skills.

Longer term this could be automated — a GitHub Action that sends a published post to a translation model, then loads the result into WordPress as a draft where a translation editor reviews and approves it. It could also live partly outside the repo, with approval happening after the fact rather than as a gate. The goal is to distribute this work rather than make it dependent on a paid staffer, and to remove the need to ask permission before contributing.

If anyone already knows of a toolchain or process for this, please say so. I'd much rather adopt something that works than stand up and maintain our own infrastructure.

## What I'm looking for

Ideas or helping hands for:

- Thoughts on the approach
- Pointers to existing tooling
- Anyone in

items.title: llama : integer type consistency in `llama.h`
items.author: MarcusDunn
items.body_excerpt:
# Feature Description

llama.h should prefer to use `sized` (always) + `signed` (mostly) integers.

# Motivation

The integer types in `llama.h` right now are.

| Count | Type            |
|---------|------------------|
| 33      | `int`              |
| 10      | `int32_t`       |
| 24      | `uint32_t`     |
| 2        | `int64_t`       |
| 2        | `uint64_t`    | 

In #4540 there was a discussion around preferences for integer types on new methods. 

Avoiding `int` makes cross platform code simpler at essentially no cost.
Signed makes arithmetic simpler at the cost of some bits if you need something large.

# Possible Implementation

1. Change all `int`'s to `int32_t`
2. As code changes try to prefer signed integers.

We could also do some higher-impact things, but I'd take the lower-impact slower changes over a large find-and-replace.

items.title: bug: a client-set `X-Conversation-Id` disables disconnect-cancellation and accumulates uncapped resumable-stream sessions, can cause memory DoS
items.author: Yunzez
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

`llama-server`, git `4b1a27f` (`version: 0.5.0-dev (build 1)`), CPU build, Linux x86_64, `Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf`. No special launch flag (the resumable-stream manager starts unconditionally at boot).


### Operating systems

Linux

### Which llama.cpp modules do you know to be affected?

llama-server

### Command line

```shell
llama-server -m Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct-Q4_K_M.gguf --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8137 -c 2048 -np 1 --no-webui python3 repro_llamacpp_stream_session_dos.py --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8137
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Repro script: [repro_llamacpp_stream_session_dos.py](https://gist.github.com/Yunzez/f99b245d040ac2604178c1bef9541d6b#file-repro_llamacpp_stream_session_dos-py)

The resumable-stream session manager keys a per-request session on the **client-controlled** `X-Conversation-Id` header. When that header is present, two things go wrong, both exploitable by an unauthenticated client:

**(A) A socket disconnect no longer cancels the generation.** With `X-Conversation-Id`, `server_res_spipe::should_stop()` (`tools/server/server-stream.cpp:622-628`) returns `spipe->is_cancelled()`, which is set only by an explicit `DELETE /v1/stream` — instead of `!conn_alive()`. So a streaming request whose client hangs up keeps the inference slot busy generating to its natural stop. An attacker fires `stream:true` requests with a large `max_tokens` and drops each connection immediately; every abandoned request still consumes a full generation and pins a slot. 

Measured on a single-slot server (`-np 1`): after abandoning one stream, a normal follow-up request was blocked **36.9 s** (the whole generation) with the header, versus **0.07 s** without it (disconnect cancels normally).

**(B) Sessions accumulate with no cap and a 300 s post-completion TTL.** Each session buffers up to `STREAM_SESSION_MAX_BYTES = 4 MiB` of SSE output (`server-stream.cpp:18`) and is retained for `STREAM_SESSION_TTL_SECONDS = 300 s` **after** the generation completes before the GC removes it (`gc_loop`, `server-stream.cpp:356`). `create_or_replace` (`:235`) just `emplace`s into an `unordered_map,  **there is no cap on the number of sessions**. A client that sends streaming requests with a fresh `X Conversation-Id` each time and never issues `DELETE /v1/stream` accumulates ~`rate × 300 s` sessions, each holding up to 4 MiB, eventually will cause memory exhaustion.

Ablation confirms the header is the cause: 150 streaming requests **without** the header grow `VmHWM` by ~0 MB (sessions are evicted on completion — `on_complete` at `server-stream.cpp:638`), while 150 **with** unique headers retain their sessions (monotonic growth; at large `max_tokens` each retains up to 4 MiB).

### First Bad Commit

_No response_

<details>
<summary>Logs</summary>

```console

```
</details>

comments.author: benthecarman
comments.body:
A related problem: sessions live in one global map (`g_stream_sessions`, `server-stream.cpp:65`), keyed only by the client-supplied `X-Conversation-Id`. Nothing ties a session to the caller's API key. So anyone who knows or guesses another client's ID can:

- read that client's buffered output: `GET /v1/stream` (`:454`)
- cancel their generation: `DELETE /v1/stream` (`:561`)
- replace their session by sending their own request with the same ID; `create_or_replace` cancels the existing session (`:235-255`)

Also, a `DELETE` with an unknown ID writes every live conversation ID to the log at WARN (`:297-304`).

This only matters when several clients share one server and IDs aren't random (the web UI uses UUIDs). One possible fix is to scope sessions to the API key that created them, and to stop logging live IDs.

items.title: [RFC]: Store-to-TENT QoS Integration Boundary for Foreground Transfers and Background Offload
items.author: catyans
items.body_excerpt:
### Changes proposed

## Summary

This RFC discusses how Mooncake Store traffic should participate in TENT QoS so that latency-sensitive transfers are protected from background offload traffic.

A representative serving workload has two priority classes:

- **HIGH**: foreground point-to-point KV handoff, such as Prefill-to-Decode (P2D), and foreground remote-prefix fetch.
- **LOW**: background writes to DRAM, local SSD, remote memory, or remote storage.

The main contention is on NIC TX and accelerator PCIe outbound bandwidth. A background Store write should not delay a foreground KV handoff that gates time-to-first-token. This RFC compares three integration boundaries:

1. **Option A — route all storage data movement through TENT.**
2. **Option B — use layered QoS and unified admission while retaining existing executors.**
3. **Option C — route only the network portion of remote Store traffic through TENT.**

The proposed rollout is **C first, then B if PCIe-side interference remains measurable**. Option A should remain a longer-term choice only if TENT is intentionally expanded into a general data-movement runtime.

This RFC is an integration proposal. It does not redefine the intent schema, QoS contract, budget scheduler, execution plan, or local admission queue proposed in #2865, #2856, #2866, #2863, and #2132. Instead, it asks how Mooncake Store should consume those mechanisms and where the ownership boundary should be.

## Motivation

Consider the following traffic classes:

| Traffic | Typical resources | Priority | Reason |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Foreground P2D KV handoff | accelerator PCIe OUT + NIC TX | HIGH | decode cannot start until the KV state arrives |
| Foreground remote-prefix fetch | NIC RX + accelerator PCIe IN, depending on placement | HIGH | a hit avoids repeated prefill computation |
| DRAM offload | accelerator PCIe OUT + memory bandwidth | LOW | background cache management |
| Local SSD write | accelerator PCIe OUT + memory bandwidth + NVMe | LOW | background persistence/eviction |
| Remote Store write | accelerator PCIe OUT, depending on GDR/staging, + NIC TX | LOW | background persistence/write-through |

Foreground prefix fetch often uses the opposite direction from background writes, so it should remain concurrent when the resources do not conflict. The scheduler must therefore reason about resources and direction; a single global HIGH/LOW gate would unnecessarily serialize independent RX/IN and TX/OUT work.

The required behavior is cooperative preemption:

```text
foreground HIGH arrives
  -> stop admitting new conflicting LOW slices
  -> allow already-submitted DMA/WQE/I/O to complete
  -> run HIGH
  -> resume LOW using otherwise-idle capacity
```

Already-posted WQEs and already-submitted DMA or NVMe operations generally cannot be revoked. Therefore, the protection bound depends on both slice size and the **global LOW in-flight window**, not on queue ordering alone.

## Current code shape

The observations below use commit [`9c6125f`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/commit/9c6125f3e9ecf667907f2fd3cea17a783a8a4791).

### Store traffic does not have one execution path

Store `Put` dispatches disk writes to `PutToLocalFile`, while memory and NoF replicas go through `TransferSubmitter` ([`client_service.cpp`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/9c6125f3e9ecf667907f2fd3cea17a783a8a4791/mooncake-store/src/client_service.cpp#L2031-L2070)).

`TransferSubmitter` then selects local memcpy, Transfer Engine, SPDK NoF, or file-read execution depending on replica type and locality ([`transfer_task.cpp`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/9c6125f3e9ecf667907f2fd3cea17a783a8a4791/mooncake-store/src/transfer_task.cpp#L981-L1028)). These executors do not share one priority scheduler.

The file-put path performs synchronous accelerator-to-host copying into a pinned buffer before submitting `StorageBackend::StoreObject` to the write pool ([`client_service.cpp`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/9c6125f3e9ecf667907f2fd3cea17a783a8a4791/mooncake-store/src/client_service.cpp#L3361-L3415)). Deferring this copy requires an explicit buffer-lifetime contract; queueing a raw pointer after the caller may reuse it would be unsafe.

### Store priority is not propagated to TENT

Remote memory replica transfers construct the legacy `Transport::TransferRequest` ([`transfer_task.cpp`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/9c6125f3e9ecf667907f2fd3cea17a783a8a4791/mooncake-store/src/transfer_task.cpp#L1198-L1235)). The legacy request has no intent or QoS priority field ([`transport.h`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/9c6125f3e9ecf667907f2fd3cea17a783a8a4791/mooncake-transfer-engine/include/transport/transport.h#L60-L71)), and the adapter does not populate those fields when creating `tent::Request` ([`transfer_engine.cpp`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/9c6125f3e9ecf667907f2fd3cea17a783a8a4791/mooncake-transfer-engine/src/transfer_engine.cpp#L611-L626)). The effective result is the TENT default priority rather than Store-aware classification.

### TENT already contains useful QoS primitives

TENT RDMA slicing preserves request priority and passes it into device selection and worker dispatch ([`rdma_transport.cpp`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/9c6125f3e9ecf667907f2fd3cea17a783a8a4791/tent/src/transport/rdma/rdma_transport.cpp#L415-L529)). RDMA workers maintain three priority queues and select HIGH before MEDIUM before LOW ([`workers.cpp`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/9c6125f3e9ecf667907f2fd3cea17a783a8a4791/tent/src/transport/rdma/workers.cpp#L240-L263), [`workers.cpp`](https://github.com/kvcache-ai/Mooncake/blob/9c6125f3e9ecf667907f2fd3cea17a783a8a4791/tent/src/transport/rdma/workers.cpp#L386-L400)).

However:

- `SharedSlotManager` provides cross-process slot visibility/gating, not a cross-process priority queue or global LOW in-flight budget.
- The optional local admission queue is process-lo

items.title: GSP: grammar-conditioned sparse LM-head projection - replication and SGLang integration feedback wanted
items.author: StealthEyeLLC
items.body_excerpt:
I am sharing an open research artifact that may be relevant to SGLang's structured-generation path.

GSP (Grammar-Conditioned Sparse Projection) consumes a packed grammar legality mask before/during the target-model LM-head projection instead of computing the full vocabulary projection and masking afterward.

The current artifact includes:
- packed-mask row-sparse Triton projection for latency-oriented decoding
- batched block-GEMM that skips grammar-inactive vocabulary tiles
- density-aware dense fallback for permissive/mixed states
- support/top-1 correctness checks
- raw paired end-to-end Qwen3.5-2B results

On the reference RTX 5060 Laptop GPU, 30 paired AB/BA trials gave median end-to-end ratios of 1.0756x (enum JSON), 1.0642x (tool-call JSON), and 1.0842x (nested-array JSON). The free-string control is not claimed as a reliable mean speedup.

This is not claiming first invention of batch-1 grammar-aware LM-head filtering; the contribution boundary is the packed-mask batched execution, heterogeneous routing, and controlled target-model evaluation.

I would especially value:
- SGLang integration feedback
- datacenter GPU replication
- heterogeneous-batch measurements
- negative results / dense-winning crossover cases

Release, verified preprint, source, raw evidence:
https://github.com/StealthEyeLLC/grammar-sparse-projection/releases/tag/v0.1.1

items.title: Questions on Triton basic concepts
items.author: peastman
items.body_excerpt:
I'm just getting started with Triton.  I can't find any documentation on some very basic concepts.  If you can point me to something I missed I'd be grateful.  If not, perhaps someone could answer these questions?

What types of values can be passed to a kernel?  PyTorch tensors obviously, as well as ints, floats, and bools.  Anything else?

The grid is defined by a lambda that takes a single argument called `meta`.  What is `meta`?

How do I access a single element of a tensor?  Say `a` and `b` are tensors and `i` is an int.  I want to write `c = a[i]*b` to multiply `b` by an element of `a`.  That produces an error.  What's the correct way of doing it?

What is the difference between a `tensor_descriptor` and a `TensorDescriptor`?  What is each used for and how do I use them?

What is the exact significance of annotating an argument with `tl.constexpr`?  Does it mean the kernel will get recompiled every time a new value of that argument is encountered?  What can be done with a constexpr value that can't be done with other ones?

How about `tl.const`?  Is it just for error checking, to avoid accidentally modifying something that shouldn't be modified, or does it have other effects?

Thanks for your help!

items.title: LMCacheMPConnector loads full model on each GPU instead of sharding with tensor-parallel-size=2 (gemma-4-12B-it)
items.author: wyadvd-dotcom
items.body_excerpt:
## Environment

- LMCache: 0.5.3rc1 (upgraded from 0.5.2 to fix a separate reshape crash - confirmed fixed in this version)
- vLLM: 0.26.0
- Model: google/gemma-4-12B-it
- Hardware: 2x RTX 3090 (24GB each), tensor-parallel-size=2
- Connector: LMCacheMPConnector, kv_role=kv_both, kv_connector_module_path=lmcache.integration.vllm.lmcache_mp_connector

## Bug

With --tensor-parallel-size 2 and the LMCacheMPConnector wired in, each GPU loads the FULL model (approx 22.5GB) instead of properly sharding it in half across the two GPUs. This causes CUDA OOM during startup even though the model comfortably fits when sharded (per-GPU weight footprint should be approx 11.8GB with TP=2, per vLLM's own reported figures without LMCache).

Reproduced twice, in full isolation, with two different config forms (module_path explicit vs default resolution) - identical failure signature both times.

TP=1 does not work around this either: the full unsharded model (approx 22.5GB) plus any KV cache does not fit on a single 23.56GB card.

## What works

Plain vLLM (no LMCache, --tensor-parallel-size 2) shards correctly and runs stably - confirms the sharding issue is specific to the LMCacheMPConnector interaction with TP=2, not a general vLLM/Gemma-4 problem.

## Expected

LMCacheMPConnector should respect vLLM's existing tensor-parallel sharding rather than causing each rank to load the full model.

## Notes

This is a known-good model per LMCache's own Gemma 4 recipe (https://docs.lmcache.ai/recipes/gemma4.html), listed as "Validated with LMCache" for google/gemma-4-12B-it specifically - so this looks like a regression or an edge case not covered by that validation. The recipe's example command does not specify TP, and testing suggests the issue is specifically in the TP=2 sharding path.

Happy to provide full logs/config from both isolated reproduction runs on request.

items.title: [Bug] DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash + DSPARK: unbounded SparsePrefillWorkspace allocation OOM-crashes the whole TP group
items.author: hasan-emre-dinc
items.body_excerpt:
### Checklist

- [x] I searched related issues but found no solution.
- [x] The bug persists in the latest version.
- [x] Issues without environment info and a minimal reproducible demo are hard to resolve and may receive no feedback.
- [x] If this is not a bug report but a general question, please start a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions. Otherwise, it will be closed.
- [x] Please use English. Otherwise, it will be closed.

### Describe the bug

Serving **DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash** with **DSPARK speculative decoding** (`--speculative-algorithm DSPARK`) and **fp8_e4m3 KV cache** on **TP2, 2×B300 (288GB)**, the server passes startup and serves normal traffic fine, but a deep queue of long-context requests (170k–212k prompt tokens each) draining into a single prefill step reliably OOM-crashes the whole TP group:

```
torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 27.20 GiB.
GPU 0 has a total capacity of 267.68 GiB of which 26.77 GiB is free. Including
non-PyTorch memory, this process has 240.52 GiB memory in use. Of the allocated
memory 235.23 GiB is allocated by PyTorch, with 5.54 GiB allocated in private
pools (e.g., CUDA Graphs), and 1.43 GiB is reserved by PyTorch but unallocated.
```

Both TP ranks hit the same error at the same time. The scheduler raises, and the whole server process exits (`kill_process_tree`). Every in-flight request drops. A second replica took over the failover traffic and hit the same crash 12 minutes later, at a smaller allocation size (15.40 GiB tried, 12.74 GiB free). So this is not a one-off. It reproduces whenever the queue depth and context length are large enough compared to whatever memory happens to be free at the time.

Traceback (identical shape on both occurrences, both ranks):
```
Scheduler hit an exception: Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 5696, in run_scheduler_process
    scheduler.run_event_loop()
  File "sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py", line 1839, in run_event_loop
    ... dispatch_event_loop -> forward
  File "sglang/srt/layers/attention/deepseek_v4_backend.py", line 3904, in _forward_prefill_sparse
    workspace = self.sparse_prefill_workspace.get(
                ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "sglang/srt/layers/attention/dsv4/sparse_prefill_utils.py", line 100, in get
    self._buffer = torch.empty(
                   ^^^^^^^^^^^^
torch.OutOfMemoryError: CUDA out of memory. Tried to allocate 27.20 GiB. ...
```

Batch state at the moment of the first crash: `#running-req: 0, #queue-req: 73, #pending-token: 337719` (a 73-request queue draining at once). Second occurrence: `#running-req: 4, #queue-req: 16, #pending-token: 388518`.

**Analysis.** `SparsePrefillWorkspace.get()` in `sparse_prefill_utils.py` reallocates its buffer with a plain `torch.empty(...)` call whenever the requested size is bigger than the current buffer. There is no check before this call:

```python
def get(self, num_tokens, dtype=torch.bfloat16):
    assert num_tokens > 0
    current_capacity = self._buffer.shape[0] if self._buffer is not None else 0
    current_dtype = self._buffer.dtype if self._buffer is not None else None
    if num_tokens > current_capacity or dtype != current_dtype:
        self._buffer = torch.empty(
            (num_tokens, 1, WORKSPACE_DIM), dtype=dtype, device=self.device,
        )
    return self._buffer[:num_tokens]
```

It is called from `_forward_prefill_sparse` with `num_tokens = n_compressed + cache.swa_token_ids.shape[0]`. That is the size of the compressed-region gather plus the SWA-region gather for every request in that prefill step. There is no `mem_get_info` check and no chunking anywhere in this path.

This is not bounded by `--max-prefill-tokens`. That flag only caps new tokens admitted per step. The crashing batch shows `#new-token: 16384`, right at that cap, so the throttle was respected and it still was not enough. It is also not bounded by `--chunked-prefill-size`. Grepping the file shows this flag is never read or enforced against this workspace. So a deep queue of long-context requests can push `n_compressed + swa_token_ids` well past what the new-token cap limits, and the allocation just tries for whatever that adds up to. There is no fallback.

This looks like the same bug class as #30505 (unbudgeted prefill transients in DSA's `flash_mla_with_kvcache` on GLM-5.2) and the budget-check gap we already fixed in the DSV4 indexer's MQA-logits path (related to #34155 and #33246). But this is a different call site, `SparsePrefillWorkspace`, and it has no budget or chunking guard at all.

**Suggestion.** Add the same kind of guard used for the DSV4 indexer's MQA-logits budget check. Read `torch.cuda.mem_get_info()` before the `torch.empty(...)` call in `SparsePrefillWorkspace.get()`. Then either chunk the prefill batch to fit, or raise an error that can be retried, instead of letting an oversized allocation take down the whole TP group. A single request failing is a much better outcome than the whole server crashing on one bad batch.

items.title: [Bug]: SM120 CUTLASS blockwise FP8 GEMM rejects N % 128 != 0 (Invalid status; kv_a_proj N=576 in DeepSeek shapes)
items.author: waynehacking8
items.body_excerpt:
### Your current environment

RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell (SM120), CUDA 13.0, torch 2.11.0+cu130, current main (f7fc0ca99) with the precompiled nightly kernels.

### Describe the bug

The SM120 CUTLASS c3x blockwise FP8 GEMM (`scaled_mm_blockwise_sm120_fp8.cu`) rejects every problem whose weight output dim N is not a multiple of 128, failing with `cutlass_gemm_caller, .../cutlass_gemm_caller.cuh:52, Invalid status` (CUTLASS `can_implement` fails). All three tile configs in `scaled_mm_blockwise_sm120_fp8_dispatch.cuh` (default 128x128x128, pingpong 64x128x128, swap-ab 128x32x128) reject these shapes, so it is not M-range dependent.

Sweep on the RTX PRO 6000 with fp32 scales, via `ops.cutlass_scaled_mm` exactly as `CutlassFp8BlockScaledMMKernel.apply_block_scaled_mm` calls it (M in {1,16,32,64,83,128,256,512} x K in {1024, 7168}):

| N | result |
|---|---|
| 512, 1536, 7168 | OK at every M/K (max rel err 2-3e-3 vs fp32 dequant reference = bf16 rounding) |
| 576, 2112 | `Invalid status` at every M/K |

N=576 is `kv_a_proj_with_mqa` (512+64) in DeepSeek V3-family models, so any block-FP8 DeepSeek-shaped checkpoint hits this on SM120 once it routes to the CUTLASS kernel. The existing test `tests/kernels/quantization/test_block_fp8.py::test_w8a8_block_fp8_cutlass_matmul` (M=32, N=576, K=7168) fails on SM120 today with exactly this error, while the same test passes on SM90 CI - the alignment requirement is specific to the SM120 kernel.

#47988 makes `CutlassFp8BlockScaledMMKernel.can_implement` decline unaligned-N layers on SM12x so kernel selection falls through to Triton, which serves them correctly. That is a selection-level workaround; the kernel-level gap remains and is worth fixing in the dispatch (e.g. a compatible epilogue/tile config for ragged N, or padding), at which point the `can_implement` guard can be relaxed.

Related: #47818 (SM120 block-FP8 dispatch crash for ue8m0 scales, same code path); #40016 is the same failure class on SM90 for the M dim (swap_ab, non-multiple-of-4 M).

### Before submitting a new issue...

items.title: [Feature]: FlashInfer-CUTLASS NVFP4 MoE lacks SWIGLUSTEP activation (blocks Step-3.7-Flash-NVFP4 at TP=8)
items.author: kenzhangwangshu
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

The FlashInfer-CUTLASS NVFP4 MoE backend rejects models using the clipped-SwiGLU activation (`SWIGLUSTEP`). `vllm/model_executor/layers/fused_moe/experts/flashinfer_cutlass_moe.py` (main, L187-193):

```python
def _supports_activation(...):
    return activation in [
        MoEActivation.SILU,
        MoEActivation.GELU_TANH,
        MoEActivation.RELU2_NO_MUL,
        MoEActivation.SWIGLUOAI,
    ]
```

`MoEActivation.SWIGLUSTEP` (used by Step-3.7) is not in the list, so the backend is unavailable for `stepfun-ai/Step-3.7-Flash-NVFP4`.

**Why it matters:** that checkpoint has `moe_intermediate_size=1280`, i.e. 160 per rank at TP=8, which is unaligned for the other NVFP4 backends as well: the TRT-LLM path hit the shuffle-alignment assert (#46879, relaxed by #46880), and CUTLASS intermediate-size padding is pending #48624. FlashInfer-CUTLASS would be a natural fallback for such shapes, but it cannot express the model's activation — as of July 2026 the released checkpoint could not shard 8-way on any NVFP4 backend (verified on 8× B300, v0.24.0 and nightly `2afa3f7e9`).

Pitch: add `SWIGLUSTEP` support to the FlashInfer-CUTLASS NVFP4 MoE path (kernel capability permitting), or document the supported-activation matrix per NVFP4 backend so unservable (model × TP) combinations fail with an actionable message.

### Alternatives

- Land #48624 (CUTLASS padding) and serve via the padded CUTLASS path — this issue would then be about backend feature-parity rather than a hard blocker.
- Re-quantized checkpoint with TP-friendly intermediate size (checkpoint-publisher side).

### Additional context

items.title: [Bug]: Cross-request context contamination via shared-prefix KV reuse in PD disaggregation with automatic prefix caching — clean with `--no-enable-prefix-caching`
items.author: Siquan-Li
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With automatic prefix caching enabled (the default) in a NIXL prefill/decode disaggregated deployment serving DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, responses intermittently contain **content from other requests** — cross-request context contamination ("crosstalk"). We have a scriptable reproducer on `/v1/chat/completions` (details below): with a long **identical shared prefix** across requests, 46/48 *sequential* requests returned another request's canary code; at concurrency 128 it was 122/128. Disabling prefix caching on the prefill node **and** all decode nodes (`--no-enable-prefix-caching`) eliminated the contamination.

## Deployment topology (at reproduction time)

```
Clients (multi-turn agent sessions; every request starts with the same large system prompt)
        |
        v
vllm-router 0.1.15  --policy round_robin --kv-connector nixl   (port 30000)
        |
   +----+------------------+
   v                       v
Prefill node              2x Decode nodes
1x node, 8x H100, TP=8    1x node each, 8x H100, TP=8
kv_producer  :8001        kv_consumer  :8002
        \____ NIXL KV transfer ____/
```

(Since 2026-10-12 we run 2P1D; all reproduction data below was collected on the 1P2D topology above.)

## Environment

- vLLM 0.31.0, built from main @ `db9527a46` (2026-10-02), local build tagged `+cu129`; torch 2.13.0+cu129, transformers 5.17.0, nixl 1.4.1
- Driver 550.54.15, nodes of 8× H100 80GB (sm90)
- Model: DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash (1M context), `FLASHMLA_SPARSE_DSV41` attention backend, block size 64
- Speculative decoding: `{"method":"dspark","num_speculative_tokens":5,"draft_sample_method":"probabilistic","rejection_sample_method":"block","enable_adaptive_verification":true}`
- `--max-num-batched-tokens 4096 --max-num-seqs 32 --gpu-memory-utilization 0.92`
- Note: PR #57662 (fix for #57661) was **not merged** at the time of writing, so this build cannot contain it.

## Symptom

Every request shares a long common prefix — in the wild this was Claude Code on the Anthropic-compatible `/v1/messages` endpoint, whose fixed large system prompt is identical across all sessions. With automatic prefix caching on, users in **different, unrelated sessions** intermittently received responses containing content from *another* session (the model "remembered" details, file names, or instructions belonging to someone else's conversation). Affected requests completed with HTTP 200; no errors or warnings in server logs.

## Reproducer (scriptable, `/v1/chat/completions`)

Design: N requests, each consisting of a **long identical shared prefix** plus a per-request distinct tail that embeds a unique canary code. After all responses complete, each output is scanned for canary codes belonging to *other* requests ("foreign" hits).

Results with automatic prefix caching **enabled** (default):

| Scenario | Requests | Outputs containing a foreign canary code |
|---|---|---|
| Sequential (C=1) | 48 | **46/48** |
| Concurrent (C=128) | 128 | **122/128** |

Key observations:

- Concurrency is **not** required — sequential single-stream requests contaminate at ~96%. Sharing a long identical prefix is the trigger.
- Canaries that varied the prefix, or shared only long *suffixes*, did **not** reproduce; earlier negative canary results were a design gap, not evidence against the bug.
- With `--no-enable-prefix-caching` on P **and** both D nodes: 0 foreign hits, and the Claude Code symptom disappeared entirely (verified by the same users plus a 16-way concurrent keepalive, ~3,000 rounds over 17 h).

The canary script is available on request.

## What we have *not* isolated

- We disabled prefix caching on all three nodes at once, so we cannot attribute the reuse to the prefill-side cache, the decode-side cache, or the P↔D KV-transfer interplay (e.g. a consumer trusting producer block IDs for freed/reused blocks, or refcount/eviction asymmetry between P and D).
- No root-cause analysis on the vLLM side yet; happy to invest in narrowing this down with maintainer guidance.

## Hypothesis (unverified)

Under PD disaggregation, prefix-cache blocks belonging to a completed request are re-served to a later request that hashes to the same shared prefix, but the physical KV content behind those blocks has been freed/reassigned — so the later request decodes against another request's KV. The serial (C=1) repro suggests the race is between request completion/reuse bookkeeping rather than simultaneous scheduling.

## Why this is not #57661

#57661 (and fix PR #57662 — still unmerged) describes NIXL transfer regions deduplicated by `base_addr` alone, truncating the compressor `state_cache` transfer for hybrid-attention layers, producing **garbled/empty output**. Our failure mode is different:

1. Symptom: our outputs are coherent but contain **another request's content**; we never observed garbling or empty content/reasoning fields.
2. Toggle sensitivity: our contamination disappears completely with `--no-enable-prefix-caching`; the region-geometry bug in #57661 is independent of the prefix-caching toggle.
3. Mechanism: truncated/misaligned compressor state cannot inject well-formed content from a different request.

We plan to validate our repro against #57662's branch as well, to rule out any interaction; both issues affect the same model + NIXL PD combination with silent HTTP-200 failures.

## Related issues

- #57661 — NIXL P/D silent output corruption (hybrid-attention region dedup), fix PR #57662 (unmerged at writing)
- #56009 — request/response cross-talk symptom, no root cause identified
- #52627 — silent output corruption in 1P1D NIXL PD, different connector combination
- #47930 — DSpark draft acceptance collapse with automatic prefix caching (another prefix-caching × disaggregation interaction)

## Offer

We keep a H100 1P2D/2P1D testbed with this exact model and can: share the canary script, run targeted repro attempts on candidate patches (including #57662), or provide `collect_env.py` output on request.

items.title: What is the first practical limit of persistent KV across Agent steps?
items.author: RyanX0198
items.body_excerpt:
Hi maintainers — I’m Rui from Psync.labs. Recent sampling and decode-interface work led me to a question about long-running local Agent workloads.

Persistent KV could reduce repeated prefill, but only if cache identity, layout, eviction and framework boundaries stay correct as models, adapters and stages change. Which condition is most likely to invalidate the idea in practice: layout incompatibility, model or tokenizer changes, fragmentation, eviction quality loss, scheduler interference, or missing cross-framework contracts?

One counterexample or minimum test would be especially useful. @yzh119

— Rui, Psync.labs

comments.author: eprogressing
comments.body:
For an agent that changes adapters or rewrites its prompt between steps, I would check **cache identity/correctness before fragmentation or scheduling**. That is a conditional priority, not a measured ranking of workloads.

A concrete counterexample is switching from adapter A to adapter B while retaining A's KV. If B changes the value projection (or earlier hidden states), identical token IDs and identical tensor shapes do not make those cached values valid for B. Similarly, editing earlier tool results breaks reuse past the unchanged token prefix in an ordinary causal transformer. Rendering the same conversation differently can also change that prefix.

I would start with this small integration test:

1. Under A, prefill a short token prefix P, then process suffix S using the cached prefix. Compare the next-token logits with a fresh A forward pass on P+S, within an appropriate numerical tolerance.
2. Use a distinct, nonzero B adapter that affects `v_proj`. Repeat with a fresh B prefill as the reference. Your cache manager should reject A's cache; forcibly reusing it is the negative control, which can expose a discrepancy.
3. Edit one early token in P and verify that cache lookup stops at the unchanged prefix. Check logits, rather than just generated text: argmax can hide a difference.

This is consistent with [vLLM's prefix-cache design](https://docs.vllm.ai/en/latest/design/prefix_caching/), which keys blocks using the parent hash, block tokens and extra hashes such as LoRA IDs. Adapter IDs also need versioning/invalidation if their weights can change in place.

After that, check the storage contract separately: [FlashInfer's KV layout documentation](https://docs.flashinfer.ai/tutorials/kv_layout.html) specifies NHD/HND layouts and page metadata. Matching semantics alone does not make a buffer portable between frameworks.

Prepared with Codex assistance from the linked documentation. The integration test above was initially a proposal; the execution update below now supplies an actual mechanism test. Is your agent retaining one model/adapter with append-only history, or switching adapters and rewriting history?


---
**GPU experiment update (2026-10-11):** I ran the actual Transformers/PEFT forward path on an A100-SXM4-40GB, plus CPU controls: Torch 2.14.1+cu130, Transformers 5.19.0, PEFT 0.21.2. This is a random three-layer Llama (hidden 64, four attention heads/two KV heads), with rank-four v_proj LoRA; it does not exercise FlashInfer's attention kernel or a production agent cache manager.

Across seeds 0/1/2, CPU/CUDA and float32/float64, all 72 comparison expectations held. Correct same-adapter reuse, an adapter-name change with exactly zero update, and reuse limited to the two tokens preceding a prefix edit agreed with fresh forwarding (maximum absolute logit error <=1.49e-7; predeclared tolerances float32 1e-5 / float64 1e-10). Forcibly reusing A's KV with nonzero B produced max-absolute differences 0.2205–0.2727; retaining the old full prefix after the edit produced 0.1082–0.2622. Each stale-cache case changed argmax in only 4/12 trials, so comparing all logits matters. Each path used a newly created cache with asserted sequence lengths.

This supports the specific correctness counterexample, not a universal ranking against fragmentation/scheduling. It does not measure answer quality, throughput, cross-framework layout compatibility, or automatic rejection by a cache manager. [Reproduction scripts, full inputs/logits, versions and results](https://gist.github.com/eprogressing/84db3e068aabbe449f8629a3f362a6e5). Prepared with Codex assistance; these runs were actually executed.

comments.body:
**Документация: Работа с `llama.cpp` b6286 (август 2025)**

**1. Изменения в архитектуре и API**

*   **Изменение публичного API:** Прямой доступ к внутренним библиотекам `ggml` и `gguf` через их заголовочные файлы (`ggml/ggml.h`, `ggml/gguf.h`) **больше не является публичным или рекомендуемым**. Функции вроде `gguf_init_from_file`, `gguf_get_n_tensors` и т.д. скрыты.
*   **Унификация API:** Всё взаимодействие с моделью, её метаданными и тензорами теперь должно происходить **только** через унифицированный API, предоставляемый в **`include/llama.h`** (и `include/llama-cpp.h` для C++).
*   **Изменение структуры `include`:** Публичные заголовки теперь находятся непосредственно в `include/`. Внутренние заголовки `ggml` перемещены в `ggml/include/`.

**2. Создание собственного примера/приложения (например, `qedit`)**

*   **Расположение:** Поместите исходный код примера (например, `qedit.cpp`) и его `CMakeLists.txt` в подкаталог `examples/<имя_примера>/` внутри корня проекта `llama.cpp`. Например: `llama.cpp/examples/qedit/`.
*   **`CMakeLists.txt` примера:**
    ```cmake
    cmake_minimum_required(VERSION 3.16)
    project(<имя_примера> CXX) # Замените <имя_примера> на имя вашего проекта

    set(TARGET <имя_примера>)
    add_executable(${TARGET} <имя_файла>.cpp) # Замените <имя_файла>.cpp на имя вашего .cpp файла

    target_compile_features(${TARGET} PRIVATE cxx_std_17)

    # Указываем include-путь к llama.h
    target_include_directories(${TARGET} PRIVATE
        ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/include    # папка с llama.h
        # ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/common   # Если используете заголовки из common
        # ${CMAKE_SOURCE_DIR}/ggml/include # Только если требуется прямой доступ к внутренним ggml (не рекомендуется)
    )

    # Линкуем необходимые библиотеки
    target_link_libraries(${TARGET} PRIVATE
        # common     # Если используете утилиты из common
        llama        # ОСНОВНАЯ библиотека, предоставляющая API из llama.h
        # ggml       # Обычно не нужно явно указывать, так как llama зависит от ggml.
                     # Но можно оставить для ясности.
        # ggml-cuda  # НЕ НУЖНО. Отдельная цель ggml-cuda НЕ СОЗДАЕТСЯ.
                     # Функциональность CUDA интегрирована в основную библиотеку ggml.
        ${CMAKE_THREAD_LIBS_INIT} # Если требуется
    )
    ```
*   **Использование API:** В коде вашего примера используйте только функции, объявленные в `include/llama.h`. Примеры функций:
    *   `llama_backend_init()`, `llama_backend_free()`: Инициализация/деинициализация бэкенда.
    *   `llama_model_default_params()`: Получение параметров модели по умолчанию.
    *   `llama_load_model_from_file()`: Загрузка модели.
    *   `llama_model_meta_count()`, `llama_model_meta_key_by_index()`, `llama_model_meta_val_str_by_index()`: Доступ к метаданным модели.
    *   `llama_model_n_embd()`, `llama_model_n_ctx_train()`, `llama_model_n_params()`: Получение информации о модели (некоторые могут требовать активного контекста).
    *   `llama_free_model()`: Освобождение модели.

**3. Сборка проекта `llama.cpp`**

*   **Конфигурация CMake:**
    *   Используйте CMake для генерации проекта сборки.
    *   Для включения поддержки CUDA используйте опцию `-DGGML_CUDA=ON` (устаревшая `LLAMA_CUBLAS=ON` больше не поддерживается).
    *   Пример команды для Visual Studio 2022:
        ```bash
        cmake .. -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A x64 -DGGML_CUDA=ON -DLLAMA_CURL=OFF -DLLAMA_BUILD_COMMON=ON -DLLAMA_BUILD_EXAMPLES=ON
        ```
*   **Сборка библиотек:**
    *   При включении `GGML_CUDA=ON` и `BUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON` (по умолчанию для MSVC):
        *   Исходники CUDA (`ggml/src/ggml-cuda/*`) добавляются в сборку основной библиотеки `ggml`.
        *   Создаются файлы `bin/Debug|Release/ggml.dll` (содержит и CPU, и CUDA код) и `bin/Debug|Release/ggml.lib` (библиотека импорта для этой DLL).
    *   Основная библиотека `llama.lib` зависит от `ggml.lib`. Линковка с `llama.lib` предоставляет доступ ко всей функциональности, включая CU

items.title: Feature Request: Expose Speculative Decoding (MTP / Draft) in public C API (llama.h) for downstream bindings
items.author: zsogitbe
items.body_excerpt:
### Feature Description

Expose Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) and speculative decoding capabilities in the public C API (`llama.h`) and export them in dynamic shared libraries (`llama.dll`, `libllama.so`, `libllama.dylib`).

Specifically, this feature request entails:

1. **Public C API Access:** Making speculative decoding workflows—currently encapsulated in `common/speculative.cpp`—accessible via stable C functions in `llama.h`.
2. **High-Level Speculative Orchestration:** Providing a high-level speculative context API to handle draft generation, verification, KV cache synchronization, and multi-pass decoding natively, rather than requiring wrapper languages to implement complex tensor plumbing downstream.
3. **Downstream Interop:** Enabling language bindings (C#, Python, Rust, Swift, Go) to run multi-token prediction and draft verification natively through the exported shared library without depending on internal `common/` headers or custom forks.

### Motivation

Currently, downstream bindings (like LLamaSharp, llama-cpp-python, and Rust wrappers) are unable to utilize the incredible speedups provided by Speculative Decoding and Multi-Token Prediction (MTP).

The recent unifications for MTP (e.g., `--spec-type draft-mtp`) and other speculative methods (EAGLE, n-gram, DFlash) are fantastic, but the orchestration logic lives entirely inside `common/speculative.cpp`. Because `common/` is not exported to the shared library (`llama.dll` / `libllama.so`), pure C API consumers are locked out of these features.

Initially, we attempted to implement the MTP drafting loop manually in C# for LLamaSharp. However, after reviewing `speculative.cpp`, we realized the native MTP implementation is too complex to replicate safely downstream:

* It requires a dual-context architecture (`ctx_tgt` and a dedicated `ctx_dft` with `LLAMA_CONTEXT_TYPE_MTP`).

* It relies on extracting and passing dense hidden state embeddings directly into the evaluation batch (`batch.embd` / `llama_get_embeddings_nextn_ith`) instead of just token IDs.

* It dynamically handles layer offsets (`llama_set_nextn_layer_offset`) for `chain_heads` architectures.

Attempting to rebuild this intricate, multi-pass autoregressive logic across P/Invoke boundaries in wrapper languages is highly brittle and creates severe technical debt.

### Possible Implementation

We are hoping the maintainers can consider formalizing speculative decoding into `llama.h` to help binding authors:

**The Ideal Solution (A Stable Speculative API)**
Introduce a formal `llama_speculative_*` or `llama_draft_*` API suite into `llama.h`. Similar to how the modern `llama_sampler` API abstracts the sampling chain, an opaque speculative context could handle the draft-and-verify loop, RoPE shifts, and KV cache rollbacks internally. Bindings would simply feed the prompt and receive verified tokens.

*Conceptual Example:*

```c
// Initialize a speculative context managing both target and draft models
LLAMA_API struct llama_speculative_context * llama_speculative_init(
    struct llama_context * ctx_tgt, 
    struct llama_context * ctx_dft,
    const struct llama_speculative_params * params
);

// A unified decode/sample loop that handles the draft/verify internally
LLAMA_API void llama_speculative_decode(
    struct llama_speculative_context * spec_ctx,
    struct llama_batch * batch
);

// Extract the accepted tokens after verification
LLAMA_API int32_t llama_speculative_get_accepted_tokens(
    struct llama_speculative_context * spec_ctx,
    llama_token * out_tokens,
    int32_t max_tokens
);

```

With models like DeepSeek V3/R1, Qwen 3.6, and Gemma 4 relying heavily on MTP for performance, this is becoming a critical feature for the broader ecosystem. If you are open to exposing an experimental API, we would love to collaborate by immediately testing it downstream in C# and reporting back!

### Prerequisites

- [x] I am running the latest code. Mention the version if possible as well.
- [x] I carefully followed the [README.md](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/blob/master/README.md).
- [x] I searched using keywords relevant to my issue to make sure that I am creating a new issue that is not already open (or closed).
- [x] I reviewed the [Discussions](https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/discussions), and have a new and useful enhancement to share.

items.title: Eval bug: SIGSEGV in CPU compute path, thread-count-dependent race (Android/aarch64, Tensor G5), not content-dependent
items.author: KorbenD3P0
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

```
version: 0.4.0-dev (build 1, commit ad6c668)
built with Clang 21.1.8 for Android aarch64
```
Built from source via cmake, Release config, no custom flags.

### Operating systems

Other (Android 17, via Termux — not a supported OS but the CPU backend/toolchain is standard aarch64 clang)

### GGML backends

CPU

### Hardware

Pixel 10 Pro XL, Google Tensor G5 (codename `laguna`), 8 CPU cores.

### Models

Reproduced on two unrelated models, which points at the shared CPU compute path rather than anything model-specific:
- `Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct-GGUF` (bartowski, Q4_K_M) via `llama-cli`
- `SmolVLM-500M-Instruct-GGUF` (ggml-org, Q8_0) + matching mmproj (f16) via `llama-mtmd-cli`, during the text-generation step (image encoding itself completed fine)

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Reproducible SIGSEGV that depends on `-t` (thread count), not on prompt content in any way I could find — and it isn't even deterministic per thread count, which is what points to a genuine race rather than an input-triggered bug:

- `-t 1` — never crashed, across dozens of runs with varied prompts/lengths.
- `-t 4` — crashed **intermittently** on byte-identical input. Concretely: feeding the exact same prompt string via `-p "<text>"` vs via `-f <file-with-same-text>` changed the outcome (one crashed, one didn't) on the same model, same machine, back to back. That's the strongest signal this is a race, not a content-dependent parsing bug.
- `-t 6` and above — crashed reliably, every single time, across many repeated runs.

Minimal repro (adjust thread count to see the pattern):

```
./build/bin/llama-cli -m qwen2.5-3b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf \
  -p "Today: 9am Math, 2pm Physics lab. 3 unread emails, one from professor about assignment deadline. Write one short digest sentence under 200 chars." \
  -n 60 -c 2048 -t 6 --single-turn --log-disable
```

At `-t 6+`: reliably `Segmentation fault (core dumped)`, exit code 139.
At `-t 1`: completes normally every time.
At `-t 4`: crashes some runs, not others, on identical input.

Also reproduced the same signature (crash during generation, not during model load or image encoding) on `llama-mtmd-cli` with SmolVLM at `-t 4`, resolved by dropping to `-t 1` there too — same fix, same apparent cause, different binary/model.

Happy to provide a debug build with a backtrace, or test a patch, if that would help narrow it down — just didn't want to sit on a reproducible crash without reporting it.

### First Bad Commit

Not bisected — this is the first commit I built from (ad6c668), so I can't say whether it's a regression or has always been present on this platform.

### Relevant log output

```
$ ./build/bin/llama-cli -m qwen2.5-3b-instruct-q4_k_m.gguf -p "..." -n 60 -c 2048 -t 6 --single-turn --log-disable
Segmentation fault         ./build/bin/llama-cli -m ... -t 6 --single-turn --log-disable
exit code: 139
```

items.title: Eval bug: LFM2.5-24B-A2B emits Qwen3-Coder-style <tool_call> XML as content — calls silently lost (lfm2moe)
items.author: leon-strong
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

With LiquidAI's **LFM2.5-24B-A2B** (`arch = lfm2moe`), the model intermittently emits tool calls in the **Qwen3-Coder-style XML** shape as *plain text*. `llama-server` returns `finish_reason: "stop"` with empty `tool_calls` and the block in `content`, so the call is **silently lost** (clients show raw XML in the transcript). The LFM2.5 parser only accepts the vendor's control-token form, so this shape cannot be recovered.

Emitted (content, verbatim):

```
<tool_call>
<function=edit>
<parameter=i>[/tmp/mdhtml/build.mjs#2ff4]</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>
```

and in another turn a whole unified diff inside `<parameter=i>…</parameter>`.

## Environment

- `llama.cpp` master `fcac19079` (build 6785), HIP/ROCm 10.0.x, gfx1100 (RX 7900 XTX), WSL2. Server: `llama-server -m LFM2.5-24B-A2B-QAD-Q4_0.gguf -c 131072 -fa on -ngl 999` (f16 KV).
- Model: `LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B-GGUF` → `LFM2.5-24B-A2B-QAD-Q4_0.gguf`, sha256 `d1c03f73ecaf61017d70419eec9e5dc0b05d50ae26c23d522829b934fbabf8a5`; the same behaviour was observed with Unsloth's `LFM2.5-24B-A2B-UD-Q4_K_XL.gguf` on the same binary.
- Client: OpenAI-compatible (`/v1/chat/completions` and `/v1/responses`, both with `tools`).

## What does work

- The GGUF template's native form parses fine: the great majority of turns return proper `tool_calls` (or `function_call` items on the Responses path) with `finish_reason: "tool_calls"`.
- `common/chat.cpp` correctly selects the LFM2.5 path (`common_chat_params_init_lfm2_5`, `tool_list_tokens = false`) for this template (it contains `List of tools: [` and no `<|tool_list_start|>`).
- Upstream's own `test-chat` agrees: a byte copy of the GGUF template (plus one appended system-prompt sentence, see below) is detected as `peg-native`, and the bundled `LFM2.5-Instruct` / `LFM2.5-8B-A1B` parser cases all pass on this build.
- Minimal probe that parses correctly:
  `POST /v1/chat/completions {"messages":[{"role":"user","content":"Call the tool get_weather for Paris."}],"tools":[{"type":"function","function":{"name":"get_weather",…}}]}`
  → `tool_calls: [{"function":{"name":"get_weather","arguments":"{\"city\":\"Paris\"}"}}]`, `finish_reason: "tool_calls"`.

## When it breaks

Both observed failures came **after a run of tool-schema errors** (a client-side "anchored patch" edit tool rejected ~8 consecutive calls: wrong intent-field length, missing `[PATH#HASH]` anchor, no hunk header, …). The model then stopped using `[name(args)]` and wrote the Qwen3-Coder XML above as ordinary content; the server had nothing to parse. `common/parsers/lfm2.cpp` requires the literals `<|tool_call_start|>` / `<|tool_call_end|>` around a python-style call, and its PEG tool grammar is only armed once that control token appears (`p.trigger_rule(...)` in `common_chat_params_init_lfm2`), so free-form XML in content is expected to be swallowed as content — consistent with #27772 being the generic mechanism.

## Notes

- The vendor template advertises tools only as a JSON list (`List of tools: [ … ]`, no syntax guidance) — the same convention as the bundled `models/templates/LFM2.5-8B-A1B.jinja` — so the call syntax is expected to come from training.
- A one-sentence system-prompt reminder appended by a local template copy ("…emit a single call in square brackets with Python-style arguments: [name(arg1=value1, arg2=value2)]. Never wrap calls in `<tool_call>`, `<function>` or `<parameter>` XML tags.") **did not prevent** the drift in the same scenario; it is not included here as a fix, only to say the obvious prompt-side nudge was tried.
- Minor, possibly model-side: one parsed call's `arguments` string came back with a **duplicate key** — `{"i":"/tmp/mdhtml/build.mjs","i":"const legend …"}` (we cannot see the raw pre-parse text). If the parser can emit duplicate JSON keys (e.g. the same arg name accepted twice), downstream parsers silently collapse them; mentioning it in case it is worth guarding.

## Question

Is the intended behaviour "the model must emit the control-token form, everything else is out of scope", or would a recovery path for the Qwen3-Coder XML shape be acceptable in the LFM2.5 parser (like other archs tolerate well-known alternate shapes)? Related items: #30118 (same shape for Qwen3.6 — a maintainer comment there notes an attempted `tool_call_starts.push_back("<function=")` was considered unusable), #20245 (older LFM2.5 shown-as-text, fixed before the PEG parser), #27772.

items.title: Eval bug: MiniCPM-V 4.7 places answers too low when asked where something is in an image
items.author: SunflowersLwtech
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version

```
$ llama-server --version
version: 0.6.0-dev (build 11609, commit fcac19079)
```

The code involved is unchanged on current master (`318a471`).

### Operating systems

Linux

### GGML backends

Vulkan

The positions are computed on the CPU side; a CPU-only build gives the same positions.

### Hardware

AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395 (Radeon 8060S)

### Models

```
openbmb/MiniCPM-V-4.7-35B-A3B-gguf: MiniCPM-V-4_7-35B-A3B-Q4_K_M.gguf, mmproj-model-f16-4x.gguf
openbmb/MiniCPM-V-4.7-1B-gguf: MiniCPM-V-4_7-1B-F16.gguf, mmproj-model-f16.gguf (position check only)
```

### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Ask MiniCPM-V 4.7 for the box of an element on a screenshot. With llama.cpp the answer is usually placed too low. The official demo of the same model (Hugging Face Space `openbmb/MiniCPM-V-4.7-Demo`) does not do this.

MiniCPM-V 4.7 reads an image as a small overview plus a grid of tiles, separated in the prompt by marker tokens (`</image>`, `<slice>`, `</slice>`, and a newline at the end of each row). Each prompt token has a position of three values: time, row and column. llama.cpp numbers the markers one after another, like text. The official implementation (`get_rope_index` in transformers) places `<slice>` and `</slice>` at the corners of their tile, and `</image>` and the row newlines just outside the image. The image tokens themselves have the same positions in both, so in our tests questions about image content were not affected; only answers that depend on where things are go wrong.

Present since #29416 (`69f201a`).

Results (18 questions on two screenshots, 35B Q4_K_M, `mmproj-model-f16-4x.gguf`, temperature 0, official system prompt; a hit is an answer whose centre is inside the target box; coordinates are the model's 0-1000 scale):

| | hits | mean vertical offset | median distance to official answers |
|---|---|---|---|
| llama.cpp b11609 | 3/18 | +60.3 (too low) | 79.8 |
| official demo (Hugging Face Space, 2026-10-14) | 14/18 | -0.9 | 0 |

Steps, using the files in https://github.com/SunflowersLwtech/minicpmv47-llamacpp-repro (screenshots, questions, `run_grounding.py`, and the official answers in `reference/`):

```sh
llama-server -m MiniCPM-V-4_7-35B-A3B-Q4_K_M.gguf --mmproj mmproj-model-f16-4x.gguf \
  --jinja -c 16384 -ngl 999 -fa on --port 8080
python3 run_grounding.py --server http://127.0.0.1:8080 --out answers.jsonl \
  --reference reference/official-vllm-4x.jsonl
```

The README there also has a unit test that needs no model, and a token-by-token comparison of positions against transformers.

### First Bad Commit

`69f201a` (#29416, model : support MiniCPM-V 4.7)

### Relevant log output

```
$ python3 run_grounding.py ... (llama.cpp b11609)
hits: 3/18
mean dy (0-1000, + = too low): +60.3
median distance to reference (0-1000): 79.8  (max 145.0, n=18)

$ python3 positions/compare_positions.py reference.tsv llama_positions.txt   (MiniCPM-V 4.7 1B, 528-token prompt, b11609)
reference tokens: 528   compared: 527   same position: 483
different position: 44   missing in llama.cpp: 0
  differs  idx    39      '<image>' reference (T,H,W)=(39, 38, 38)  llama.cpp=(39, 39, 39)
  differs  idx   100     '</image>' reference (T,H,W)=(39, 55, 63)  llama.cpp=(41, 41, 41)
  differs  idx   101      '<slice>' reference (T,H,W)=(39, 39, 39)  llama.cpp=(42, 42, 42)
  differs  idx   166     '</slice>' reference (T,H,W)=(39, 46, 46)  llama.cpp=(44, 44, 44)
  differs  idx   167      '<slice>' reference (T,H,W)=(39, 39, 47)  llama.cpp=(45, 45, 45)
  ...
```

The second log comes from the token-by-token comparison in that README. (T,H,W) is time, row, column. Token 39 is the start of the image.

items.title: ROCm Upgrade from 7.2.4 to 10.1.0
items.author: thelittlefireman
items.body_excerpt:
Following https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/pull/29910.

I ask AI to generate a python script to compare ISA between ROCm 7.2.4 and ROCm 10.1.0 (on gfx906)

**TLDR;**
ROCm 10.1 introduce massive regressions in multiples kernels (~126) but also improve some others. At least 66 Kernels need a fix and 112 kernels need to be looked at closely.
This seems to be related to long vgpr live range issue.

I also try to compile/compare some LLVM options :
- `-mllvm -amdgpu-sched-strategy=max-ilp` [reddit](https://www.reddit.com/r/LocalLLaMA/comments/1wyq8r7/comment/pegd00r/?utm_source=share&utm_medium=web3x&utm_name=web3xcss&utm_term=1&utm_content=share_button) or [https://github.com/mixa3607/ML-gfx906/releases#release-20260808180342](https://github.com/mixa3607/ML-gfx906/releases#release-20260808180342)
- `-fno-offload-lto` [https://github.com/ROCm/llvm-project/issues/4434](https://github.com/ROCm/llvm-project/issues/4434)

but it make regression even worse.

I think the best for now is to write somewhere that's we support only ROCm 7.2.X version for now and maybe later open a (huge) PR and fix every regressions (maybe with some `__builtin_amdgcn_sched_group_barrier`)

<details markdown="block">
  <summary>General analysis</summary>

v27 Metric | ROCm 7.2.4 | ROCm 10.1 | Change
-- | -- | -- | --
Static VGPR spill stores | 3,995 | 5,087 | +27.3%
Kernels with increased spills | — | 66 | Regression
Kernels with decreased spills | — | 50 | Improvement
Kernels with newly introduced spills | — | 47 | Regression
Kernels with eliminated spills | — | 12 | Improvement
Static ISA instruction count | 4,317,692 | 4,282,323 | -0.82%
s_waitcnt instructions | 293,942 | 286,684 | -2.47%
Total code size | 20.66 MB | 20.60 MB | -0.33%

</details>

<details markdown="block">
  <summary>Kernel family analysis</summary>

| Family                        | Spills changes | Occupancy Improve / Regression | Instructions counter delta |
| ------------------------------ | -------------------------- | ------------------------------- | -------------------- |
| `mul_mat_vec_f`                | 0                          | 142 / 0                         | -1 280               |
| `mul_mat_vec_q`                | 0                          | 49 / 22                         | -9 649               |
| `mul_mat_vec_q_moe`            | 0                          | 16 / 1                          | -336                 |
| `flash_attn_ext_vec`           | -402                       | 15 / 3                          | -12 564              |
| `flash_attn_tile`              | -175                       | 12 / 3                          | -4 925               |
| `rms_norm_f32`                 | 0                          | 8 / 0                           | -31                  |
| `mul_mat_q`                    | +417                       | 46 / 42                         | -2 501               |
| `lightning_indexer_kernel_vec` | +1 177                     | 0 / 0                           | +1 750               |
</details>

items.title: smallwords: one vocabulary for prompts, GBNF, JSON Schema, and validation
items.author: cmccomb
items.body_excerpt:
I built `smallwords` because controlled vocabularies tend to drift across four separate parts of an LLM application: the prompt, the grammar, the schema, and the validator. `smallwords` puts a single `WordlistSpec` at the center and generates all four from it.

```bash
pip install smallwords
```

```python
from smallwords import OutputResources, OutputShape, allow_input_words
from smallwords.prompts import build_prompt

spec = allow_input_words("moby_898", "missile")
shape = OutputShape(min_words_per_line=6, max_words_per_line=11, max_lines=3)
resources = OutputResources.from_wordlist(spec, shape=shape)
prompt = build_prompt("explain", source_text, wordlist=spec)

grammar = resources.gbnf
schema = resources.json_schema(key="answer")
result = resources.validate(model_output)
```

The model-backed example starts with this line:

> By subtracting where it is from where it isn't, or where it isn't from where it is, it obtains a difference, or deviation.

The same local Granite 4.2 model then generated three constrained rewrites through `llama-server`:

**Simple**

> The missile is now where it is.  
> The missile should be where it should be.  
> The difference tells the missile how far to move.

**Pirate**

> First place is where the ship is now.  
> Second place is where it should be.  
> Difference tells the crew which way to sail.

**Cowboy**

> Where the cattle are now is the first place.  
> Where the ranch is is the second place.  
> The difference tells the cowboy which way to ride.

Each run uses a task-focused subset to keep its GBNF compact, then validates the result against both that subset and the complete preset. The simple case adds only the essential topic word `missile`. Pirate and cowboy use size-neutral remixes of the 898-word base list.

The hard contract covers vocabulary, punctuation, capitalization, line count, and words per line. Style hints remain prompt guidance, so the grammar constrains the allowed language without encoding a fixed sentence. I also disabled shared prompt-cache reuse in the live examples so fixed-seed sampled runs remain stable across repeated requests.

The package is MIT licensed, typed, and supports Python 3.10 and newer. I would value feedback on vocabulary expansion policies, output shapes, and grammar-sampling edge cases that appear in real llama.cpp workflows.

- Repository: https://github.com/cmccomb/smallwords
- Documentation: https://cmccomb.github.io/smallwords/
- PyPI: https://pypi.org/project/smallwords/

items.title: Eval bug: rpc-server -c: cache files truncated on disk-full are later served as valid cache hits → silent weight corruption / garbage output
items.author: tobenator1200-lab
items.body_excerpt:
### Name and Version version 0.6.0-dev (build 968, commit 10a60cf ### Operating systems Linux ### GGML backends CUDA, RPC ### Hardware V100 in a KVM guest as the RPC server, client with RTX 5070 Ti ### Models Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0 / UD-Q8_K_XL ### Problem description & steps to reproduce

Summary

With rpc-server -c, when the cache filesystem runs full, set_tensor leaves zero-byte cache files behind (the write failure is not checked). On every later model load the client's SET_TENSOR_HASH probe hits that file, get_cached_file returns it without checking size or content, and the server answers result = 1. The client therefore skips sending the tensor, and the affected weights are never actually written to the device. No error or warning is logged anywhere.

The model loads normally and runs at normal speed, but produces fluent text that degrades into digit soup — which looks like a quantization or GPU-numerics problem rather than a cache problem. In my case it took two evenings of bisecting (quant type, BF16 tensors, CUDA graphs, ECC, test-backend-ops — all fine) before toggling -c turned the fault on and off deterministically.

Environment

  • llama.cpp commit 10a60cf (same commit on client and server); behaviour of the relevant code is unchanged on current master (see "Root cause")
  • RPC server: Tesla V100-PCIE-32GB (sm_70), KVM guest (Ubuntu Server 24.04, driver 580.178.04, CUDA 13.0), 56 GB root disk
  • Client: llama-server on the host (RTX 5070 Ti), --rpc <guest>:50052 --device RPC0
  • Models: Qwen3.8-27B Q8_0 and UD-Q8_K_XL (~28 GB each) affected; UD-Q4_K_M (~16 GB, cached earlier while space was available) unaffected

Evidence

Cache directory after the problem appeared (disk at 100 %): 77 zero-byte files, written in two bursts that coincide exactly with the first loads of the two Q8 models:

$ df -h ~
/dev/mapper/ubuntu--vg-ubuntu--lv   56G   54G     0 100% /
$ find ~/.cache/llama.cpp/rpc -size 0 | wc -l
77
$ ls -laS --time-style=full-iso ~/.cache/llama.cpp/rpc | tail -4
-rw-rw-r-- 1 user user 0 2026-10-10 05:23:34.369399299 +0000 e5e90a16751af795
-rw-rw-r-- 1 user user 0 2026-10-10 05:23:34.143396155 +0000 fd2dfb81fb1ea48f
-rw-rw-r-- 1 user user 0 2026-10-14 19:11:33.562701065 +0000 fffe16879088ccaf
...

(full listing attached)

Controlled A/B with everything else fixed (same model, same seed, same prompt, same client command; only the server's -c flag changed):

rpc-server | Output -- | -- without -c | correct, coherent answer -c (cache containing the zero-byte files) | "3/2/0279362202067758992765827979272782797202727622705292902723..." -c, cache wiped, enough free space — load #1 and reload #2 | correct, identical to the no-cache output

Results were deterministic and repeatable by toggling the flag.

Root cause (current master, ggml/src/ggml-rpc/ggml-rpc.cpp)

Write side, rpc_server::set_tensor — stream state is never checked, so a failed write leaves an empty or short file under the hash name:

cpp
std::ofstream ofs(cache_file, std::ios::binary);
ofs.write((const char *)data, size);
LOG_INFO("[%s] saved to '%s'\n", __func__, cache_file.string().c_str());

Read side,
