items.title: [Bug]: `/metrics` (iteration-stats) route blocks the serve event loop — a 2 s Prometheus scrape inflates request latency 5–60× and cuts prefill throughput ~5× (4× RTX 5060 Ti TP4, Qwen3.5 hybrid-GDN NVFP4 27B, 1.3.0rc29)
items.author: sean640112
items.body_excerpt:
> **Update (2026-10-09): the root cause is not sm120.** The "fixed" per-request cost comes from the `/metrics` iteration-stats route blocking the serve event loop: a 2 s Prometheus scrape inflates request latency 5–60× and cuts prefill throughput ~5×. Controlled A/B, py-spy stacks and the Prometheus-side numbers are in the [follow-up comment](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/issues/19623#issuecomment-6076428189) below.

# ~6 s fixed per-request latency floor on sm120 (4× RTX 5060 Ti, TP4) with a Qwen3.5 hybrid-GDN 27B NVFP4 checkpoint

## Summary

On a 4× RTX 5060 Ti (sm120) box serving a **dense hybrid GDN + full-attention 27B** NVFP4 checkpoint with `trtllm-serve` (PyTorch backend, TP4), we measure a **~6 s per-request floor on time-to-first-token that is independent of prompt length**. A 212-token request takes **6.06 s** to first token (8.0 s total), and the floor persists at every length we tested (212 → 59,571 tokens). Requests are reproducible to ±5 ms across 12 measurements in 3 separate server starts.

The same hardware, same checkpoint, same prompt, same client, served by SGLang gives **0.26–0.30 s** for the identical request. `trtllm-serve` therefore looks ~20× slower on short requests, while its *marginal* prefill throughput is only ~2.6× lower (~2,143 tok/s vs ~5,600 tok/s).

We have ruled out MTP/spec-decode, scheduler policy, `max_seq_len`, chunked prefill, the CUDA caching allocator, and thinking-mode as causes (details below). We would like to know whether this per-request floor is **expected on sm120 for hybrid GDN models**, or a bug — and which knob/diagnostic we should look at next. We are happy to run any instrumentation you suggest.

## Environment

| | |
|---|---|
| GPU | 4× NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5060 Ti 16 GB, compute capability **12.0 (sm120)**, TP=4 |
| Driver | 610.57.04 |
| CUDA toolkit | 13.3 (`nvcc` 13.3, `CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-13.3`) |
| OS / Python | Linux, Python 3.12.11 (venv) |
| TensorRT-LLM | **1.3.0rc29.dev202609240000** (nightly from 2026-09-24; PyPI 1.2.1 does not contain `modeling_qwen3_5.py`, hence nightly) |
| torch | 2.14.0+cu132 |
| flashinfer-python | 0.6.18 |
| triton | 3.8.0 |
| nvidia-cutlass-dsl | 4.8.0.dev0 |
| tensorrt / tensorrt_cu13 | 10.14.1.48.post1 |
| MPI | OpenMPI 5.0.10 (`mpi4py` bootstrap path) |
| Model | `nvidia/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4` — `architectures: ["Qwen3_5ForConditionalGeneration"]`, `model_type: qwen3_5`; 64 layers, hidden 5120, 24 Q heads, 4 KV heads |
| Quantization | ModelOpt `MIXED_PRECISION`: **FP8 per-tensor on 208 layers** (`block_size` absent) + **NVFP4 `group_size: 16` on 193 layers**, `kv_cache_quant_algo: null` |

Note on the attention backend: your hardware support matrix lists sm120 as supporting NVFP4 / MXFP4 / FP8 (per-tensor) / FP8 KV cache, which covers this checkpoint's formats — so the quantization scheme itself should be fully supported on sm120.

## How to reproduce

Server (the `mpirun -n 1` wrapper and `OMPI_MCA_*` are needed on this host because `import tensorrt_llm` otherwise blocks in the mpi4py `MPI.COMM_WORLD` initialization, and this host's own hostname resolves to loopback only):

```bash
export CUDA_HOME=/usr/local/cuda-13.3
export OMPI_MCA_btl_tcp_if_include=lo OMPI_MCA_oob_tcp_if_include=lo
mpirun -n 1 --oversubscribe trtllm-serve serve /path/to/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4 \
  --host 127.0.0.1 --port 1234 --tp_size 4 \
  --max_seq_len 140000 --max_batch_size 8 \
  --served_model_name qwen3.8-27b \
  --free_gpu_memory_fraction 0.80 \
  --extra_llm_api_options opts.yaml
```

`opts.yaml`:
```yaml
enable_chunked_prefill: true
max_num_tokens: 8192
speculative_config:
  decoding_type: MTP
  max_draft_len: 3
  speculative_model: /path/to/Qwen3.8-27B-NVFP4
```

Client — a minimal stdlib-only streaming client (this is the "probe" used for every number below; it measures the first chunk that carries `choices[0].text`/`delta.content`):

```python
import json, time, urllib.request
prompt = open("/path/to/corpus.txt").read()[:600]          # → 212 tokens
body = {"model": "qwen3.8-27b", "prompt": prompt, "max_tokens": 1, "temperature": 0, "stream": True}
req = urllib.request.Request("http://127.0.0.1:1234/v1/completions",
        data=json.dumps(body).encode(), headers={"Content-Type": "application/json"})
t0 = time.time(); ttft = None
with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=900) as r:
    for raw in r:
        s = raw.decode().strip()
        if not s.startswith("data: "): continue
        if s[6:] == "[DONE]": break
        d = json.loads(s[6:])
        ch = d.get("choices") or []
        if ch and ch[0].get("text"):
            ttft = time.time() - t0; break
print("TTFT", ttft)
```

## Measured results (same probe, same prompts, same box)

| prompt tokens | path | TRT-LLM stream TTFT | TRT-LLM non-stream total | SGLang stream TTFT | SGLang non-stream total |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **212** | completions | **6.053–6.062 s** (n=5) | 7.995–8.035 s | **0.262 s** | 0.304 s |
| 222 | chat (medium template) | 12.11 – **22.21 s** (unstable across restarts) | 14.06 – 26.19 s | 0.268 s | — |
| 7,172 | completions | 10.10 s | 12.02 s | 0.243 s *cached* | 1.84 s *cached* |
| 12,131 | completions | 12.12 s | 14.06 s | — | — |
| 28,008 | completions | — | 20.13 s | — | 6.15 s *cached* |
| 59,571 | completions | — | 36.26 s | — | — |
| 65,032 | chat | 56.52 s | 56.45 s | — | — |

*("cached" = the SGLang side hit its radix prefix cache on the shared corpus prefix, so those cells are not a like-for-like prefill comparison.)*

Least-squares fit of the completions path (`total = C + N/R`, 5 points spanning 212 → 59,571 tokens):
**C = 8.10 s, R = 2,143 tok/s, R² = 0.9966** — i.e. a very large constant plus a modest rate term. (The streaming TTFT is ≈ 1.9 s lower at every point, i.e. TTFT ≈ 6.1 s + N/2143.)

For reference, an independent client (vLLM's `bench serve` against the same server) measured prefill throughput of **453 / 1,014 / 1,302 tok/s** at 8K / 32K / 64K with meanTTFT 16.15 / 29.28 / 46.44 s, i.e. the same
score_reasons: 匹配 KV 与存储、Serving 与评测、Kernel 与正确性、工程与测试

items.title: CUTLASS 4.8.0
items.author: Junkai-Wu
items.body_excerpt:
### CuTe DSL
* New features
  - Initial Rubin support to accelerate dense GEMMs. The following features are available:  
    - CuTe DSL and CuTe extensions
      - Support for higher-throughput FP8 (MMA_K=64) and FP4 (MMA_K=128) Tensor Core MMA instructions
      - B collector reuse 
      - Extended TMEM size from 512 COL to 576 COL
      - Larger shared memory allocations (328KB)
      - Enhanced mixed precision throughput (FP8/FP4)
      - Softmax acceleration related features
    - Primitives
      - Support for higher-throughput FP8 (MMA_K=64) and FP4 (MMA_K=128) Tensor Core MMA instructions
      - B collector reuse
      - Extended TMEM size from 512 COL to 576 COL
      - Larger shared memory allocations (328KB)
      - Enhanced mixed precision throughput (FP8/FP4)
      - Softmax acceleration related feature
      - 2:4 sparsity support for FP4

  - CuTe DSL extensions has several new features:
    - CTA-V maps are now inferred automatically for `cute_ext` TMA load, store, multicast, and reduce-store operations. Explicit CTA-V maps remain supported as overrides.
    - Added asynchronous atomic TMA reduce-store and sparse MMA operations.
    - Added reusable `cute_ext` GEMM mainloop and TMA epilogue helpers.
    - Added opt-in TMEM accumulator-buffer planning, including overlapping ping-pong storage for capacity-constrained kernels.
    - Improved device-side TMA descriptor updates and grouped GEMM performance through SMEM-staged updates, workspace reuse, and reduced prologue and synchronization overhead.
  - This release includes an opt-in preview of the CuTe DSL extensions (`cute_ext`) compiler pipeline for ordinary Cute DSL kernels. This pipeline lets user mix `cute_ext` APIs directly into `@cute.jit` and `@cute.kernel` code and is required for kernels that mix the two API surfaces. You may test this feature with the following:
  `CUTE_DSL_USE_EXTENSION_COMPILER=1 python your_program.py`
The pipeline is expected to preserve program behavior and performance, but generated PTX/SASS may differ.  Note that this pipeline will become the default in the future, no earlier than 4.10.
  - Added examples for better control over Primitives' compiler warnings/errors introduced in 4.7.0.  See the `CuTeDSL/experimental/compiler_diagnostic/` directory.
  - IKET Profiler Tool
    - Rubin kernels (sm107) can now be profiled.
    - It is now possible to only dump timing data for a specific cluster to reduce profiling overhead.  Previously all clusters were profiled.
    - Task Scheduling can instrument the schedule with IKET ranges when constructing TaskManager objects (`iket_enable_profiling=True`).  Task execution will generate an IKET range and individual pipeline stages in a schedule may generate separate ranges (`iket_profiling_stages`).
  - A number of new examples were added in this release:
    - Rubin (CuTe):
      - Dense GEMM for legacy data type with B collector reuse as applicable
      - Grouped GEMM with B collector reuse
      - Dense blockscaled GEMM with FP4/FP6/FP8 mixed precision and UE5M3 / block-32 scale-factor support
      - Grouped blockscaled GEMM with B collector reuse as applicable
      - Blockwise GEMM
    - Rubin (CuTe extension):
      - Support for higher-throughput FP8 (MMA_K=64) and FP4 (MMA_K=128) blockscaled GEMM with UE5M3 scale-factor
      - Grouped GEMM with B collector reuse
    - Blackwell (CuTe extension):
      - Dense GEMMs
        - Back-to-back GEMM
        - Blockscaled GEMM
        - Persistent GEMM with alpha/beta scaling
        - CLC scheduler/dynamic persistent GEMM
        - GLU GEMM
        - Mixed input GEMM
        - Planar complex GEMM
        - Input transform GEMM
        - GeForce pingpong dense GEMM
        - Blackwell Ultra blockscaled GEMM
      - Dense Convolutions
        - Implicit-Gemm Fprop Conv
        - Blocksclaed Implicit-Gemm Fprop Conv
        - GeForce Implicit-Gemm Fprop Conv
        - GeForce Blockscaled Implicit-Gemm Fporp Conv 
      - Attention
        - GQA Decode
      - Grouped GEMM
        - Unscaled and blockscaled grouped GEMM
      - Top-K
    - Ampere (CuTe extension):
      - SIMT GEMM
  - CuTe DSL now supports x86_64 Windows
  - CuTe DSL AoT now supports new host target: QNX8.0 
  - Notebooks are restructured under examples/python/CuTeDSL/cute/notebooks and new notebooks for primitives will be added under examples/python/CuTeDSL/notebooks 
  - Numpy is now not a default dependency

items.title: [Perf][SM103] GQA fp8 decode: the direct trtllm-gen entry runs ~1.15x behind FI's own BatchDecode wrapper on the same shapes
items.author: brandonfzhang
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

On captured GQA decode traffic (16 q-heads / 1 kv-head per rank, head_dim 128,
fp8 KV), the **direct** trtllm-gen decode entry — the path vLLM integrates — is
**~1.15x behind FlashInfer's own `BatchDecodeWithPagedKVCacheWrapper`**
(GPU-time-weighted; cute-dsl backend at long KV, trtllm-gen-via-wrapper at short
KV). The wrapper forms also beat the best non-FI rival (vLLM's FA fp8) on most of
the traffic, so this within-FI gap is the difference between FI winning and losing
the cell as integrated. We see the same direct-vs-wrapper gap on two different
models' serves (Nemotron-3-Ultra and MiniMax-M3, both vLLM).

## Environment

- NVIDIA GB300 (SM103); CUDA 13.0; FlashInfer 0.7.1rc5
- Timing: CUPTI, 20 interleaved rounds, SM clock locked 2070 MHz, fp64 gates
- Shapes + weights from live serving of the published Nemotron-3-Ultra vLLM GB300
  recipe (TP4; speculative decode q=6 plus q=1 traffic)

## Exact call parameters

GQA paged decode: `num_q_heads=16`, `num_kv_heads=1`, `head_dim=128`,
q and KV `float8_e4m3fn`, paged KV with `page_size=32`, bf16 output;
`q_len=1` rows below (the serve also runs q_len=6 speculative verify — see ask 2).

## Measurements — q=1, 16/1 heads, head_dim 128, fp8 KV (µs, top classes by GPU time)

| batch | kv_len | direct trtllm-gen | wrapper (best backend) | vLLM FA fp8 |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 65536 | 21.6 | 18.8 (cute-dsl) | 22.6 |
| 1 | 131072 | 27.8 | 23.3 (cute-dsl) | 26.1 |
| 1 | 262144 | 32.5 | 27.9 (cute-dsl) | 32.5 |
| 2 | 131072 | 24.9 | 22.9 (cute-dsl) | 27.9 |
| 2 | 262144 | 35.3 | 32.9 (cute-dsl) | 38.8 |
| 1 | 8192 | 8.2 | 6.9 (trtllm-gen) | 14.0 |
| 2 | 4096 | 7.2 | 6.0 (trtllm-gen) | 11.3 |

Note the short-KV rows: even *trtllm-gen itself* is faster through the wrapper than
through the direct entry, so part of the gap is entry-point overhead/config rather
than kernel choice.

## Why this is a FlashInfer issue, not an integration nit

The obvious rejoinder — "vLLM should just call the wrapper" — doesn't hold yet: at
the serve's dominant q=6 speculative-verify traffic, the wrapper forms are **not
eligible at all** at this geometry, so the direct entry is the only FI decode path
that covers the whole regime, and an integration reasonably wants one
CUDA-graphable decode path rather than a per-q_len API switch. Given FI's current
surface, vLLM's pick is the correct one — and FI loses the cell with it. Both
fixes live in FlashInfer:

## Ask

1. Extend the wrapper/cute-dsl decode eligibility to q_len > 1 (speculative verify,
   q=6 here) at this head geometry — this is what unblocks integrations from using
   the fast forms at all.
2. Bring the direct trtllm-gen decode entry to parity with the wrapper (or route it
   through the same backend selection): the short-KV rows above show the *same
   backend* running faster through the wrapper, so the overhead is in the entry
   point itself, and fixing it speeds up every existing integration with no
   framework change.

## Related

- #6558 (within-FI form gap of the same kind: allreduce AUTO vs best form)

items.title: [Bug]: ModelClaim engine crashes with IndexError in kvcached get_new_blocks after the controller raises its KV limit above the engine's initial block pool
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

A vLLM engine started by the ModelClaim runtime (kvcached-patched) crashes with `IndexError` after the controller raises its KV limit above the KV block pool the engine allocated at startup. EngineCore exits, the runtime restarts the engine (`restart_count` +1), and every request to that model fails until it is back (about 40 s for an 8B model).

```
File ".../vllm/v1/core/single_type_kv_cache_manager.py", line 399, in allocate_new_blocks
    new_blocks = self.block_pool.get_new_blocks(num_new_blocks)
File ".../kvcached/integration/vllm/patches.py", line 1003, in get_new_blocks
    block = self.kv_block_pool[bid]
IndexError: list index out of range
EngineCore encountered a fatal error.
```

What we observed:

1. vLLM sizes the block table once, at engine start: `self.kv_block_pool = [KVCacheBlockClass(i) for i in range(num_gpu_blocks)]`. For a single Qwen3-8B-FP8 engine on an A100-40GB this is 26.2 GiB of blocks (kvcached log: `Using kvcached process-local KV capacity: ... available=28173858448 bytes`).
2. When that engine is alone on the card, `planKVLimits` gives it the engine's held KV plus the whole remaining card, 29.0 GiB. Nothing caps the limit at the engine's initial pool ([kvplan.go#L114-L127](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/main/pkg/controller/modelclaim/kvplan.go#L114-L127)). The event reads `KV limit set to 29.0 GiB, from 26.2 GiB`.
3. kvcached then hands out block ids up to the new limit. An id at or above `num_gpu_blocks` indexes past `kv_block_pool`.

We hit the crash 4 times in one benchmark run:

- **History captured:** in the two crashes whose limit history we captured, the engine had been raised above its initial pool. One of them crashed 4 minutes after its limit had been lowered from 29.0 GiB back to 9.2 GiB, when a second engine was placed. Lowering the limit afterwards did not prevent the crash.
- **History not captured:** the other two engines ran in the same setup, alone on the card first.
- **Never above the pool:** engines whose limit never exceeded their initial pool never crashed, across dozens of KV-saturating runs. These include engines placed next to an existing engine and engines started in pairs or groups.
- **Above the pool, no crash:** two engines were raised above their pool briefly and did not crash: a 0.6B engine at concurrency 1 (36.7 vs 34.9 GiB), and an 8B engine under load for 90 s. Exceeding the pool is necessary but not sufficient; the crash depends on how many blocks get allocated afterwards.
- **Prefix caching and reset:** prefix caching makes it trigger sooner, but it is not required: one crash happened with `--no-enable-prefix-caching`. `/reset_prefix_cache` is not required either.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Deploy a warm pool with one GPU (`samples/modelclaim/warm-runtime-pool.yaml`, 1× A100-40GB) and no pool policy annotation.
2. Apply one ModelClaim alone on that pod:
   ```yaml
   spec:
     modelName: qwen3-8b-z
     artifactURL: huggingface://Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8
     engine: vllm
     perGPU:
       maximumFootprint: 10752Mi
       kvFloor: 2Gi
     engineConfig:
       args:
         --max-model-len: "8192"
         --max-num-seqs: "32"
         --max-num-batched-tokens: "2048"
   ```
3. Check the event `KV limit set to 29.0 GiB, from 26.2 GiB` (runtime snapshot `kv_capacity_bytes: 31132614656`).
4. Send RAG-shaped load directly to the engine port. Repeat with `--seed 1`, `2`, `3`:
   ```bash
   vllm bench serve --backend openai-chat --base-url http://<pod-ip>:<engine-port> \
     --endpoint /v1/chat/completions --model qwen3-8b-z --tokenizer Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8 \
     --dataset-name random --random-input-len 1024 --random-output-len 128 \
     --num-prompts 300 --request-rate 32 --max-concurrency 16 --ignore-eos --seed 1
   ```
   Runs 1 and 2 complete 300/300. Run 3 crashed after 144 requests, and the snapshot showed `restart_count: 1`.

### Expected behavior

- The controller never sets an engine's KV limit above the KV capacity the engine sized its block table for at startup. Room on the card beyond that stays unassigned, or goes to other engines.
- Suggested fix: the runtime reports each engine's initial KV capacity in the snapshot (the kvcached segment's `total_size` when the engine came up, or `num_gpu_blocks` × block bytes). `planKVLimits` caps `kvLimitBytes` at it. Add a regression test where a single engine on a card gets a capped limit.
- kvcached should also clamp or reject a limit beyond `num_gpu_blocks` instead of handing out out-of-range block ids. We will report that side to ovg-project/kvcached.

### Environment

- Image `ghcr.io/ovg-project/kvcached-vllm:kvcached-v0.1.6-vllm-v0.30.0` (vLLM 0.30.0, kvcached 0.1.6), runtime built with `make docker-build-kvcached-runtime`.
- 1× NVIDIA A100-SXM4-40GB, driver 570.148.08, single-node minikube.
- Models: Qwen/Qwen3-8B-FP8 (all 4 crashes) and Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B.

### Area

Orchestration (controllers, CRDs)

items.title: Should LMCacheMPConnector honor kv_transfer_config.kv_role — or is MP mode intentionally always-kv_both?
items.author: kezboard233
items.body_excerpt:
## Context

We run a production-shaped POC on 8×V100 (two vLLM TP4 instances of Qwen3.8-27B-FP8 sharing one LMCache MP server with a CPU L1 tier) and filed #5143 with a runtime-verified repro: an engine launched with `kv_role="kv_consumer"` still stores every request's KV into the shared L1 — a single 32K-token cold request produced `168 × "Stored 784"` lines (= full prefix × 4 TP ranks), and the only engine that received any request in that window was the `kv_consumer` one.

We later found #4665 (closed by its author without maintainer response) reporting the same mechanism from the CacheBlend angle: the single-process connector honors `kv_role` / `skip_save`, the MP connector honors neither. As of today's `dev`, `lmcache_mp_connector.py` still contains no occurrence of `kv_role` / `kv_consumer` / `kv_producer` / `force_skip_save`.

## The design question

Before we contribute a patch, we want to check intent: **is MP mode intentionally "every connected engine writes"?** Two readings:

1. **Contract gap** — vLLM makes `kv_role` mandatory, documents it as "Whether this vLLM instance produces, consumes KV cache, or both", and exposes `is_kv_producer` / `is_kv_consumer` for connectors to branch on; LMCache's own single-process adapter honors it (`force_skip_save` in `vllm_v1_adapter.py`). Under this reading we'd gladly contribute a small PR that skips store-metadata generation when `is_kv_consumer` (mirroring the single-process gate), so warm-then-read-only fleets and PD-style topologies become possible on the MP path.

2. **Intentional always-kv_both** — the MP tier is a shared scratch space where every connected engine contributes. Under this reading we'd instead ask for the intent to be documented, plus ideally a one-line warning at connector init when `kv_role != "kv_both"`, so users aren't misled (we only noticed via instrumented counter evidence ourselves).

Happy to do either — a steer from maintainers decides which.

(Impact context: no correctness issue — stored content is identical — but a consumer-role engine burns D2H bandwidth and shared-L1 capacity; a 32K prefix on our model is ≈8.6 GB across 4 ranks.)

items.title: [Performance]: Beam search re-materializes Result.output_token_ids from pybind once per beam
items.author: yifanQi98
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

#### Background

For beam-search requests, `GenerationResultBase._handle_response` iterates over beams and calls `_handle_sequence` once per beam:

```python
finish_reasons = response_result.finish_reasons
# output_token_ids = (beams, tokens)
if self.sampling_params.use_beam_search:
    for beam_idx, _ in enumerate(response_result.output_token_ids):   # result.py:692
        self._handle_sequence(finish_reasons, response_result,
                              beam_idx, logprobs_result,
                              req_perf_metrics_dict)
```

`_handle_sequence` then reads the same property again, once per call:

```python
if self.sampling_params.use_beam_search:
    output.token_ids = [
        *decoder_output_prefix,
        *response_tensors.output_token_ids[src_idx],      # result.py:402
    ]
else:
    ...
    output.token_ids.extend(response_tensors.output_token_ids[src_idx])   # result.py:407
```

`LlmResult.output_token_ids` is not in `LlmResult.py_result_properties`, so `LlmResult.__getattr__` falls through to `getattr(self._result, item)` on the **pybind** `bindings.executor.Result`. That property returns a freshly built nested Python list on every access — it is not cached on either side:

```python
>>> a, b = llm_result.output_token_ids, llm_result.output_token_ids
>>> a is b
False
>>> a[0] is b[0]
False
>>> a == b
True
```

So for a request with `N` beams, one response converts the full `(N, tokens)` structure from C++ **N + 1 times** when once is sufficient. Because the per-conversion cost is itself O(N · tokens), the redundant work is **quadratic in beam width**.

This is the dominant host-side cost for the "short decode length, very wide beams" pattern (e.g. SID / generative-recommendation serving with `n = best_of = 500`, `max_tokens = 3`), where `_handle_sequence` does almost no work per beam other than these reads.

#### Measurement

Offline, no GPU, no model, no executor. A real `bindings.executor.Result` is constructed and populated (`output_token_ids` is settable), wrapped in a real `LlmResult`, and the **real** `GenerationResultBase._handle_sequence` is driven once per beam, reproducing the body of `_handle_response`'s beam loop. (Correction added after review: this driver loop used `range(BEAM)` and so did not include the loop head's own `enumerate(response_result.output_token_ids)` read. It therefore measures N reads per response rather than the N+1 a real response performs; at 500 beams that is one extra ~26 us read, about 0.2% of the effect.)

Three arms, interleaved, `gc.collect()` before every sample, median of 25:

- **A stock** — real `_handle_sequence` against the real `LlmResult`
- **C patched** — the same real source, textually rewritten so `response_tensors.output_token_ids` resolves to a binding materialized **once per response**; every other attribute still reads the real `LlmResult` per beam, so this arm does not overstate the win. (Correction added after review: the rewrite binds the value through a module-level global to model the hoist. It is semantically the suggested fix but is not literally the final parameter-passing form; the re-measurement below uses the real patch.)
- **B snapshot** — every attribute pre-materialized, with the snapshot itself built outside the timed region. It bounds the achievable *saving*; it is **not** a measurement of what any real memoizing implementation would cost, since that implementation has to build and consult its cache inside the timed region

Access counts were obtained by running the real code path against a counting forwarder, not by reading the source by hand. For one 500-beam response:

| attribute | reads | served by |
|---|---|---|
| `time_breakdown_metrics` | 1000 | instance attr (cheap) |
| `output_token_ids` | **500** | **pybind** |
| `request_perf_metrics` | **500** | **pybind** |
| `cum_log_probs` / `log_probs` / `generation_logits` / `additional_*_outputs` | 500 each | `py_result` (Python-side) |
| `finish_reasons` | 1 | pybind |

Total 4501 attribute reads per response, 1001 of them pybind-served.

##### Results (ms per response, `tokens = 3`)

| beams | one pybind read | A stock | C patched | C saving | B upper bound | B saving |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 | 0.53 µs | 0.122 | 0.120 | −0.002 (1.6%) | 0.097 | −0.025 (20.5%) |
| 20 | 1.25 µs | 0.195 | 0.187 | −0.008 (4.1%) | 0.127 | −0.068 (34.9%) |
| 100 | 6.25 µs | 1.016 | 0.458 | −0.558 (54.9%) | 0.303 | −0.713 (70.2%) |
| 300 | 16.20 µs | 5.848 | 1.047 | −4.801 (82.1%) | 0.682 | −5.166 (88.3%) |
| **500** | **25.94 µs** | **14.428** | **1.543** | **−12.885 (89.3%)** | 0.985 | −13.443 (93.2%) |

At 500 beams, **89% of the per-response beam loop is redundant pybind re-conversion of one property.** 100 → 500 beams is 5× the width and 23× the waste, confirming the quadratic behaviour.

In this harness the effect at beam=20 is inside its noise floor (arm C's delta is 0.008 ms against a per-sample sd of 0.03–0.04 ms). That is a limit of this harness's precision, **not** a general threshold: the re-measurement below, using the real patch and 60 interleaved pairs, resolves a repeatable 0.025–0.028 ms saving at 20 beams with a 95% CI of [0.0250, 0.0306]. The saving is simply small there, and it grows quadratically.

##### Cross-check

Two independent estimates of the same quantity agree:

- micro: 500 reads × 25.94 µs = **12.97 ms**
- macro: arm A − arm C = **12.89 ms**
- ratio **0.99**

The residual between arm C and arm B (0.558 ms at 500 beams) is **not** mostly `request_perf_metrics`. Corrected attribution, measured directly rather than inferred from the residual: a per-read micro-benchmark puts `request_perf_metrics` at **0.241 µs** unset / **0.361 µs** set, so its 499 per-beam reads are worth **0.120 ms** (unset) / **0.180 ms** (set) per response, and hoisting it in situ measures 0.165 ms. The larger share of the residual is the per-beam group served Python-side by `PyResult` (`log_probs`, `cum_log_probs`,

items.title: [Bug]: trtllm-serve /v1/chat/completions rejects the standard OpenAI field prompt_cache_key with 400
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

TensorRT-LLM main @ 15f060c9f8, `trtllm-serve` (any model, any GPU).

### Reproduction

    curl -s localhost:8000/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
      "model": "<model>",
      "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}],
      "prompt_cache_key": "session-1234"
    }'

or with the OpenAI Python client: `client.chat.completions.create(..., prompt_cache_key="session-1234")`.

### Expected behavior

The request is served. `prompt_cache_key` is part of OpenAI's Chat Completions request body (a hint for prompt-cache routing), and clients built on it may set it on every request of a session.

### Actual behavior

The request fails validation with `extra_forbidden` ("Extra inputs are not permitted") for `prompt_cache_key`, because `ChatCompletionRequest` inherits `extra="forbid"` from `OpenAIBaseModel` and has no such field. `ResponsesRequest` already accepts it (it switched to `extra="allow"`, and the comment there names `prompt_cache_key` as one of the fields real clients send), so the same client works against `/v1/responses` but not against `/v1/chat/completions`.

### Additional notes

KV cache reuse in TensorRT-LLM needs no client hint, and `cache_salt` is the field that isolates cached prefixes, so the field can be accepted and ignored, the same way `parallel_tool_calls` and `user` are. PR to follow.

items.title: [Bug]: Grouped MLA generation cubins are registered as Dense in kernelMetaInfo.h but named and selected as Causal
items.author: lucifer1004

### System Info

TensorRT-LLM main, `cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/trtllmGenKernels/fmha/cubin/kernelMetaInfo.h` (artifacts from #19591). On release/1.3 the table is split per architecture since #20022; the same rows are in `kernelMetaInfoSm100f.h` and `kernelMetaInfoSm107.h` (see the location list below). Seen on SM107; the SM100f rows have the same pattern.

### Who can help?

@pengbowang-nv @farazkh80 (#15009)

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Reproduction

All 36 grouped MLA generation cubins (`fmhaSm100fKernel_...` and `fmhaSm107aKernel_Qkv{Bfloat16,E4m3}OBfloat16HQk576HV512{,HVPerCta128,HVPerCta256}PagedKvCausalP32...VarSeqQ64Kv128{Static,Persistent}GroupedKeepsAbForGen`; per architecture 9 with BF16 and 9 with E4M3 Q/KV, 18 for `kSM_100f`, 18 for `kSM_107`) have `Causal` in the function name, but their `mMaskType` field is `0` (`TrtllmGenAttentionMaskType::Dense`). Locations:

- main @ 13e19d6cf3, `kernelMetaInfo.h`: SM100f BF16 lines 19057-19110, SM100f E4M3 19347-19400, SM107 BF16 20903-21019, SM107 E4M3 21907-22023.
- release/1.3 @ c9d1169641 (after #20022): `kernelMetaInfoSm100f.h` lines 243-296 (BF16) and 533-586 (E4M3); `kernelMetaInfoSm107.h` lines 887-1003 (BF16) and 1835-1951 (E4M3). The values are unchanged by the split. The grouped P128 E4M3 H128 cubins added there for SM107 are registered with `mMaskType = 1` (Causal), so only the HQk576 grouped MLA rows are affected.

`mMaskType` is part of the hash that the cubin path looks up (`hashFromFmhaOptions` -> `hashID`). With `FmhaOptions::mSelectsGroupedMla = true`, the autotuner selects the grouped kernel with a causal mask for MLA generation with multiple query tokens, so the lookup fails (`Trtllm-gen kernels not found`), and the only remaining route is NVRTC. On SM107, NVRTC currently fails for these configurations (separate issue). We had to map Causal back to Dense for grouped MLA kernels in `algoFilterForCubinPath` before the cubins could be used.

With that mapping, the cubins give the expected causal result: compared with the non-grouped kernel on SM107, outputs are bit-identical for KV lengths 16 and 64, and at most 2 bf16 ulp apart from 256 up to 128K. So the kernels behave as their names say, and only the metadata is off. #15009 also mentions that its re-exported rows were changed to `maskType=Causal` "to match the shipped lib's grouped mask rewrite".

### Expected behavior

The registered mask type matches what the kernel implements and what the selector asks for, so that grouped MLA generation cubins can be found without a remapping.

### actual behavior

`mMaskType = Dense` for kernels named `...Causal...`; the cubin lookup misses them when grouped MLA selection is enabled.

### additional notes

This does not affect main today because `mSelectsGroupedMla` is never set in TensorRT-LLM. It blocks enabling it (#15009), together with the missing `cumSeqLensQ/Kv` in the MLA generation path (#20375). If the right fix is on the export side, a regenerated `kernelMetaInfo.h` (`kernelMetaInfoSm100f.h` / `kernelMetaInfoSm107.h` after #20022) would be enough; otherwise I can send the remapping as a small PR.

Related: #20375, #20377, #20382 (FP8-KV grouped MLA hang for head counts that do not divide 64).

items.title: [Bug]: FP8-KV MLA generation hangs on SM107 with the grouped trtllm-gen E4M3 kernels when heads per rank do not divide 64 (e.g. 12)
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- GPU: SM107, 8 GPUs over 2 nodes (TP8 attention)
- TensorRT-LLM main @ 69a455ae974bcf9582c9a2cc4f7fd9a5f75680fe (code and cubin list checked there), PyTorch backend, TRTLLM attention backend
- Model: MLA model with 96 query heads -> 12 heads per rank at TP8 (kv_lora_rank 512, qk_rope_head_dim 64)
- kv_cache_config.dtype: fp8, tokens_per_block 32, MTP speculative decoding with 8 query tokens per step
- Grouped (tokens x heads in one Q tile) MLA generation kernel selection enabled locally (`FmhaOptions::mSelectsGroupedMla`; main does not set it, see #15009)

### Who can help?

@pengbowang-nv @farazkh80

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Reproduction

1. Serve the model with `kv_cache_config.dtype: fp8` and grouped MLA generation selection enabled.
2. Startup never finishes: every rank stops in the first generation-shape attention call of the warmup (num_tokens=8, num_gen_requests=1, KV length 8). GPU utilization stays at 100 %, nothing is logged after `Attention workspace size is not enough, increase the size from 0 bytes to ...`. `TRTLLM_ENABLE_PDL=0` does not change it.
3. A host-side backtrace of a rank shows the main thread inside the next cuBLAS call (`cublasGemmStridedBatchedEx -> cuKernelSetAttribute`), i.e. queued behind a kernel that never completes.
4. With synchronizing checkpoints in `MLA.forward_absorption_generation`: the q_nope bmm and `mla_rope_generation` (FP8 Q quantization, FP8 KV append, bmm scales) complete; the attention op does not. A sync right after the FMHA launch in `TllmGenFmhaRunner::run` never returns. The selected cubin is `fmhaSm107aKernel_QkvE4m3OBfloat16HQk576HV512HVPerCta256PagedKvCausalP32VarSeqQ64Kv128StaticGroupedKeepsAbForGen` (grid 2x2x1, numHeadsQ 12, maxSeqLenQ 8, multiCtasKv off for this KV length).

Standalone reproduction with the FMHA runner only (no model): `TllmGenFmhaRunner(E4M3, E4M3, E4M3, BF16)`, paged KV page 32, MLA head dims 576/512, 1 KV head, generation kernel, grouped selection enabled, seqLenQ 8 (12 heads also hangs at seqLenQ 1, 4, 5, 6), seqLenKv 2048:

| numHeadsQ | 4 | 6 | 8 | 10 | 12 | 14 | 16 | 20 | 24 | 32 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| FP8 (E4M3 Q/KV) grouped | ok | **hangs** | ok | **hangs** | **hangs** | **hangs** | ok | **hangs** | **hangs** | ok |
| BF16 grouped (checked: 12, 16) | — | — | — | — | ok | — | ok | — | — | — |

The FP8 kernel completes only when numHeadsQ divides the 64-row Q tile. BF16 grouped kernels with 12 heads are fine.

### Expected behavior

The FP8 grouped MLA generation kernel works for any head count, or is not selected for head counts it cannot handle.

### actual behavior

The FMHA kernel never completes; the process hangs with the GPU at 100 %.

### additional notes

**Analysis.** In `makeTmaShapeStrideQ` (`cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/trtllmGenKernels/fmha/trtllmGen_fmha_export/KernelParams.h`), for `mGroupsTokensHeadsQ`:

~~~
numTokensPerTileQ = numTokensPerTileQ / numGroupedHeads;   // 64 / 12 = 5
tileShapes = {clampedHeadDimQ, numGroupedHeads, 1, numTokensPerTileQ};  // 5 tokens x 12 heads = 60 rows
~~~

so the Q TMA box covers 60 of the 64 tile rows. The comment there says padding at the end of the tile is allowed. The BF16 cubins handle it; the E4M3 cubins never finish, which looks like the kernel waits for a full 64-row tile (a transaction byte count or row bookkeeping derived from tileSizeQ instead of from the box). Unchanged on current main.

**Reachability on main.** Main never sets `mSelectsGroupedMla`, so this hang is latent there today. But the precompiled SM107 E4M3 MLA generation cubins are KeepsAb only (Dense / Sliding / Sparse, plus the grouped ones above); there is no SwapsAb E4M3 MLA generation cubin. Non-grouped FP8 MLA generation on SM107 therefore goes to NVRTC and fails with `Array.cpp:376 Out-of-bound access` (#20377, case 2, including the 2048-query-token shape). I think the two are likely the same coverage gap seen from two sides: shapes without an E4M3 cubin fail in NVRTC, and the existing grouped E4M3 cubins hang when 64 % numHeadsQ != 0. The only FP8 MLA generation path that works on SM107 right now seems to be grouped selection with 4/8/16/32 heads per rank.

**Workaround** (removes the hang in our runs). In `AttentionOp::mlaGeneration` (TRTLLM-Gen path), when the selected kernel is grouped E4M3, Q is decode-size (<= 16 tokens) and `64 % numHeadsQ != 0`: copy Q into a zero-padded `[numTokens, nextPow2(numHeadsQ), 576]` FP8 buffer, run the FMHA with `mNumHeadsQ = mNumHeadsQPerKv = nextPow2(numHeadsQ)` and a padded BF16 output, then copy the real heads of O back (two small row-copy kernels; MLA heads are independent, so padded heads only produce output that is dropped). Not used when softmax stats, attention sinks or an output scale-factor buffer are requested. I have not opened a PR for it: it only matters once grouped selection is enabled (#15009, #20375, #20376), so it would be dead code on main as is; it could go in together with that change.

Possible proper fixes: (a) make the E4M3 grouped kernels handle a partial last tile like the BF16 ones; (b) build the Q TMA box from whole tokens rounded up, with OOB fill and row masking; (c) exclude such head counts from grouped selection for FP8 (on SM107 this currently lands on the NVRTC failure in #20377, so it needs that fixed too).

**End-to-end with the workaround** (one serving run, TP8 over 2 nodes, 8 query tokens per step, batch 1; the build also includes the split-KV reduction change from #20380; bf16 KV vs fp8 KV):

- Without the workaround: all ranks hang in the first generation warmup, as above. With it: startup completes, including CUDA graph capture for batch 16..1; no new errors in the logs.
- Decode step period (median, ms), bf16 KV -> fp8 KV: 2K 12.57 -> 12.64, 32K 12.87 -> 12.85, 128K 13.62 -> 13.39.
- Per MLA call (8 query tokens, 1 sequence): BF16 grouped with 12 heads vs FP8 grouped with 16 padded heads: 2K 12.16 v

items.title: [DCP] `dcp.save` silently keeps one rank's copy when values under the same key differ across ranks, e.g. RNG state
items.author: Qinyu-Xu
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.distributed.checkpoint.save` treats a value under the same key on every rank as replicated. It keeps only one rank's copy and drops the others (see #120356). When the value is per-rank state, for example Python or NumPy RNG state, every rank restores that one copy on load, and the other ranks' state is lost.

In the example below, each rank seeds Python's `random` with `1234 + rank` and saves its state under the key `rng`. After loading, all four ranks restore rank 0's state.

```python
import os, random, tempfile
import torch.distributed as dist
import torch.distributed.checkpoint as dcp
import torch.multiprocessing as mp


def run(rank, path):
    os.environ.update(MASTER_ADDR="localhost", MASTER_PORT="29513")
    dist.init_process_group("gloo", rank=rank, world_size=4)
    random.seed(1234 + rank)

    dcp.save({"rng": random.getstate()}, checkpoint_id=path)
    expected = random.random() 

    state = {"rng": random.getstate()}
    dcp.load(state, checkpoint_id=path)
    random.setstate(state["rng"])
    got = random.random()

    print(f"rank {rank}: expected {expected:.4f}  got {got:.4f}", flush=True)
    dist.destroy_process_group()


if __name__ == "__main__":
    mp.spawn(run, args=(tempfile.mkdtemp(),), nprocs=4)
```

Output:

```
rank 0: expected 0.9665  got 0.9665
rank 1: expected 0.9086  got 0.9665
rank 2: expected 0.5334  got 0.9665
rank 3: expected 0.1487  got 0.9665
```

#### Why this matters

Saving RNG state is meant to make a resumed run continue exactly like an uninterrupted one. However, when every rank's RNG state collapses to one rank's, exact continuation no longer holds. RLinf ran into this problem and fixed it in RLinf/RLinf#1570. They report that their original checkpoint "restored incorrect rank RNG streams and diverged during continuation".

Also, in some setups, ranks are seeded differently so that dropout masks or MoE router noise are independent across ranks. After the collapse, all ranks draw the same values, so this independence is lost. For example, Megatron-LM seeds its RNG per rank for independent MoE router noise. NVIDIA/Megatron-LM#6858 fixed a resume that restored other ranks' streams in its own checkpoint format, and left a TODO for the same defect in its `fsdp_dtensor` format, which saves with `dcp.save`([source](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM/blob/3914483fd325e053797aff3fa431d4a3141139aa/megatron/training/checkpointing.py#L573-L577)).

#### Where it happens

When building its save plan, every rank adds a write request for each value, so every rank asks to write `rng`:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/54b9926ebf45a422247d8a72011dcbde9eb90f3d/torch/distributed/checkpoint/default_planner.py#L555-L559

The coordinator then removes duplicates in `dedup_save_plans`. It groups requests by key alone and keeps only one rank's request for each key:

https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/54b9926ebf45a422247d8a72011dcbde9eb90f3d/torch/distributed/checkpoint/_dedup_save_plans.py#L36-L55

#### Expected behavior

1. Warn when values under the same key differ across ranks. Each rank could hash its non-tensor values while building its local plan. The hashes would travel with the local plans that are already gathered on the coordinator, so the coordinator could compare them cheaply.
2. Document the requirement. The documentation should state that values under the same key must be identical on every rank.

### Versions

items.title: [RFC] Make generic code paths device-agnostic: remove hardcoded CUDA-specific assumptions to support third-party accelerator backends
items.author: jishuangfeng
items.body_excerpt:
Author
@jishuangfeng 
@dingsheng758 

## Summary

PyTorch provides the `PrivateUse1` extension point, which allows out-of-tree (OOT) accelerator backends to register device modules, `DeviceInterface`, autocast rules, and so on. In practice, however, a large amount of **generic** framework code still hardcodes CUDA-specific assumptions:

- Closed device whitelists such as `("cuda", "xpu")`, `["cuda", "xpu", "mtia"]`, `{"cuda", "cpu", "xpu", "hpu", "mps"}`;
- `"cuda"` as a default device, or unconditional calls to `torch.cuda.*`;
- Per-device if/elif branches and "probe xpu first, then fall back to cuda" style environment probing;
- Device-specific components statically bound, with no registration extension point.

For OOT accelerator backends, the consequences are: features silently skipped, state already collected but discarded by gating (a few of these are latent correctness bugs that affect even in-tree devices), `torch.compile` behavior diverging from eager, and backend authors being forced to copy whole modules or monkey-patch internal functions.

Based on our hands-on decoupling experience with a `PrivateUse1` backend, this issue categorizes the problem space into **three major categories** and proposes a recommended decoupling approach for each. All proposals rely only on mechanisms that already exist in-tree — `torch.accelerator.*`, `DeviceInterface` + `get_interface_for_device()`, `get_registered_device_interfaces()`, `register_*()` registries, and `_get_custom_mod_func` auto-discovery — without introducing new core abstractions. The added surface is limited to thin capability-declaration hooks and explicit registration functions (Proposals 1-B / 1-D), all of which reuse the existing `DeviceInterface` / registry patterns.

**Problem overview:**

| # | Category | Typical pattern | Typical symptom for OOT backends |
|---|----------|-----------------|----------------------------------|
| 1 | Hardcoded whitelists | Feature gating enumerates a fixed device set | Silently excluded from features; state collected but discarded by gating; forced to monkey-patch multiple namespaces just to opt in |
| 2 | Hardcoded device branches | Per-device if/elif chains and environment probing | Branches cannot be extended to new backends; wrong device selected on mixed-backend machines; heuristics never take effect for new backends |
| 3 | Hardcoded device API calls | Generic paths directly call `torch.cuda.*` | Blocked, crashed, or silently falling back to CPU; other in-tree devices cannot reuse the logic either |

Each proposal below is a small, self-contained change with zero behavior change for in-tree devices (CUDA/CPU/XPU/MPS/MTIA); unregistered devices take the default path unless they explicitly opt in.

## Category 1 — Hardcoded whitelists

**Problem.** Feature gating and per-device behavior heuristics enumerate fixed device sets, or branch on `is_cuda` / `is_xpu` flags. This implicitly assumes that "the set of backends is closed". Consequences:

- Newly registered backends are silently excluded from features (RNG state usage, compile support checks, attention validation, quantization fusion, mkldnn fusion, ...);
- In some places, state has already been collected for all accelerators but is then discarded by whitelist gating — for example, RNG state is already collected for all accelerators via `torch.accelerator`, yet a hardcoded `{"cuda", "xpu"}` gate decides that this state is never used and silently falls back to CPU state. **This is a latent correctness bug, not just a missing feature**;
- Closed, literal capability sets are **imported by value** into multiple namespaces, so OOT backends must monkey-patch multiple places to opt in — fragile and error-prone.

**Typical patterns:**

```python
# Pattern A: closed set for feature validation
supported_devices = {"cuda", "cpu", "xpu", "hpu", "mps"}

# Pattern B: module-level constant tuple
GPU_BENCHMARK_DEVICE_TYPES = ("cuda", "xpu", "mtia")
def _get_default_gpu_device_type() -> str:
    avail_gpus = [
        device_type
        for device_type in GPU_BENCHMARK_DEVICE_TYPES
        if getattr(torch, device_type).is_available()
    ]
    if len(avail_gpus) > 1:
        raise AssertionError(
            f"expected at most one available GPU type, got {avail_gpus}"
        )
    return "cuda" if len(avail_gpus) == 0 else avail_gpus.pop()

# Pattern C: inline set membership check
if self._device.type in {"cuda", "xpu"}:
    ...

# Pattern D: closed capability set imported by value + gating
from .utils import SUPPORTED_MKLDNN_DEVICES   # ("cpu", "xpu")
if get_device_type(x) not in SUPPORTED_MKLDNN_DEVICES:
    raise AssertionError(...)

# Pattern E: the same feature whitelisted in multiple places with inconsistent sets
x.device.type in ("cpu", "cuda")          # check site 1
x.device.type in ("cpu", "cuda", "xpu")   # check site 2
```

**Proposed decoupling approaches.**

### Proposal 1-A: registry-derived predicates

Replace literal tuples with predicates that query the device registry. For example, delegate to the existing `torch._inductor.utils.get_gpu_type()` — this function enumerates all registered backend devices via `get_registered_device_interfaces()`, based on `DeviceInterface.is_gpu()`. Any backend that registers a `DeviceInterface` whose `is_gpu()` returns `True` is discovered automatically, with no per-feature registration step.

```python
def _get_default_gpu_device_type() -> str:
    from torch._inductor.utils import get_gpu_type

    return get_gpu_type()
```

### Proposal 1-B: registry + public `register_*()` API (capability gating with explicit backend opt-in)

Replace the hardcoded whitelist with a registry seeded with the original whitelist contents, and expose a public registration API so that a backend can opt in with a single call in its own initialization code:

```python
# In the library: default registry = a snapshot of the original whitelist; in-tree behavior is byte-for-byte identical
_WOQ_INT8PACK_FUSION_DEVICES = {"cpu

items.title: [MPS] `index_reduce` amax/amin fail to propagate NaNs for float16 and float32
items.author: jianzhi-1
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

On MPS, `torch.index_reduce` with `reduce="amax"` or `"amin"` does not propagate NaNs for `torch.float16` and `torch.float32`. `torch.bfloat16` behaves correctly.

The observation is that, given an array with `NaN` present,
1. CPU always returns `NaN`
2. MPS returns a finite value within the array OR the reduction identity (i.e. `-inf` or `+inf`) depending on the argument `include_self: bool` (`True` and `False` respectively).

To reproduce:

```python
import torch

print(torch.__version__)
print("MPS available:", torch.backends.mps.is_available())

cases = (
    (float("nan"), 1.0, True),
    (1.0, float("nan"), True),
    (1.0, float("nan"), False),
)

for dtype in (torch.float16, torch.float32, torch.bfloat16):
    for reduce in ("amax", "amin"):
        for base, src, include_self in cases:
            outputs = []
            for device in ("cpu", "mps"):
                x = torch.tensor([base], dtype=dtype, device=device)
                source = torch.tensor([src], dtype=dtype, device=device)
                index = torch.tensor([0], device=device)
                result = torch.index_reduce(
                    x,
                    0,
                    index,
                    source,
                    reduce=reduce,
                    include_self=include_self,
                )
                outputs.append(result.cpu().tolist())

            print(
                dtype,
                reduce,
                base,
                src,
                include_self,
                "CPU:", outputs[0],
                "MPS:", outputs[1],
            )
```

Expected output:

The CPU and MPS results should both contain NaN in every case.

Actual output:

```text
float16 amax nan 1.0 True   CPU: [nan] MPS: [1.0]
float16 amax 1.0 nan True   CPU: [nan] MPS: [1.0]
float16 amax 1.0 nan False  CPU: [nan] MPS: [-inf]
float16 amin nan 1.0 True   CPU: [nan] MPS: [1.0]
float16 amin 1.0 nan True   CPU: [nan] MPS: [1.0]
float16 amin 1.0 nan False  CPU: [nan] MPS: [inf]

float32 amax nan 1.0 True   CPU: [nan] MPS: [1.0]
float32 amax 1.0 nan True   CPU: [nan] MPS: [1.0]
float32 amax 1.0 nan False  CPU: [nan] MPS: [-inf]
float32 amin nan 1.0 True   CPU: [nan] MPS: [1.0]
float32 amin 1.0 nan True   CPU: [nan] MPS: [1.0]
float32 amin 1.0 nan False  CPU: [nan] MPS: [inf]

bfloat16 amax nan 1.0 True  CPU: [nan] MPS: [nan]
bfloat16 amax 1.0 nan True  CPU: [nan] MPS: [nan]
bfloat16 amax 1.0 nan False CPU: [nan] MPS: [nan]
bfloat16 amin nan 1.0 True  CPU: [nan] MPS: [nan]
bfloat16 amin 1.0 nan True  CPU: [nan] MPS: [nan]
bfloat16 amin 1.0 nan False CPU: [nan] MPS: [nan]
```

### Preliminary investigation

The culprit is `aten/src/ATen/native/mps/kernels/Indexing.metal:IndexReduceOp`. The templates `amin` and `amax` uses Metal built-ins `min` and `max` instead of PyTorch's c10 metal operations (i.e. `c10::metal::min` and `c10::metal::max`). The native Metal kernels do not support NaN propagation in these cases. Using the `c10::metal` versions allow NaN to be propagated correctly. 

The apparent cause is `IndexReduceOp` in `aten/src/ATen/native/mps/kernels/Indexing.metal`:

```metal
return min(a, b); // return c10::metal::min(a, b);
return max(a, b); // return c10::metal::max(a, b);
```

Should be a simple fix - I can get it.

### Agent details

This initial analysis, reproduction matrix, and proposed fix were prepared with Codex. I've updated the issue description to make it more intuitive.

items.title: [RFC]: Support Encode/Prefill/Decode (EPD) Disaggregation in AIBrix Gateway
items.author: varungup90
items.body_excerpt: ### Summary This RFC proposes adding Encode/Prefill/Decode (EPD) disaggregation support to AIBrix Gateway. Today, AIBrix supports Prefill/Decode (PD) disaggregation. With growing multimodal workloads, the encoding stage can also become a significant and independently scalable part of inference. EPD disaggregation separates inference into three stages: * Encode (E): Process multimodal inputs such as image, video, or audio and generate intermediate representations. * Prefill (P): Process prompt tokens and encoder outputs and generate KV cache. * Decode (D): Perform autoregressive token generation. The Gateway should become aware of these worker roles and route requests to the appropriate Encode, Prefill, and Decode worker pools. ### Motivation Encode, Prefill, and Decode have different compute and memory characteristics. Running all stages on the same workers can lead to resource contention and makes it difficult to scale each stage independently. EPD disaggregation enables: * Independent scaling of Encode, Prefill, and Decode workers. * Better resource utilization for multimodal workloads. * Different hardware or parallelism configurations for each stage. * Isolation of expensive multimodal encoding from Prefill/Decode workloads. * Reuse of the existing AIBrix PD routing architecture for multimodal serving. vLLM has started supporting disaggregated encoder architectures, including EPD-style deployments: * https://docs.vllm.ai/projects/ascend/en/latest/user_guide/feature_guide/epd_disaggregation.html * https://docs.vllm.ai/en/stable/features/disagg_encoder/ ### Proposed Change Extend AIBrix Gateway’s existing PD disaggregation support to understand an additional Encode worker role. Conceptually: For multimodal requests, the Gateway should: 1. Identify compatible Encode, Prefill, and Decode workers. 2. Select workers using the existing AIBrix load-balancing framework. 3. Pass the required routing/transfer metadata to the inference engine. 4. Allow the inference engine and its connectors to handle encoder-output and KV-cache transfers. For text-only requests, the Encode stage can be bypassed and existing PD routing can continue to be used. The implementation should reuse the existing PD routing infrastructure as much as possible rather than introducing a separate routing architecture. Initial Scope * Add encode as a supported worker role alongside prefill and decode. * Discover and maintain Encode/Prefill/Decode worker pools. * Extend PD routing to select a compatible E/P/D execution path. * Support multimodal requests requiring an Encode stage. * Keep encoder-output and KV-cache transfer outside of the Gateway. * Add basic stage-level routing metrics and failure handling. Future work can explore encoder-cache-aware routing, heterogeneous hardware selection, and independent autoscaling of E/P/D worker pools. Open Questions * Should Encode workers be shared across multiple Prefill/Decode pools? * What metadata should the Gateway provide to coordinate encoder-output transfer? * Should worker selection happen in E → P → D order, or should Decode/Prefill capacity drive the selection first? * How much of the existing PD router can be generalized into an EPD stage-aware router? ### Alternatives Considered _No response_ ### Area Not sure

items.title: [Bug] /v1/messages/count_tokens returns 501 through the gateway
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` can't be used through the gateway. vLLM and SGLang both serve it next to `/v1/messages`, and it's what the Anthropic SDK calls for `client.messages.count_tokens()`.

The request does reach the gateway plugin, because it matches the `/v1/messages` PathPrefix on both the reserved route and the per-model routes. But `validateRequestBody` matches paths exactly and has no case for it, so the plugin answers `501 unknown request path`.

Adding the case alone isn't enough. The response is just `{"input_tokens": N}`, with no `model` or `usage`, so `processLanguageResponse` treats it as an unknown response and replaces it with a 500. `/tokenize` ran into the same thing and is excluded in `isLanguageRequest` for that reason (#2732).

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Deploy a vLLM model behind the gateway.
2. Send `POST /v1/messages/count_tokens` with `{"model": "<model>", "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": "hi"}]}`.
3. The gateway returns 501 `unknown request path`.

I hit both the 501 and the 500 in unit tests against main (9190b145). I haven't run it on a live cluster.

### Expected behavior

The request is routed by `model` like `/v1/messages`, and the engine's response is passed back unchanged. There's nothing to meter, since the endpoint only counts tokens.

### Environment

- AIBrix version: main (9190b145)
- LLM(s) being used: vLLM, SGLang

Area: Gateway

items.title: [Bug] Evicting one branch of the Preble prefix tree drops pods from its parent prefix
items.author: hmdsefi
items.body_excerpt:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

`LPRadixCache.evictNode` in `pkg/utils/prefixcacheindexer/tree.go` removes the evicted node's pods from every parent node. It does not check whether another child of that parent still has the pod.

prefix-cache-preble records the target pod on every node of the request's path (`PostRouteUpdate`), so a parent prefix lists every pod that cached any of its branches. When one branch expires, the parent and the root lose those pods, even if another branch on the same pod is still cached. Requests that share the parent prefix then no longer match that pod, and the router falls back to cost-based routing.

## Steps to Reproduce

Unit level, with `NewLPRadixCache(2)`:

1. `AddPrefix([1 2 3], "m1", "default/p1")`, `AddPrefix([1 2 4], "m1", "default/p1")` and `AddPrefix([1 2 4], "m1", "default/p2")`. The tree is `[1 2]` with the children `[3]` and `[4]`.
2. Make only the `[4]` node older than the 5 minute TTL and call `Evict(time.Now())`.
3. Call `MatchPrefix([1 2 9], "m1", [p1, p2])`.

At d0500b03 it returns the matched tokens `[1 2]` and no pods.

## Expected behavior

`[1 2]` should still match p1, which still caches `[1 2 3]`. p2 only had `[1 2]` through the evicted branch, so it is right to drop p2.

## Environment

- AIBrix version: main at d0500b03
- Deployment environment: unit test of pkg/utils/prefixcacheindexer
- Cloud provider (if applicable): n/a
- LLM(s) being used: not model specific
- Client library version (if applicable): n/a

## Area

Gateway

I'd like to fix this. I have a change with tests ready and will open a PR.

items.title: [Bug] A recovered Batch job past its window with no execution metadata never finishes expiring
items.author: Jackmeson1
items.body_excerpt:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

An in-progress Batch job that is already past its completion window when the metadata service recovers it, and that has no execution metadata (`status.execution is None`), never finishes expiring. It stays `in_progress` with the `expired` condition set, and clients keep seeing `in_progress`.

On recovery, `job_committed_handler` (`python/aibrix/aibrix/batch/batch_manager.py:554` at `99325e7`) does not schedule overdue work and calls `expire_job` instead. For an in-progress job, `expire_job` (line 1184) persists the expired condition and leaves finalization to the live driver it then signals. A recovered job has no driver. The orphan cleanup path that would finish it runs only when `job_expired.status.execution is not None` (line 1258). Every later expiry pass from the scheduler then returns early, because the job is already `IN_PROGRESS` with `EXPIRED` (line 1215). Nothing else owns the job, so it never becomes terminal.

The same recovery with `execution = {}` (not `None`) does finish `expired`, and an overdue `created` job finalizes `expired` as expected (`batch-api.rst:147` documents expiry after the window).

## Steps to Reproduce

From `python/aibrix` at `99325e7`, put this in `tests/batch/` and run it with `pytest`:

<details><summary>test_overdue_recovery.py</summary>

```python
import os
from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone

import pytest

os.environ.setdefault("SECRET_KEY", "test-secret-key-for-testing")

from aibrix.batch.batch_manager import BatchManager
from aibrix.batch.job_entity import (
    BatchJob,
    BatchJobEndpoint,
    BatchJobSpec,
    BatchJobState,
    BatchJobStatus,
    CompletionWindow,
    ConditionType,
    ObjectMeta,
    TypeMeta,
)
from aibrix.context import InfrastructureContext
from aibrix.metadata.api.v1.batch import _batch_job_to_openai_response


class _Scheduler:
    def __init__(self):
        self.appended = []

    def append_job(self, job_id):
        self.appended.append(job_id)


def _overdue_in_progress_job(job_id, execution):
    created = datetime.now(timezone.utc) - timedelta(hours=25)
    job = BatchJob(
        typeMeta=TypeMeta(apiVersion="batch/v1", kind="Job"),
        metadata=ObjectMeta(
            name=f"job-{job_id}", namespace="default", uid=f"uid-{job_id}",
            creationTimestamp=created, resourceVersion=None, deletionTimestamp=None,
        ),
        spec=BatchJobSpec(
            input_file_id=f"input-{job_id}",
            endpoint=BatchJobEndpoint.CHAT_COMPLETIONS.value,
            completion_window=CompletionWindow.TWENTY_FOUR_HOURS.expires_at(),
        ),
        status=BatchJobStatus(
            jobID=job_id, state=BatchJobState.IN_PROGRESS,
            createdAt=created, inProgressAt=created,
        ),
    )
    job.status.request_counts.total = 1
    job.status.execution = execution
    return job


@pytest.mark.asyncio
@pytest.mark.parametrize("execution", [None, {}], ids=["execution-none", "execution-empty"])
async def test_recovered_overdue_in_progress_job_expires(execution):
    manager = BatchManager(InfrastructureContext())
    scheduler = _Scheduler()
    manager.set_scheduler(scheduler)
    job = _overdue_in_progress_job(f"overdue-{execution is None}", execution)

    await manager.job_committed_handler(job)  # recovery after a restart
    await manager.expire_job(job.job_id)  # the scheduler's next expiry pass

    assert scheduler.appended == []  # overdue work is not scheduled
    current = manager._done_jobs.get(job.job_id) or await manager.get_job(job.job_id)
    assert current.status.state == BatchJobState.FINALIZED, (
        f"state={current.status.state.value} condition={current.status.condition} "
        f"client={_batch_job_to_openai_response(current).status}"
    )
    assert current.status.condition == ConditionType.EXPIRED
    assert _batch_job_to_openai_response(current).status == "expired"
```

</details>

`execution-empty` passes. `execution-none` fails with:

```text
AssertionError: state=in_progress condition=expired client=in_progress
```

The test calls the recovery handler and one more expiry pass directly; it does not restart a process against durable storage.

## Expected behavior

A recovered job past its window finishes `expired` (state `finalized`, condition `expired`, client status `expired`), the same as when it has an empty execution record or was still `created`.

## Environment

- AIBrix version: `main` at `99325e7`
- Deployment environment: Batch API, metadata service recovery; reproduced in-process on Linux, Python 3.10.12
- LLM(s) being used: none

## Area

Batch

I don't plan to send a fix for this soon, so anyone is welcome to take it. A fix probably belongs in `expire_job`: route a recovered job that has no live driver and no execution reference through the existing stopped-job finalization, without stamping `FINALIZED` directly and so bypassing output finalization.

This report was prepared with AI assistance (Claude Code); the test above was run against `main`.

items.title: [Bug] KPA panic mode never holds replicas and reports idle workloads as panic
items.author: AarnavNoble
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

KPA's panic mode doesn't behave as its code describes, and part of that code can never run. Before sending a fix I'd like to agree on which behavior is wanted, since there are two reasonable directions (below).

**1. The "no scale-down while in panic" rule is dead code.** `computeTargetReplicas` (`pkg/controller/podautoscaler/algorithm/kpa.go`) keeps the highest pod count seen during panic in `maxPanicPods` and refuses to go below it:

```go
// We do not scale down while in panic mode. Only increases will be applied.
if desiredPodCount > maxPanicPods { ... context.SetMaxPanicPods(maxPanicPods) }
desiredPodCount = maxPanicPods
```

But the context the controller passes in is `baseScalingContext`, where `GetMaxPanicPods()` returns `0` and `SetMaxPanicPods` is a no-op (`pkg/controller/podautoscaler/context/context.go`). The controller also builds a new context on every reconcile, so `InPanicMode` doesn't carry over either. Each reconcile therefore just takes `max(stable, panic)` for that reconcile, and the panic-mode recommendation can go down while still in panic. The unit tests use `mockScalingContext`, which does store `MaxPanicPods`, so they pass while production never gets this behavior.

**2. An idle workload is reported as panic.** `shouldEnterPanicMode` returns `true` whenever `StableValue <= 0`, so zero traffic (stable 0, panic 0) produces the reason `"panic mode scaling"` and the `Operating in panic mode.` log line.

**3. Panic entry doesn't use Knative's rule.** Panic is entered when `panic / stable > panicThreshold`. Knative enters panic when the panic-window pod count is at least `panicThreshold` times the ready pods (`dppc / readyPods >= panicThreshold`) and stays in it until a full stable window has passed without that. The code computes `isOverPanicThreshold` with Knative's rule but only logs it.

In practice the default 5-minute scale-down cooldown (`stabilizeRecommendation`) hides most of point 1, since it keeps the highest recommendation of the last 5 minutes anyway. With a shorter `scale-down-cooldown-window`, nothing holds replicas during a burst.

### Steps to Reproduce

Calling `KPAAlgorithm.ComputeRecommendation` the way the controller does (a fresh `NewBaseScalingContext()` per call, one `POD` metric `concurrency` with `targetValue: "10"`, default annotations):

| Call | Current pods | Stable value | Panic value | Desired | Reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4 | 10 | 25 | 8 | panic mode scaling |
| 2 | 8 | 3 | 6.5 | 6 | panic mode scaling |
| 3 | 4 | 0 | 0 | 2 | panic mode scaling |

Call 2 is still in panic (6.5 / 3 > 2) but recommends fewer pods than call 1, and `GetMaxPanicPods()` is still `0` after both calls. Call 3 has no traffic and is labeled panic.

### Expected behavior

- No `panic` label (reason, log, metrics) when there is no traffic.
- One of these for panic hold, which is what I'd like your input on:
  - **A. Implement it.** Keep panic state per PodAutoscaler across reconciles (the reconciler already keeps per-PodAutoscaler state, such as the recommendation history in `stabilizeRecommendation`, and releases it on delete), enter panic with Knative's `dppc / readyPods >= panicThreshold`, and hold the peak until a stable window passes without panic.
  - **B. Remove it.** Drop `maxPanicPods`, `GetMaxPanicPods`/`SetMaxPanicPods` and the hold logic, document that KPA scales on `max(stable, panic)` while panicking, and leave holding replicas to the scale-down cooldown.

A is closer to Knative and to KPA's docs. B is smaller and keeps one mechanism for holding replicas. I'm happy to send a PR for whichever you prefer, along with the idle-panic fix.

### Environment

- AIBrix version: `main` at 177ba311
- Deployment environment: unit-level reproduction against the KPA algorithm and the real `baseScalingContext`

### Area

Orchestration (controllers, CRDs)

items.title: [Feature][ModelClaim] Lower Retry-After for a sleeping model from 10 s to 3 s; a wake takes 2.5–3.1 s
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 Feature Description and Motivation

When a request names a sleeping ModelClaim, the gateway answers `503` with `Retry-After: 10` and asks the controller to wake the model. The wake itself takes 2.5–3.1 s, so a client that honours `Retry-After` waits 10 s for a model that has been ready for about 7 s.

We measured this through Envoy and the gateway on a single A100-40GB, sleeping each model with level-1 sleep and then sending one request:

| Model | Sleeping → Active | First 200, client retries every 1 s | First 200, client honours `Retry-After` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Qwen3-0.6B | 2.5 s | 3.05 s | 10.05 s |
| Qwen3-1.7B | 2.7 s | 3.05 s | 10.05 s |
| Qwen3-8B-FP8 | 3.1 s | 4.06 s | 10.05 s |

The claim stays in the `Sleeping` phase for the whole wake and then moves straight to `Active`, so every 503 in that window carries the sleeping-state value. In a 16-minute run with 12 models taking turns on one card, all 28 requests that found their model asleep had their first token at 10.0–10.1 s. Once awake, the engine answered them in about 40 ms.

The 10 s comes from the default `modelClaimRetryAfterSeconds` ([modelclaim_wake.go#L46](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/main/pkg/plugins/gateway/modelclaim_wake.go#L46)). `modelClaimRetryAfter` picks the value by the controller's reason only ([gateway_req_body.go#L428-L442](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/main/pkg/plugins/gateway/gateway_req_body.go#L428-L442)). A sleeping claim usually carries no reason, so it gets the same 10 s as a claim that is starting from scratch, which takes 40–53 s.

### Use Case

Long-tail models that sleep when idle and are woken by their next request: the first request after an idle period is the one users notice. Cutting its wait from 10 s to the time the wake actually takes makes request-triggered wake usable for interactive traffic.

### Proposed Solution

1. Choose the Retry-After by the binding's state as well as by its reason. A claim in the `sleeping` state with no reason gets 3 s. Everything else keeps today's values:

   | Case | Retry-After |
   | --- | --- |
   | `sleeping`, no reason (a wake in progress) | 10 s → **3 s** |
   | `activating` (a fresh start) | 10 s |
   | `WaitingForRoom`, `MakingRoom` | 20 s |
   | `Moving` | 30 s |

2. With 3 s, from the numbers above, a small model's first retry at 3 s finds it ready. An 8B model's first retry is a little early, so it succeeds on the second retry at 6 s. Either way the wait drops from 10 s to 3–6 s.

3. A client that retries earlier sends more requests while the model wakes. A retry that still finds the model asleep only costs a 503. The gateway does not ask for the same wake twice (`RequestWake` returns false for a wake already asked for).

4. Optionally make the value configurable, for example an environment variable on the gateway, so operators running larger models can raise it.

A gateway-side bounded hold would remove the client retry altogether. That is a larger change and could follow separately. Related: #2925 (declarative Wake policy), which keeps today's `OnDemand` request-triggered wake.

### Area

Gateway

items.title: `tt.scan`/`tl.cumsum` hits an internal `AddPartialReduce` assert when `num_ctas > 1`
items.author: dequeueing
items.body_excerpt:
Launching a kernel that runs `tl.cumsum` (any `tt.scan`) under a multi-CTA layout (`num_ctas >= 2`) triggers an internal consistency assertion in the scan lowering:

```
triton-opt: .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157:
void AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
```

**Expected**: either a clean diagnostic telling the user that scan is not supported under multi-CTA layouts, or correct codegen.
**Actual**: the internal assert fires. On a bare `triton-opt` run this is a `SIGABRT`; through the Python frontend the same assertion is surfaced as an opaque `RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed` after the assert text is printed, rather than a user-facing diagnostic.

The assert exists to catch a block-count mismatch, and it does — but the failure mode gives the user no hint that `num_ctas` is the problem.

This is **not** the same defect as the batched-dot `num_ctas` crash fixed by #11811 / reported in #11808. That bug lived in `TritonNvidiaGPUAssignCGALayoutsPass` (a rank mismatch while *assigning* the CGA layout). The IR reproducer below never runs that pass — the `CGALayout` is already written into the encoding and it crashes later, inside `ConvertTritonGPUToLLVM`'s scan lowering. On the Python frontend the same kernel does go through `AssignCGALayouts` successfully and only aborts at lowering. So this survives the #11811 fix; I have not rebuilt past that commit to confirm on current `main`, but the failing code path (`ScanOpToLLVM`, not `AssignCGALayouts`) is untouched by it.

## Reproducer 1 — `tl.cumsum` + `num_ctas=2`

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def scan_k(x_ptr, o_ptr, M: tl.constexpr, N: tl.constexpr, AX: tl.constexpr):
    om = tl.arange(0, M); on = tl.arange(0, N)
    x = tl.load(x_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :])
    r = tl.cumsum(x, axis=AX)
    tl.store(o_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], r)

x = torch.randn(32, 32, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
o = torch.empty(32, 32, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
scan_k[(1,)](x, o, 32, 32, 0, num_ctas=2)   # <- num_ctas=2 triggers it
```

Output (the assert message is emitted, then the pipeline reports a generic failure):

```text
python: .../ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157: ... AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
...
RuntimeError: PassManager::run failed
```

`num_ctas=1` compiles and runs correctly. The crash is independent of the scan axis and of which tensor dimension the CGA layout splits.

## Reproducer 2 — `triton-opt` (offline, no GPU)

`repro.mlir`:

```mlir
#b = #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread=[1,1],threadsPerWarp=[1,32],warpsPerCTA=[4,1],
                  order=[1,0], CGALayout=[[1,0]]}>
module attributes {"ttg.num-ctas"=2:i32,"ttg.num-warps"=4:i32,
                   "ttg.threads-per-warp"=32:i32} {
  tt.func @p(%v:tensor<32x32xf32,#b>) {
    %r = "tt.scan"(%v) <{axis = 0 : i32, reverse = false}> ({
    ^bb0(%a:f32,%b:f32):
      %s = arith.addf %a, %b : f32
      "tt.scan.return"(%s) : (f32) -> ()
    }) : (tensor<32x32xf32,#b>) -> tensor<32x32xf32,#b>
    tt.return
  }
}
```

```text
$ triton-opt repro.mlir --allocate-shared-memory-nv \
    --convert-triton-gpu-to-llvm=compute-capability=90 -o /dev/null
triton-opt: .../ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157: ... AddPartialReduce(...):
Assertion `numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelElementsPerThread *
scanElementsPerThreads == srcValues.size()' failed.
(SIGABRT, exit 134)
```

## Controls

- **`num_ctas=1`** (drop the `CGALayout`): compiles cleanly (rc 0).
- **`tt.reduce` with the same 2-CTA `CGALayout`**: compiles cleanly **and produces numerically correct output** (`tl.sum` + `num_ctas=2` matches the reference). Reduction lowering accounts for the CTA dimension; scan lowering does not.
- The assert fires for every scan configuration I tried: any scan axis, 2D or 3D tensors, `num_ctas=2` or `4`, and CGA splits on either dimension. The gap is systemic to `tt.scan` under multi-CTA, not tied to one config.
  - The **same assertion text is reached at two sites**, chosen by how many warps carry unique data along the scan axis (`axisNumWarps`). With the layouts Triton picks for the Python reproducer, `axis=0` goes through `AddPartialReduce` at `ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`, while `axis=1` on a 2D tensor (and the scan axis of a 3D tensor) takes the `axisNumWarps==1` fast path and fires the identical assert inside `AddPartialReduceOneWarp` at `ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:263`. A hand-written layout that puts several warps on the scan axis hits `:157` instead — so the site is decided by `axisNumWarps`, not by rank. Both come from the same `ScanLoweringHelper` block-count math, so the suggested fix below covers both.

<details>
<summary>Relevant native stack frames (triton-opt)</summary>

```text
#17 AddPartialReduce(...)
      .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:184:63
#21 (anonymous namespace)::ScanOpConversion::emitFastScan(
      mlir::triton::ScanOp, ..., mlir::triton::TargetInfoBase const&) const
      .../lib/Conversion/TritonGPUToLLVM/ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:522:3
#22 ConvertOpToLLVMPattern<mlir::triton::ScanOp>::matchAndRewrite(...)
#27 (anonymous namespace)::OperationLegalizer::legalize(mlir::Operation*)
```
</details>

Note on the two line numbers: the assert that fails is at **`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`** (the `numScanBlocks * ... == srcValues.size()` check). The `#17` frame prints `184:63` because `-O2` attributes the inlined cold `__assert_fail` block to the next source line — the `__assert_fail` call is preceded by `mov $0x9d, %edx` (`0x9d = 157`), confirming the assert's own line argument is 157. The `#18–#20` frames are inlined `SmallVector` destructors on the same PC, not real calls.

## Root cause

`AddPartialReduce` (`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157`) asserts:

```cpp
assert(numScanBlocks * numParallelBlocks * parallelE

comments.author: he-yufeng
comments.body:
Verified against current main (`aad2a60d9`, local `triton-opt` built with `TritonRelBuildWithAsserts`, pinned LLVM 24.0.0git): this is fixed by #11990.

Running the exact pipeline from the report (`--allocate-shared-memory-nv --convert-triton-gpu-to-llvm=compute-capability=90`):

| config | result |
|---|---|
| repro as posted (scan axis 0, `CGALayout=[[1,0]]`, split along the scan axis) | clean `error: TODO: unsupported scan layout`, exit 1, no assert |
| scan axis 1, split along axis 1 | same clean error |
| scan axis 0, `CGALayout=[[0,1]]` (split along the non-scan axis) | compiles, exit 0 |
| scan axis 1, split along axis 0 | compiles, exit 0 |
| `num_ctas=1` control | compiles, exit 0 |

No SIGABRT anywhere. The two assert sites (`ScanOpToLLVM.cpp:157` and `:263`) are still in the tree but no longer reachable from these inputs. The mechanism matches the #11990 description: scan-axis CTA splits now fail `ScanLoweringHelper::isSupported()` via `getCTASplitNum(...)[axis] != 1`, and non-scan-axis partitions use the per-CTA shape in `getNonAxisNumBlocks()` / `getAxisBlockStride()`, which is what the assert's block-count product needed.

One observation in case anyone touches this code: the rejection text is the pre-existing placeholder `TODO: unsupported scan layout`, which does not tell the user that `num_ctas` is the trigger. Not worth a PR on its own, but if the scan-axis case is meant to stay unsupported, naming the cause there would save the next person a source build.

Suggest closing this as fixed by #11990.
