items.title: [Perf][SM103] MLA ragged prefill (trtllm-gen): runtime is flat in query count at fixed KV — chunked prefill (small q over long KV) up to 10x behind FA4
items.author: brandonfzhang
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary

On captured MLA context-chunk prefill traffic (Kimi-K3 geometry), FlashInfer's
trtllm-gen ragged prefill shows a shape pathology: **its runtime is nearly constant
in the number of queries at a fixed KV length** (~965 µs at KV 66304 whether q is
128 or 640), as if the kernel's work scales with KV rather than q. FA4 scales with
q, so on the chunk-append regime — small/medium q against a long accumulated KV,
which is where chunked prefill lives — FI is **5–10x behind**. On the big causal
self-chunk FI actually *wins* (214 vs 268 µs at q=kv=16384). Cell-level, FI's best
prefill form is 1.14x (bf16) / 1.19x (fp8-KV) behind the best rival,
GPU-time-weighted over the captured traffic.

Both references are public: FA4 is `flash_attn/cute` in Dao-AILab/flash-attention
(and the kernel SGLang's Kimi fork dispatches); `tokenspeed-mla` is on PyPI (MIT)
and leads the fp8-KV leg.

## Environment

- NVIDIA GB300 (SM103); CUDA 13.0; FlashInfer 0.7.1rc5
- Timing: CUPTI device time, 20 interleaved rounds, SM clock locked 2070 MHz,
  fp64 reference gates
- Shapes captured from live serving of the published Kimi-K3 GB300 recipes

## Exact call parameters

Ragged (varlen) MLA context-chunk attention, un-absorbed form: `num_q_heads=12`
(per-rank shard), `d_qk=192` (128 NoPE + 64 RoPE), `d_v=128`, bf16 q/kv,
`batch_size=1` varlen, `return_lse=True`; `is_causal=False` for chunk-append rows
(q attends to the accumulated prefix), `True` for self-chunk rows. FI candidate:
the trtllm-gen ragged prefill entry; rival: FA4 varlen at identical signatures.

## Measurements (µs; total_q / total_kv are the exact varlen lengths)

| total_q | total_kv | causal | FI trtllm-gen | FA4 | FI behind |
|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 59 | 44800 | no | 656.3 | 69.9 | **9.4x** |
| 128 | 12416 | no | 188.1 | 32.6 | 5.8x |
| 128 | 66304 | no | 969.1 | 95.5 | **10.1x** |
| 256 | 66304 | no | 966.4 | 206.9 | 4.7x |
| 512 | 66304 | no | 969.3 | 395.7 | 2.4x |
| 640 | 66304 | no | 964.0 | 396.4 | 2.4x |
| 1831 | 66304 | no | 928.9 | 901.4 | 1.03x |
| 16128 | 66304 | no | 2851.3 | 2777.3 | 1.03x |
| 16384 | 16384 | yes | 214.4 | 267.9 | **FI 1.25x ahead** |

Note the FI column at kv=66304: 969 / 966 / 969 / 964 µs for q = 128…640 — flat in
q, converging with FA4 only once q is large enough that both kernels are KV-bound.
The causal self-chunk row shows the kernel is competitive when q ≈ kv.

## Ask

Make the ragged prefill cost scale with q at small q (tile/CTA scheduling over the
q dimension, or an early-exit split over KV): the chunk-append regime is the
steady state of chunked prefill, and it is the single largest attention-side loss
we measured for FlashInfer on this platform.

## Related

- #6489 / #6485 (CAKE Rubin ragged-sequence kernels — adjacent, training-side)

items.title: gemma4:26b concurrent decode loses EOS (length at num_predict); qwen3.8-27b IDENTICAL dual on same GB10/Ollama harness is 3/3 clean
items.author: scottmcmorrow

items.title: [Bug]: classic RDMA context disabled by PORT_ERR never recovers when PORT_ACTIVE isn't seen
items.author: ironashram
items.body_excerpt:
### Bug Report

## Summary

A local IB port flapped three times for about 7 s each. Every classic-engine `WorkerPool` on that HCA processed the first `IBV_EVENT_PORT_ERR`, disabled its context and disconnected all endpoints. No further async event was ever logged for that HCA, including the `PORT_ACTIVE` 7 s later, although the port has been ACTIVE ever since. The context stayed inactive for 43 minutes, until the process was restarted. All KV transfers needing that rail failed for that whole time.

In the classic engine, a context disabled by a fatal async event can only come back through the `IBV_EVENT_PORT_ACTIVE` branch of `WorkerPool::handleContextEvent()`. Nothing re-checks the port afterwards. #3799 added exactly that safety net (`Workers::resumePausedContexts()`, a 1 Hz `ibv_query_port` poll) to TENT only. The classic `WorkerPool` on main still has no fallback.

## Environment

- Mooncake `mooncake-transfer-engine-cuda13` 0.3.13.post1 (pip wheel), classic `rdma_transport` (no `MC_USE_TENT`)
- SGLang PD disaggregation with the Mooncake KV transfer backend and Mooncake Store (HiCache)
- 8x B200 per node, 8x ConnectX-7 (MT4129) NDR 400G IB rails per node, firmware 28.47.2682
- Host: kernel 7.0.0-38-generic, DOCA-OFED 26.04-1.1.0 (`mlx5_core` 26.04-1.1.0)
- Container userspace: rdma-core / libibverbs1 50.0-2ubuntu0.2
- `MC_PKEY_INDEX=1`

## Timeline (UTC)

Kernel journal on the node with the failing HCA (`mlx5_0`). Nothing in the window for any other HCA on that node.

```
12:46:19 mlx5_core 0000:18:00.0 mlx5_0: Port: 1 Link DOWN
12:46:26 mlx5_core 0000:18:00.0 mlx5_0: Port: 1 Link INIT
12:46:26 mlx5_core 0000:18:00.0 mlx5_0: Port: 1 Link DOWN
12:46:26 mlx5_core 0000:18:00.0 mlx5_0: Port: 1 Link ACTIVE
12:46:39 mlx5_core 0000:18:00.0 mlx5_0: Port: 1 Link DOWN
12:46:46 mlx5_core 0000:18:00.0 mlx5_0: Port: 1 Link INIT
12:46:46 mlx5_core 0000:18:00.0 mlx5_0: Port: 1 Link DOWN
12:46:46 mlx5_core 0000:18:00.0 mlx5_0: Port: 1 Link ACTIVE
12:51:38 mlx5_core 0000:18:00.0 mlx5_0: Port: 1 Link DOWN
12:51:45 mlx5_core 0000:18:00.0 mlx5_0: Port: 1 Link INIT
12:51:45 mlx5_core 0000:18:00.0 mlx5_0: Port: 1 Link DOWN
12:51:45 mlx5_core 0000:18:00.0 mlx5_0: Port: 1 Link ACTIVE
```

The port has stayed ACTIVE since 12:51:45: `state` 4, `link_downed` unchanged, symbol / receive / link-recovery / integrity error counters all 0.

Mooncake, in the engine processes using `mlx5_0`. There are five `WorkerPool`s on that HCA (one per transfer-engine instance in the pod), and each logged exactly this once:

```
W1015 12:46:19.248450  3526 worker_pool.cpp:1014] Worker: Received context async event unknown for context mlx5_0
W1015 12:46:19.250267  3526 worker_pool.cpp:1014] Worker: Received context async event port error for context mlx5_0
I1015 12:46:19.373971  3526 worker_pool.cpp:1087] Worker: Context mlx5_0 is now inactive due to fatal event: 10
```

From 12:46:19 until the restart at about 13:29, those processes logged no other `Received context async event`, no `scheduled recovery probe` and no `is now active after recovery delay` line for `mlx5_0`. That covers the two later flaps and all three link-ups. Every async event read is logged at WARNING (`worker_pool.cpp:1014`), so no event for that context was read after 12:46:19.

Peers kept hitting the dead rail:

```
E1015 12:46:22.928117  3542 worker_pool.cpp:654] Worker: Process failed for slice (opcode: 0, source_addr: 0x..., length: 17408, dest_addr: 0x..., local_nic: mlx5_1, peer_nic: <peer>@mlx5_0, dest_rkey: ..., retry_cnt: 0, max_retry_cnt: 9): transport retry counter exceeded
W1015 12:46:22.928141  3542 worker_pool.cpp:1395] Rail paused: peer=<peer>@mlx5_0 error_count=5 pause_ms=30000
```

On the SGLang side that showed up as a steady rate of `KVTransferError: Decode instance could be dead, remote mooncake session ... failed` and `Failed to get kvcache from prefill instance`, mostly on the DP rank bound to `mlx5_0`, for the 43 minutes until the restart. The restarted process came up on the same HCA and transfers have succeeded since.

## Code analysis (main at 3aa0f716)

- `WorkerPool::handleContextEvent()`: `IBV_EVENT_PORT_ERR` (and DEVICE_FATAL, CQ_ERR, WQ_FATAL, LID_CHANGE) clears `recovery_activate_after_ns_`, calls `context_.set_active(false)` and `disconnectAllEndpoints()`.
- The only thing that arms recovery for that state is the `IBV_EVENT_PORT_ACTIVE` branch, which calls `scheduleContextRecovery()`. `maybeActivateRecoveredContext()` (called on every `monitorWorker()` iteration) does nothing while `recovery_activate_after_ns_` is 0.
- There is no `ibv_query_port` in the classic `worker_pool.cpp`. The calls in `rdma_context.cpp` are in GID reprobe / refresh and in device open only.
- #3559's TTL reactivation applies to breaker-disabled contexts only. Its description says fatal async events own the inactive state.
- #3799 fixed both halves of this for TENT: it drains the async fd, and it adds a 1 Hz `ibv_query_port` resume for paused contexts. The classic engine already drains (`doProcessContextEvents()` loops to EAGAIN), but it never got the poll.
- #3523 (defect C) says the classic engine is protected because its monitor worker "unconditionally re-activates contexts every second". That doesn't match v0.3.12, v0.3.13.post1 or main: since the delayed recovery from #2959, a fatal-event-disabled classic context is re-enabled only by `PORT_ACTIVE`.

## What we don't know yet

We can't tell from the logs whether `PORT_ACTIVE` was never delivered to these processes or delivered and never read. The fd is drained to EAGAIN, so the edge-triggered race fixed in #3799 for TENT doesn't explain it. Either way, one missed event leaves the context dead for the life of the process.

Two smaller observations, in case they're relevant:
- The `unknown` event right before `PORT_ERR`. Our libibverbs 50.0 has no name for it, so it's presumably an event type newer than rdma-core 50 delivered by the 7.0 / DOCA-OFED 26.04 kernel. We haven't decoded its numeric type.
-

items.title: torch.fx.Tracer.record_stack_traces is broken in torch 2.4.0
items.author: gilfree
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

`torch.fx.Tracer` has a `record_stack_traces` member. It does not give the correct stack trace, starting with torch  2.4 RC.

I am not sure it is part of the external API, but it was nice to have. The following is working in 2.3, but broken in 2.4RC


```python
import torch.fx
class M1(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = torch.nn.Linear(1, 1)
    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.linear(x)
class M2(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.m1 = M1()
    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.m1(x)
m = M2()
tracer = torch.fx.Tracer()
tracer.record_stack_traces=True
graph = tracer.trace(m)
sym=torch.fx.GraphModule(m,graph)
print(sym.print_readable())
assert 'code: return x + self.linear(x)' in sym.print_readable()
assert 'code: return x + self.m1(x)' in sym.print_readable()
```

It was broken in this PR: https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/pull/121449/ where you stopped using the find_user_frame (or an equivalent function) to filter non user stack traces.

Something along these lines can be probably used as a fix:

```python
    def create_proxy(self, kind, target,args, kwargs, name, type_expr = None, proxy_factory_fn = None):
....
     if self.record_stack_traces and not proxy.node.stack_trace:
            proxy.node.stack_trace = _find_user_frame2_4(''.join(CapturedTraceback.extract().format()))


    def _find_user_frame2_4(self, stack_trace):
        stack_trace=stack_trace.split('\n')
        if 'torch/fx/proxy.py' in stack_trace[-3]:
            stack_trace=stack_trace[:-1]
            while len(stack_trace)>2 and '/fx/' in stack_trace[-2]:
                stack_trace=stack_trace[:-2]
        return '\n'.join(stack_trace)
```

Notes:
- I am not sure why you don't see the effect in `torch.export.export`.
- `torch.export.unflatten` looses stack trace for collapsed modules.

items.title: [Bug] NVGPUWarpSpecialization: `Unexpected op` in backward-slice when `tl.gather` feeds `tl.dot` (sm90)
items.author: dequeueing
items.body_excerpt:
## Summary
A `tl.gather` result used as a `tl.dot` operand inside `tl.range(..., warp_specialize=True)` aborts the `NVGPUWarpSpecialization` pass at `WSDataPartition.cpp:330` (`llvm_unreachable("Unexpected op")`) during backward-slice partitioning — `tt.gather` is not in the op whitelist. `num_ctas=1`, `num_warps=4`.

## Reproducer
Save the following script as `repro.py` and run with `python repro.py`:

```python
import torch, triton, triton.language as tl

@triton.jit
def k(a_ptr, b_ptr, c_ptr, M: tl.constexpr, N: tl.constexpr, K: tl.constexpr):
    om = tl.arange(0, M); on = tl.arange(0, N); ok = tl.arange(0, K)
    acc = tl.zeros([M, N], dtype=tl.float32)
    for i in tl.range(0, 4, warp_specialize=True):
        a = tl.load(a_ptr + om[:, None] * K + ok[None, :] + i * M * K)
        b = tl.load(b_ptr + ok[:, None] * N + on[None, :] + i * K * N)
        idx = tl.full([M, K], 1, tl.int32)
        a = tl.gather(a, idx, axis=1)          # gather result feeds tl.dot
        acc += tl.dot(a, b)
    tl.store(c_ptr + om[:, None] * N + on[None, :], acc)

M = N = K = 128
a = torch.randn(4 * M * K, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
b = torch.randn(4 * K * N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float16)
c = torch.empty(M * N, device="cuda", dtype=torch.float32)
k[(1,)](a, b, c, M, N, K, num_ctas=1, num_warps=4)
```

## Crash
Expected: the kernel compiles and runs (as it does when `warp_specialize=True` is removed), or fails with a user-facing diagnostic. Actual: compiler crashes with an internal assertion/error.

```
UNREACHABLE executed at <triton_src>/third_party/nvidia/hopper/lib/Transforms/WarpSpecialization/WSDataPartition.cpp:330!
```

## Root cause
`getBackwardSliceToPartition`'s op whitelist does not include `tt.gather`; reaching it hits `llvm_unreachable` rather than a graceful "unsupported" diagnostic. The identical kernel compiles and runs normally when `warp_specialize=True` is removed.

## Environment
Triton `42c5e89c3` (2026-09-11, `TritonRelBuildWithAsserts`), NVIDIA H800 (sm_90a), `num_ctas=1`, `num_warps=4`. Deterministic.

items.title: [AMD] CoalesceAsyncCopy produces a layout the direct-to-LDS lowering cannot coalesce when a warp spans more than the fastest shared dimension
items.author: bogdan-petkovic
items.body_excerpt:
### Describe the bug

### Describe the bug

`TritonAMDGPUCoalesceAsyncCopy` can rewrite an async copy into a src layout that the direct-to-LDS lowering then rejects on GFX9. It happens when the blocked order and the shared order differ and a warp has more lanes than the fastest shared dimension has elements.

For a swizzled shared encoding the pass distributes the lanes and warps along the shared order and then rebuilds the blocked encoding with the original blocked order (added in #10928). The order of a blocked encoding also decides how the lanes are linearized, so once the lanes span more than one dimension, the first lanes walk along the dimension that is strided in LDS and the writes are no longer coalesced. This only works while all lanes of a warp fall in the fastest shared dimension, like the 64x2 tile in the tests of #10928.

The existing test `async_copy_different_order` in `test/TritonGPU/amd/amd-coalesce-async-copy.mlir` already shows it. Its expected layout, `threadsPerWarp = [32, 2], warpsPerCTA = [1, 4], order = [1, 0]` for an `order = [0, 1]` shared layout, fails the same way when it is lowered.

### Reproducer

Triton main at 20d9d98fead78c2f65e1b3ba5a7881d86a836dad. No GPU needed, this is a compile failure.

`repro.mlir`, a 16x4 f32 copy with 2 warps on gfx950:

```mlir
#blocked = #ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [1, 1], threadsPerWarp = [16, 4], warpsPerCTA = [2, 1], order = [1, 0]}>
#shared = #ttg.swizzled_shared<{vec = 1, perPhase = 1, maxPhase = 1, order = [0, 1]}>
#smem = #ttg.shared_memory
module attributes {"ttg.num-ctas" = 1 : i32, "ttg.num-warps" = 2 : i32, "ttg.target" = "hip:gfx950", "ttg.threads-per-warp" = 64 : i32} {
  tt.func @copy(%input: tensor<16x4x!tt.ptr<f32>, #blocked> {tt.contiguity = dense<[1, 4]> : tensor<2xi32>, tt.divisibility = dense<[16, 16]> : tensor<2xi32>, tt.constancy = dense<[1, 1]> : tensor<2xi32>},
                %view: !ttg.memdesc<16x4xf32, #shared, #smem, mutable>) {
    %token = ttg.async_copy_global_to_local %input, %view : tensor<16x4x!tt.ptr<f32>, #blocked> -> <16x4xf32, #shared, #smem, mutable>
    tt.return
  }
}
```

```
triton-opt repro.mlir --tritonamdgpu-coalesce-async-copy=gfx-arch=gfx950 --allocate-shared-memory --convert-triton-amdgpu-to-llvm=gfx-arch=gfx950
```

```
repro.mlir:7:14: error: cannot lower 'ttg.async_copy_global_to_local' to a direct-to-LDS copy: the resulting writes into shared memory are not coalesced for a vectorization of 1 element(s). Adjust the blocked or shared encoding so each warp writes a contiguous range.
```

CoalesceAsyncCopy rewrites the src to `#ttg.blocked<{sizePerThread = [1, 1], threadsPerWarp = [16, 4], warpsPerCTA = [1, 2], order = [1, 0]}>`. Lanes 1 to 3 then take the next columns, 16 elements apart in LDS. The same tile with `order = [0, 1]` lowers to a single buffer load to LDS:

```
sed 's/warpsPerCTA = \[2, 1\], order = \[1, 0\]/warpsPerCTA = [1, 2], order = [0, 1]/' repro.mlir > shared-order.mlir
triton-opt shared-order.mlir --allocate-shared-memory --convert-triton-amdgpu-to-llvm=gfx-arch=gfx950
```

And the existing test case:

```
awk 'BEGIN{RS="// -----\n"} /async_copy_different_order/' test/TritonGPU/amd/amd-coalesce-async-copy.mlir > different-order.mlir
triton-opt different-order.mlir --tritonamdgpu-coalesce-async-copy=gfx-arch=gfx942 --allocate-shared-memory --convert-triton-amdgpu-to-llvm=gfx-arch=gfx942
```

fails with the same error.

### How we hit it

In rocmlirTriton (https://github.com/ROCm/rocmlirTriton) a non-power-of-two K tile is split into power-of-two segments, so a K tile of 36 has a last segment of 4. For f32 convolutions on gfx950 with an M tile of 16 or 32 the copy of that segment is a 16x4, 32x2 or 16x8 tile, which is exactly this case. Our weekly tuning ran into it on 677 configs. We disabled those tile sizes on gfx950 for now.

In our tree, falling back to the shared order when the rebuilt encoding cannot be lowered fixed all of them and left the code of every config that already compiled unchanged. We did not send that as a PR because it calls `canLoadDirectToLDS` from the pass, and a fix that builds the right layout up front seems preferable. Happy to test any fix.


### Environment details

Triton main at 20d9d98fead78c2f65e1b3ba5a7881d86a836dad, built from source with CMake (TritonRelBuildWithAsserts, nvidia and amd backends, only the triton-opt target) against the prebuilt LLVM from cmake/llvm-info.json (b010a18d2b648cab83c83967ff26b8fde11acdc6). Ubuntu 22.04.5 on x86_64, GCC 11.4.

No GPU is needed, this is a compile failure in triton-opt and the target comes from gfx-arch (gfx950 for the reproducer, gfx942 for the existing test case). We first hit it compiling f32 convolutions for gfx950 in rocmlirTriton, whose vendored Triton has the same CoalesceAsyncCopy code.

Picking this up. I read the pass and the mechanism checks out: the swizzled branch distributes lanes along the shared order and then stamps the original blocked order back on, which re-linearizes the lanes. Once a warp spans more than the fastest shared dimension, consecutive lanes walk a dim that is strided in LDS, and the rewritten copy is exactly what the direct-to-LDS lowering rejects.

items.title: [Tracking][Spec Decode] Adaptive DSpark Bring-Up Tracker
items.author: benchislett
items.body_excerpt: Tracking issue to organize the adaptive verification support for DSpark speculative decoding ## Backend Support Adaptive verification has a firm requirement that the attention backend must not use the CPU-side query lengths as a source-of-truth, instead using the gpu tensors (so that we can run the confidence-based assignment on the GPU without synchronizing the CPU). Additionally, kernels must be able to support decode batches where requests have different query lengths per request. Currently, the following backends are known to support variable lengths: - FLASH_ATTN - DSV4 Attention **TODO**: - Hybrid / Linear attention (requires significant effort) - - Mamba (for NVIDIA Nemotron models) - - GDN (for Qwen3.x models) - - Kimi KDA (for Kimi K3) - DSV3-style MLA - FlashInfer GQA: - - TRTLLM kernel support exists, just needs to be plugged into vLLM. Minor change. - - CUTLASS backend of FlashInfer may need additional support to avoid the cpu query lengths ## Online Profiling The initial version does profiling at startup to estimate the verification step time by replaying the recorded CUDA graphs. This is known to have some drift: We want to extend this to fully online profiling in the future. However, there are some challenges that make this tricky: - Online profiling may lead to "dead spots": one-time latency spikes make a certain batch size appear unattractive, leading to the adaptive verifier to never select that batch size, which leads to negative feedback and stale data limiting our range of profiled values. Generally there is an "exploration vs exploitation" problem here, as well as a requirement for some way to detect and eliminate outliers (such as those caused by JIT compilation) - Variable sequence lengths make it hard to measure a single reliable estimate of execution time for a given number of tokens. In practice we will want some way to account for this: either tracking measured points in 2D (num_tokens, max_seq_len or mean_seq_len), or estimating the overhead added per-token of KV reads ## Tuning Confidence Scores The confidence scores are not always perfectly calibrated. In particular, it seems like the deeper positions have higher variance and some bias in their expectation. The DSpark paper suggests [Sequential Temperature Scaling (STS)](https://arxiv.org/html/2607.05147v1) as an online solution to calibrating these estimates. I did not see much benefit when adding this feature, but we should experiment more thoroughly and assess the potential benefit of improved confidence estimates. Here are the results from one run with DSV4-Flash-0731: ## First-Class Observability ### Exposing Timings and Adaptive-SD Metrics Now that we are profiling different phases of the worker execution (model runner, proposer), and tracking the step time by batch size, we will want to expose these to the user for observability. This will help with performance tuning and development, as well as for monitoring of production deployments at scale. We will want to propagate the metrics to both the prometheus / frontend, as well as to the iteration-level logging feature. We will also want some way to report our other metrics for adaptive verification: confidence success rate (mismatch between "expected" AL and "achieved" AL), performance model reliability (difference between "expected" step time and "actual" step time), etc. ### Benchmarking Compatibility Adaptive speculative decoding will change what it means for speculative decoding to have high acceptance rate. AL is no longer a "golden" metric for success. As a start, this PR enables detailed, per-request and per-step speculative decoding metrics to be exposed in the OpenAI response. This can be used to report exact speculative decoding statistics and aggregated on the client to fit the use-case. https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/48915 ## Feature Compatibility - [ ] Logprob extraction support ([see here](https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/47808#discussion_r3723768178))

items.title: VisitorRowReduction::Callbacks::reduction is declared to return ElementCompute but has no return statement
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`VisitorRowReduction::Callbacks::reduction` in `include/cutlass/epilogue/threadblock/fusion/visitor_store.hpp` (lines 551-560) is declared to return `ElementCompute` but contains no `return` statement; control flows off the end of a non-void function, which is undefined behavior. Compilers flag it (`-Wreturn-type` / nvcc equivalent).

The result is currently benign because the only call site (line 508) discards the return value. The function also duplicates the existing shared helper `fragment_reduce` (line 214) that the Col and Scalar reduction visitors already use at lines 330 and 748.

### Suggested fix

Either change the signature to `void`, or delete the private duplicate and call `fragment_reduce<RegReduceFn, RoundStyle>(reduce_buffer, result)` like the sibling visitors.

items.title: numeric_limits constants wrong for float_ue8m0_t::lowest, tfloat32_t::epsilon and half_t::epsilon
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

Three `numeric_limits` members return values inconsistent with the types' own encodings. Each was checked by compiling against include/ only and printing the results.

#### 1. `float_ue8m0_t::lowest()` returns the maximum magnitude

`include/cutlass/float8.h` lines ~1482 and ~1638 (std and platform specializations):

```cpp
static cutlass::float_ue8m0_t lowest() { return cutlass::float_ue8m0_t::bitcast(0xfe); }
```

`0xfe` is exponent 254, i.e. +2^127 - the same value as `max()`. For this unsigned format the smallest finite value is `bitcast(0x00)` = 2^-127 (`BitRepresentation::MIN_VALUE == 0`). This looks like a copy of the signed e4m3 constant into a signless type.

```
ue8m0 lowest=1.70141e+38 min=1.17549e-38 max=1.70141e+38 ; lowest<=min -> VIOLATED
```

Any code seeding a min-reduction or clamping with `lowest()` starts from +2^127 instead of 2^-127; `ue8m0` is the MX block-scale type, so scale-selection code is exposed.

Fix: `bitcast(0x00)` in both specializations (or derive from `BitRepresentation::MIN_VALUE`). Related but distinct from the FP6 `lowest()` report (#3493), which covers `float_subbyte.h`.

#### 2. `tfloat32_t::epsilon()` is a subnormal garbage constant

`include/cutlass/tfloat32.h` line ~312:

```cpp
static cutlass::tfloat32_t epsilon() { return cutlass::tfloat32_t::bitcast(0x1000); }
```

`0x00001000` decodes to a denormal (~1.4e-41). TF32 has 10 mantissa bits, so machine epsilon is 2^-10 (fp32 bits `0x3A800000`). The comment above it even says "smallest finite value", which suggests the member's intent drifted.

```
tf32 epsilon=0 bits=00001000 ; expected 2^-10 ~ 0.000976562
```

Fix: `bitcast(0x3A800000)`.

#### 3. `half_t::epsilon()` is off by 2x

`include/cutlass/half.h` lines ~618 and ~686 (both specializations):

```cpp
static cutlass::half_t epsilon() { return cutlass::half_t::bitcast(0x1800); }
```

`0x1800` = 2^-9. fp16 declares `digits == 10`, so machine epsilon should be 2^-10 = `0x1400`. The sibling `bfloat16_t` is internally consistent (digits 7, eps 2^-7):

```
half epsilon=0.00195312 (expected 2^-10 = 0.0009765625) ; bf16 epsilon=0.0078125 (correct)
```

Fix: `bitcast(0x1400)` in both places.

items.title: zipped/tiled divide with a dynamic tiler skips divisibility checks on static layouts and returns a non-size-preserving layout
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

When a zipped/tiled divide receives a *dynamic* tiler against a *fully static* layout, the divisibility requirement is checked nowhere, and the result is a silently non-size-preserving layout.

```cpp
#include "cute/layout.hpp"
#include <iostream>
int main() {
    using namespace cute;
    auto L = make_layout(make_shape(_12{}, make_shape(_4{}, _8{})),
                         make_stride(_7{}, make_stride(_1{}, C<30>{})));
    auto d = zipped_divide(L, 128);   // 128 does not divide size(L) == 384
    print(d);
    print(" size="); print(size(d));   // 288
}
```

Actual output:

```
((12,4,2),(1,1,3)):((_7,_1,_30),(896,11,90))
 size=288
```

`size(d) == 288 != size(L) == 384`, strides run past the layout's cosize (896), and no diagnostic of any kind fires. Each individual configuration is handled correctly on its own:

- fully static tiler: compile-time `static_assert` fires ("Shape Divisibility Condition"),
- fully dynamic operands: the runtime assert catches it,
- mixed static layout / dynamic tiler: the static path's runtime check is compiled out (the shapes are static, so the dynamic assert sees nothing to test) and the static check cannot see the dynamic tiler, so every guard is skipped.

The Python port asserts on the same input, which highlights the gap when cross-checking.

### Suggested fix

In the mixed case, emit a runtime divisibility check (or a `CUTE_GCC_UNREACHABLE`-style guarded assert) comparing the dynamic tiler size against the known static layout size before performing the division, so misuses fail loudly instead of producing layouts whose size differs from the input.

items.title: maximum_active_blocks wrappers pass int into CudaHostAdapter* and no longer compile
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

Since 3.4, `GemmUniversalBase::maximum_active_blocks` takes a `CudaHostAdapter*`:

```cpp
// include/cutlass/gemm/device/gemm_universal_base.h:350
static int maximum_active_blocks(CudaHostAdapter *cuda_adapter = nullptr)
```

but the 2.x-style device wrappers still declare the pre-3.4 signature `(int smem_capacity = -1)` and forward the int into that pointer parameter, which does not convert:

```cpp
static int maximum_active_blocks(int smem_capacity = -1) {
  return UnderlyingOperator::maximum_active_blocks(smem_capacity);   // int -> CudaHostAdapter*: error
}
```

Calling any of these wrappers fails to compile:

```
error: argument of type "int" is incompatible with parameter of type "cutlass::CudaHostAdapter *"
```

Affected call sites (all forwarding `smem_capacity`):

- `gemm/device/gemm_universal.h:393-394`
- `gemm/device/gemm_universal_adapter.h:738-739` (2.x alias path)
- `gemm/device/rank_k.h:462`
- `gemm/device/rank_2k.h:499`
- `gemm/device/symm.h:554`
- `gemm/device/gemm_universal_with_broadcast.h:337`
- `gemm/device/gemm_universal_streamk_with_broadcast.h:337`
- `gemm/device/gemm_universal_with_absmax.h:355`
- `gemm/device/gemm_with_k_reduction.h:366`
- `gemm/device/gemm_layernorm_mainloop_fusion.h:336-337`

The 3.x adapter (`gemm_universal_adapter.h:270`) already updated its own declaration correctly (`maximum_active_blocks(int /* smem_capacity */ = -1)` ignoring the value), so only these forwarders were missed. Nothing in-tree calls them anymore (the profiler moved to the new API), which is why CI does not see it.

Reproduction: compile a TU that calls e.g.

```cpp
#include "cutlass/gemm/device/gemm.h"
using Gemm = cutlass::gemm::device::Gemm<float, cutlass::layout::ColumnMajor,
                                         float, cutlass::layout::ColumnMajor,
                                         float, cutlass::layout::RowMajor>;
int n = Gemm::maximum_active_blocks();
```

with nvcc or g++ against the current headers; it errors at the forwarded argument.

### Suggested fix

Drop the unused parameter in the ten wrappers to match the base signature (`maximum_active_blocks()` with no arguments), mirroring what `gemm_universal_adapter.h:270` already does.

items.title: EllGemm ColumnMajor-output workspace sizing uses the unswapped problem shape and undersizes split-K semaphores
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`device::EllGemm` computes its split-K semaphore workspace size from an unswapped problem shape, while `initialize()` builds the launch grid from the swapped one, so for rectangular problems on ColumnMajor outputs the workspace is sized for a different grid than the one that runs.

```cpp
// include/cutlass/gemm/device/ell_gemm.h:747-753  (get_workspace_size)
cutlass::gemm::GemmCoord tiled_shape = threadblock_swizzle.get_tiled_shape(
  args.problem_size,                       // (m, n, k)
  {ThreadblockShape::kM, args.ell_blocksize, ThreadblockShape::kK},
  args.split_k_slices);
...
bytes += sizeof(int) * size_t(tiled_shape.m()) * size_t(tiled_shape.n());

// include/cutlass/gemm/device/ell_gemm.h:768-773  (initialize)
cutlass::gemm::GemmCoord grid_shape = threadblock_swizzle.get_tiled_shape(
  {args.problem_size.n(), args.problem_size.m(), args.problem_size.k()},   // transposed
  {ThreadblockShape::kM, args.ell_blocksize, ThreadblockShape::kK},
  args.split_k_slices);
```

The transpose is intentional at the launch site (the kernel consumes the swapped convention), but the sizing call must match it. Arithmetic example with `ThreadblockShape = 128x128x32`, `split_k_slices = 4`, `m = 264`, `n = 136`: sizing yields `tiled_shape.m() * n() = 15 * 2 = 30` semaphores (120 bytes after the ell-block N scaling), while the launched grid is built from `(136, 264)` and needs `18` tiles along one axis instead of `15`, i.e. more semaphore slots than were allocated and zeroed. The reverse aspect ratio over-allocates harmlessly; the bad direction gives an undersized, partially uninitialized semaphore buffer feeding split-K accumulation.

The RowMajor-output specialization does not swap and is consistent.

### Suggested fix

Pass the same swapped problem shape to `get_tiled_shape` inside `get_workspace_size`:

```cpp
threadblock_swizzle.get_tiled_shape(
  {args.problem_size.n(), args.problem_size.m(), args.problem_size.k()}, ...)
```

items.title: [BUG] Constexpr missing in dynamic control-flow regions
items.author: nodeeeeee
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

## Motivation

I encountered this while implementing FlashAttention. The implementation naturally groups the load and MMA paths into JIT methods on a compile-time configuration object, and selects between them using the runtime warp index. A reduced version looks like this:

```python
class FlashAttention:
    @cute.jit
    def load(self, tensor, pipeline):
        ...

    @cute.jit
    def mma(self, tensor, pipeline):
        ...


@cute.jit
def fa4_device_body(
    fa: cutlass.Constexpr[FlashAttention],
    tensor: cute.Tensor,
    storage,
):
    warp_idx = cute.arch.make_warp_uniform(cute.arch.warp_idx())

    pipeline = make_pipeline(
        storage=storage,
        num_stages=fa.num_stages,
    )

    if warp_idx < 4:
        cute.arch.setmaxregister_decrease(fa.num_producer_regs)
        fa.load(tensor, pipeline)
    else:
        cute.arch.setmaxregister_increase(fa.num_mma_regs)
        fa.mma(tensor, pipeline)
```

Here, `self` in `FlashAttention.load()` and `FlashAttention.mma()` is a compile-time method receiver. The `fa` parameter in `fa4_device_body()` refers to the same kind of compile-time object, made explicit by its `Constexpr` annotation.

Writing the device body as an actual instance method makes this code compile, but only because the compiler has a special case that excludes a receiver whose name is literally `self`. Passing the same object as a named `Constexpr[FlashAttention]` parameter should have equivalent staging semantics, but currently does not.

## Problem

CuTe DSL treats `Constexpr[T]` parameters as compile-time Python meta values. They do not have an MLIR representation and must not become arguments or results of runtime control-flow regions.

However, when a method is called through a `Constexpr` receiver inside a dynamic `if`, the receiver is incorrectly captured as a region argument:

```python
class Receiver:
    @cute.jit
    def store(self, output):
        ...


@cute.kernel
def kernel(receiver: cutlass.Constexpr[Receiver], output: cute.Tensor):
    tidx, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()

    if tidx == Int32(0):
        receiver.store(output)
```

The region analyzer currently treats the base object of every method call as a mutable runtime value, except when its name is literally `self`.

Consequently, `receiver` is added to the values carried through the dynamic `if`. Lowering then attempts to flatten the plain Python `Receiver` instance into MLIR values and fails with:

```text
error[TYPE_DYNAMIC_EXPR_UNSUPPORTED]:
A value carried through this `if` is a plain Python value (Meta value)
(a `Receiver`) that cannot be turned into a Runtime value (Staged value)
```

This means `self.method()` works because of the existing `self` special case, while an explicitly annotated `receiver: Constexpr[Receiver]` does not, despite having the same staging semantics.

## Root cause

`Constexpr` is a property of the original function parameter binding. The AST preprocessor removes parameter annotations while transforming the function, so the later control-flow region analysis no longer knows which names refer to `Constexpr` parameters.

`RegionAnalyzer.visit_Call()` therefore sees only a method call on a Python object and adds its receiver to `invoked_args`.

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL 4.7/4.8 regression: FlashAttention-4 SM100 forward kernel spills registers (0 -> 176 B) vs 4.5.1, ~3% slower on B300
items.author: zpcore
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

With identical kernel source, CuTe DSL 4.7.x/4.8.0 generates PTX for the FlashAttention-4 SM100 forward kernel (`flash_attn.cute.flash_fwd_sm100.FlashAttentionForwardSm100`) that spills registers, where CuTe DSL 4.5.1 generated PTX that does not. The kernel is at the 128-register cap in both cases (512 threads per CTA), so the extra pressure becomes local-memory spills. The varlen causal fwd+bwd step is about 2–3% slower on B300.

The regression is in the generated PTX, not in ptxas: the 4.8.0 PTX still spills when assembled with the older ptxas 13.2, while the 4.5.1 PTX assembled with that same ptxas does not.

**Resource usage, same FA4 source (`fa4-v4.0.0.beta16`), same quack-kernels 0.4.1, sm_103a**

| Kernel | CuTe DSL 4.5.1 | CuTe DSL 4.8.0 |
|---|---|---|
| `FlashAttentionForwardSm100` | 128 regs, 0 B stack, 0 spill stores/loads, 5272 SASS instr | 128 regs, **112 B stack, 176 B spill stores / 176 B spill loads** (44 STL / 33 LDL), 5768 SASS instr |
| `FlashAttentionBackwardSm100` | 128 regs, 8 B stack, 1 STL / 5 LDL | 128 regs, 24 B stack, 24 B spill stores / 60 B spill loads (4 STL / 13 LDL) |

MMA (`UTCHMMA`/`UTCQMMA`), `MUFU`, and packed FP32 (`FFMA2`/`FMUL2`/`FADD2`) instruction counts in the forward kernel are identical between the two versions, so the difference is spill traffic rather than different math.

**PTX vs ptxas cross-check (forward kernel PTX from `CUTE_DSL_KEEP=ptx`)**

| PTX from | assembled with | Result |
|---|---|---|
| CuTe DSL 4.5.1 (PTX ISA 9.1) | ptxas 13.1 and 13.2 | 0 B stack, 0 B spills |
| CuTe DSL 4.8.0 (PTX ISA 9.4, `.version` lowered to 9.2) | ptxas 13.2 | 112 B stack, 176 B spill stores / 176 B spill loads |

Neither PTX contains `.local` declarations, so the spills are introduced by ptxas from register pressure in the 4.8.0 PTX.

`CUTE_DSL_COMPILER_OPT="remarks{ptx}"` with `CUTE_DSL_LINEINFO=1` on 4.8.0 reports the spills for both forward and backward, and marks `flash_attn/cute/tile_scheduler.py:923` (the varlen scheduler's `_get_num_m_blocks`, loading `cu_seqlens`) as the likely pressure region.

**Timing (B300, varlen causal, bf16, head_dim 128, fwd+bwd, median of 20 steps after 3 warmups, runs interleaved on one GPU)**

| Shape | CuTe DSL 4.5.1 | CuTe DSL 4.8.0 |
|---|---|---|
| 8192 tokens × 32 heads, 4 docs | 1.206–1.245 ms | 1.222–1.234 ms |
| 32768 tokens × 32 heads, 8 docs | 5.300–5.329 ms | 5.486–5.488 ms (+3%) |
| 32768 tokens × 16 heads, 1 doc | 12.35–12.38 ms | 12.71–12.84 ms (+3%) |

CuTe DSL 4.7.0 and 4.7.1 (measured with quack-kernels 0.6.5) show the same slowdown as 4.8.0. The current FA4 release (`fa4-v4.0.0.beta32`) with quack-kernels 0.6.5 on CuTe DSL 4.8.0 is within noise of beta16 on 4.8.0, so the difference tracks the DSL version, not the FA4 or quack version. I could not test 4.5.3 or 4.6.x with this FA4 source (import errors unrelated to the kernel), so the regression landed after 4.5.1 and by 4.7.0.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

1. Environment: NVIDIA B300 SXM6 (sm_103a), driver 590.48.01, PyTorch 2.11 (CUDA 13.0), Python 3.12.
2. FA4 source: `Dao-AILab/flash-attention` at tag `fa4-v4.0.0.beta16`, installed with `pip install --no-deps --no-build-isolation flash_attn/cute`.
3. Install `quack-kernels==0.4.1` (`--no-deps`) and one of:
   - `nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.5.1` with `nvidia-cutlass-dsl-libs-cu13==4.5.1` (apache-tvm-ffi 0.1.6)
   - `nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.8.0` with `nvidia-cutlass-dsl-libs-cu13==4.8.0` (apache-tvm-ffi 0.1.11)
4. Run the script below with `CUTE_DSL_KEEP=ptx,cubin CUTE_DSL_DUMP_DIR=<dir>`, then `cuobjdump --dump-resource-usage <dir>/*flash_fwd_sm100*.cubin`.

quack-kernels 0.4.1 annotates with `cute.core.ThrMma`/`ThrCopy`, which 4.8.0 exposes only on `cute`; the script aliases them so the same quack source imports on both DSL versions.

```python
import importlib.metadata as md
import json
import sys

import torch
import cutlass.cute as cute

for _name in ("ThrMma", "ThrCopy", "TiledMma", "TiledCopy"):
    if not hasattr(cute.core, _name) and hasattr(cute, _name):
        setattr(cute.core, _name, getattr(cute, _name))

from flash_attn.cute.interface import flash_attn_varlen_func


def bench(total, heads, head_dim, docs):
    torch.manual_seed(0)
    q, k, v = (
        torch.randn(total, heads, head_dim, device="cuda", dtype=torch.bfloat16, requires_grad=True) for _ in range(3)
    )
    cu = torch.linspace(0, total, docs + 1, device="cuda").round().to(torch.int32)
    max_seqlen = int((cu[1:] - cu[:-1]).max())

    def step():
        out = flash_attn_varlen_func(
            q, k, v, cu_seqlens_q=cu, cu_seqlens_k=cu, max_seqlen_q=max_seqlen, max_seqlen_k=max_seqlen, causal=True
        )
        out = out[0] if isinstance(out, tuple) else out
        out.float().square().mean().backward()

    for _ in range(3):
        step()
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    times = []
    for _ in range(20):
        start, end = torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True), torch.cuda.Event(enable_timing=True)
        start.record()
        step()
        end.record()
        torch.cuda.synchronize()
        times.append(start.elapsed_time(end))
    return round(sorted(times)[10], 3)


shapes = [(8192, 32, 128, 4), (32768, 32, 128, 8), (32768, 16, 128, 1)]
print(json.dumps({
    "cutlass_dsl": md.version("nvidia-cutlass-dsl"),
    "gpu": torch.cuda.get_device_name(),
    "median_ms": {f"{t}x{h}h_d{d}_{n}docs": bench(t, h, d, n) for t, h, d, n in shapes},
}))
```

**Expected behavior**

CuTe DSL 4.8.0 generates PTX for this unchanged kernel source with register pressure comparable to 4.5.1, so the forward kernel does not spill and runs at 4.5.1 speed. If this is a deliberate lowering change, guidance on a compile option or kernel-side change that avoids the spill would help.

**Environment details**

- GPU: NVIDIA B300 SXM6 (sm_103a), driver 590.48.01
- CuTe DSL: 4.5.1 (good), 4.7.0 / 4.7.1 / 4.8.0 (spills), CUDA 13 libs
- ptxas used in the cross-check: 13.1, 13.2
- PyTorch 2.11, CUDA 13.0, Python 3.

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL from_dlpack rejects float8_e4m3fn tensors (dtype_map lists Float8E5M2 only)
items.author: Vinnie6167
items.body_excerpt:
## Describe the bug

`cutlass.cute.runtime.from_dlpack` rejects `torch.float8_e4m3fn` tensors:

```
KeyError: Unsupported element type in dlpack: 'Float8E4M3FN'. Supported types are:
['Bool', 'Int64', 'Int32', 'Int16', 'Int8', 'UInt64', 'UInt32', 'UInt16', 'UInt8',
 'Float64', 'Float32', 'Float16', 'BFloat16', 'Float8E5M2']
```

The runtime already decodes the DLPack type code and reports the element type as
`Float8E4M3FN` (the string comes out of `libcute_dsl_runtime.so`, which also knows
`Float8E4M3`, `Float8E4M3FNUZ`, `Float8E8M0FNU`, `Float4E2M1FN`, ...). Only the Python
lookup table in `TensorDescriptor.element_type` /
`python/CuTeDSL/cutlass/base_dsl/runtime/tensor_descriptor.py` stops at `Float8E5M2`, so
every other 8-bit float that the runtime recognizes is rejected at import time even though
`cutlass.Float8E4M3FN` is a fully supported kernel element type.

PyTorch is not the limiting side: `torch.empty(8, dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn).__dlpack__()`
succeeds on torch 2.11 and the capsule round-trips through `torch.from_dlpack`.

## Steps/Code to reproduce bug

```python
import torch
from cutlass.cute.runtime import from_dlpack

x = torch.empty(8, dtype=torch.float8_e4m3fn, device="cuda")
t = from_dlpack(x, assumed_align=16)   # KeyError: Unsupported element type in dlpack: 'Float8E4M3FN'
```

## Expected behavior

`from_dlpack` returns a `cute.Tensor` with `element_type == cutlass.Float8E4M3FN`, the same
way it does for `torch.float8_e5m2`.

## Workaround in use

Callers currently export the storage as `uint8`/`int8` and overwrite `element_type`
afterwards, e.g. FlashInfer does this in `flashinfer/gemm/kernels/bmm_fp8_blackwell.py`,
`flashinfer/attention/cute_dsl/fmha.py`, and pending PR flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#5533:

```python
t = from_dlpack(x.view(torch.uint8), assumed_align=16)
t.element_type = cutlass.Float8E4M3FN
```

Adding the missing names to the `dtype_map` (at least `Float8E4M3FN`; ideally the other
strings the runtime emits) would let these call sites drop the reinterpretation.

## Environment details

- nvidia-cutlass-dsl 4.8.0 (`nvidia_cutlass_dsl_libs_cu13-4.8.0`), and `main` as of 2026-10-07
- torch 2.11.0+cu130
- Linux x86_64, CUDA 13.0

items.title: [BUG] CuTe DSL: SIGSEGV compiling integer ** (int32/int64), including 2 ** 3
items.author: JayceSu98
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

Compiling a CUDA kernel containing `x ** y`, where both operands are loaded
from integer CUDA Tensors, terminates the Python process with SIGSEGV (exit
status 139) inside `cute.compile()`.

The reproducer uses only small positive inputs: `x = 2`, `y = 3`, with expected
output `8`. It does not involve zero bases, negative exponents, overflow, or
Python-valued constant evaluation. Compilation does not return, and the kernel
is not launched.

This reproduces for both `int32` and `int64` with native NVIDIA CuTeDSL wheels:

- **4.5.2**;
- **4.8.0 (final release, cu12)**;
- **4.8.0.dev0 (cu12)**, tested separately before checking the final release.

For 4.8.0 final, the frontend and compiler were freshly installed into an
isolated target from matching 4.8.0 wheels. No source changes or custom compiler
forks were used.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

Save this as `minimal_integer_pow.py` in an environment with native NVIDIA
CuTeDSL and CUDA-enabled PyTorch:

```python
import argparse

import cutlass
import cutlass.cute as cute
import torch
from cutlass.cute.runtime import from_dlpack


@cute.kernel
def pow_kernel(a: cute.Tensor, b: cute.Tensor, out: cute.Tensor):
    i, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()
    x = a[i]
    y = b[i]
    out[i] = x ** y


@cute.jit
def launch(a: cute.Tensor, b: cute.Tensor, out: cute.Tensor):
    pow_kernel(a, b, out).launch(grid=(1, 1, 1), block=(128, 1, 1))


def main():
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--dtype", choices=("int32", "int64"), default="int32")
    args = parser.parse_args()
    print("CuTeDSL", cutlass.__version__, flush=True)
    print("PyTorch", torch.__version__, "CUDA runtime", torch.version.cuda,
          flush=True)
    print("GPU", torch.cuda.get_device_name(0), flush=True)
    print("dtype", args.dtype, "runtime inputs: a=2, b=3", flush=True)
    dtype = getattr(torch, args.dtype)
    a = torch.full((128,), 2, dtype=dtype, device="cuda")
    b = torch.full((128,), 3, dtype=dtype, device="cuda")
    out = torch.full_like(a, -123)
    handles = [from_dlpack(t, assumed_align=16) for t in (a, b, out)]
    print("COMPILE_BEGIN", flush=True)
    compiled = cute.compile(launch, *handles)
    print("COMPILE_OK", flush=True)
    compiled(*handles)
    torch.cuda.synchronize()
    result = out.cpu()
    assert torch.equal(result, torch.full_like(result, 8)), result
    print("PASS: synchronized output = 8", flush=True)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

Run each dtype in a separate process:

```bash
python minimal_integer_pow.py --dtype int32
echo "exit=$?"
python minimal_integer_pow.py --dtype int64
echo "exit=$?"
```

Observed with 4.8.0 final:

```text
CuTeDSL 4.8.0
PyTorch 2.7.0+cu128 CUDA runtime 12.8
GPU NVIDIA A100-PCIE-40GB
dtype int32 runtime inputs: a=2, b=3
COMPILE_BEGIN
PROCESS_EXIT_STATUS 139
```

`COMPILE_OK` is never reached. The shell reports `Segmentation fault`.
The int64 case also exits with status 139 during compilation.
4.5.2 additionally prints `!!!!!!! Segfault encountered !!!!!!!`.

**Expected behavior**

The kernel should compile and produce `8` for all elements. If runtime integer
exponentiation is not supported by this compilation path, an explicit compiler
diagnostic would be preferable to a process-level crash.

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**

- Environment location: Docker, Linux x86_64.
- GPU: NVIDIA A100-PCIE-40GB (SM80).
- Python: 3.10.
- PyTorch: 2.7.0+cu128; PyTorch CUDA runtime: 12.8.
- CUDA Toolkit: 12.9.
- NVIDIA driver: 610.43.02.
- CuTeDSL: 4.5.2; 4.8.0 final with `nvidia-cutlass-dsl`, `libs-base`,
  `libs-core`, and `libs-cu12` all at 4.8.0; separately 4.8.0.dev0 cu12.
- Reproduced with file caching disabled (`CUTE_DSL_ENABLE_FILE_CACHING=0`).
- The reproducer compiles an `@cute.jit` launcher, not a bare `@cute.kernel`.

The container originally had older user-space driver libraries. Matching host
driver libraries were selected for these test processes without replacing the
system installation. The CUDA execution controls below successfully compiled,
launched, synchronized, and checked device output with that same setup.

**Additional context**

Control cases use the same Tensor-loaded inputs `2` and `3`, the same
128-thread block, and the same DLPack/compilation bridge. Successful cases
synchronize the device and check every output, rather than only compiling.

| Expression | 4.5.2 int32 / int64 | 4.8.0 final cu12 int32 / int64 |
|---|---|---|
| `x ** y` | Both SIGSEGV during compilation | Both SIGSEGV during compilation |
| `x + y`, `x * y`, `x // y`, `x % y` | Both pass | Both pass |
| `x - y`, `x / y`, `-x`, `abs(x)` | Both pass | Not tested |
| `cutlass.min`, `cutlass.max`, `==`, `<` | Both pass | Not tested |
| `&`, `\|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>` | Both pass | Not tested |
| float32 `x ** y` | Pass, output 8 | Pass, output 8 |

Integer true division controls use float32 output. These are bounded controls,
not exhaustive coverage of all scalar operations or input domains.

The 4.5.2 pre-lowering IR contains `math.ipowi` on the loaded integer values.
An earlier GDB run stops inside the native NVIDIA `_cutlass_ir.so`, but does
not provide useful symbols. We have not identified a specific internal pass
root cause or established that every affected version has the same root cause.

We found the older floating-point power discussion #2296, but it concerns
`v ** 1.3`, increased compilation time, and a suspected runtime hang, rather
than this positive-integer compilation SIGSEGV. We could not find a matching
public issue or a documented fix for this integer-power reproducer.

Could you help clarify whether Tensor-loaded integer `**` is intended to be
supported, and whether this crash matches a known issue or existing fix?

items.title: [Feature request] `torch.export` .save/.load could support `safetensors` and/or `weights_only=True`
items.author: stu-twelvelabs
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

Today, torch.export will load tensors via
```
def deserialize_torch_artifact(serialized: Union[Dict[str, Any], Tuple[Any, ...], bytes]):
    if isinstance(serialized, (dict, tuple)):
        return serialized
    if len(serialized) == 0:
        return {}
    buffer = io.BytesIO(serialized)
    buffer.seek(0)
    # weights_only=False as we want to load custom objects here (e.g. ScriptObject)
    artifact = torch.load(buffer, weights_only=False)
    assert isinstance(artifact, (tuple, dict))
    return artifact
```
Security teams really don't like this I have learned 🙂. In the interest of leveraging the awesome benefits of export more safely, it would be amazing to add optional support for any or all of `safetensors` and/or `weights_only=True`!

Thank you for all the work on `torch.export`, it has a very promising future!

### Alternatives

_No response_

### Additional context

_No response_

cc @chauhang @penguinwu @avikchaudhuri @gmagogsfm @zhxchen17 @tugsbayasgalan @angelayi @suo @ydwu4

Hi PyTorch team 👋 and @stu-twelvelabs ,

I'd like to work on this issue and propose a secure enhancement to the `deserialize_torch_artifact` function.

Intent
- Add an optional `safe: bool` parameter to control the use of `weights_only=True` in `torch.load`, which avoids deserializing pickled custom objects—helpful for security-sensitive environments.
- Add support for the `safetensors` format behind a new `use_safetensors: bool` flag, using `safetensors.torch.load` for loading serialized weights safely and efficiently.
- Preserve backward compatibility and ensure existing usage of the function remains unaffected.
- Raise a PR with clear tests and documentation for the new parameters.

This change directly addresses the security concerns mentioned in the issue. Please assign it to me if it’s available—I'd be happy to contribute this enhancement.
@pytorchbot if possible please assign the issue to me .

Thanks!

comments.author: AbhijatSaxena
comments.body:
Hi, a question about how this relates to [CVE-2026-4538](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-4538) ("deserialization in the pt2 Loading Handler", listed against 2.10.0). Scanners now flag torch 2.14.1 for it with no fixed version. The only PyTorch reference on the NVD record is #176791, which added a `weights_only` flag to `torch.export.load` and was closed by its author a week before the CVE was published, so this issue seems to be the closest place to ask.

On current main, `deserialize_torch_artifact` tries `weights_only=True` and falls back to `weights_only=False` ([serialize.py#L446-L458](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e342e9a9d7123c2b78940da0ea3fdb0dfa9beeb0/torch/_export/serde/serialize.py#L446-L458)). Pickled weights/constants are loaded with `weights_only=False` ([_package.py#L889-L895](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e342e9a9d7123c2b78940da0ea3fdb0dfa9beeb0/torch/export/pt2_archive/_package.py#L889-L895), [L947-L953](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e342e9a9d7123c2b78940da0ea3fdb0dfa9beeb0/torch/export/pt2_archive/_package.py#L947-L953)), and custom/opaque objects go through `_pickle_load_obj` / `pickle.loads` ([L970-L980](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e342e9a9d7123c2b78940da0ea3fdb0dfa9beeb0/torch/export/pt2_archive/_package.py#L970-L980)). The `torch.export.load` docstring already says "uses pickle under the hood ... Never load data from an untrusted source" ([__init__.py#L350-L351](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/e342e9a9d7123c2b78940da0ea3fdb0dfa9beeb0/torch/export/__init__.py#L350-L351)), and that warning is in 2.14.1 too.

So two questions, mainly so advisory databases can be told something definite:

1. Is that docstring warning the official position, i.e. loading `.pt2` from untrusted sources isn't supported and CVE-2026-4538 is expected behaviour rather than a bug?
2. Or is the plan to provide an opt-in safe path, along the lines of #199042 (currently open, superseding #191149), with the default flipped later as was done for `torch.load`?

Either answer would help. Thanks!

items.title: [ray.data] when using a custom filesystem the error message is wrong when aiohttp is not installed.
items.author: Mortimerp9
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

```
fs=MyFileSystem()
ray.data.read_parquet(
        pq_path,
        filesystem=fs,
    )
```
ray data will use path_util to check the filesystem:
https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/master/python/ray/data/datasource/path_util.py#L78-L91

While doing so, it will try to do `from fsspec.implementations.http import HTTPFileSystem`. This will fail if `aiohttp` has not be installed properly, however, the error message is the one prebuilt earlier, which complains about the custom fs not implementing the right API. If it can't import HTTPFileSystem, the error message should be different. It would also help to have the source exception (instead of `from None`) as this would point out to the real error from the get go.

### Versions / Dependencies

ray 2.35.0

### Reproduction script

see code snippet above: ```
fs=MyFileSystem()
ray.data.read_parquet(
        pq_path,
        filesystem=fs,
    )
```

I cannot provide the custom filesystem implementation though.

### Issue Severity

Low: It annoys or frustrates me.

comments.author: miggle711
comments.body:
I looked into this on current master.

The custom-filesystem case from the report no longer reaches the HTTP import. `_validate_and_wrap_filesystem` now raises a clear `TypeError` naming the type if the filesystem isn't a pyarrow or fsspec one, and `_get_fsspec_http_filesystem()` is only called for http(s):// paths. I never saw the reporter's filesystem, so I can't say their exact case is covered.

However, the underlying problem still exists for http(s):// paths. `_get_fsspec_http_filesystem()` in python/ray/data/datasource/path_util.py catches `ModuleNotFoundError` for the whole `fsspec.implementations.http` import and raises "Please install fsspec to read files from HTTP." from None. fsspec's HTTP module imports aiohttp at import time, so with fsspec installed and aiohttp missing (which is what `pip install "ray[data]"` gives, since the data extra has fsspec but not aiohttp), the message blames the wrong package and drops the real cause. The path is then skipped with a warning, and the user ends up with "no files found".

Proposed fix: branch on `e.name` in that except. Keep the current message for fsspec, and otherwise name the missing module and chain with `from e`. This gives what the issue asks for: a different message, with the source exception attached. 

I could make a small PR plus a unit test if the contributors agree. ;)

items.title: [Data] Add opt-in full schema inference to read_orc
items.author: jiangxt2
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

With DataSourceV2, `read_orc` infers its schema from up to 16 eligible files. A column appearing only in a later-discovered file can therefore be absent from the planned Dataset schema. Could `read_orc` offer an opt-in `merge_schema=True` argument that considers every eligible ORC file before returning the Dataset? The default should retain the current bounded sample, following the contract of Parquet PR #66522. Full inference has additional file-listing and metadata-read costs, which should be documented along with the candidate-file behavior across repeated Dataset actions. A request for full inference should be rejected clearly when DataSourceV2 is disabled.

This request concerns schema discovery. The existing nested-field reader failure on PyArrow 17 is tracked separately in #67064.

### Use case

A batch ETL job appends ORC files to a dataset over time. The dataset has more than 16 eligible files, and an optional `campaign_id` column appears only in a file outside the V2 planning sample. An analytics job needs the complete schema when constructing downstream projections and transforms; increasing the sample limit would only move the point at which a later field can be missed. An opt-in full-inference mode would let that job accept higher planning cost while keeping ordinary reads on the existing bounded path.

items.title: [Bug] Console-created deployments are not discoverable by the AIBrix data plane
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
A deployment created from the Console can reach `Ready`, and its generated Service can handle requests directly, but the AIBrix Gateway does not discover it.

The generated Pod template currently has only the Console/application labels ([code](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a40be9ba404730e4be2d2a0820942bca79275dc6/apps/console/api/deployment/provider/kubernetes.go#L633-L642)). It is missing the AIBrix model labels defined in [`pkg/constants/model.go`](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a40be9ba404730e4be2d2a0820942bca79275dc6/pkg/constants/model.go#L23-L37), such as `model.aibrix.ai/name` and `model.aibrix.ai/port`. The [mocked app manifest](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a40be9ba404730e4be2d2a0820942bca79275dc6/development/app/config/templates/deployment/deployment.yaml#L6-L23) shows the expected shape.

To reproduce:

1. Create a deployment in Console with the dev [`mock-vllm` template](https://github.com/vllm-project/aibrix/blob/a40be9ba404730e4be2d2a0820942bca79275dc6/apps/console/api/store/demo.go#L569-L590).
2. Wait for it to become ready.
3. Inspect the Pod labels with `kubectl get pods --show-labels`.
4. Port-forward the generated Service: `/v1/chat/completions` works.
5. Send the same request through the AIBrix Gateway: the model has no discovered backend.

A Console deployment reported as ready should also be callable through the AIBrix data plane.

The fix will likely need to map the Console Model's `serving_name`, the effective container port, and the template engine to the canonical AIBrix labels. Please reuse the existing label constants. If a different model-name mapping is intended, it should be documented as part of the change.

This is complete when the mock model can be deployed from Console and reached through the Gateway, with a small rendering test plus an end-to-end check.

Related: #2202, #2198

items.title: [Bug] vLLM classification models can't be reached through the gateway
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

vLLM serves its classification API at `POST /classify` (`vllm/entrypoints/pooling/classify/api_router.py`), and has done so since at least v0.9. The gateway only knows `/v1/classify`, which is SGLang's OpenAI-style route. #1905 added that path as the vLLM endpoint, but vLLM doesn't serve it.

So a vLLM classification model can't be reached through the gateway on either path:

- `POST /classify` matches no HTTPRoute, so Envoy returns 404 before the plugin ever sees it. Even with a route, `validateRequestBody` has no case for it and would answer 501.
- `POST /v1/classify` is routed, but the vLLM pod answers 404.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Deploy a vLLM sequence-classification model behind the gateway.
2. Send `POST /classify` with `{"model": "<model>", "input": "some text"}`. Envoy returns 404.
3. Send the same body to `/v1/classify`. The request reaches the pod, which returns 404.

I found this by reading the routes and code on main (9190b145) and confirmed the 501 with a unit test. I haven't run it on a live cluster.

### Expected behavior

`POST /classify` is routed by `model` to that model's pods, the same way `/tokenize` and `/pooling` are.

### Environment

- AIBrix version: main (9190b145)
- LLM(s) being used: vLLM

Area: Gateway

items.title: [Bug] Request trace never uses some log2 token buckets because the index is truncated
items.author: hmdsefi
items.body_excerpt:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

`RequestTrace.getTraceKey` in `pkg/cache/trace.go` builds the `input:output` trace key from the log2 token buckets:

```go
inputIndex := int64(inputBucket / RequestTracePrecision) // Convert to int without precision loss.
```

`getTokenBucket` rounds log2(tokens) to a multiple of 0.1, but `bucket / 0.1` is not always an exact integer in floating point, and `int64(...)` truncates. For the 4.3 bucket the quotient is `42.999999999999993`, so the index is 42. Of the indexes 0 to 200, ten are never produced (43, 81, 86, 91, 162, 167, 172, 177, 182 and 187), and their requests are counted under the index below.

This affects the trace the gateway writes for the GPU optimizer when `AIBRIX_GPU_OPTIMIZER_TRACING_FLAG` is on. The optimizer reads the index back as log2(tokens) times 10, so a 20-token request is read as about 18 tokens and a 270-token request as 256.

## Steps to Reproduce

```go
trace := cache.NewRequestTrace(0)
key, _ := trace.AddRequestTrace("req", 20, 270, "")
```

At d0500b03 `key` is `42:80`. log2(20) is 4.32 and log2(270) is 8.08, so it should be `43:81`.

## Expected behavior

The index should be the rounded bucket times 10, so every bucket can appear in the trace.

## Environment

- AIBrix version: main at d0500b03
- Deployment environment: unit test of pkg/cache
- Cloud provider (if applicable): n/a
- LLM(s) being used: not model specific
- Client library version (if applicable): n/a

## Area

Gateway

I'd like to fix this. I have a change with tests ready and will open a PR.

items.title: [Bug] VTC token tracker keeps a user under totals it no longer has after a partial prune
items.author: hmdsefi
items.body_excerpt:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

In `UpdateTokenCount` (`pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/vtc/token_tracker.go`):

```go
oldTotal := t.userTotals[user]
t.pruneExpiredBucketsAndUpdateState(user, cutoff)
totalAfterPruning := t.userTotals[user]
...
newTotal := totalAfterPruning + newTokens
t.updateUserTotalAndMinMax(user, oldTotal, newTotal)
```

When pruning removes some but not all of the user's buckets, `pruneExpiredBucketsAndUpdateState` already moves the user in `totalsToUsers` from `oldTotal` to `totalAfterPruning`. The last call then removes the user from `oldTotal`, where it no longer is, and adds it under `newTotal`. The user stays listed under `totalAfterPruning` as well.

`GetMinTokenCount` then reports a total that no user has, and the VTC router computes its bucket size, `(min + max) / 2`, from it. With steady traffic most updates prune part of the window, so `totalsToUsers` gets a new stale entry on almost every update.

## Steps to Reproduce

Tracker with a 100 ms window (`WithWindowSize(100), WithTimeUnit(Milliseconds)`):

1. `UpdateTokenCount(ctx, "user1", 100, 0)`, and a few milliseconds later `UpdateTokenCount(ctx, "user1", 30, 0)`.
2. Once the first bucket has left the window and the second has not, call `UpdateTokenCount(ctx, "user1", 50, 0)`.
3. `GetTokenCount` for user1 and `GetMaxTokenCount` are 80, but `GetMinTokenCount` is 30, and `totalsToUsers` lists user1 under both 30 and 80.

In a loop of 50 updates with 5 buckets in the window, one user ended up with 45 entries in `totalsToUsers`, and the min was 65 while the user's total was 285.

## Expected behavior

After an update the user is listed only under its current total, and the min and max come from current totals.

## Environment

- AIBrix version: main at d0500b03
- Deployment environment: unit test of pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/vtc
- Cloud provider (if applicable): n/a
- LLM(s) being used: not model specific

items.title: [Bug] Preble histogram keeps an entry for every tree node it has recorded
items.author: hmdsefi
items.body_excerpt:
## 🐛 Describe the bug

`SlidingWindowHistogram.update` in `pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms/prefix_cache_preble.go` adds the decode length of each routed request to `perNodeTotalDecodeLengths`, a map keyed by the tree node of the request's prompt.

The histogram's other maps keyed by tree node (`histogram`, `nodeToCount`, `hitTokens`, `promptTokens`, `decodingSize` and `podAllocations`) are cleaned up in two places: `removeOldEntries` when the node's entries leave the sliding window, and `removeEvictedNodes` when the prefix cache evicts the node. `perNodeTotalDecodeLengths` is cleaned up in neither, and nothing reads it.

So with prefix-cache-preble the map gets an entry for every prompt node the router records, and keeps it for the life of the gateway process. Evicted nodes stay reachable from it. Prompts are mostly distinct, so the map grows with the number of routed requests.

## Steps to Reproduce

Unit level:

1. Build the histogram as `newTestRouter` in `prefix_cache_preble_test.go` does, and add a prefix to the cache.
2. Call `update` for that node, then either `removeOldEntries` with a time past the sliding window or `removeEvictedNodes` with the node.
3. The other maps keyed by tree node no longer have the node, but `perNodeTotalDecodeLengths` still does.

## Expected behavior

Once a node's entries have expired, or the node has been evicted, the histogram should not keep the node.

## Environment

- AIBrix version: main at d0500b03
- Deployment environment: unit test of pkg/plugins/gateway/algorithms
- Cloud provider (if applicable): n/a
- LLM(s) being used: not model specific

items.title: [Bug] KV event sync never matches engine-reported prefixes with the default block size
items.author: theminjunchoi
items.body_excerpt:
With `AIBRIX_PREFIX_CACHE_KV_EVENT_SYNC_ENABLED=true`, the prefixes the engines report through KV events never match a request, at least with the default settings.

The two sides cut prompts into blocks differently. The router turns the prompt into bytes, 4 per token, and splits them every `AIBRIX_PREFIX_CACHE_BLOCK_SIZE` bytes. A BlockStored event is hashed one engine block at a time, and an engine block is `block_size` tokens. So the hashes only line up when the env value happens to be 4 × the engine's block size. For vLLM's default 16-token blocks that's 64. The code default is 16, and the gateway manifests and release overlays set 128.

Here's what `SyncPrefixHashTable` on main returns for a prompt whose blocks a vLLM pod reported, with 16-token blocks:

| AIBRIX_PREFIX_CACHE_BLOCK_SIZE | match |
|---|---|
| 16 | 0% |
| 64 | 100% |
| 128 | 0% |

Nothing logs an error. Routing still matches the hashes the router records for its own picks, so KV sync quietly behaves like the standard mode, and since those hashes never match an engine block, BlockRemoved events can't clean them up either. Setting the env to 64 doesn't really fix it. Block size depends on the model and attention backend, and one env value covers every model the gateway serves.

The events already carry the engine's block size, so the index can learn it per model and split requests to match. I have a PR ready.

items.title: [Bug] Gateway swallows ext_proc Send error when model is empty
items.author: franzego
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

Server.sendProcessingResponse in pkg/plugins/gateway/gateway.go:807 gates all Send-error handling on len(st.model) > 0. Early rejections (401 auth, unknown path, header validation) have model == "", so if srv.Send() fails (Envoy canceled/closed), the error is dropped, nil is returned, and Process loops back into Recv() on a dead stream. Transport failure is hidden; no log / send_envoy_proxy metric for those requests. 

I have a fix for this and will link a PR to it soon.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Unit: mock ExternalProcessor_ProcessServer.Send to return errors.New("transport closed"), call with processState{model: ""} — old code returns nil.
2. Live: trigger an early ImmediateResponse (bad API key) while Envoy cancels concurrently — Send returns Canceled, Process still returns nil.

### Expected behavior

Send errors always log + propagate to end the stream. Metrics + finishRequestCount stay guarded by model != "" since AddRequestCount never ran for model-less requests.

### Environment

- AIBrix version: main @ 8f50bab8
- Component: pkg/plugins/gateway

### Area

Gateway

items.title: [Bug] PD routing runs the prefill before the requestsInflight cap is checked
items.author: AarnavNoble
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

With `pd` routing and a config profile that sets `requestsInflight`, the per-replica cap is checked only after the prefill leg has already run. A request rejected with 429 still costs a full prefill, and leaves KV on the prefill pod for a decode that never comes. Before sending a fix I'd like to agree on the intended behaviour, since there are a few reasonable directions (below).

**How the two meet.** `applyConfigProfile` (`util.go`) sets the profile's strategy to `least-request` when `requestsInflight` is set. A model-wide `lockedRoutingStrategy` takes precedence over that, and so does a `routing-strategy` header, unless `authoritativeRoutingPolicy` is set. The docs' own `lockedRoutingStrategy` example is `"pd"`. So a PD model with a capped profile routes through `pd` with the cap active. Copilot's review of #2726 raised the same precedence point, asking for the limits to either override incompatible strategies or be rejected. That thread has no reply.

**Order of operations for one request** (`HandleRequestBody` → `selectTargetPod`):

1. `filterSaturatedReplicaInflight` (`gateway.go`) drops pods whose running count is already at the cap. Its comment calls it a best-effort pre-filter, with the hard cap enforced later.
2. `router.Route` → `pdRouter.Route` selects prefill and decode pods and calls `doPrefillRequest`:
   - **vLLM** (`IsAsync() == false`): the prefill HTTP call completes before `Route` returns.
   - **SGLang**, and TRT-LLM generation-first: the prefill leg is dispatched in a goroutine. For SGLang it uses `context.WithoutCancel` (the default `AsyncDispatchPolicy`).
3. Only then does `enforceReplicaInflight` (`gateway_req_body.go`) run the atomic `AdmitPodRunningRequest` on the target pod, which is the decode pod. If that pod is full, the request gets 429.

**Why the race is wide.** Between steps 1 and 3 the decode pod's count hasn't been incremented. For vLLM, that window lasts the whole prefill call. Every request that arrives during one prefill sees the same pre-increment count, passes the pre-filter for the same decode pod, and runs its own prefill. Only one fits under the cap, and the rest are rejected after their prefill has finished.

**What a rejected request costs**
- **vLLM:** a complete prefill on the prefill pod. Its KV blocks are held for a decode pull that never comes, until the engine's own KV-transfer timeout frees them.
- **SGLang:** the prefill leg isn't cancelled by the 429. It waits on a bootstrap that never comes until `AIBRIX_PREFILL_REQUEST_TIMEOUT` (30s by default). For that time the prefill pod's `PrefillRequestTracker` count stays raised, which feeds prefill selection. After the timeout it sends `/abort_request` to a decode pod that never received the request.
- **Gateway accounting is fine.** `finishRequestCount` still releases the token-load charges.

Under a burst this is load-amplifying: the pods are full, and every rejected request still adds prefill work and holds KV.

### Steps to Reproduce

Found by reading the code on `main` (a502f652). The call order is `gateway_req_body.go` (`selectTargetPod`, then `enforceReplicaInflight`) and `pd/router/router.go` (`Route`, then `doPrefillRequest`). I haven't run it on a cluster. A unit-level reproduction is straightforward with a counting prefill server, `requestsInflight: 1` and two concurrent requests: two prefill calls are made and one request gets 429. I can add that as a test.

### Expected behavior

A request that will be rejected by the decode pod's `requestsInflight` cap shouldn't start a prefill. Three options, roughly from most to least complete:

- **A. Admit the decode pod before prefill.** After `Select` picks the decode pod, `pdRouter.Route` runs the same atomic admission, through a callback the gateway puts on the routing context, before calling `doPrefillRequest`.
  - If the decode pod is full, `Route` returns the existing inflight-exceeded error, and no prefill starts.
  - `enforceReplicaInflight` skips a request whose target was already admitted.
  - A prefill failure after admission releases it on the existing error path.
  - This keeps the hard cap and removes the wasted work.
  - It could also go further: try the next decode candidate instead of rejecting.
- **B. Undo the prefill on rejection.** Keep the current order. When `enforceReplicaInflight` rejects a PD request, cancel the async prefill leg and abort the prefill request on the prefill pod.
  - Smaller change.
  - vLLM still pays the full prefill, since it has already finished; only the KV is freed sooner.
- **C. Treat the combination as unsupported.** Following the #2726 review comment: either ignore `requestsInflight` for `pd`, logging a warning, or reject a profile that combines a capped profile with a `pd` lock.
  - Simplest.
  - It drops the cap for PD deployments, which are the ones with the most expensive requests.

I'd lean towards A and can send a PR for it, plus the reproduction test. If you'd rather have B or C, I can do that instead.

### Environment

`main` at a502f652. Affects `pd` routing with any engine, when a config profile sets `requestsInflight`.

### Area

Gateway (PD routing, config profiles)
