items.title: [BUG] Cache policy from `cute.copy` is dropped when the copy atom is created with `invariant=True`
items.author: kainzhong
items.body_excerpt:
### Which component has the problem?

CuTe DSL

### Bug Report

**Describe the bug**
When you create a copy atom with `invariant=True` and pass a L2 cache policy to `cute.copy`'s `cache_policy` param, it will be silently dropped.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

```python
"""Minimal repro: CopyG2ROp(invariant=True) + cute.copy(cache_policy=...) drops the L2 policy.

Usage: python repro.py {inv,noinv}   (profile with ncu and read the SASS of `k`)
"""
import sys
import torch
import cutlass
from cutlass import cute, BFloat16, Int64, Float32
from cutlass.cute.runtime import from_dlpack

INVARIANT = sys.argv[1] == "inv"

@cute.kernel
def k(mX: cute.Tensor, mY: cute.Tensor):
    tidx, _, _ = cute.arch.thread_idx()
    policy = cute.arch.inline_ptx(
        "createpolicy.fractional.L2::evict_first.b64 {$w0}, {$r0};",
        write_only_types=[Int64], read_only_args=[Float32(1.0)])
    load = cute.make_copy_atom(cute.nvgpu.CopyG2ROp(), BFloat16, num_bits_per_copy=256,
                               invariant=INVARIANT)
    src = cute.make_tensor((mX.iterator + tidx * 16).align(32), cute.make_layout(16))
    r = cute.make_rmem_tensor((16,), BFloat16)
    cute.copy(load, src, r, cache_policy=policy)
    dst = cute.make_tensor(mY.iterator + tidx * 16, cute.make_layout(16))
    cute.autovec_copy(r, dst)

@cute.jit
def launch(mX: cute.Tensor, mY: cute.Tensor):
    k(mX, mY).launch(grid=[1, 1, 1], block=[32, 1, 1])

x = torch.randn(512, dtype=torch.bfloat16, device="cuda"); y = torch.empty_like(x)
launch(from_dlpack(x, assumed_align=32), from_dlpack(y, assumed_align=32))
torch.cuda.synchronize()
assert torch.equal(x, y)
print("ok", "invariant=" + str(INVARIANT))
```

Run `CUTE_DSL_KEEP_PTX=1 python cutedsl_invariant_cache_policy_repro.py` and examine the PTX, you can see `ld.global.nc.v8.b32` doesn't have the cache hint despite we did pass one in CuTeDSL.

Run `CUTE_DSL_KEEP_PTX=1 python cutedsl_invariant_cache_policy_repro.py --no-invariant` which will use `invariant=False`, and examine the PTX, this time the cache hint presents: `ld.global.L2::cache_hint.v4.b64`

**Expected behavior**
I can use both cache policy and invariant hint

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**
 - Environment location: GB200, nvidia-cutlass-dsl==4.8.0

**Additional context**
Add any other context about the problem here.

items.title: [QST] SM120 FP8 MMA with FP32 accumulate, plain form against block-scaled form with unit scales
items.author: emre570
items.body_excerpt:
**What is your question?**

On an RTX 5080, the plain FP8 MMA with FP32 accumulate runs at half the rate of the block-scaled FP8 MMA with FP32 accumulate. When all scale bytes are `0x7F` (UE8M0 1.0), the two forms give equal bits.

My FP8 attention kernel in CuTe DSL used `MmaFP8Op`. I changed it to `MmaMXF8Op` with constant unit scales and no other change. The kernel time went from 123.6 ms to 83.6 ms and the output is byte-equal (sgl-project/sglang#43390). So a user can do this today. My question is about the default.

1. Is there a reason to keep the plain form for E4M3 x E4M3 with FP32 accumulate on SM120?
2. If there is no reason, do you want `MmaFP8Op` and `rr_op_selector_sm120` to emit the block-scaled form with unit scales for this case? I can send a PR.

### Related report

The same behavior is reported in flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#5963 for the FlashInfer SM120 FP8 attention kernel, with RTX 5090 numbers and a bit-identity check. That issue also points to the MXFP8 attention work in flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#3628 and flashinfer-ai/flashinfer#4149. The numbers below add an RTX 5080 and a CUTLASS GEMM measurement to that report.

### Scope

E4M3 x E4M3, FP32 accumulate, one RTX 5080 (driver 595.99.02, CUDA 13.3, CUTLASS `ffa119a12`). I did not measure other types or other cards.

### Raw MMA rate

Independent MMA chains, no memory access, 84 SMs. The rate is the same from 4 to 32 warps per SM.

| instruction | TFLOP/s |
|---|---:|
| `kind::f8f6f4.m16n8k32 ... f32.e4m3.e4m3.f32` | 246 |
| `kind::mxf8f6f4.block_scale.scale_vec::1X.m16n8k32 ... f32.e4m3.e4m3.f32.ue8m0` | 489 |

### Bit equality

- Random finite inputs. 0 of 704,643,072 accumulator registers differ.
- Negative control with scale 2.0. 704,643,071 registers differ.
- Edge cases (subnormal, ±448, NaN bytes, accumulator start at zero, FLT_MAX, subnormal, infinity, NaN). 30 classes, 176,160,768 registers each, 0 bits differ.

### CUTLASS GEMM

I used the SM120 `CollectiveBuilder` with `OpClassTensorOp`, pingpong schedule, tile 128x128x128, FP32 output. Then I changed only the instruction in `SM120_16x8x32_TN<float_e4m3_t, float_e4m3_t, float>` to the block-scaled form. The scale `0x7F7F7F7F` stays in a register. There is no scale factor tensor and no additional load. The patch is 34 lines.

I measured 30 shapes from real models. All 30 give 0 different output words. Five examples:

| shape source | M x N x K | plain | patched | speedup |
|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| Wan 2.2 14B, `to_q` | 32760 x 5120 x 5120 | 236.1 | 398.6 | 1.69x |
| Llama 3.3 70B, MLP up | 4096 x 28672 x 8192 | 234.7 | 398.1 | 1.70x |
| FLUX.1-dev, FFN up | 4608 x 12288 x 3072 | 231.8 | 393.3 | 1.70x |
| MiniMax-H3, FFN up | 30272 x 14336 x 5376 | 234.6 | 363.5 | 1.55x |
| Gemma 3 27B, MLP up | 128 x 21504 x 5376 | 195.8 | 203.4 | 1.04x |

TFLOP/s. The speedup is 1.55x to 1.72x for the 22 shapes with M of 4096 or more. It is 1.04x to 1.82x for the 8 shapes with M = 128, where the low end is DRAM-bound.

Nsight Compute on the stock plain kernel shows the tensor pipe 96% busy. The MMA instruction rate is 47.9% of the peak.

One caution. These numbers use `max_swizzle_size = 8`. With the default of 1, three large shapes become DRAM-bound and the patched kernel is slower than the plain kernel (0.88x). I can open a different issue for that with the data.

### Where the plain form is used

- CuTe DSL `MmaFP8Op`
- `rr_op_selector_sm120` in `sm120_mma_builder.inl`, `sm120_array_mma_builder.inl` and `sm120_blockwise_mma_builder.inl`

cuBLASLt on the same card uses `QMMA.SF.16832.F32.E4M3.E4M3.E8` in its FP8 GEMM kernel and no plain `QMMA`.

I can share the benchmark source, the patch and the raw results if they are useful.

items.title: [BUG] sm120 GEMM hangs when K = 0 (grouped and non-grouped) after can_implement(), initialize() and run() return success
items.author: vera-rubin
items.body_excerpt:
**Describe the bug**

On sm120, a CUTLASS 3.x GEMM with K = 0 passes `can_implement()`, and `initialize()` and `run()` return `kSuccess` in the tested release builds. The records show zero-K kernels not completing within 10, 15 or 60 seconds.

- **Grouped GEMM, where K = 0 is documented as supported.** With the sm120 ptr-array kernel, the recorded K = {128, 0, 256, 0} and {0, 0, 0, 0} groups do not complete within the recorded timeouts, while {128, 128, 128, 128} and {256, 512} pass. The mainloop source indicates that one K = 0 group is sufficient. CHANGELOG 4.3.0 says ([CHANGELOG.md L715](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/CHANGELOG.md?plain=1#L715)):

  > Enable GEMM_K = 0 in grouped gemm.

  The same case was fixed for Hopper in #2547 and for sm100 grouped GEMM in #2746.
- **Non-grouped GEMM, a validation gap.** The docs don't say whether K = 0 is supported, and a debug build stops at `assert(gmem_prob_shape[0] >= 1)` in `make_tma_copy_desc` ([copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp L957](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cute/atom/copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp#L957)). A release build (`-DNDEBUG`, as the examples use) prints `Error: Failed to initialize the TMA descriptor 1` to stderr, `initialize()` still returns `kSuccess`, and the launched kernel does not complete before the recorded timeout. With M = 0 or N = 0, the same kernel's `run()` returns `Error Internal` instead. Upstream examples 79a (NVFP4) and 79c (MXFP8 x MXFP6) time out at `--k=0`. Our own tests time out the same way with FP8 (cooperative and pingpong) and NVFP4 cooperative kernels at 128x128, and with FP8 at 300x392 with L = 2 and with beta = 0. They use real (non-null) A/B buffers.

A caller whose K can be 0 at run time (for example a weight-gradient GEMM for an MoE expert that received no tokens) is an illustrative scenario. This makes reachability plausible, not demonstrated for a deployed SM120 framework, product, or protected workload.

The submitted computation does not complete within the recorded timeout. Software waiting for it can lose availability; recovery and impact on other GPU users were not assessed. No confidentiality or integrity failure was demonstrated.

**Cause (our reading):**

1. The producer issues TMA loads only inside `for ( ; k_tile_count > 0; --k_tile_count)` ([sm120_mma_tma.hpp L400](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_mma_tma.hpp#L400), [sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp L665](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp#L665)), so at K = 0 it loads nothing.
2. The consumer `mma()` clears the accumulators and then calls `pipeline.consumer_wait(smem_pipe_read)` unconditionally ([sm120_mma_tma.hpp L526](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_mma_tma.hpp#L526), [sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp L848](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp#L848)). No TMA transaction ever completes that barrier. The array mainloops have the same first wait ([sm120_mma_array_tma.hpp L516](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_mma_array_tma.hpp#L516), [sm120_blockscaled_mma_array_tma.hpp L934](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_blockscaled_mma_array_tma.hpp#L934)).
3. The collectives' `can_implement()` checks only TMA alignment ([sm120_mma_tma.hpp L278](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_mma_tma.hpp#L278), [sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp L399](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp#L399)). When the descriptor encode fails, [copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp L1066-L1080](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cute/atom/copy_traits_sm90_tma.hpp#L1066-L1080) prints the error and calls `assert(false)`, which `NDEBUG` compiles out, so `initialize()` still reports success.

Other architectures, read, not run (we have no sm90 or sm100 GPU):

- Hopper's ptr-array mainloop guards the first wait with `if (k_tile_count > 0)` ([sm90_mma_array_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp L533](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm90_mma_array_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp#L533)). Hopper's non-grouped mainloop has only a debug `assert(k_tile_count >= 1)` before an unconditional `consumer_wait` ([sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp L481-L487](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm90_mma_tma_gmma_ss_warpspecialized.hpp#L481-L487)).
- The sm100 mainloops skip the first wait when `k_tile_count <= 0` ([sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp L670](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm100_mma_warpspecialized.hpp#L670), [sm100_blockscaled_mma_warpspecialized.hpp L991](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/0b55a2f691d69981583568fd9eb69687b1f0de8a/include/cutlass/gemm/collective/sm100_blockscaled_mma_warpspecialized.hpp#L991)).

**What a one-line guard did.** We added `if (k_tile_count <= 0) { return; }` right after `clear(accum)` in `mma()` and rebuilt on the RTX 5090:

- In `sm120_mma_tma.hpp` and `sm120_blockscaled_mma_tma.hpp`: the non-grouped K = 0 cases we re-ran completed with D = beta*C, bit-exact against a double-precision host reference (FP8 cooperative at 128x128 and at 300x392 w

items.title: Expert Parallelism (EP) roadmap for SM12x b12x MoE kernel (b12x_fused_moe / B12xMoEWrapper)
items.author: ItamarTerem
items.body_excerpt:
Hi flashinfer team,
We're deploying a large MoE model (384 experts, top_k=8) on 8x RTX PRO 6000 (SM120/Blackwell workstation) using the b12x_fused_moe CuteDSL kernel via TensorRT-LLM's pytorch backend, and have hit the Expert Parallelism restriction:

b12x_fused_moe does not yet support Expert Parallelism
(num_local_experts={X} != num_experts={Y}).
Use a different MoE backend for EP configurations.

This comes from the explicit guard in flashinfer/fused_moe/cute_dsl/b12x_moe.py (both in the free function b12x_fused_moe and in B12xMoEWrapper.__init__), confirmed in flashinfer version 0.6.12.
Context on why this matters for us specifically: without EP, every GPU must retain workspace/routing capacity sized for the full state_E (all 384 experts), even though tensor parallelism already shards each expert's weights across GPUs. This is a meaningful, measured memory cost — in our case, the dynamic workspace's packed_input buffer alone accounts for roughly 7–11GB/GPU across a 60-MoE-layer model, purely from having to size for the worst-case "all experts active" scenario rather than a num_experts/ep_size subset.

What we're asking:

1. Is EP support for the SM12x b12x kernel family (static/dynamic/micro backends) on the roadmap, even at a preliminary stage?
2. Is there a rough timeline or tracking issue we could follow?
3. Are there known architectural blockers specific to SM120 (vs. SM100/SM103, where other kernels like MegaMoE already support EP) that make this a harder problem here?

We also note that vLLM's FlashInferB12xExperts (_supports_parallel_config) explicitly declines to use this backend when EP is requested, for the same underlying reason — so this appears to be a shared, cross-framework limitation rather than something specific to our integration.
Happy to provide more detail on our exact shapes/config if useful. Thanks for your work on this — the b12x kernel has otherwise been the only correctness-verified MoE path we've found for SM120 (CUTLASS produces silently incorrect output on this architecture in our testing).

items.title: [RFC] Removing ideep git submodule dependency from PyTorch & add oneDNN git submodule
items.author: sanchitintel
items.body_excerpt:
### 🚀 The feature, motivation and pitch

### Background

Currently, PyTorch eager-mode leverages oneDNN for x86_64 & aarch64 CPUs via [ideep](https://github.com/intel/ideep), 
which is essentially a set of headers to make [oneDNN](https://github.com/uxlfoundation/oneDNN) integration with PyTorch more convenient.

ideep is a git submodule of PyTorch, and in turn, oneDNN is a git submodule of ideep.

### Proposal

We intend to remove ideep as a submodule dependency & use oneDNN API directly in ATen because:

1. When changes in ideep are upstreamed to PyTorch, i.e. when the `ideep` submodule commit for PyTorch is updated, the underlying changes are somewhat opaque to PyTorch. This may have been a benefit when oneDNN was initially integrated with PyTorch, but as the CPU implementation is mature now, it makes more sense to integrate oneDNN directly with PyTorch. 
2. Intel XPU (`xpu` is the device name for Intel GPUs) implementation in ATen already uses oneDNN API directly.
3. We received feedback from the community on PyTorch GitHub repo to remove the ideep dependency, and directly use oneDNN.

### Impact

oneDNN will become a git submodule of PyTorch.
ideep dependency will be removed.
There will not be any performance regressions or breakages.

### Plan of action (in stages)

1. **Port ideep code to ATen** & refactor it.
This first step will simply get rid of ideep & ensure that there wouldn't be any breakages or regressions.
It entails sharing as much code as possible between x86_64, aarch64 CPUs & Intel GPU implementations.
e.g. oneDNN primitive descriptor cache code (currently, ideep has a primitive descriptor cache for CPU) could be shared between CPU & XPU implementations.
Primitive cache code could also be shared (Both the CPU & GPU implementations currently rely on oneDNN's own primitive cache, but it's possible to add one in PyTorch).

2. **Completely unify oneDNN integration for CPU & XPU**.
This means either unifying oneDNN related methods in ATen (in `aten::native::onednn` namespace) for both CPU & XPU.
Or not just sharing the `at::native::onednn` API, but the corresponding code as well (with preprocessor directives, wherever necessary, to allow some divergent code for CPU/XPU).
Currently, there isn't a clear answer as to whether the second approach would be feasible, because it may end up making the code hard-to-read.

We currently plan to proceed with Stage 1 first, but are open to any suggestions.

Thanks!

items.title: 3D Conv Slow with Large Tensors (> 2**31) Elements
items.author: viengiaan
items.body_excerpt:
### 🐛 Describe the bug

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

device = torch.device("cuda")

# Define an extremely large input tensor (exceeding 2**31 elements for a single sample), use 3d convolutions
# Total elements = 1 * 256 * 7 * 1090 * 1106 = 2,160,327,680 > 2**31 (2,147,483,648)
num_channels = 256

# Define a convolution layer
conv_layer = nn.Conv3d(num_channels, num_channels, kernel_size=3, stride=1, padding=1).to(device).half()

input_tensor = torch.randn(1, num_channels, 7, 1088, 1088, device=device).half()

# Takes 0.7 seconds
output_tensor = conv_layer(input_tensor)

# Input exceeding 2 ** 31
input_tensor = torch.randn(1, num_channels, 7, 1090, 1106, device=device).half()
# Takes 22 seconds
output_tensor = conv_layer(input_tensor)

torch.cuda.synchronize()
```

Additional Context:

- If we use input with the size less than 2^31, it takes around 0.7 seconds. But if the input is larger than 2^31, it requires 22 seconds to complete the task.
- The application of the above operation is for video diffusion.
- Similar issues are found in https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/95024 and https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/issues/152816

items.title: [Gateway] Gate raw request body logging behind verbose log levels
items.author: googs1025
items.body_excerpt:
Parent issue: #2989

## Problem

Several Gateway validators log the complete request body when JSON parsing fails. Other request-processing logs include parsed prompts or messages at `V(4)`.

These diagnostics are useful, but request bodies can contain user prompts, tool arguments, conversation history, or large encoded data. Request contents should not appear at normal production log levels.

## Proposed behavior

At normal log levels, parsing failures should record only:

- request ID;
- endpoint;
- sanitized parse reason;
- request body size.

Raw JSON content may be logged only at `klog.V(6)`.

Verbose logging must:

- include at most 4 KiB of the request body;
- record whether the value was truncated;
- never log multipart file contents, filenames, or form values;
- apply the same policy to parsed prompt or message fields;
- require no new environment variable.

Example normal log:

```go
klog.ErrorS(nil, "error to unmarshal request",
    "requestID", requestID,
    "endpoint", requestPath,
    "reason", jsonParseReason(err),
    "requestBodyBytes", len(requestBody))
```

Example verbose diagnostic:

```go
if klog.V(6).Enabled() {
    klog.V(6).InfoS("request body parse failure details",
        "requestID", requestID,
        "requestBody", truncateRequestBodyForLog(requestBody, 4096),
        "requestBodyTruncated", len(requestBody) > 4096)
}
```

## Scope

Apply this policy to the Gateway validators for Chat Completions, Responses, Completions, Embeddings, image and video generation, Tokenize, Pooling, Decisions and SystemOne where applicable, and new Score and Audio Speech validators.

Move parsed prompt/message logging from `V(4)` to the same bounded `V(6)` behavior.

## Testing

Cover:

1. Default verbosity: metadata is logged; raw body and prompt are absent.
2. `V(6)`: JSON content is present; values longer than 4 KiB are truncated; truncation is reported.
3. Multipart: file contents, filenames, and form values remain absent at every level.
4. Compatibility: existing HTTP validation responses remain unchanged.

## Non-goals

- Do not completely remove verbose request diagnostics.
- Do not add per-field redaction rules.
- Do not add a request-body logging environment variable.
- Do not log multipart contents at any verbosity.
- Do not change parsing or routing behavior.

## Acceptance criteria

- Raw JSON is absent from normal logs.
- Raw JSON is available only at `V(6)`.
- Verbose bodies are capped at 4 KiB.
- Multipart contents are never logged.
- Parsed prompt/message logging follows the same policy.
- Client-visible behavior remains unchanged.

items.title: [Feature][Rubin] Dense projection GEMMs with grad
items.author: abcdabcd987
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem

We need verified Rubin support and good performance for the dense and batched GEMMs in GLM-5.2 training. This can be solved by validated cuBLAS/cuBLASLt coverage; a new FlashInfer kernel is only needed where the library path is missing or underperforms.

The GB200 profile attributes roughly 2.27 seconds of summed GPU kernel time to dense projection GEMMs and 0.30 seconds to MLA batched GEMMs over two optimizer steps on one rank. The largest projection is `o_proj`; smaller output dimensions and the FP32 router projection also need attention.

## Requested outcome

Cover BF16 forward, input-gradient (`dgrad`), and weight-gradient (`wgrad`) GEMMs with FP32 accumulation. Accept the operand layouts actually used by training, including transposed weight views, without forcing additional copies.

For activations `X[T,K]`, weights `W[N,K]`, and output gradient `G[T,N]`, support the following operations. The reference layouts below assume contiguous row-major `X`, `W`, and `G`; all strides are in elements, not bytes.

| Operation | Usage / computation | Left operand: shape; strides | Right operand: shape; strides | Requested output: shape; strides |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Forward | `F.linear(X, W)` = `X @ W.T` | `[T,K]`; `(K,1)` | `[K,N]`; `(1,K)` | `[T,N]`; `(N,1)` |
| Input gradient | `G @ W` | `[T,N]`; `(N,1)` | `[N,K]`; `(K,1)` | `[T,K]`; `(K,1)` |
| Weight gradient | `G.T @ X` | `[N,T]`; `(1,N)` | `[T,K]`; `(K,1)` | `[N,K]`; `(K,1)` |

The transposes in this table are views, not requests to materialize transposed copies. Use explicit strides rather than relying only on `NN`/`NT`/`TN` labels, whose interpretation depends on the API's storage convention.

Provide BF16 output and an FP32 gradient-output option where supported. The router's FP32 arithmetic is a separate numerical requirement: do not silently replace it with BF16 or TF32; any faster reduced-precision mode must be explicit and validated.

## Workload and reference shapes

**`T` is irregular, generally not a power of two, and varies across batches and runs.** Recorded values are 16,231 and 16,172, not a fixed 16,384-token batch. Forward and dgrad have ragged row counts; wgrad has a ragged reduction length, and all three must support these sizes without caller-side padding.

The following table gives logical forward dimensions for the `F.linear(X, W)` pattern above, with weights stored as `[N,K]`. The backward shapes and representative layouts follow from the operation table.

| Projection | `K` | `N` | Input dtype |
|---|---:|---:|---|
| Attention output (`o_proj`) | 16,384 | 6,144 | BF16 |
| Query low-rank projection (`q_a`) | 6,144 | 2,048 | BF16 |
| Query expansion (`q_b`) | 2,048 | 16,384 | BF16 |
| KV projection (`kv_a`) | 6,144 | 576 | BF16 |
| Shared-expert gate/up, each | 6,144 | 2,048 | BF16 |
| Shared-expert down | 2,048 | 6,144 | BF16 |
| Dense MLP gate/up, each | 6,144 | 12,288 | BF16 |
| Dense MLP down | 12,288 | 6,144 | BF16 |
| Indexer query projection | 2,048 | 4,096 | BF16 |
| Indexer key projection | 6,144 | 128 | BF16 |
| Indexer head-weight projection | 6,144 | 32 | BF16 |
| Router gate | 6,144 | 256 | FP32 |

The LM-head projection `[T,6144] @ [6144,154880]` is covered by the separate chunked LM-head/loss request. Its GEMMs may reuse this implementation, but its loss and workspace requirements belong to that request.

### MLA batched projections: usage and layout

For these contractions, heads are the GEMM batch dimension, but activations use token-major `[T,H,D]` storage. A logical `[H,T,D]` batched-GEMM view must therefore not be assumed to have contiguous head-major storage.

The two forward contractions are shown below. The `einsum` expressions define the math; the output-layout requirements are stated separately because `einsum` alone does not specify physical output strides.

| Operation | Usage / contraction | Logical inputs | Required output interface |
|---|---|---|---|
| Query absorption | `einsum("thd,hdc->thc", Q, W_uk)` | `Q[T,64,192]`, `W_uk[64,192,512]` | Contiguous `[T,64,512]` for sparse attention |
| Value projection after attention | `einsum("thc,hdc->thd", A, W_uv)` | `A[T,64,512]`, `W_uv[64,256,512]` | Contiguous `[T,64,256]`, viewable as `[T,16384]` for `o_proj` |

The query and weights are slices of larger tensors, not compact independent allocations. These representative layouts follow from their parent buffers:

```python
# Parent buffers are contiguous in the stated order.
Q = q_full[:, :, :192]       # q_full: [T,64,256]
W_uk = W_kv[:, :192, :]      # W_kv:   [64,448,512]
W_uv = W_kv[:, 192:, :]

# Current query-absorption call: write directly into token-major output.
q_latent = empty((T,64,512))
bmm(Q.permute(1,0,2), W_uk, out=q_latent.permute(1,0,2))

# Value projection is followed immediately by flattening for o_proj.
out = einsum("thc,hdc->thd", A, W_uv)
out = out.reshape(T, 64 * 256)
```

In this example, `A` is the token-major attention output `[T,64,512]`. The request is to produce the value-projection result directly in the required token-major layout, so the final reshape is a view rather than an additional copy.

| Tensor | Logical shape | Element strides | Layout detail |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Q` | `[T,64,192]` | `(16384,256,1)` | Feature slice of `[T,64,256]`; not contiguous |
| `W_uk` | `[64,192,512]` | `(229376,512,1)` | Head stride retains all 448 parent rows |
| `W_uv` | `[64,256,512]` | `(229376,512,1)` | Same head stride; starts 98,304 elements into `W_kv` |
| `q_latent` output / `A` input | `[T,64,512]` | `(32768,512,1)` | Token-major |
| Requested `out` | `[T,64,256]` | `(16384,256,1)` | Token-major; flattening heads/features needs no copy |

Equivalently, the forward batched-GEMM views have the following layouts. In particular, the batch stride for a head can be smaller than the stride between token rows; the head matrices are interleaved in the token-major allocation.

| Operation | Left operand: shape; strides | Right operand: shape; strides | Reques

items.title: [Feature][Rubin] MegaMoE: MXFP8, recomputation, and clamped SwiGLU
items.author: abcdabcd987
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem

We need the MegaMoE training backend in [PR #6053](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6053) to support activation checkpointing, clamped SwiGLU, and native MXFP8 across Blackwell and Rubin. The target workloads include both 256- and 288-expert models with irregular, unequal per-rank token counts.

The GB200 benchmark at revision `072340e2` also reports 1.4–1.5× slower steps than MoK under uniform routing, and 58.9 GiB of retained output/context per layer at EP32/64 with overflow-safe schedules; the memory figure excludes symmetric workspaces ([benchmark details](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6053#issuecomment-6026084025)). These are results for that revision, not Rubin measurements or claims about later revisions.

## Requested outcome

- **Recomputation:** Add a context-only recompute API for activation checkpointing, similar to MoK's `recompute_forward_context`. Rebuild the state needed by backward without rerunning unnecessary down projections, combine, and output epilogues; validate that recomputed and saved-context backward agree.

- **GLM-5.3-Flash support:** Support 288 routed experts, including EP8 with 36 local experts and EP32 with 9. Implement clamped SwiGLU for both routed and shared experts: `silu(clamp(gate, max=10)) * clamp(up, min=-10, max=10)`, with matching backward semantics; retain the unclamped option for the GLM-5.2 workload ([GLM-5.3-Flash implementation](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/8073e6dcaea9aa4b42acf2d92ec72148786bbaeb/src/transformers/models/glm5_next/modeling_glm5_next.py#L86-L142)).

- **MXFP8:** Add native MXFP8 routed-expert forward, input gradients, and weight gradients, not fake quantization followed by BF16 GEMMs. Use a MoK-compatible recipe with caller-prequantized weights and fused activation/gradient quantization, including both operand orientations where needed; keep the shared expert in BF16 initially ([MoK reference API](https://github.com/cursor/mixture-of-kittens/blob/caeb2963f855c7ad53bb50c8bbf211086405cb98/README.md)).

- **Memory and speed:** Address the router-gradient backward overhead, capacity-sized saved routed outputs, and computation on padded source rows identified in the [GB200 benchmark comment](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6053#issuecomment-6026084025). Reduce retained activation memory without trading away numerical quality, and make performance track real work rather than pessimistic reserved capacity.

## Target hardware

Required targets are **`sm_100` (B200/GB200), `sm_103` (B300/GB300), and `sm_107` (Rubin)**. Implement and validate the requested capabilities on all three, rather than treating Blackwell as a comparison-only platform.

Expert-parallel groups must support peers spanning multiple hosts within one NVL72 NVLink domain. An inter-rack transport is not required.

## Inference engine

We use PyTorch native with a custom training integration. This request covers both forward and backward, not an inference-only operator.

## Workload and configuration

- **Data type and quantization:** BF16 baseline and native MXFP8 routed-expert training; BF16 shared expert.
- **Parallelism:** Expert parallelism within one NVLink domain, combined with expert FSDP and activation checkpointing.

`H` is hidden width and `I` is expert intermediate width. Both workloads use top-8 routing and one shared expert of width `I`.

| Workload | H | I | Routed experts | Target EP sizes | Local routed experts |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|---|
| [GLM-5.2-shaped workload](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6053#issuecomment-6026084025) | 6144 | 2048 | 256 | 4 / 8 / 16 / 32 / 64 | 64 / 32 / 16 / 8 / 4 |
| [GLM-5.3-Flash](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash/raw/main/config.json) | 4096 | 2048 | 288 | 8 / 32 | 36 / 9 |

**The real input-token count `T_r` is irregular, generally not a power of two, and changes across microbatches and runs.** Ranks in the same EP collective can have different counts, including zero; support this independently of uneven received expert loads, without caller-side activation padding.

Use roughly 8K–32K real tokens per rank as the main benchmark range, including counts such as `8191`, `16172`, `16231`, and `32767`. Token counts and routing must remain runtime inputs.

- **Layouts:** Activations are `[T_r,H]`; routing IDs and coefficients are `[T_r,8]`. Gate and up weights are separate tensors, each `[E_local,I,H]`, used as `gate_e = X_e @ W_gate[e].T` and `up_e = X_e @ W_up[e].T`. Down weights are `[E_local,H,I]`, used as `activation_e @ W_down[e].T`.

## Current workaround

The existing comparison paths are [MoK #17](https://github.com/cursor/mixture-of-kittens/pull/17) and DeepEP HybridEP plus grouped GEMMs, as described in the [benchmark setup](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6053#issuecomment-6026084025). For the measured adapter revision, activation checkpointing replays the full forward because it lacks a context-only entry point ([recompute comparison](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/6053#issuecomment-6026084025)).

## Acceptance criteria

- **Hardware coverage:** Run correctness and performance qualification on `sm_100`, `sm_103`, and `sm_107` for the listed workloads.
- **Training correctness:** Validate outputs, input gradients, routing-coefficient gradients, and all expert/shared weight gradients against independent references. Include clamp boundaries, uneven/empty ranks, skewed routing, and recomputation; support FP32 weight-gradient accumulation and document the BF16/MXFP8 numerical behavior.
- **Performance:** Compare complete forward/backward and checkpointed execution against MoK and HybridEP plus grouped GEMMs. Include scheduling, quantization, copies, and replay, and report total peak memory with matched ring sizes or an explicit latency-versus-memory comparison.

items.title: [Feature][Rubin] CAKE packed KDA grad for long ragged sequences
items.author: abcdabcd987
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem

We need an efficient KDA training path for long packed sequences with unequal document lengths, irregular tails, and variable local head counts. Context-parallel redistribution gives each rank the complete packed token axis for a subset of heads, rather than a short token shard for all heads. The supplied CP16 profile exercises four local heads (`64 / 16`); this is an important benchmark configuration, not a restriction on supported shapes.

In a GB200 training profile spanning two optimizer updates, recurrence kernels consume 6.595 s: 1.568 s original forward, 1.560 s activation-checkpoint replay, and 3.467 s backward including internal recomputation. This is 11.29% of 58.432 s summed GPU kernel duration, not a wall-time speedup estimate; communication, convolution, gate construction, and external Q/K normalization are excluded.

Existing [KDA backward PR #5376](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5376) is relevant, but its documented backward-only, fixed/equal-length and 128-aligned sequence domain does not cover this complete workload. This request is to extend and qualify existing work, not to ignore it.

## Requested outcome

Provide a supported packed KDA forward and first-order backward API with variable-length documents, variable local head counts, zero initial state per document, and practical saved-state/workspace use at long sequence lengths, including the profiled roughly 240K–261K tokens. Support standalone forward/backward and activation-checkpoint replay without requiring the caller to depend on an undocumented forward saved-tensor format.

For this 64-head model, support `H_local ∈ {1,2,4,8,16,32,64}`, corresponding to CP sizes `{64,32,16,8,4,2,1}` under head-sharded redistribution. Internal kernel specialization is fine, but the public API must not hard-code four heads. Include both small-head/long-sequence and larger-head configurations in performance qualification.

The request is for the local recurrence boundary after redistribution. It does not include distributed collectives, CP packing/permutation changes, causal convolution, projections, or output gated RMSNorm.

## Target hardware

- SM100 (B200, GB200): profiled target.
- SM103 (B300, GB300): requested target.
- Future architecture: SM107 / Rubin, retaining the scope of our other training-kernel requests.

Only GB200 supplied the profile above; please report qualification separately by architecture.

## Inference engine

PyTorch native; Custom / other. This is a training integration, not autoregressive decode.

## Affected model or model family

[GLM-5.3-Flash, pinned public configuration](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash/blob/eb9eb208eb0d988989d07a6a12d0fdeb5f52574a/config.json). The configuration has 64 KDA heads, head dimension 128, and bounded log-gate lower limit -5.

## Workload and configuration

- **Execution:** BF16 training with activation checkpointing; no activation/weight quantization in this operator.
- **Parallelism:** world size 64, CP16, EP32 in the motivating run, producing `H_local=4`. The requested kernel is single-device and accepts variable `H_local`; it does not need to know the CP group or implement collectives.
- **Head counts:** `H_local ∈ {1,2,4,8,16,32,64}`, with key/value head dimension 128. This is the required coverage for this model, not a claim that arbitrary other head counts are structurally unsupported.
- **Packed batch:** `B=1`; three or four documents in the observed invocations. Exact document boundaries were not recorded as tensor values; do not assume equal lengths or infer them from the total.
- **Token counts:** observed `S ∈ {239718, 245028, 249866, 250340, 258574, 259042, 259584, 261393}` at `H_local=4`; these are benchmark points, not an exhaustive supported range. `S` is the complete packed token count after redistribution, not the pre-redistribution local token count. Holding the packed batch fixed while changing CP changes `H_local`, not `S`.
- **Environment:** `python -m flashinfer.collect_env` output is not available with the profile.

| Operand | Shape | Dtype | Element strides / meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `q`, `k`, `v` | `[1,S,H_local,128]` | BF16 | Contiguous: `[S*H_local*128,H_local*128,128,1]` |
| `g` | `[1,S,H_local,128]` | FP32 | Same contiguous layout; preactivated natural-log decay |
| `beta` | `[1,S,H_local]` | BF16 | `[S*H_local,H_local,1]`; already sigmoid-activated |
| `cu_seqlens` | `[num_docs+1]` | Int32 | Contiguous device prefix sums, starting at 0 and ending at `S` |
| `out`, `dout` | `[1,S,H_local,128]` | BF16 | Same logical layout as `v` |
| `dq`, `dk`, `dv`, `dbeta` | Same as corresponding input | BF16 | Input-gradient storage boundary |
| `dg` | Same as `g` | FP32 | Do not narrow the log-gate gradient |

The incumbent uses chunk size 64, `safe_gate=True`, and scale `128**-0.5`. Each packed document starts from zero recurrent state; the caller does not consume a final state. Chunk size is the baseline implementation choice, not a requirement to prohibit a better algorithm.

### Precision and gate boundaries

Q/K are L2-normalized externally with epsilon `1e-6`, then stored in BF16 before entering the recurrence. Backward returns BF16 gradients to that external normalization boundary; fusing normalization must not silently remove this rounding point.

The existing gate is constructed in FP32 as `g = -5 * sigmoid(exp(A_log) * (raw_gate + dt_bias))`. `beta` is supplied after sigmoid in BF16. The core API should accept these preactivated operands; a fused raw-gate/L2 variant is optional and should be validated separately, including gradients for `raw_gate`, `A_log`, and `dt_bias`.

## Current workaround

FLA chunked KDA forward/backward with external Q/K normalization and FP32 bounded-gate construction. This works but recurrence and recomputation are a substantial training cost; an implementation supporting only equal-length 128-aligned sequences cannot replace it.

## Impact

Throughput; Memory capacity

items.title: [Feature][Rubin] CAKE four-stream mHC training at H4096 with FP32 mapping and full backward
items.author: abcdabcd987
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem

We need efficient four-stream mHC training, including normalization, mapping, collapse, residual mixing, and all activation/parameter gradients. Existing [MegaMHC exports](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/e403d30785ea9ece65a88b3337db86dcac19fef5/flashinfer/experimental/deepgemm_mega_mhc/mega_mhc.py) target H5120 with FP8-output machinery and do not expose this complete BF16-activation training backward.

In a two-update GB200 profile, mHC-only work consumes 3.151 s, or 5.39% of 58.432 s summed GPU kernel duration. This excludes the attention/MLP branch and its checkpoint replay; it is not an end-to-end speedup estimate.

The main targets are FP32 mapping GEMMs (1.537 s) and normalization/combined input-gradient work (0.987 s), rather than coefficients/Sinkhorn alone (0.039 s). A materialized normalized FP32 `[T,16384]` tensor is 0.91–0.99 GiB at the profiled token counts; this is per-tensor size, not a measured simultaneous memory peak.

## Requested outcome

Support the complete four-stream mHC connection at hidden size 4096, with runtime-variable local token counts, BF16 activation boundaries, FP32 mapping/coefficient arithmetic and gradients, and first-order backward through all mHC paths. The attention/MLP branch remains an external operation; split prepare/finish kernels are fine if the complete gradient accumulation contract is preserved.

Prioritize eliminating large intermediates or fusing normalization with mapping/gradient work. Do not limit the request to a forward Sinkhorn optimization.

## Target hardware

- SM100 (B200, GB200): profiled target.
- SM103 (B300, GB300): requested target.
- Future architecture: SM107 / Rubin, requested training support.

## Inference engine

PyTorch native; Custom / other. Training with activation checkpointing.

## Affected model or model family

[GLM-5.3-Flash, pinned public configuration](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash/blob/eb9eb208eb0d988989d07a6a12d0fdeb5f52574a/config.json), with four streams, hidden size 4096, 20 Sinkhorn iterations, and `hc_eps=1e-6`. The requested FP32 intermediate policy below is explicit; bitwise equivalence to a model implementation that rounds intermediate coefficients to BF16 is not the target.

## Workload and configuration

- **Local tokens:** observed `T ∈ {14928,15288,15566,15590,16114,16132,16164,16263}`; these are benchmark points, not an allowed-value list or a 16K maximum. Support runtime-variable `T`, including smaller/larger and irregular local shards.
- **Parallelism:** motivating run uses world size 64, CP16 and EP32; this request is for local mHC kernels, not collectives. Different CP sizes and batch layouts change local `T`; no CP16-specific geometry is required.
- **Model-fixed dimensions:** four residual streams, hidden size 4096, and the resulting 24-by-16384 mapping are not divided by CP in this path. Keep those model dimensions as the required scope rather than incorrectly replacing four streams with `4 / CP`.
- **Quantization:** none in the requested mHC path; no FP8 output requirement.
- **Environment:** `python -m flashinfer.collect_env` output is unavailable.

| Operand | Shape | Dtype | Element strides / role |
|---|---|---|---|
| Streams `X` | `[T,4,4096]` | BF16 | Contiguous `[16384,4096,1]` |
| Mapping `fn` | `[24,16384]` | FP32 | Row-major `[16384,1]`; use its transpose for forward |
| `scale`, `base` | `[3]`, `[24]` | FP32 | Contiguous |
| Collapsed input `U`, branch output `B` | `[T,4096]` | BF16 | Contiguous |
| Mixed output `Y`, upstream `dY` | `[T,4,4096]` | BF16 | Same logical layout as streams |
| `dfn`, `dscale`, `dbase` | Same shapes as parameters | FP32 | FP32 reductions and returned gradients |

### Exact function

Use `rms_eps=1e-5`, `hc_eps=1e-6`, and 20 finite Sinkhorn iterations. The following pseudocode defines the requested function, with arithmetic in FP32 except the marked activation boundaries:

```text
u = float32(X).reshape(T, 16384)
r = rsqrt(mean(u*u, axis=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-5)
z = (u*r) @ fn.T
pre  = sigmoid(z[:, :4]  * scale[0] + base[:4]) + 1e-6
post = 2 * sigmoid(z[:, 4:8] * scale[1] + base[4:8])
logits = (z[:, 8:] * scale[2] + base[8:]).reshape(T,4,4)
C = row_softmax(logits) + 1e-6
C = C / (column_sum(C) + 1e-6)
repeat 19 times:
    C = C / (row_sum(C) + 1e-6)
    C = C / (column_sum(C) + 1e-6)
U[t,d] = BF16(sum_i pre[t,i] * float32(X[t,i,d]))
B = external_branch(U)  # BF16 [T,4096]
Y[t,j,d] = BF16(post[t,j] * float32(B[t,d])
                 + sum_i C[t,i,j] * float32(X[t,i,d]))
```

`C` is indexed by source stream then destination stream. Different normalization order, epsilon placement, or differentiating an idealized converged Sinkhorn solution would change the function.

### Backward precision

Mapping GEMMs must preserve FP32-quality arithmetic; BF16/TF32 approximations should be explicit, separately validated modes rather than silent replacements. Keep mapping intermediates, coefficients, their gradients, and parameter reductions in FP32.

Return the branch-output gradient in BF16 after its complete FP32 sum. After branch backward supplies `dU`, sum the mapping, collapse, and residual-mix contributions to `dX` in FP32, then cast once to BF16. Returning three separately rounded BF16 contributions is not equivalent. Preserve sigmoid-tail gradients even when the FP32 forward sigmoid rounds to one.

## Current workaround

Custom normalization/coefficient/stream kernels plus FP32 library GEMMs and a combined autograd boundary. The implementation supports training, but mapping and large-intermediate traffic are costly; a forward-only FP8-oriented route is not a replacement.

## Impact

Throughput; Memory capacity or bandwidth; Correctness or numerical-quality risk.

## Acceptance criteria

- Validate `Y`, `dX`, `dB`, `dfn`, `dscale`, and `dbase` against independent eager references that implement the finite normalization chain and stated storage boundaries.

items.title: [Feature][Rubin] CAKE packed depthwise causal convolution + SiLU training kernels
items.author: abcdabcd987
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem

We need an efficient packed depthwise causal convolution + SiLU training operator, including input and FP32 tap gradients. This is a separate, independently usable operator ahead of KDA recurrence, not a request to fuse the entire distributed KDA layer.

In a two-update GB200 profile, this scope costs 0.987 s, or 1.69% of 58.432 s summed GPU kernel duration, including Q/K/V convolutions, checkpoint replay, preactivation recomputation in backward, and tap-gradient reductions. Communication and CP packing are excluded; the percentage is not a wall-time speedup estimate.

The current convolution already fuses SiLU. The opportunity is a faster complete training path and potentially less backward recomputation/workspace, not removing a standalone SiLU launch.

## Requested outcome

Provide packed width-four depthwise causal convolution with fused SiLU, forward and first-order backward, variable local channel counts, zero history at document boundaries, BF16 activation storage, and FP32 tap weights/gradients. Reuse relevant convolution implementation components where possible, but expose a training operator independently of recurrent attention.

For the model's 8192 channels, support `C_local ∈ {128,256,512,1024,2048,4096,8192}` as CP varies across `{64,32,16,8,4,2,1}`. The observed `C_local=512` is the CP16 benchmark, not a support restriction. Internal specialization is fine; the public API should not require a fixed CP size or 512 channels.

## Target hardware

- SM100 (B200, GB200): profiled target.
- SM103 (B300, GB300): requested target.
- Future architecture: SM107 / Rubin, requested training support.

## Inference engine

PyTorch native; Custom / other. Packed training, not decode.

## Affected model or model family

[GLM-5.3-Flash, pinned public configuration](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash/blob/eb9eb208eb0d988989d07a6a12d0fdeb5f52574a/config.json), with independent width-four Q/K/V short convolutions in the KDA layers.

## Workload and configuration

- **Packed tokens:** observed `S ∈ {239718,245028,249866,250340,258574,259042,259584,261393}`; these are benchmark points, not supported-length limits. Accept variable `S` and document counts; three or four documents were observed, not required.
- **Local channels:** `C_local = 8192 / CP = 128 * H_local` under the model's head-aligned redistribution. Required values are `{128,256,512,1024,2048,4096,8192}`; the profile uses 512, whereas CP1 uses 8192.
- **Parallelism:** motivating run uses world size 64, CP16, EP32; the requested kernel is single-device and does not perform redistribution. Holding the packed batch fixed while changing CP changes `C_local`, not the complete packed token count `S`.
- **Invocation pattern:** three independent Q/K/V convolutions per KDA layer, plus activation replay and backward.
- **Environment:** `python -m flashinfer.collect_env` output is unavailable.

| Operand | Shape | Dtype | Element strides |
|---|---|---|---|
| `x`, `y`, `dy`, `dx` | `[1,S,C_local]` | BF16 | Contiguous `[S*C_local,C_local,1]` |
| `weight`, `dweight` | `[C_local,4]` | FP32 | Contiguous `[4,1]` |
| `cu_seqlens` | `[num_docs+1]` | Int32 | Contiguous device prefix sums |

The convolution width four is model-defined, unlike the CP-dependent channel count, and remains the required tap width. There is no bias, residual operand, external initial state, or required final state. Preserve PyTorch depthwise-convolution tap order: tap 3 multiplies the current token, tap 0 the token three positions earlier; out-of-document history is zero.

### Precision and backward

Use FP32 convolution accumulation with BF16 outputs and FP32 partial/final tap-gradient reductions. The incumbent forward fuses SiLU; its backward recomputes the convolution preactivation into BF16 before evaluating the SiLU derivative. That preactivation rounding is part of the compatibility target, not permission to narrow the FP32 tap weights or their gradients.

An implementation may retain or recompute preactivation, but must state the precision boundary and report the memory/performance tradeoff. An alternative higher-precision derivative policy should be explicit and separately compared, not silently substituted.

## Current workaround

Packed FLA Triton convolution forward/backward with fused SiLU, preactivation recomputation, and FP32 partial tap-gradient reduction. It is functional; the request concerns a more efficient training replacement.

## Impact

Throughput; Memory capacity or bandwidth; API usability or integration complexity.

## Acceptance criteria

- Validate output, `dx`, and FP32 `dweight` against a document-local convolution reference with the stated activation/backward rounding boundaries.
- Cover all required `C_local` values with the same precision contract and variable token/document counts; do not specialize the API to the recorded CP16 batch geometry.
- Cover unequal document lengths, lengths smaller than four, non-64-aligned tails, and no forward/backward leakage across documents.
- Benchmark complete forward/replay/backward at the observed 512-channel shapes and representative smaller/larger channel counts, including recomputation, tap reduction, and any layout conversion. Report `S`, `C_local`, workspace, and saved tensors for each result; distinguish full correctness coverage from memory-feasible performance cases rather than extrapolating the profile's timings.
- Support a standalone convolution call; Q/K/V batching is optional and must not require KDA recurrence or distributed collectives.

## Related work, dependencies, or suggested scope

[PR #4243](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/4243) contains fused width-four convolution + SiLU + KDA decode work, but its in-place decode state/cache contract is not packed training with backward. Reuse components if useful; the requested API is a separate training operator, not just an additional decode shape.

items.author: abcdabcd987
items.body_excerpt:
## Problem

The existing CAKE RMSNorm training implementation from closed [#5679](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/5679) / [PR #5741](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5741) covers hidden widths 512, 2048, and 6144 in its [exported registry](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/e403d30785ea9ece65a88b3337db86dcac19fef5/flashinfer/jit/cake_rmsnorm_train.py). GLM-5.3-Flash also needs H1536 and H4096.

Ordinary RMSNorm consumes 0.848 s in the motivating two-update GB200 profile, including forward/replay and backward. That total includes existing H512 calls too; it is not all attributable to the two missing widths.

## Requested outcome

Add H1536 and H4096 forward/backward routes to the existing training API and kernel registry, preserving runtime-variable token counts. These are model feature widths, not CP-sharded dimensions; this remains a narrow width extension, not a new normalization family.

## Target hardware

SM100 (B200, GB200), SM103 (B300, GB300), and Future architecture: SM107 / Rubin, matching the existing training family's architecture scope. The motivating profile is GB200 only.

## Inference engine

PyTorch native; Custom / other. Training with activation checkpointing.

## Affected model or model family

[GLM-5.3-Flash public configuration](https://huggingface.co/zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash/blob/eb9eb208eb0d988989d07a6a12d0fdeb5f52574a/config.json): hidden size 4096 and query LoRA rank 1536.

## Workload and configuration

- **Shapes:** `x,dy[T,H]`, `weight[H]`; `H ∈ {1536,4096}`.
- **Tokens:** observed `T ∈ {14928,15288,15566,15590,16114,16132,16164,16263}`; benchmark examples, not supported-length limits. Preserve runtime-varying `T`, including smaller/larger and irregular row counts as batch layout and CP vary.
- **Layout:** contiguous row-major activations with strides `[H,1]`; contiguous weights.
- **Precision:** BF16 activations, upstream gradients, and affine weights; FP32 RMS/reduction arithmetic. Preserve the existing API's FP32 reciprocal-RMS and deterministic FP32 `dweight` accumulation/output; the caller can cast the final parameter gradient to its storage dtype.
- **Function:** `y = BF16((float32(x) * rsqrt(mean(float32(x)**2) + eps)) * float32(weight))`, with epsilon inside the square root.
- **Epsilon:** retain the existing configurable argument; test `1e-5` and `1e-6`.
- **Parallelism:** the profile uses CP16/EP32; the local operator requires no communication or fixed CP size. CP changes row count `T`, not the complete normalized feature width `H` in this path.
- **Environment:** `python -m flashinfer.collect_env` output is unavailable.

## Current workaround

Compiled PyTorch RMSNorm forward/backward for unsupported widths. H512 can continue using the already-supported route.

## Impact

Missing model or hardware support; Throughput; API usability or integration complexity.

## Acceptance criteria

- New forward/backward routes pass the existing training RMSNorm correctness and deterministic-reduction tests at both widths.
- Validate output, `dx`, and `dweight` at small, large, and irregular `T`, not only the observed counts; benchmark representative sizes against the current fallback and report `T` explicitly.
- Preserve existing 512/2048/6144 routes and runtime token-count behavior without recompiling for each `T`.

## Related work, dependencies, or suggested scope

Small follow-up to [#5679](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/issues/5679) / [#5741](https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/5741). Sigmoid-gated RMSNorm, mHC normalization, new FP32 affine-weight modes, residual fusion extensions, and CP layout changes are outside scope.

items.title: [Core] RESCHEDULING placement group saturates the GCS main thread when it can't be scheduled
items.author: dancingactor
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

If scheduling a placement group in the `RESCHEDULING` state fails, `GcsPlacementGroupManager` keeps retrying scheduling it(~90k retry/s), which busy-spins the GCS main thread. Every retry is guaranteed to fail the same way until the next resource sync update arrives, so retrying before then is unnecessary and only blocks the GCS main thread.

Here is the issue in detail:

- Placement group P is already scheduled successfully on nodes A and B, with one bundle on each node.
- Node A dies, so P needs to be rescheduled elsewhere, and P enters the `RESCHEDULING` state.
- `GcsPlacementGroupManager` treats a `RESCHEDULING` placement group as top priority, so it inserts P at the front of the queue.
- The cluster doesn't currently have available resources for P, so `GcsPlacementGroupManager` fails to schedule P.
- `GcsPlacementGroupManager` immediately reinserts P at the front of the queue and retries scheduling it. The cluster resources haven't been updated yet, so it fails again.
- This retry loop keeps running and busy-spins the GCS main thread, starving other tasks. It only stops when a resource sync update finally provides enough available resources for P.

In this case, every retry between two resource sync updates is completely redundant, because it is guaranteed to produce the same result.

### Proposed Change

I think Solution 1 is better because it solves busy-loop and keeps the `RESCHEDULING` PG at top priority.
|            | Solves busy-loop | Keeps `RESCHEDULING` PG top priority |
| ---------- | ---------------- | ------------------------------------ |
| master     | No               | Yes                                  |
| Solution 1 | Yes              | Yes                                  |
| Solution 2 | Yes              | No                                   |
#### Solution 1
Only retry scheduling a `RESCHEDULING` PG when a resource sync update arrives

#### Solution 2
Back off the `RESCHEDULING` PG the same way as a normal PG when retrying (the first attempt still gets top priority). This also solves the busy-loop problem, but it removes the top priority of the `RESCHEDULING` PG.

These PRs already proposed this change:
- https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65007
- https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65970


### Versions / Dependencies

- Ray: 3.0.0.dev0, built from source at commit a1a2cc64ee

### Reproduction script

``` python
import time

import psutil

import ray
from ray.cluster_utils import Cluster
from ray.util.placement_group import placement_group, placement_group_table

# Head node with 0 CPUs and two 1-CPU workers, both filled by a placement group.
cluster = Cluster(initialize_head=True, head_node_args={"num_cpus": 0})
workers = [cluster.add_node(num_cpus=1) for _ in range(2)]
ray.init(address=cluster.address)
pg_a = placement_group([{"CPU": 1}])
pg_b = placement_group([{"CPU": 1}])
ray.get([pg_a.ready(), pg_b.ready()])

# Remove pg_a's node. pg_a becomes RESCHEDULING: it's feasible, but pg_b holds the
# only remaining CPU.
node_id = placement_group_table(pg_a)["bundles_to_node_id"][0]
cluster.remove_node(next(w for w in workers if w.node_id == node_id))
while placement_group_table(pg_a)["state"] != "RESCHEDULING":
    time.sleep(0.1)
time.sleep(1)

# Nothing in the cluster changes from here on.
gcs = psutil.Process(cluster.head_node.all_processes["gcs_server"][0].process.pid)
start = placement_group_table(pg_a)["stats"]["scheduling_attempt"]
gcs.cpu_percent()
time.sleep(5)
end = placement_group_table(pg_a)["stats"]["scheduling_attempt"]
print(f"pg_a scheduling attempts in 5s: {end - start}, GCS CPU: {gcs.cpu_percent():.0f}%")
```

items.title: [Bug]: Block-scaled FP8 model fails during NVRTC warmup in a pip-less uv environment
items.author: dtemraz
items.body_excerpt:
### System Info

- TensorRT-LLM: `1.3.0rc29` (PyTorch backend)
- Python: 3.12
- Environment: virtual environment created with `uv venv` (no `pip` installed in the venv)
- GPU: H100 SXM 80 GB
- Model: `Qwen/Qwen3-4B-FP8` (block-scaled FP8)

### Who can help?

_No response_

### Information

- [ ] The official example scripts
- [x] My own modified scripts

### Tasks

- [ ] An officially supported task in the `examples` folder (such as GLUE/SQuAD, ...)
- [ ] My own task or dataset (give details below)

### Reproduction


On a machine with a supported NVIDIA GPU and working CUDA dependencies:

```bash
uv venv /tmp/trtllm-uv-repro --python 3.12
uv pip install --python /tmp/trtllm-uv-repro/bin/python \
  --index-strategy unsafe-best-match \
  --prerelease=allow \
  --extra-index-url https://pypi.nvidia.com \
  'tensorrt_llm==1.3.0rc29' 'mpmath==1.3.0'

export PATH=/tmp/trtllm-uv-repro/bin:$PATH

/tmp/trtllm-uv-repro/bin/trtllm-serve Qwen/Qwen3-4B-FP8 --backend pytorch
```

The environment has no venv-local `pip` executable unless it is installed separately. 
The failure is observed during engine warmup, at the first block-scaled FP8 GEMM JIT compilation.


### Expected behavior

TensorRT-LLM should locate the JIT include headers using the installed package's location without requiring the `pip` command to exist in the environment. If the headers cannot be located, the error should identify the missing include path or package-location lookup failure.


### actual behavior

On the tested setup, serving fails during warmup with:

```text
RuntimeError: NVRTC compilation failed
```

The failure originates in JIT include-directory discovery: getJitIncludeDirs() locates the required headers by invoking pip show tensorrt_llm and parsing the Location: field.

In a uv-created virtual environment without pip, this command may resolve to a system-level pip that cannot locate the package installed in the virtual environment. As a result, the required include paths are missing, and compilation of fp8_block_scaling_gemm fails.

The error surfaces as RuntimeError: NVRTC compilation failed, without identifying the missing include paths.

BF16 inference works in the same environment.

## Workaround

Installing `pip` into the same virtual environment and ensuring its executable is first on `PATH` resolves the issue in the tested setup.

### additional notes

.

### Before submitting a new issue...

- [x] Make sure you already searched for relevant issues, and checked the [documentation](https://nvidia.github.io/TensorRT-LLM/) and [examples](https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/tree/main/examples) for answers to frequently asked questions.

items.title: [Performance]: trtllm-gen fmhaReductionKernel walks all KV partials serially per thread; low-batch decode pays a fixed ~6-13 us per call
items.author: lucifer1004
items.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

Multi-CTA-KV generation kernels with a separate reduction (`KeepsMmaAbForGeneration` kernels with gmem reduction) finish with `fmhaReductionKernel` (`cpp/tensorrt_llm/kernels/trtllmGenKernels/fmha/fmhaReduction.cu`). At low batch its grid is tiny: for Kimi K3 MLA decode at batch 1, it is 8 x 2 CTAs for the target model and 2 x 4 for the drafter. Each thread then merges all `numCtasKv` partials of its row one after another. The kernel costs about 6.5 us per call at 2K context and 13.5 us at 128K with 64 KV splits, which is a large share of the attention time at batch 1. #15009 saw the same thing on B300 ("the only remaining gap is the generic fmhaReductionKernel, ~9.2 us flat").

Proposal: an extra template parameter `KvSplit`. The 512 threads of a CTA form `KvSplit` groups. Group g merges partials g, g + KvSplit, ... of the same rows (the same online-softmax update as today), and group 0 then merges the per-group (max, sum, O) through shared memory. Each CTA covers `1/KvSplit` of the rows, so the grid grows by `KvSplit` within the existing `2 x SMs` CTA budget, and every thread walks `KvSplit` times fewer partials. `KvSplit = 1` keeps the current kernel.

Measured on SM107 with the grouped Q64 MLA generation kernels (Kimi K3 shapes, 32 tokens per page, causal, up to 64 KV splits), p50 us per MLA call including the reduction, batch 1:

| config | 2K | 8K | 32K | 128K |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| target, 16 heads, KvSplit 1 | 14.20 | 24.56 | 29.13 | 55.81 |
| target, 16 heads, KvSplit 4 | 12.01 | 18.02 | 22.70 | 49.81 |
| target, 16 heads, KvSplit 8 | 12.30 | 17.28 | 21.74 | 49.27 |
| target, 16 heads, KvSplit 16 | 13.26 | 17.02 | 21.60 | 49.17 |
| drafter, 8 heads, KvSplit 1 | 12.80 | 22.76 | 26.77 | 50.51 |
| drafter, 8 heads, KvSplit 8 | 11.06 | 15.59 | 19.63 | 44.38 |

Outputs match KvSplit 1 to about 1e-5 in output sum and absolute sum at batch 1, 2 and 4. End to end (Kimi K3 + MTP, 8 GPUs over 2 nodes, single request, two cold starts that agree within 0.04 ms), KvSplit 8 changes the decode step by -0.10 ms at 2K, -0.23 ms at 32K and -0.21 ms at 128K, with unchanged accuracy.

PR to follow. Because I could only measure this on SM107 with the grouped MLA kernels, the PR makes it opt-in (`TLLM_FMHA_REDUCTION_KV_SPLIT`); if someone can check SM100/SM103, a default of 8 (still limited by the CTA budget) looks like the right end state.

items.title: [BUG] SM90 blockwise FP8 GEMM reuses modified B scales across M waves
items.author: 1sgtpepper
items.body_excerpt:
## Which component has the problem?

CUTLASS C++

## Bug Report

**Describe the bug**

SM90 cooperative blockwise FP8 GEMM applies the preceding M wave's A scale again when processing the next M wave. With CTA tile 256×128×128 and scale granularity 128×64×128, `D[128,0]` is **1024 instead of 512**.

**Steps/Code to reproduce bug**

In a checkout of `59e3a3338d516ca6ce0e073af8da65289678a35c`:

```sh
curl -fL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/1sgtpepper/cutlass/75e7b4a8a2859c317209d81c91c5ab9158a573e7/test/regression/fp8_scale_wave.cu -o fp8_scale_wave.cu
nvcc -std=c++17 -O3 -lineinfo --expt-relaxed-constexpr \
  -gencode=arch=compute_90a,code=sm_90a \
  -Iinclude -Itools/util/include fp8_scale_wave.cu -o fp8_scale_wave
./fp8_scale_wave
```

Inputs are FP8 E4M3 ones, with A scales 2 and 4 across the row bands and B scales 1 and 2 across the column bands.

```text
minimal l=0 m=128 n=0 actual=1024 expected=512
minimal tile=256x128x128 scale=128x64x128 stages=3 problem=256x128x128x1 mismatches=16384 FAIL
```

**Expected behavior**

Each M wave multiplies its own A scale by the original B scale for the current K tile.

**Environment details (please complete the following information):**

- CUTLASS `59e3a3338d516ca6ce0e073af8da65289678a35c`, main as of September 8, 2026. The affected collective is byte-identical in `v4.8.0dev` and `v4.7.1`; these releases were not executed.
- H100 80GB HBM3, driver 580.95.05; CUDA 13.1.1.
- Modal cloud GPU, Ubuntu 24.04 container, Linux x86_64.

**Additional context**

The `ScaleMsPerWave == 1 && ScaleNsPerTile > 1` path modifies B-scale registers reused by successive M waves, in both the main loop and drain. Reloading B's original scales makes all ten `--all` cases pass; restoring the old code restores the same six failures.

items.title: [Serve] [RFC] Computed Retry-After for backpressure rejections
items.author: vinay7373
items.body_excerpt:
## Motivation

PR #65193 added `BackpressureConfig`. Deployments can now reject backpressured requests with a 429 and a static `Retry-After` header. Each caller (proxy or `DeploymentHandle`) has its own request queue, and at the time of a backpressure rejection a static `Retry-After` value can be incorrect in both directions. If the queue is deep and the static value is too short, clients retry into another rejection, adding load exactly when the system is trying to shed it. If the queue drains fast and the value is too long, capacity sits idle while clients wait.

This proposal computes the `Retry-After` value from observed load. This makes the header a reliable estimate of when capacity will be available, instead of a number the operator guessed. This was the original shape of the production request behind #65193 and it fits the discussion there about making 429 the default at some point.

No OSS inference server does this today (TGI, Triton, NVIDIA Dynamo and TorchServe all reject without a retry hint). The closest prior art is cloud-side (Azure OpenAI's `retry-after-ms`, AWS's `x-amz-retry-after`) and per-client rate limiters, where the value can be exact because a rate window is a clock. Capacity recovery is not a clock, so here the value is an estimate at any layer.

## Goals

- An opt-in `BackpressureConfig` policy that computes `Retry-After` from load signals the rejecting component already has.
- Keep the rejection path as cheap as it is today. No RPCs, locks or extra work on reject-and-respond.
- Degrade gracefully: computed, else static, else no header. Never fail or delay a rejection.

## Non-goals

- Changing when requests are rejected. Admission control is a separate discussion.
- Guaranteeing admission at the suggested time. The header is a hint, not a reservation.
- Changing the default rejection status code. Tracked separately.
- Implementing any further policy, such as the cluster-informed one (see "Future policies").

## Proposed API

```python
from ray.serve.config import BackpressureConfig

@serve.deployment(
    max_queued_requests=64,
    backpressure_config=BackpressureConfig(
        status_code=429,
        retry_after_policy="queue_drain_rate",   # NEW: "static" (default) | "queue_drain_rate"
        retry_after_s=5,                         # static value; also the fallback for computed policies
    ),
)
```

`retry_after_policy` is a named policy instead of a bare `"auto"` so future strategies can be added without changing what existing configs mean.

## Proposed design

This design adds a new field to `BackpressureConfig` called `retry_after_policy`, and one new policy named `queue_drain_rate` that computes `Retry-After` from the rejecting component's observed queue depth and drain rate.

The overall mechanism has 3 basic aspects: (i) how to compute the `Retry-After` value (what the `queue_drain_rate` policy implements), (ii) where to compute it, and (iii) who stamps the header and emits it to the client.

These boil down to emission and estimation. Emission answers (iii) and is fixed: the rejecting component stamps the header. Estimation covers (i) and (ii): one shared implementation, invoked at the two places Serve rejects today, each feeding its own local signals.

### The `queue_drain_rate` policy (this proposal)

```
retry_after = ceil(observed_queue_depth / drain_rate)
```

- **The numerator is the depth observed at rejection.** It is at least `max_queued_requests`, since a rejection only fires once the queue has reached the cap, and occasionally a little above it: the router's check is not atomic, and replica-rejected requests re-enter the queue behind new arrivals. The raise site already holds this number (it is in the `BackPressureError` message today), so using the observed value costs nothing and is exact.
- **`drain_rate` is the live signal**: how fast the queue empties, updated at the end of every interval as `drain_rate = 0.3 * rate_over_last_interval + 0.7 * previous_drain_rate`. `rate_over_last_interval` is the fresh measurement: requests drained during the interval that just ended. `previous_drain_rate` is this same formula's output from the previous update, so it carries the whole history with older intervals fading out. The 70% weight on the trend keeps lumpy traffic from whipping the value around (completions land in bursts, so a single interval can read 0 or 3x the true rate), and the 30% on the fresh measurement keeps the estimate chasing real load changes within a few intervals. The split, the interval length and the warmup threshold are implementation constants with environment-variable overrides, like Serve's other internal tunables, not new `BackpressureConfig` fields. The update runs on a lightweight background timer in the component's existing metrics machinery (default 1s). An interval with zero completions counts as a real observation when work is in flight, since that is what slow drain looks like, but idle intervals (nothing running or queued) skip the update instead of decaying the rate. The rate counts as warm after a configurable minimum number of counted intervals; until then the fallback applies.
- **Two call sites, one implementation.** On the proxy path the router rejects; its drain rate is its own assignment throughput, from a monotonic counter added at the existing send event (the current per-replica counter is an in-flight gauge, so it can't provide a rate). The rate is fleet-blended: faster replicas take more assignments, so mixed hardware is priced in. On direct ingress the replica rejects; its drain rate is its own completion rate, and its queue is drained only by itself. Same formula, different local inputs, different values, each describing its own queue. A replica's value is a conservative upper bound, since a retry may be re-balanced to a replica that frees up sooner.
- **Clamp to [1, 60] seconds.** Common client SDKs ignore `Retry-After` above 60s.
- **Jitter (for example +/-20%) is applied in the shared heade

comments.author: johntaylor-cell
comments.body:
My main concern is how this RFC and direct-ingress work together.  Serve is moving toward direct-ingress with HAProxy as the default, and on that path the router is no longer the module that rejects the request.  HAProxy will sit between the client and Serve, and it already has retry-after functionality (as does Envoy).  Both implement it very differently from what the RFC proposes.  Their calculation is time-based so it is more exact than the proposed prediction.  It is also per-client, and HAProxy exposes queue-based metrics so the limit can fire only under real back pressure.  I suggest we provide a way to enable that functionality in HAProxy, which Serve already generates config for but does not use today.

If we also want retry-after on the router path (when direct-ingress is disabled), I would try to duplicate HAProxy's time-based functionality, rather than use a forecast. That is a larger change than this RFC scopes, since admission control is listed as a non-goal, but I think it is worth deciding explicitly rather than estimating.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
Thanks for the review. Breaking it down into where we agree and where we don't.

**Where we agree:**

1. The RFC did not cover the direct-ingress path. That was a real gap and I updated the RFC. Short version: on direct ingress the same policy runs at the replica, using its own queue depth divided by an EWMA of its own completion rate. Same formula, one shared estimator implementation, two call sites. A replica's queue is drained only by itself, so that vantage is even simpler than the router's.

2. Per-client rate limiting at the HAProxy layer is valuable. It answers "this client exceeded its quota", and its Retry-After can be exact because a rate window is a clock. That is complementary to this RFC, which answers "the deployment is out of capacity, here is when to come back". I would support that as a separate proposal and am happy to file it.

**Where we don't agree, and why:**

1. "HAProxy will sit between the client and Serve" as the rejector. Not for backpressure today. On the direct-ingress path the replica rejects the request (see the "Request dropped due to backpressure" emission sites in [replica.py on the ray-2.58.0 tag](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/blob/ray-2.58.0/python/ray/serve/_private/replica.py)). HAProxy passes the replica's response through, and its errorfiles only rewrite HAProxy-generated errors. #65193 shipped 429 + Retry-After on this path, tested with `RAY_SERVE_ENABLE_DIRECT_INGRESS=1`.

2. "Functionality Serve already generates config for but does not use". I checked `haproxy_templates.py`: no stick-tables, no track-sc, no deny rules, no Retry-After anywhere in the generated config. Enabling this would be new work, not switching on something dormant.

3. "Their calculation is time-based so it is more exact than the proposed prediction". I checked the [HAProxy docs](https://www.haproxy.com/documentation/haproxy-configuration-tutorials/security/traffic-policing/) on this. HAProxy's computed Retry-After is `http-after-response set-header Retry-After %[src,table_expire(...)]`: the time until the client's stick-table rate-limit record expires. That is per-client policing, and it is exact because a rate window is deterministic. For capacity overload (server maxconn queue full, `timeout queue` expiring) the docs show no Retry-After computation: that 503 ships without a hint. The queue timer measures elapsed wait, not time until capacity returns. When capacity frees depends on service completions and arrivals, and no layer can know that exactly, including HAProxy, which cannot see how long the inference ahead of a request will take. Any capacity Retry-After is an estimate at every layer. That is why the RFC ships an acceptance criterion and telemetry to measure the estimate, instead of claiming exactness.

Rate limiting and capacity backpressure are different problems. An exact time-based Retry-After exists for the first and cannot exist for the second. This RFC is scoped to the second, now explicitly works on both ingress paths, and leaves room for a HAProxy rate-limiting proposal alongside it.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@johntaylor-cell 

My thoughts on your a HA Proxy based admission control and what I see as limitations:

- As you mentioned the HAProxy queue resets on every reload and Serve reloads HAProxy on every replica-set change. So the primary queue evaporates exactly during autoscaling churn (your own finding).
- Composition traffic never passes HAProxy, so the Serve backstop must stay. That means 3 admission systems with 3 threshold vocabularies to keep coherent.
    - Users configuring three queueing layers instead of one: per-server `maxconn` plus timeout queue in HAProxy, `max_queued_requests` at handles, `max_ongoing_requests` at replicas. Three knobs at three levels in different units (connections vs requests, per instance vs per caller vs per replica) that all have to be sized against each other and re-sized as the cluster scales. Mis-size any pair and you get double queueing or shedding while replicas sit idle. That is more error prone, not simpler.
- The default proxy path gets nothing from it.
- Per-deployment BackpressureConfig granularity would have to be re-expressed in generated HAProxy config.
- Moving where queueing happens is an admission-control redesign, which this RFC explicitly scopes out as a non-goal.
- On jittered-static vs computed: 
    - jitter only spreads retries around a center, it cannot make the center reliable. With `retry_after_s` we already ship the option to set a fixed, guessed value at config time, so a jittered constant is not a new proposal, it is [#65193](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65193) plus jitter. Drain rate moves 10-100x across load regimes, so the constant is wrong exactly when it matters. A 5s center against a 60s real drain means every jittered retry comes back early and gets refused again. Guessing that constant is the problem this RFC exists to remove. So a computed value using drain rate is more reliable. And @suppagoddo 's suggestion for A/B against a jittered-static baseline will show it under real workloads and make this measurable.
