@abrarsheikh to summarize the whole review thread and the current state of RFC:

Updated the RFC based on the review so far and it came out simpler. 
One policy, `queue_drain_rate` which computes `retry_after` on rejection using below formula:
```
retry_after = ceil(max_queued_requests / drain_rate)
```
Where:
- `max_queued_requests`: the numerator is the configured cap (depth at rejection is always the cap) and 
- `drain_rate` is a smoothed measure of how fast the rejecting component's queue empties which is assignment throughput at the router, completion rate at the replica. 

The value is clamped to [1, 60]s and jittered in the shared header helper so the static path gets jitter too, falls back to the static retry_after_s when the rate isn't warm, and the acceptance test is an A/B against a jittered-static baseline measured on suggested delay vs observed local drain time.

comments.author: JerryChaox
comments.body:
hello guys, some information and test for this RFC.

I tested the proposal on Ray 2.58.0 and found two implementation details worth checking before coding it.

First, num_requests_sent_to_replicas is an in-flight gauge: it increments on send and decrements on completion. It cannot directly provide assignment throughput, so the router likely needs a monotonic counter at the accepted-assignment event.

Second, router queue depth is not always equal to max_queued_requests at rejection. Internal replica rejection can cause requests to re-enter after new requests occupy temporarily freed slots. With a cap of 8, 1,418 of 17,270 router rejection events had an observed depth of 9–11. I did not observe this on the direct-replica path.

I also compared the computed policy with a tuned jittered-static baseline over 90 held-out distributed runs. Conditional local-drain header MAE was 1.865s for the computed policy and 1.141s for static 2s. The computed policy generated fewer attempts, so this looks like a precision versus retry-cost tradeoff rather than a clear winner.

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
@JerryChaox Thanks for testing the approach and for those valuable findings. Here are my thoughts on each of them:

1. Agree (and my earlier comment was wrong on this) that `num_requests_sent_to_replicas` is an in-flight gauge, increments on send (`router.py:404`) and decrements on completion (`router.py:412`). I will fix this by adding a new monotonic assignment counter at the same send event. So the raise site and the counters live on the same object and the drain rate is still a derivation over local state.

2. This is a great find. Agreed. This finding makes the formula better: use the observed depth at rejection as the numerator instead of the configured cap. The raise site already holds that number, it is in the BackPressureError message today.

3. On your third observation, the A/B test: I see how a static value wins on a homogeneous workload, where a good constant like your 2s can be guessed or tuned in advance. But the whole purpose of this RFC is the case where the constant cannot be guessed in advance, because load regimes vary and move the drain rate. I'd like to know: a) Did drain time vary across your 90 runs? b) Was the 2s tuned per workload or once overall?

Your fewer attempts observation is the most interesting part. MAE weighs a 1s early and a 1s late suggestion equally, but the costs are not equal: early means a wasted attempt plus more load on a system that is already shedding, late means idle wait. So I think we should use a asymmetric or composite metric that penalizes wasted attempts (penalize early more than late).

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
Acceptance criteria spec:

1. Ground truth: Each rejection records the observed depth D and the drain counter value at that moment. Ground truth T is the wall time until the counter advances by D: assignments at the router, completions at the replica on direct ingress. This measures what the header claims, that the observed backlog clears. It does not measure whether a specific retry gets admitted, since that depends on other clients' arrivals. T stays measurable under continuous overload because the counter keeps advancing even when the queue never dips below the cap.
2. Metric: An asymmetric loss between the suggested delay `s` and `T`: `0.75 * max(T - s, 0) + 0.25 * max(s - T, 0)`. One second too early costs 3x one second too late, because an early retry wastes an attempt and adds load while the system is shedding and a late one only waits, bounded by the clamp. The minimizer of this loss is the 75th percentile of the drain time distribution, so the estimator gets a concrete target. MAE is reported as secondary for comparability. Scoring is offline over logged pairs, on the pre-jitter post-clamp value.
3. Baseline: The comparison arm is jittered static, with the constant tuned only on calibration runs disjoint from the evaluation set (rule: 75th percentile of calibration drain times, one global constant). A per-scenario tuned static is also reported. Runs are open loop (clients ignore the header) with autoscaling off and a pinned replica set.

@suppagoddo For me to run the above acceptance test I'll need one structured record per rejection with `policy id, fallback rung used, observed depth, drain rate estimate and warm flag, pre-jitter and post-jitter values, and the counter value at rejection`. Plus the counter itself readable by a test harness at sub-second granularity. Everything already exists at the raise site or in estimator state; the cost is one log line on a path that already logs a warning today. Please make sure this record emission is part of your implementation.

Pass bar (proposal): 
- Computed beats the static baseline on the primary loss by at least 20% in aggregate across the scenarios
- is never more than 10% worse in any single scenario
- the undershoot rate lands at 25 +/- 10 points
- and cold start falls back to the static value cleanly.

cc. @JerryChaox @abrarsheikh @johntaylor-cell

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
**AI serving regimes for the acceptance runs**

Now that the implementation is up for review (#66798), here are the regimes the acceptance runs will cover. The runs collect the metrics defined in my acceptance comment above. The scenarios its pass bar refers to are drawn from these regimes. I'm deriving the regimes from real-world AI serving, using two characteristics: load and completion.

What a regime is: An AI serving regime is a recurring pattern of load and completion at the component that rejects requests. Load is how requests arrive. Completion is how they finish: how long each one runs, how many run at once, and whether they finish one at a time or in batches.

**Why these two (load and completion)?**
Ground truth in the acceptance spec is the time for the drain counter to advance by the observed depth: assignments at the router, completions at the replica on direct ingress. Both count the completion process, seen from each vantage, since the router hands a queued request to a replica when one finishes. So completion sets the drain time directly. Load decides when the queue overflows and what the estimator sees between rejections, such as idle gaps. Latency is an outcome of both, not an input.

Completion is the important half in AI serving, because processing time is not known when a request arrives. A generative model decides its output length while it generates, and in production "the remaining output length of an LLM request is not conditioned on the generated length so far" [1]. Drain speed cannot be computed from what is in the queue. It has to be measured from completions.


**Completion regimes:** 
The estimator samples once per second, so what matters is how far apart completions arrive at that scale.

| Regime | Examples | Completions | Evidence |
|---|---|---|---|
| W1 Real-time predictive | vision, ranking, LLM code completion | Dense: many per second | Latency bounds of 15 to 250 ms [2]. Code completion has a median output of 13 tokens [3] |
| W2 Batched execution | `@serve.batch`, dynamic batching | Grouped: a batch finishes together | Each response returns once its whole batch is evaluated [4] |
| W3 Interactive LLM | chat on continuous batching | Dense to moderate: seconds each, many at once | A median of 129 output tokens [3] at 20 to 50 tokens/s [5] |
| W4 Long-running LLM | reasoning, long context, agent steps | Sparse: minutes each, few at once | A mean of 3,880 output tokens [6]. Long contexts limit how many run at once [7] |

**Load regimes:**

| Regime | Arrivals | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| L1 Steady | A constant rate. The runs use fixed-interval schedules so repeated runs are comparable | MLPerf's Server scenario models online load with Poisson arrivals [2] |
| L2 Bursts and idle gaps | High-rate bursts separated by silence | API traffic is "aperiodic... characterized by burstiness" [8]. Short-term arrivals are "often bursty (CV > 1)" [1] |
| L3 Mix shift | A steady rate, but the request mix changes, so completions speed up or slow down | Services have "widely different prompt and token distributions" [3]. In one 48-hour window, 29 of 2,412 clients sent 90% of requests [1] |

**Scenarios:** 
|# | Cell | Completions | Expected drain time | Load |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| S1 | W1, L1 | every 0.25 s | 2 s | 2x drain |
| S2 | W3, L1 | every 2.5 s | 20 s | 2.5x drain |
| S3 | W1 to W3, L3 | every 0.25 s, then every 1 s | 4 s, then 16 s | 2x drain |

comments.author: vinay7373
comments.body:
From the above clearly EWMA's loss is 74% lower overall than static jitter. Though the results above show a clear gain, it falls short when completions are seconds apart:
1. Long requests, one completion every 8 s: never early, but clients waited 15 to 17 s longer than needed on average.
2. Batched, 8 requests finishing together every 4 s: early only 2 to 3% of the time, and clients waited about 6 s longer than needed.
3. Steady slow, one completion every 2.5 s: the estimate swings both ways. On the proxy path it was early 45% of the time. On both paths, when it was late, clients waited 9 to 12 s longer than needed.
4. Beyond cap, one completion every 8 s with 30 requests waiting: the true wait is 240 s. Without the 60 s cap, the EWMA would have sent a median of 382 s, and up to about 2,400 s (40 minutes). These are rejections from the first 180 s of each run, while the drain held at one every 8 s.

**Main cause for the above limitation:** The EWMA counts drains in each one-second sample and divides the depth by that rate. When completions are seconds apart, most samples count zero. The rate falls at every empty second and dividing by a small rate gives a long wait. When the next completion comes, the rate jumps back up. So the estimate follows the time since the last completion, not the real drain speed. For example, with one completion every 4 s and 8 requests ahead, the true wait is 29 to 32 s, but the EWMA's estimate moves between 20 and 59 s.

Lets take LLM serving as an example. After bit research on how requests complete in LLM serving, I found that what matters is not just how long each request runs, but how far apart completions are at the component that rejects. That gap is about how long one request runs, divided by how many requests run at the same time. For example, if a replica runs 40 requests at once and each takes 20 s, one finishes every 0.5 s or if it can run only 2 at once, one finishes every 10 s. LLM requests run for seconds to minutes. Memory for long contexts limits how many run at once on a replica and batched work finishes in groups. So in Batched execution (W2), Long-running LLM (W4) and Interactive LLM (W3) when a replica runs only a few requests at once, completions at the rejecting component are seconds apart or come in groups. These patterns are common in LLM serving and they are where a per-second rate breaks down. So we want to measure the drain in a way that does not depend on completions landing inside each one-second sample.

To address the above, I would like to propose **The busy clock**:
The PR already keeps one running total for each component, the drain counter. The busy clock adds a second running total: busy seconds.
- A drain is one step of the drain counter: an assignment at the router, or a completion at a replica.
- A busy second is a second in which the component had work pending or saw a drain. These are the seconds the PR's sampler already counts. Idle seconds, which the PR skips, are not added, so the busy clock stops when the component is idle.
- Seconds per drain is busy seconds divided by drains over a recent window. It is the average time the component needs for one drain while it is working.
- The window is the most recent stretch of busy time that holds at least 8 drains and at least 10 busy seconds. Each limit protects one kind of workload:
  - When completions are seconds apart, the 8 drains matter. They keep the estimate from resting on one or two gaps. With one completion every 8 s, the window stretches to about 64 s.
  - When there are many completions per second, 8 drains can pass in a fraction of a second. The 10 busy seconds keep the estimate from jumping with every small burst.
  - The window only sets how far back the estimate looks. The estimate is still updated every second and every rejection is answered at once. Until 10 busy seconds have passed, the window is all the busy time so far, so warmup still takes 3 counted seconds. If the last 10 minutes of busy

items.title: Async actor fiber stack protection is re-anchored after the first Python call on CPython 3.14
items.author: guoshengCS
items.body_excerpt:
## Environment

  - OS: Linux
  - Python: CPython 3.14.7
  - Ray: 2.57.0
  - Workload: high-concurrency async actors
  - Async actor tasks are executed using Ray's Boost.Fiber task runner.

  ## Background

  We originally observed continuous memory growth when running Ray async actors
  on CPython 3.14.

  The issue appears related to CPython 3.14 stack protection retaining the runner
  thread's pthread stack bounds while Python object deallocation occurs on a
  Boost fiber stack.

  Related upstream work:

  - [Issue #63290](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues/63290)
  - [PR #64772](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/64772), which re-anchors
    CPython's stack protection to the current async-actor fiber
  - [PR #65177](https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65177), which
    cherry-picked #64772 into the Ray 2.57 release branch

  After upgrading from Ray 2.55.0 to `ray==2.57.0`, the memory growth disappeared.
  However, the same workload started failing intermittently with:

  ```
  ^[[36m(RouterManager pid=17880, ip=10.17.71.27)^[[0m [2026-09-12 03:10:57,784 C 17880 18485] task_receiver.cc:136:  An unexpected system state has occurred. You have likely discovered a bug in Ray. Please report this issue at https://github.com/ray-project/ray/issues and we'll work with you to fix it. Check failed: objects_valid 1 return objects expected, 1 returned. Object at idx 0 was not stored.
^[[36m(RouterManager pid=17880, ip=10.17.71.27)^[[0m *** StackTrace Information ***
^[[36m(RouterManager pid=17880, ip=10.17.71.27)^[[0m /opt/venv/python3.14.7/lib/python3.14/site-packages/ray/_raylet.so(+0x181494a) [0x7f606f81494a] ray::operator<<()
^[[36m(RouterManager pid=17880, ip=10.17.71.27)^[[0m /opt/venv/python3.14.7/lib/python3.14/site-packages/ray/_raylet.so(_ZN3ray6RayLogD1Ev+0x469) [0x7f606f816f79] ray::RayLog::~RayLog()
^[[36m(RouterManager pid=17880, ip=10.17.71.27)^[[0m /opt/venv/python3.14.7/lib/python3.14/site-packages/ray/_raylet.so(_ZN3ray4core12TaskReceiver25HandleTaskExecutionResultENS_6StatusERKNS_17TaskSpecificationERKNS0_19TaskExecutionResultERKSt8functionIFvS2_S9_IFvvEESB_EEPNS_3rpc13PushTaskReplyE+0xf96) [0x7f606ec203e6] ray::core::TaskReceiver::HandleTaskExecutionResult()
^[[36m(RouterManager pid=17880, ip=10.17.71.27)^[[0m /opt/venv/python3.14.7/lib/python3.14/site-packages/ray/_raylet.so(+0xc20d22) [0x7f606ec20d22] ray::core::TaskReceiver::ExecuteTask()
^[[36m(RouterManager pid=17880, ip=10.17.71.27)^[[0m /opt/venv/python3.14.7/lib/python3.14/site-packages/ray/_raylet.so(_ZN3ray4core32UnorderedActorTaskExecutionQueue31AcceptRequestOrRejectIfCanceledENS_6TaskIDERNS0_13TaskToExecuteE+0x131) [0x7f606ec32cc1] ray::core::UnorderedActorTaskExecutionQueue::AcceptRequestOrRejectIfCanceled()
^[[36m(RouterManager pid=17880, ip=10.17.71.27)^[[0m /opt/venv/python3.14.7/lib/python3.14/site-packages/ray/_raylet.so(+0xc3361b) [0x7f606ec3361b] std::_Function_handler<>::_M_invoke()
^[[36m(RouterManager pid=17880, ip=10.17.71.27)^[[0m /opt/venv/python3.14.7/lib/python3.14/site-packages/ray/_raylet.so(+0xc303e7) [0x7f606ec303e7] std::_Function_handler<>::_M_invoke()
^[[36m(RouterManager pid=17880, ip=10.17.71.27)^[[0m /opt/venv/python3.14.7/lib/python3.14/site-packages/ray/_raylet.so(+0xc36264) [0x7f606ec36264] boost::fibers::worker_context<>::run_()
^[[36m(RouterManager pid=17880, ip=10.17.71.27)^[[0m /opt/venv/python3.14.7/lib/python3.14/site-packages/ray/_raylet.so(+0xc36010) [0x7f606ec36010] boost::context::detail::fiber_entry<>()

  This resembles the failure mode discussed in PR #57253 (https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/57253): if task_execution_handler raises before entering the task-handling code that converts exceptions into return objects, Cython may continue by returning an OK status without producing the expected objects. The later objects_valid CHECK then masks the original exception.

  ## Experiment with PR #65119

  We also tested Ray 2.57.0 with the exact fiber stack-boundary tracking changes
  from PR #65119 (https://github.com/ray-project/ray/pull/65119).

  That PR replaces the estimated fiber stack range used by #64772 with the exact
  allocation recorded by FiberStackRegistry.

items.title: [Core/Auth] Enable token authentication by default for all clusters in Ray 2.61
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
Since Ray 2.59, token authentication is on by default only for local clusters. Every other cluster (started by hand, by `ray up` and the autoscaler, by KubeRay, or by the Anyscale platform) still runs with auth disabled, so anyone who can reach its ports can run arbitrary code. Ray 2.61 makes token auth the default for every cluster. `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` stays the opt-out.

Design:

- `AUTH_MODE` defaults to `"token"` in `src/ray/common/ray_config_def.h`. The local-cluster special cases added in #64755, #66467 and #66778 are deleted, since every path is already in token mode.
- One place creates the token: `Node(head=True)`. Connecting nodes and clients never create one; without a token they fail fast with an error that names `ray get-auth-token` and the `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` opt-out.
- The token never goes on a command line. `ray up` ships it to the head node as a file mount, the head ships it to the worker nodes it launches, and `image_uri`/`container` workers get it as a read-only file mount.
- A client in token mode talking to a cluster that opted out gets an error instead of silent success. gRPC servers in disabled mode reject requests that carry a token. HTTP clients check `GET /api/authentication_mode` instead, because reverse proxies in front of a disabled dashboard can send their own `Authorization` header (the former `kuberay-auth.md` guide set one up with kube-rbac-proxy; also ray-project/kuberay#1824, #42606).


How users use it in 2.61. Every sub-issue PR must keep these flows working as shown:

1. Local development, no setup. The head creates `~/.ray/auth_token`, and everything in the same HOME reads it.

```bash
ray start --head
ray start --address=127.0.0.1:6379   # a second node on the same machine
python -c "import ray; ray.init()"   # a driver
```

A bare `ray.init()` needs no setup: it connects to the running local cluster if there is one, and otherwise starts a new one.

2. A cluster built by hand across machines. The token file must be copied from the head to each machine; the token never goes on a command line.

```bash
# head machine
ray start --head
# worker machine, after the head's ~/.ray/auth_token is copied here
ray start --address=<head-ip>:6379
```

Without the copy, `ray start --address` fails at once with an error that says to run `ray get-auth-token` on the head and copy the token.

3. `ray up`. No token steps: `ray up` creates the token on the operator's machine if needed and ships it to the head node. The head ships it to every worker node it launches, including ones the autoscaler adds later.

```bash
ray up cluster.yaml
ray dashboard cluster.yaml &
ray job submit --address http://127.0.0.1:8265 -- python script.py
```

4. A client on another machine. Clients on the head machine, or on the machine that ran `ray up`, already have the token. Any other machine needs the token file copied to it.

```bash
# after the head's ~/.ray/auth_token is copied to this machine
ray job submit --address http://<head-ip>:8265 -- python script.py
```

`RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH` is only needed when the token file lives somewhere other than `~/.ray/auth_token`.

5. Opting out. Every node and every client sets `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled`. The head logs a warning that auth is disabled.

```bash
RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled ray start --head
RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled ray start --address=<head-ip>:6379
RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled ray job submit --address http://<head-ip>:8265 -- python script.py
```

A node or client that leaves out `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` fails with an error telling it to set it: AuthModeMismatch if it has a token, the missing-token error if it doesn't. For `ray up`, put `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` in the cluster YAML's start commands.

6. Mismatches never fall back to auth off. A worker or client with no token, a different token, or a different auth mode than the head fails right away with an error that names the fix. It does not hang or connect without auth.

Rules every sub-issue PR must keep:

- Auth is on unless `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` is set. No code decides auth on or off from whether a cluster is local, new, or started by a particular entry point.
- A head node started with `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` logs a warning once, from `Node(head=True)`, saying auth is disabled and anyone who can reach the cluster's ports can run code. Worker nodes, drivers and clients don't warn.
- Only a head node (`Node(head=True)`) creates a token. Worker nodes, drivers, `ray://` clients, the CLI and the SDKs never create one, because a token made on a client can't match the cluster's. The one exception is `ray up`, which creates the cluster and ships its token to the head node, which ships it to the worker nodes it launches.
- Token source precedence stays `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN` > `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH` > `~/.ray/auth_token`.
- The token never appears on a command line, in `ps`, in logged environment variables, or in log output. Pass it as a file.
- A mismatch always fails, never falls back to auth off:

| Cluster | Node or client | Result |
|---|---|---|
| token | token, same token | works |
| token | token, different token | rejected |
| token | token mode, no token | fails before connecting |
| token | `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` | rejected (missing token) |
| `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` | token mode | rejected (AuthModeMismatch) |
| `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` | `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` | works |

- Every auth error names its fix: run `ray get-auth-token` on the head and copy the token, or set `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` if the cluster opted out. A rejected node or client must show that error, not hang or time out.
- `GET /api/authentication_mode` stays unauthenticated; it reveals only the mode, and the client-side mismatch check depends on it.
- The dashboard never rejects a request because of its `Authorization` header; reverse proxies in front of a disabled dashboard can send their own. HTTP mismatches are detected on the client.
- Local development stays zero-config: `ray start --head`, then `ray star

items.title: [Core/Auth] Reject gRPC requests that carry a token on clusters with auth disabled
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
A server with an empty token accepts every request (`server_call.h`), so a client in token mode talking to a cluster with `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` succeeds silently. The client should be told to opt out too.

Change:

- A server in disabled mode rejects any request that carries a token with `UNAUTHENTICATED` and "AuthModeMismatch: cluster has RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled; set it on the client too". Apply it in `ServerCall::ValidateAuthenticationToken` (keep the Kubernetes token exception) and in the Python gRPC server interceptor in `grpc_utils.py`, which is then always installed.
- `AuthenticationError.__str__` leaves out the "get a token" help for this message.
- Test: a disabled cluster with a driver that also sets `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` and has a token file works; a driver that doesn't set it gets the AuthModeMismatch error.
- Test: `ray start --address` in token mode against a head with `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` fails with AuthModeMismatch, without hanging or timing out.

HTTP is out of scope here (see #67053).

items.title: Illegal memory access in triton kernel and non-determinism codegen
items.author: xw285cornell
items.body_excerpt:
Hi team, we seem to identified an issue that triton is generating non-deterministic codegen results, and in certain cases (small chances) it seems to have illegal memory access due to out of bound access in shared memory. 
The triton code is fairly simple (shown below). We run the code many times (disabled pytorch's codegen cache) and it seems it produced different shared memory: 
Most of times: 
{"name": "triton__0d1d2d3d4", "shared": 2560, "num_warps": 4, "num_stages": 1}
Sometimes: 
{"name": "triton__0d1d2d3d4", "shared": 544, "num_warps": 4, "num_stages": 1}

So sometimes it only asks for 544 bytes for shared memory space which might lead to out of bound access to shared mem. We checked and ttir is the same across the two runs, but llir is different. Wondering if you can shed some lights on this (and whether the codegen is deterministic. Also this is still on llvm IR - not sure if it repros in MLIR. 

```
from torch._inductor.triton_ops.autotune import pointwise

@pointwise(
    size_hints=[262144, 64],
    tile_hint=TileHint.DEFAULT,
    filename="notebook",
    meta={
        "signature": {0: "*bf16", 1: "*fp32", 2: "*bf16", 3: "i32", 4: "i32"},
        "device": 0,
        "constants": {},
        "mutated_arg_names": [],
        "configs": [instance_descriptor(divisible_by_16=(0, 1, 2, 3), equal_to_1=())],
    },
)
@triton.jit
def triton_(
    in_ptr0,
    in_ptr1,
    out_ptr0,
    xnumel,
    ynumel,
    XBLOCK: tl.constexpr,
    YBLOCK: tl.constexpr,
):
    xnumel = 262144
    ynumel = 62
    xoffset = tl.program_id(0) * XBLOCK
    xindex = xoffset + tl.arange(0, XBLOCK)[:, None]
    xmask = xindex < xnumel
    yoffset = tl.program_id(1) * YBLOCK
    yindex = yoffset + tl.arange(0, YBLOCK)[None, :]
    ymask = yindex < ynumel
    x0 = xindex % 512
    x1 = xindex // 512
    y2 = yindex
    x3 = xindex
    tmp0 = tl.load(
        in_ptr0
        + (
            512
            + x0
            + (1536 * x1)
            + (786432 * y2)
            + (786432 * (((x0 + (512 * x1)) // 262144)))
        ),
        xmask & ymask,
    ).to(tl.float32)
    tmp1 = tl.load(in_ptr1 + (512 + x0), xmask)
    tmp2 = tmp1.to(tl.float32)
    tmp3 = tmp0 + tmp2
    tmp4 = 2.8284271247461903
    tmp5 = tmp3 / tmp4
    tl.store(
        out_ptr0 + (y2 + (62 * x3) + tl.zeros([XBLOCK, YBLOCK], tl.int32)),
        tmp5,
        xmask & ymask,
    )
```

items.title: [CI] Installation E2E test step grew from ~9 min to ~41 min since July
items.author: Jeffwan
items.body_excerpt:
**Area:** Testing (E2E)

## Summary

In the `Installation Tests` workflow, the `Run installation e2e tests` step went from 9m15s in mid-July to 40m36s now, and the whole workflow from about 20 minutes to 54. The `installation-test` job has a 75-minute timeout.

Measured on two runs of the same workflow:

- July 13: https://github.com/Jeffwan/aibrix/actions/runs/29281096831/job/86923371188
- October 8, `a228471` (main at #2930): https://github.com/Jeffwan/aibrix/actions/runs/37735233267/job/113174859334

## Numbers

| | Jul 13 | Oct 8 |
|---|---|---|
| Whole workflow | 20.5 min | 54 min |
| `Run installation e2e tests` step | 9m15s | 40m36s |
| Test packages | 1 (`./test/e2e`) | 13 |
| Top-level tests | 44 | 180 |
| Sum of test time | 486s | 2,123s |
| Compile time before the first test | 47s | 3m08s |

October 8 time per package. All packages run one after another (`go test -p 1`):

| Package | Time |
|---|---|
| gateway/routing | 527s |
| controller/roleset | 360s |
| controller/stormservice | 257s |
| gateway/pd | 218s |
| controller/podset | 206s |
| controller/modeladapter | 169s |
| controller/modelclaim | 163s |
| controller/raycluster | 117s |
| controller/modelwarmup | 46s |
| gateway/api | 32s |
| controller/modelrouter | 25s |
| controller/autoscaling (+ external-metrics) | ~5s |

## Why it grew (about +31 min)

### 1. New controller lifecycle E2E tests: about +19 min

Controller tests went from about 204s (only `TestRoleSetInPlaceUpdate`) to 1,348s. Every new package runs on the same kind cluster, one after another, so each one adds its full time to the step.

| Change | Package time now |
|---|---|
| StormService E2E (#2733, Sep 16) | 257s |
| PodSet lifecycle E2E (#2751, Sep 20) | 206s |
| ModelAdapter E2E no longer skipped (#2657, Sep 3) | 169s |
| ModelClaim E2E (#2460 Jul 18, expanded through #2929 Oct 8) | 163s |
| RayClusterFleet lifecycle E2E (#2753, Sep 20) | 117s |
| ModelWarmup E2E (#2769, Oct 2) | 46s |
| ModelRouter lifecycle E2E (#2743, Sep 19) | 25s |
| RoleSet historical-node (#2628) and drain (#2736) tests enabled in CI | roleset 202s → 360s |

### 2. Gateway tests: about +8 min

Gateway tests went from about 282s to 777s.

- **Each request to the mock is about 3.3× slower (#2383, Jul 14).** That change turned on capacity-aware latency in the mock by default. A request with no `max_tokens` now sleeps about 0.03s + 2ms × `randint(10, 500)` output tokens. That averages about 0.55s, where it used to be a fixed 0.2s.
  - 30 pod-discovery requests: 6.3s → 20.8s.
  - The 8 routing tests present in both runs: 163s → 351s in total. `TestRandomRouting` went 21s → 67s; the VTC tests went from about 21s to 52–61s.
- **New tests:**
  - power-of-two routing: 137s
  - PD failure, bucketing and watchdog tests: `gateway/pd` is 218s now
  - backend-request and API endpoint tests

### 3. Build overhead: about +4 min

#2676 (Sep 8) split the suite into packages and added `go test -p 1`. The `-p` flag limits concurrent compile actions as well as test binaries, so all compilation is now serial:

- compile time before the first test: 47s → 3m08s
- about 5–9s of compiling and linking before each of the 13 packages

items.author: xiaonans
items.body_excerpt:
**What is your question?**
I want to write my own fused fp16xfp16 gemm kernel with CUTE, but I can not find a tutorial/sample code with a performance comparable to cublas. 

I noticed there are some tutorials in https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/tree/main/examples/cute/tutorial, which has fp32xfp32 and int8xint8 gemm. But the performance of int8xint8 gemm is not good enough. I also noticed a 3rd party of fp16xfp16 gemm with CUTE https://github.com/leimao/CUDA-GEMM-Optimization?tab=readme-ov-file, but as shown in the readme, the performance is yet not comparable to cublas. So I wonder whether CUTE can give an official fp16xfp16 gemm kernel with good performance, so that I can develop based on that?

comments.author: Bogumil-Sapinski-Mobica
comments.body:
Hi,
I have added PR https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/pull/1843
I added it because:
- torch::kBFloat16 is a best match for bf16 type
- torch::kBFloat16 is used in pytorch benchmarks (pytorch/benchmarks/static_runtime/test_static_runtime.cc) and unit tests (pythorch/test/cpp/api/functional.cpp TEST_F(FunctionalTest, ELU))
- bf16 is already mapped to kBFloat16 in other place of cutlass (cutlass/python/cutlass/utils/datatypes.py is_torch_available()) in library_to_torch_dict. However it has different value types than _CUTLASS_TYPE_TO_TORCH_TYPE

However I have some doubts:
- as I mentioned in PR description in pytorch/test/cpp/api/support.h void assert_tensor_equal() kBFloat16 type is cast to kFloat32 because some tensor operations are not available for kBFloat16
- at::kBFloat16 is not exposed explicitly in torch namespace in pytorch/torch/csrc/api/include/torch/types.h.

I was not able to run 02_pytorch_extension_grouped_gemm.ipynb with my changes so I have no living proof that it works at least in this example. Any advice how to import pytorch from local repo will be welcome.

items.title: Five conv filter tile access iterators invert the byte scaling in add_pointer_offset (8/sizeof_bits instead of sizeof_bits/8)
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

Five conv filter tile access iterators invert the byte scaling in `add_pointer_offset`: they compute `pointer_offset * 8 / sizeof_bits<Element>::value` where every sibling iterator uses `pointer_offset * sizeof_bits<Element>::value / 8`.

Affected sites:

- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/conv2d_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_analytic.h:194
- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/conv2d_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_fixed_channels.h:165
- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/conv2d_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_few_channels.h:167
- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/conv3d_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_analytic.h:160
- include/cutlass/conv/threadblock/depthwise_fprop_filter_tile_access_iterator_direct_conv_optimized.h:162

For fp32 (32 bits) the inverted form is a silent no-op multiplier of 8/32 vs the correct 4; for fp16 it scales offsets by 1/2 instead of 2. All 30+ sibling iterators (activation/dgrad/wgrad variants) use the correct form, e.g. conv2d_dgrad_filter_tile_access_iterator_analytic.h:187.

Currently latent: no in-tree caller passes nonzero element-granularity pointer offsets into these mainloop A/B iterators (kernels call `add_pointer_offset` on the epilogue D iterator only). The defect surfaces for any external user advancing these public iterators manually.

items.title: Sparse split-K kernels offset the E operand without the kElementsPerElementE division
items.author: VaggelisGian
items.body_excerpt:
### Description

`SparseGemmSplitKParallel`-style serial split-K in `include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/sparse_gemm.h` offsets the E (metadata) operand by the wrong amount for slices beyond the first:

```cpp
// sparse_gemm.h:237
cutlass::MatrixCoord tb_offset_E{
  threadblock_tile_offset.m() * Mma::Shape::kM,
  threadblock_tile_offset.k() * params.gemm_k_size / kSparse,   // missing / kElementsPerElementE
};
```

The E iterator's extent is expressed in packed element-E columns and divides twice (`sparse_gemm.h:269`, `problem_size_k / kSparse / kElementsPerElementE`), and the sibling kernel `gemm_sparse_universal.h:622` divides twice as well when offsetting:

```cpp
cutlass::MatrixCoord tb_offset_E{
  threadblock_tile_offset.m() * Mma::Shape::kM,
  offset_k / kSparse / kElementsPerElementE,
};
```

With the missing division, every K-slice `>= 1` of a split-K sparse GEMM starts its metadata reads far past the end of the packed E tensor; all accesses are predicated off and the slice runs on zero-filled (invalid) metadata.

Concrete numbers: fp16 (`kElementsPerElementE == 2`), K=128, `split_k_slices = 2`: slice 1 has an E extent of 4 columns while its offset column is 32. Zero valid accesses.

The same formula is duplicated in two more copies of this kernel body:
- `sparse_gemm_with_absmax.h:322`
- `sparse_gemm_with_visitor.h:153`

Reachability note: nothing in-tree exercises it (`device::SparseGemm` with `split_k_slices > 1`; example 15 uses one slice), so this is latent, but the wrapper accepts split-K (`device/sparse_gemm.h` passes `args.batch_count` through).

### Suggested fix

Divide by `kElementsPerElementE` in the offset at all three sites, matching `gemm_sparse_universal.h`:

```cpp
threadblock_tile_offset.k() * params.gemm_k_size / kSparse / kElementsPerElementE,
```

items.title: [Store] Does Mooncake store plan to support awareness of layers, chunk ordering, and TP?
items.author: Hadigan
items.body_excerpt:
It looks like the current Mooncake store does not have awareness of layer granularity, chunk order (earlier vs. later chunks), or TP ranks. This can cause problems during cache eviction:

1. The store might evict KVs for only some layers, forcing prefill to recompute all layer KVs for those tokens.
2. The store might evict the KVs corresponding to the earliest chunk(s) of a token sequence, forcing prefill to recompute KVs for all chunks/tokens.
3. The store might evict KVs produced by some TP ranks, forcing all TP ranks to recompute KVs.

I think the Mooncake store should be aware of layers, chunk ordering, and TP. On eviction, it should evict a token’s KV caches for all layers and for all TP ranks together (i.e., keep KV state complete per token). 
From the chunk-order perspective, eviction policies should prefer removing KVs for later chunks first rather than evicting early-chunk KVs that make prefill expensive.

items.title: [Core/Auth] Create the auth token when any head node starts
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
Under a token default, every head must be able to create the token. Today only `ray.init()` creates one: `ray start --head` with no token fails with `AuthenticationError`, and `ray.cluster_utils.Cluster()` builds `Node(head=True)` directly, so its GCS crashes on `Check failed: has_token || ignore_auth_mode` (`authentication_token_loader.cc:115`) and the user only sees `Timed out waiting for file .../gcs_server_port_...`.

Change:

- `Node.__init__` with `head=True` calls `ensure_token_if_auth_enabled(create_token_if_missing=True)` before starting the GCS. This covers `ray start --head`, `ray.init()`, C++/Java drivers and `Cluster()`.
- Remove the token-creation calls in `worker.py` (new-cluster path) and `scripts.py` (`ray start --head`).
- Connecting paths keep `create_token_if_missing=False`.

No behavior change while the default is still `disabled`.

items.title: [Core/Auth] Distribute the auth token to ray up and autoscaler nodes via file_mounts
items.author: MortalHappiness
items.body_excerpt:
`ray up` clusters need the token on the head and every worker, without putting it on a command line. Passing it as an env var in the start commands puts it in `ps` on both ends of the SSH command and twice in the `ray up` console log.

Change:

- In `_set_up_config_for_head_node` (`autoscaler/_private/commands.py`), before the file mounts are rewritten, add a file mount for `~/.ray/auth_token` unless `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` is set locally or the YAML already mounts that path. The source follows token precedence: `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN` written to a 0600 temp file, else `RAY_AUTH_TOKEN_PATH`, else `~/.ray/auth_token` (created with `generate_and_save_token` if missing). The autoscaler reuses `file_mounts` for workers.
- Opting out: the user sets `RAY_AUTH_MODE=disabled` on the nodes in the cluster YAML. `ray up` never copies the local auth mode to the nodes.
- Existing `ray up` clusters relaunch once after upgrading, because the new file mount changes the runtime hash. Call this out in the PR so it reaches the release notes.
- Also cover `--no-monitor-on-head`, which skips `_set_up_config_for_head_node`.
- The fake multi-node docker provider skips `file_mounts`, so add the token file to the shared `node_spec["volumes"]` in `fake_multi_node/node_provider.py`, mounted read-only at `/home/ray/.ray/auth_token`.
- Test: a fake-provider cluster with `RAY_AUTH_MODE=token` scales up a worker that joins.

To check: whether launcher file mounts reach the container in Docker mode, and whether rsync keeps mode 0600.

items.title: [Core] C++ tests fail to build on macOS without --dynamic_mode=off
items.author: dancingactor
items.body_excerpt:
### What happened + What you expected to happen

On macOS, building a C++ test fails:

```
$ bazel test //src/ray/gcs/tests:gcs_placement_group_manager_test
ERROR: /private/var/tmp/_bazel_ryanchen/5221b57a12346d5b9f26ffbb4c5beac0/external/com_google_googleapis/google/rpc/BUILD.bazel:23:14: Linking external/com_google_googleapis/google/rpc/libstatus_proto.upb.dylib failed: (Exit 1): cc_wrapper.sh failed: error executing CppLink command (from target @@com_google_googleapis//google/rpc:status_proto) 
  (cd /private/var/tmp/_bazel_ryanchen/5221b57a12346d5b9f26ffbb4c5beac0/sandbox/darwin-sandbox/3998/execroot/io_ray && \
  exec env - \
    PATH=/bin:/usr/bin:/usr/local/bin \
    PWD=/proc/self/cwd \
    ZERO_AR_DATE=1 \
  external/local_config_cc/cc_wrapper.sh @bazel-out/darwin_arm64-opt/bin/external/com_google_googleapis/google/rpc/libstatus_proto.upb.dylib-2.params)
# Configuration: 027e5668f8aa2f880a108404b0ae57c26e88f88eb018fd4d5ea01e61f460fbe5
# Execution platform: @@internal_platforms_do_not_use//host:host

Use --sandbox_debug to see verbose messages from the sandbox and retain the sandbox build root for debugging
Undefined symbols for architecture arm64:
  "_google_protobuf_Any_msg_init", referenced from:
      _google_rpc_Status_submsgs in status.upb.o
ld: symbol(s) not found for architecture arm64
clang: error: linker command failed with exit code 1 (use -v to see invocation)
Target //src/ray/gcs/tests:gcs_placement_group_manager_test failed to build
```

**Adding `--dynamic_mode=off` avoids this failure, which is also what macOS CI does (`ci/ray_ci/macos/macos_ci.sh`). But it makes the test build slow and not user friendly**

### Root cause

- Ray's macOS cc toolchain doesn't enable `supports_dynamic_linker`, so a native `cc_library` is built static-only on macOS.
- `@upb//bazel:upb_proto_library.bzl` (the version pinned by grpc 1.58) calls `create_linking_context_from_compilation_outputs` with `disallow_dynamic_library` set only for Windows. As a result it still emits a nodeps `.dylib` for each proto.
- That dylib is linked with only its own object file. Linux tolerates the undefined symbols in shared libraries; macOS `ld` rejects them.

Newer protobuf already fixed this in its bundled upb (`bazel/private/upb_proto_library_internal/cc_library_func.bzl`):

```python
disallow_dynamic_library = cc_common.is_enabled(..., "targets_windows") or not cc_common.is_enabled(..., "supports_dynamic_linker"),
```

### Proposed fix

Backport that one line as a patch. Then declare `upb` in `bazel/ray_deps_setup.bzl` before `grpc_deps()`, with the same URL and sha256 grpc pins plus the patch. This is the same approach Ray already uses for `com_google_protobuf`. It makes no change on Linux, where `supports_dynamic_linker` is enabled. The patch can be dropped once Ray moves to a gRPC version that uses protobuf's bundled upb.

I tested it locally on macOS:
- With the patch, `bazel test //src/ray/gcs/tests:gcs_placement_group_manager_test` builds and passes without `--dynamic_mode=off`.
- With the patch removed, the link error above comes back.

### Versions / Dependencies

**Environment:** macOS 15.6.1 (arm64), Xcode 26.0.1, Bazel 7.5.0, `master`

### Reproduction script

bazel test //src/ray/gcs/tests:gcs_placement_group_manager_test

### Issue Severity

Medium: It is a significant difficulty but I can work around it.

items.title: SM120 (RTX PRO 6000) MoE backend gaps: MoeConfig.backend schema missing MegaMoE entries, and no EP-capable path for this hardware
items.author: ItamarTerem
items.body_excerpt:
Hi TensorRT-LLM team,
Deploying a large MoE model (Kimi-K2.7-Code-NVFP4, 384 experts) on 8x RTX PRO 6000 (SM120) via the pytorch backend, trtllm-serve, version 1.3.0rc20. Two related findings we wanted to raise:

1. MoeConfig.backend's pydantic Literal doesn't include MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL/MEGAMOE_DEEPGEMM, even though create_moe.py's dispatch logic already handles both as real branches. Setting moe_config.backend: MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL in extra_llm_api_options.yaml fails pydantic validation before create_moe.py is ever reached, even though the underlying backend selection logic supports it. This looks like the config schema hasn't caught up to the dispatch logic yet.
2. More fundamentally: none of the EP-capable MoE backends currently work on SM120 in this build.
 - MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL / MEGAMOE_DEEPGEMM: both explicitly require SM100/SM103 ("MegaMoECuteDsl requires SM100 family (SM100 or SM103); got SM120"), and fall back to CutlassFusedMoE.
 - WIDEEP: not SM-gated, but its GEMM compute still routes through the same CUTLASS kernel that produces silently incorrect output on SM120 in our testing, and additionally hit a binding mismatch in this build (run_moe() is missing value for argument '_37') before we could evaluate EP itself.
 - CUTEDSL (b12x): the only backend we've confirmed produces correct output on SM120, but has no EP support at the flashinfer level (num_local_experts != num_experts raises NotImplementedError in b12x_fused_moe).

Net result: there is currently no correct + EP-capable MoE path for SM120 in this stack, which limits per-GPU memory headroom for large-expert-count models on this hardware class.
Questions:

1. Is SM120 support planned for any of the MegaMoE/WideEP paths, or is SM100/SM103-first prioritization intentional for the near term?
2. Should we file the MoeConfig.backend schema gap as a separate, smaller issue, since that looks like a straightforward fix independent of the larger EP question?
3. Is there a recommended path for SM120 users running large MoE models today, or is CUTEDSL/no-EP the expected configuration for this hardware class in the current release?

Happy to share full repro steps/configs if helpful. Thanks for your work on this — appreciate the pointers.

shortlist.title: [good-first-issue] tests: make flaky vllm_bench throughput comparisons reproducible
shortlist.author: maobaolong
shortlist.body_excerpt:
Parent tracker: #5313 · Onboarding: #3372

## Confirmed flaky behavior

`k3-multiprocess-test / vllm / vllm_bench / zmq` changes its throughput verdict without a source update:

| Build #5340, September 29, 2026 (UTC) | Result |
| --- | --- |
| [Original job](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5340#01a0eab1-a517-4a38-8163-b0ec7cfaff63) | LMCache throughput **7.34% slower** than baseline; fails the 5% limit |
| [Retry](https://buildkite.com/lmcache/k3-multiprocess-test/builds/5340#01a0eaba-4671-4f79-a910-4a02cfa0cadf) | LMCache throughput **0.62% faster** than baseline; passes |

Both are `dev` builds of **`9e8226dd49728769843bf6f586b00b33ab616125`**, with no PR-base merge, vLLM **`0.30.1rc1.dev244+g0da126676`**, and torch **`2.13.0+cu130`**. Both baseline and LMCache completed all 50 requests with 500400 input tokens. This is an intermittent benchmark verdict, not an installation failure.

The inputs are not reproducible across those attempts: the original uses seed `1790644335`, the retry `1790645482`. Each attempt uses the same seed for its own baseline/LMCache pair, but the default `RANDOM_SEED` comes from `date +%s`. The seed change is a confirmed confounder; it is **not proven to be the sole cause** of the throughput fluctuation.

## Bounded good-first task

Make this benchmark's inputs reproducible across retries, and make the comparison auditable. This is the first test-harness improvement for the confirmed flake, not a production performance optimization.

1. Replace the clock-derived default seed with a documented stable default; continue honoring an explicit `RANDOM_SEED` override.
2. Save a small comparison manifest next to `baseline.json` and `lmcache.json`: effective seed, model, request count and lengths, actual checkout SHA, installed vLLM/torch versions, and the two throughput values/verdict. Keep any new diagnostics local to this workload.
3. Preserve separate attempt results when used in CI. Follow the existing result-directory/cleanup conventions, and ensure the manifest is accessible in the job log or a public Buildkite artifact rather than merely naming a container-local file.
4. Add focused CPU-only regression coverage using stub benchmark commands: default seed is repeatable, both sides receive it, an override is honored, and success/failure summaries retain the actual numbers.

Keep the 5% throughput limit, request/token checks, and cache-retrieval validation. Do not add blanket retries, remove assertions, or present a fixed seed as proof of a resolved performance issue. #5227 already added retry mitigation; this task addresses reproducibility within the workload.

Starting points, checked at `42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052`:

- [Workload seed and result comparison](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/workloads/vllm/vllm-bench.sh).
- [Result cleanup/copying](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/scripts/cleanup.sh).
- [Buildkite step and existing retry policy](https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache/blob/42be9c7439a1eb0b17bf6b7565a894a9743fd052/.buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/pipeline.yml).

## Acceptance

- [ ] Default inputs are identical across attempts; explicit overrides still work.
- [ ] A reviewer can recover both results, the effective inputs, versions, and verdict from public job output/artifacts.
- [ ] Stubbed CPU coverage exercises default/override and passing/failing results.
- [ ] GPU validation reports first-attempt results with a fixed seed; remaining fluctuation is reported as unresolved rather than hidden.
- [ ] Existing behavioral assertions and thresholds remain effective.

## Reproduce the CI workload

The evidence below comes from CI; this issue does not claim a local GPU reproduction. Use a dedicated Linux x86_64 GPU test host with Docker and NVIDIA Container Toolkit, two available CUDA GPUs capable of running separate `Qwen/Qwen3-14B` servers, sufficient host RAM for the default 80 GiB LMCache buffer (plus the mock L2 storage for the L2 case), and disk/network access for the image, wheels, and model. CI uses CUDA 13.0, Python 3.12, and a 1 GiB `/dev/shm`. A maintainer can run the GPU validation for a contributor who only has a CPU machine.

These commands build the public CI image recipe, explicitly start Bash, and pin the historical LMCache and vLLM revisions. They are a reproduction recipe, not a fully locked copy of every historical dependency or GPU scheduling condition. Run from a fresh directory; make the actual PR against current `dev`.

```bash
git clone https://github.com/LMCache/LMCache.git
cd LMCache
git checkout 9e8226dd49728769843bf6f586b00b33ab616125
docker build -t lmcache-flake-ci \
  -f .buildkite/k3_harness/ci-base.Dockerfile .
docker run --rm --gpus '"device=0,1"' --shm-size=1g \
  --entrypoint bash \
  -v "$PWD:/workspace/LMCache" -w /workspace/LMCache \
  -e MAX_JOBS=1 \
  -e INFERENCE_ENGINE=vllm \
  -e LMCACHE_REQUEST_TRANSPORT=zmq \
  -e LMCACHE_PR_BASE_MERGE=never \
  -e PINNED_VLLM_VERSION=0.30.1rc1.dev244+g0da126676 \
  -e PINNED_VLLM_ARCHIVE_INDEX_URL=https://wheels.vllm.ai/0da126676e38f5dc1b02b2c4f48dc85f90f5a79f/cu130 \
  lmcache-flake-ci -c '
    set -e
    source /opt/venv/bin/activate
    command -v git uv python3 nvcc gcc g++
    nvidia-smi
    git config --global --add safe.directory /workspace/LMCache
    .buildkite/k3_tests/multiprocess/run.sh vllm_bench
  '
```

Use the linked failed and passed jobs as the initial reproduction pair. For subsequent GPU runs, record the actual checkout SHA, installed package versions, GPU model, input settings, and first-attempt result. A green retry alone does not show that the underlying fluctuation was fixed.

## Claim and contribution rules

This is primarily for a new contributor. Claim **one active sub-issue at a time** by commenting `/claim` here; check existing comments and ass

shortlist.title: Refactor: TRTLLMHAAttnBackend should not inherit from FlashInferAttnBackend when reuse is small
shortlist.author: merrymercy
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Summary

`TRTLLMHAAttnBackend(FlashInferAttnBackend)` (in `python/sglang/srt/layers/attention/trtllm_mha_backend.py`) inherits from `FlashInferAttnBackend`, but it reuses very little from the parent. Almost all attention-specific behavior is overridden, and some inherited setup is allocated-but-never-used. We should reconsider this inheritance: **if the reuse is small, we should not inherit from `FlashInferAttnBackend`** — inheriting directly from the base `AttentionBackend` (and pulling in only the small bits of plumbing that are actually shared) would be cleaner.

### What is actually reused

The only real reuse comes from `super().__init__(...)`:
- `req_to_token_pool`, `token_to_kv_pool`
- `max_context_len`, `skip_prefill`, `use_sliding_window_kv_pool`
- the `kv_indptr` / `kv_last_page_len` buffers (used by the companion `TRTLLMHAAttnMultiStepDraftBackend` draft steps)
- `forward()` dispatch — which actually comes from the base `AttentionBackend`, not from FlashInfer.

### What is overridden (not reused)

Essentially all the attention logic:
- `init_forward_metadata`, `init_cuda_graph_state`, `init_forward_metadata_out_graph`
- `forward_decode`, `forward_extend` (call `flashinfer.decode.trtllm_batch_decode_with_kv_cache` / `flashinfer.prefill.trtllm_batch_context_with_kv_cache` directly)
- `get_cuda_graph_seq_len_fill_value`, `_resolve_swa_kv_pool`
- it uses its own `TRTLLMMHAMetadata` and its own page-table builder.

### Inherited-but-unused / redundant work

Because the TRTLLM kernels use a completely different API, part of the parent `__init__` is wasted:
- Parent builds `prefill_wrapper_ragged`, `prefill_wrappers_paged`, `decode_wrappers`, and the `FlashInferIndicesUpdater*` objects — TRTLLM-MHA never uses them.
- Parent sets `self.workspace_buffer` to the shared `global_workspace_buffer`, but the child **replaces** it with its own zero-init `global_zero_init_workspace_buffer`.
- `max_context_len` and `_swa_kv_pool` are set by the parent and then re-set by the child.

### Proposal

- Evaluate inheriting `TRTLLMHAAttnBackend` directly from `AttentionBackend` instead of `FlashInferAttnBackend`.
- Move the small amount of genuinely shared init plumbing into a thin shared helper/mixin (e.g. pool/buffer setup) rather than dragging in the full FlashInfer wrapper/indices-updater allocation.
- Avoid allocating FlashInfer wrappers and updaters that the TRTLLM path never uses.
- Apply the same review to `TRTLLMHAAttnMultiStepDraftBackend(FlashInferMultiStepDraftBackend)`.

As a general guideline: **do not inherit from `FlashInferAttnBackend` when the reuse is little** — prefer inheriting from the base `AttentionBackend` and sharing only what is actually common.

### Good first issue

This is a good first issue: it is well-scoped, localized to `trtllm_mha_backend.py` (plus the base classes), and mostly a refactor with clear before/after behavior to validate against existing tests.

shortlist.title: [Performance]: spec-decode boot-to-boot throughput dispersion on L4 (CV up to 13.92%), resolved in 0.30.0
shortlist.author: akshathtiwari
shortlist.body_excerpt:
### Proposal to improve performance

Not a proposal so much as a measurement suggestion. Speculative-decoding throughput on this stack is boot-dependent to a degree a single-boot benchmark cannot see: on 0.29.0 / L4, twelve boots of a byte-identical configuration gave CV 13.92% in one container and 3.73% in another. Anything comparing speculative configurations from one boot each is partly measuring which boot it got.

0.30.0 looks much better on this axis (0.99% and 1.61% across two containers on different physical cards), so this may already be resolved. I am reporting it mainly because the mechanism is not what I assumed, and the protocol seems worth having on record either way.

### Report of performance regression

Reporting this because 0.30.0 appears to resolve it, and the obvious explanation turns out to be wrong, so something else changed and I would like to know what.

**Setup.** Qwen3-4B target, `z-lab/Qwen3-4B-DFlash-b16` drafter, 5 speculative tokens, bf16 weights, `--kv-cache-dtype auto`, FlashInfer pinned. GSM8K, concurrency 1, one fixed prompt set replayed on every boot. 12 boots per arm inside a single container, one physical GPU per session (UUID recorded). The harness speaks HTTP only and never imports vLLM.

Throughput at concurrency 1, output tokens/s:

| card | engine | session | default | --enforce-eager | ratio | default CV |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| L4 (SM89) | 0.29.0 | A | 39.2 | 80.5 | **0.487** | **13.92%** |
| L4 (SM89) | 0.29.0 | B | 61.2 | 79.7 | **0.768** | **3.73%** |
| L4 (SM89) | 0.30.0 | C | 82.8 | 81.6 | **1.014** | 0.99% |
| L4 (SM89) | 0.30.0 | D | 78.2 | 77.0 | **1.017** | 1.61% |
| A10 (SM86) | 0.29.0 | E | 132.6 | 138.3 | 0.959 | 2.08% |

Each ratio is the default arm divided by the eager arm measured in the same container, so session and card effects cancel. On 0.29.0/L4 the CUDA-graph path runs at 49% and 77% of the eager path; on 0.30.0 it reaches parity. Acceptance length is flat throughout (tau 4.11-4.15), so this is throughput rather than a change in what the drafter gets accepted.

### Misc discussion on performance

Two observations, one related issue, and a question.

**1. The CUDA-graph fallback still fires on 0.30.0.** I had assumed the improvement was the speculative path gaining full graphs. It is not. The warning is byte-identical on both versions and capture proceeds under PIECEWISE in each:

> CUDAGraphMode.FULL_AND_PIECEWISE is not supported with spec-decode for attention backend FlashInferBackend (support: AttentionCGSupport.UNIFORM_SINGLE_TOKEN_DECODE); setting cudagraph_mode=PIECEWISE

Backend selection is unchanged too: both versions log FLASHINFER for the target and FLASH_ATTN for the second selection. So neither graph mode nor backend choice explains the difference.

**2. On 0.29.0 the dispersion magnitude is itself not reproducible.** Two twelve-boot measurements of the identical configuration gave CV 13.92% and 3.73%, with means 39.2 and 61.2 tok/s. The effect is present in both; its size is not a property of the configuration. The eager arm is stable across every session measured (80.5, 79.7, 81.6, 77.0 on L4; 138.3 on A10), which is what makes it usable as a control.

**Related, but I do not think it is the same thing: #58677.** That reports the draft model's torch.compile cache identity flipping between exactly two values across restarts with byte-identical argv, attributed to the shared VllmConfig being mutated in-place during the main model's warmup and CUDA-graph-capture phase, before the draft head compiles. Two differences: the symptom there is startup recompile cost rather than steady-state throughput, and it reports 0.27.1 affected with 0.29 appearing immune, whereas what I measure is on 0.29.0.

Still, the shape is close enough that I would rather ask than assume: **if VllmConfig is mutated in place during graph capture and that mutation reaches what the draft compiles to, could the same mechanism produce a steady-state throughput difference and not only a cache-key difference?** My measurements begin after the server reports healthy, so any recompilation has finished by then.


**The question.** What changed between 0.29.0 and 0.30.0 on this path, given the fallback and the backend selection are identical in both? If a specific PR is responsible I would rather cite it than guess. I looked at #53867, #51700, #54646 and #52228 and could not attribute it from the release notes alone.

**Possibly relevant.** The effect is much weaker on an A10 (ratio 0.959) than on an L4 (0.487 and 0.768) at the same engine version. The A10 has 24 GiB against the L4's 22.03 GiB usable, and this configuration sits close enough to the memory ceiling that --enforce-eager alone decides whether an fp8_e4m3-KV variant boots at all. So capacity pressure may matter more here than architecture. I have not separated the two.

**Reproduction.** Harness, raw append-only records, analysis scripts and the engine logs are at https://github.com/akshathtiwari/spec-fp8-study (archived at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23033168). The boot-variance runs are one command each and the per-session numbers regenerate from the stored records. Happy to run further configurations if a specific one would help; the full sweep is a couple of GPU-hours.

### Your current environment (if you think it is necessary)

Not `collect_env.py` output: the engine runs in an ephemeral container on a rented GPU, so this machine's environment is not the one under test. These are the fields the harness records per measurement, read from nvidia-smi and from the running server.

```text
GPU         NVIDIA L4 (SM89, 22.03 GiB usable) and NVIDIA A10 (SM86)
            one physical card per session, gpu_uuid recorded per record
driver      580.95.05
CUDA        13.0
torch       2.13.0+cu130
vLLM        0.29.0 and 0.30.0, pinned by image digest. Version is read from
            the server's /version endpoint and checked against the declared
            value before any measu

comments.author: akshathtiwari
comments.body:
Correction to the "possibly relevant" paragraph in my original post.

I wrote that the A10 has 24 GiB against the L4's 22.03 GiB usable, and offered memory capacity as the likelier of two readings for why the deficit is weak on the A10. **That is wrong.** Both cards report **22.5 GiB** in my own records, and I had never checked the field before writing it. Capacity is not the difference between them.

What does differ, from the same records:

| | VRAM | arch | max SM clock | power limit |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| L4 | 22.5 GiB | SM8.9 | 2040 MHz | **72 W** |
| A10 | 22.5 GiB | SM8.6 | 1695 MHz | **150 W** |

So the card showing the deficit has less than half the power budget. That is a better fit for the symptom than capacity ever was: CUDA graphs run the work faster, faster work draws more power, and a 72 W part can hit its cap and clamp — variably, depending on thermal history, which would also explain why the dispersion magnitude itself does not reproduce between sessions. The eager arm runs slower, stays under the cap, and is stable in every session measured.

I want to be clear that this is a hypothesis and **my data cannot test it.** I was recording `clocks.max.sm` and `power.limit`, which are what the card is permitted to do, not what it did. A throttling explanation is precisely what configured limits cannot see.

I have since added sampling of achieved SM clock, power draw and `clocks_throttle_reasons.*` across the measurement window, and a run is in flight. If `sw_power_cap` is active during the default arm and not during the eager arm, that is the driver answering the question directly rather than me inferring it from a clock curve. I will post the result either way, including if it kills the hypothesis.

The throughput numbers and the ratio table in the original post are unaffected by this — they are measured, and the correction is to an explanation I attached to them.

shortlist.title: Restart-proof KV cache for llama-server: 40K-token TTFT 155s to 6s after reboot
shortlist.author: qqkzlm
shortlist.body_excerpt:
Every restart wipes your prefill. Server crash, box reboot, model reload — a 40K-token agentic prompt pays the full ~155s prefill again before the first token.

I patched llama-server to persist KV-cache prefix checkpoints to disk and auto-restore the longest matching prefix on boot. Same prompt after a restart: **first token in ~6s instead of ~155s** (2.1s disk read once + decode). No client changes, no re-architecture — the server just remembers.

Measured on GTX 1080 8GB, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, `-c 92160`:

- Cold: 151s prefill → first token at ~155s
- Warm (post-restart): 2.1s disk read (first request only) → first token at ~6s
- Checkpoints keyed by model + ctx + KV quant (wrong config = ignored, never corrupted); disk-budget eviction included

Single-commit patch (86KB): https://github.com/qqkzlm/llama-cpp-prompt-disk-cache — `git am` onto the PrismML `prism` branch, four flags (`--slot-save-path`, `--checkpoint-min-step`, `--ctx-checkpoints`, `--prompt-cache-disk-budget`).

One MoE lesson from the same box: keep experts on GPU, let KV follow the layers — pushing 20 MoE layers to CPU collapsed prefill 265→30 tok/s, which no cache can fix.

Happy to upstream behind a flag if maintainers are interested.

comments.author: qqkzlm
comments.body:
Update to the README since this went up — three things worth calling out for anyone trying it:

**1. Prebuilt CUDA binaries exist for both platforms.** The `v0.2.3` release ships `llama-server-win-cuda-v0.2.3.zip` and `llama-server-linux-cuda-v0.2.3.tar.gz`. The Linux package is built for `sm_61`/Pascal, so it also runs on GTX 10-series. No build needed:

```bash
./llama-server -m model.gguf -c 32768 --host 0.0.0.0 --port 8000 \
  --slot-save-path /var/tmp/kvstore/model \
  --prompt-cache-disk-budget 20 --checkpoint-min-step 2048 --ctx-checkpoints 64
```

**2. Only one flag is actually required.** `--slot-save-path` is the only one you must pass — `--prompt-cache-disk-budget` and `--prompt-cache-disk-path` are silently ignored without it, and entries land in `<slot-save-path>/pdcache`. `--prompt-cache-disk` is **enabled by default**, so passing it is optional; use `--no-prompt-cache-disk` to turn the cache off.

**3. Cache hits require a byte-identical prompt prefix.** Only the common prefix from token 0 onward is reused. If you prepend a timestamp or a random ID, everything after it misses and the cache is effectively unused. Put stable content first (system prompt, tool definitions, long docs) and per-turn content last — opencode / Claude Code already do this, so it works out of the box.

The README now has a "when does the cache hit / when does it miss" section covering this, a flag-duty table, and a Chinese-first three-step guide (the repo README is now Chinese-primary). A Windows `start-llama-server.bat` is included in the zip if you want a prompt-driven launcher instead of a command line.

Still happy to upstream this behind a flag if maintainers are interested — the whole feature is one commit touching `tools/server/server-prompt-disk.cpp` (~900 lines) plus slot/task integration.

shortlist.title: [Bug] Decode Throughput Inconsistency Between bench_serving and Engine Logs
shortlist.author: leepoly
shortlist.body_excerpt: ### Checklist - [x] 1. I have searched related issues but cannot get the expected help. - [x] 2. The bug has not been fixed in the latest version. - [x] 3. Please note that if the bug-related issue you submitted lacks corresponding environment info and a minimal reproducible demo, it will be challenging for us to reproduce and resolve the issue, reducing the likelihood of receiving feedback. - [x] 4. If the issue you raised is not a bug but a question, please raise a discussion at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/discussions/new/choose Otherwise, it will be closed. - [x] 5. Please use English, otherwise it will be closed. ### Describe the bug Hi, I encountered an inconsistency in decode throughput reporting. When benchmarking with the bench_serving script, the reported TPOT is **much lower** than the decode throughput logged by the engine. This gap is significant for **small models or high concurrency settings**. ### Reproduction #### start the server ``` python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path Qwen/Qwen2.5-0.5B \ --trust-remote-code \ --tp 1 \ --load-format dummy \ --port 30000 --host 127.0.0.1 ``` #### benchmark (seqlens 2048 concurrency 16) ``` python3 -m sglang.bench_serving \ --backend sglang \ --dataset-name random \ --random-range-ratio 1.0 \ --random-input-len 2048 \ --random-output-len 256 \ --num-prompts 16 \ --max-concurrency 16 \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 30000 ``` Observed Results: - The bench_serving script reports a median TPOT of 4.45 ms, equating to a token throughput of 224 $\times$ 16 = 3584 tokens/second. - However, the engine logs show a decode throughput of 7026 tokens/second. The gap between these metrics is significant and raises concerns about potential discrepancies in throughput measurement. Please let me know if you need additional details or logs to assist in troubleshooting. ### Environment Python: 3.10.0 (default, Mar 3 2022, 09:58:08) [GCC 7.5.0] CUDA available: True NVIDIA H800 GPU CUDA_HOME: /usr/local/cuda NVCC: Cuda compilation tools, release 12.6, V12.6.85 CUDA Driver Version: 535.129.03 PyTorch: 2.5.1+cu124 sglang: 0.4.1.post5 flashinfer: 0.1.6+cu124torch2.4 triton: 3.1.0 transformers: 4.48.0 torchao: 0.7.0 numpy: 1.26.4

comments.author: YEXINGZHE54
comments.body: I think it's just a difference between  long-time metric and short-time peak metric. From the perspective of bench_serving, estimating token throughput using TPOT (Time Per Output Token) provides a comprehensive evaluation over the entire testing period. On the other hand, the throughput printed in the engine log refers to the number of tokens generated within a single logging interval (which can be understood as the time for 40 consecutive decodes) divided by the time taken. Clearly, the data in the engine log is influenced by various factors, including: the potential interleaving of the prefill phase between decodes, which extends the total time; additionally, the amount of remaining memory also affects the number of tokens output per decode. Of course, the core issue here is that the engine log records short-term peak throughput, and similar results might be obtained if using the P25 (25th percentile) of TPOT for estimation.

comments.author: Tshiyao
comments.body:
I think I've found the cause. In multiple tests, when the backend is specified as "sglang," the `flush_cache` function is called to clear the cache.

 If `flush_cache` is executed successfully, there will be an inconsistency in the Decode Throughput between `bench_serving` and `engine logs`, specifically, `bench_serving` will be lower than `engine logs`. 

If `flush_cache` fails, the difference in Throughput between the two is within an acceptable range.

I speculate that the time loss caused by the successful execution of `flush_cache` might be the reason. The Decode Throughput in `engine logs` is not affected by this, but `bench_serving` is. I'm still not sure how to fix it. Does anyone have any suggestions?

When the backend is specified as "sglang," the following code is called to flush the cache，code in [here](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/9cf407729441a18561ee5a8b2c1e3e535ba817f9/python/sglang/bench_serving.py#L961):
```python
# Flush cache
if "sglang" in backend:
    requests.post(base_url + "/flush_cache")
```

The specific implementation of `flush_cache` can be found [here](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/blob/9cf407729441a18561ee5a8b2c1e3e535ba817f9/python/sglang/srt/managers/scheduler.py#L1677):
```python
def flush_cache(self):
    """Flush the memory pool and cache."""
    if len(self.waiting_queue) == 0 and (
        self.running_batch is None or len(self.running_batch.reqs) == 0
    ):
        self.tree_cache.reset()
        self.tree_cache_metrics = {"total": 0, "hit": 0}
        if self.grammar_backend:
            self.grammar_backend.reset()
        self.req_to_token_pool.clear()
        self.token_to_kv_pool.clear()

        if not self.spec_algorithm.is_none():
            self.draft_worker.model_runner.req_to_token_pool.clear()
            self.draft_worker.model_runner.token_to_kv_pool.clear()

        self.num_generated_tokens = 0
        self.forward_ct_decode = 0
        self.spec_num_total_accepted_tokens = 0
        self.spec_num_total_forward_ct = 0
        torch.cuda.empty_cache()
        logger.info("Cache flushed successfully!")
        if_success = True
    else:
        logging.warning(
            f"Cache not flushed because there are pending requests. "
            f"#queue-req: {len(self.waiting_queue)}, "
            f"#running-req: {0 if self.running_batch is None else len(self.running_batch.reqs)}"
        )
        if_success = False
    return if_success
```

comments.author: ptimizeroracle
comments.body:
I went through both sides of this with the current code (main @ 99b9109). Happy to turn any of it into a fix if wanted, but evidence first.

**The two numbers are different estimators, not two measurements of the same thing:**

| | bench_serving | engine log |
|---|---|---|
| definition | TPOT-derived, per request: `(latency − ttft)` over `output_len − 1`, averaged across the whole run, client-side | `num_generated_tokens / gap_latency` where `gap_latency` is the time since the previous log line (`scheduler_components/metrics_reporter.py:799,894`) |
| window | entire run: queueing, any cold start, `[DONE]` tail included | one reporting interval, near-instantaneous |

So bench < engine is expected whenever the run has any ramp-up: the engine line reads close to a short-window peak, the bench number is a whole-run average.

Three smaller things verified along the way (all `python/sglang/benchmark/serving.py` unless noted):

1. TPOT arithmetic is the standard upstream vLLM formula (`(latency − ttft)/(output_len − 1)`, `:1136`): sound.
2. `itl` is recorded per stream **event**, not per token (`:334-337`, `:466+`). Events carrying several tokens (stream-interval batching, speculative decoding) contribute one itl sample, so `len(itl) < output_len − 1` and ITL percentiles conflate event latency with token latency. A retokenized correction already exists, but only for the `sglang-oai` backends (`:1131-1135`, `:1145-1155`); the completions/chat paths don't get it. I wrote CPU unit tests pinning this behavior (sum(itl) + [DONE]-tail == latency − ttft exactly; mean(ITL) > TPOT for the same request from denominators alone). Happy to PR them.
3. `should_flush_cache` is `("sglang" in backend AND SGLANG_IS_IN_CI) or --flush-cache` (`:1467-1471`), not default-on, so the cold-start mechanism discussed earlier in this thread needs CI or the explicit flag to apply to a default run.

If it's useful, the options I see: (a) a note in the bench output clarifying the window difference vs engine logs, (b) an engine-side long-window average for apples-to-apples runs, (c) extending the retokenized ITL path to the other backends. Which, if any, would you want?

shortlist.title: llama-quantize: GGML_ASSERT(size mismatch) when quantizing mmproj files containing 3D conv tensors (gemma4v audio conv1d)
shortlist.author: mrBenBern
shortlist.body_excerpt:
Quantizing the gemma-4-E2B combined mmproj (vision+audio, gemma4v/gemma4a projectors) from F16 to Q8_0 aborts with:

  llama-quant.cpp:1365: GGML_ASSERT(gguf_get_tensor_size(...) == new_size) failed

Repro:
  llama-quantize --allow-requantize mmproj-F16.gguf out.gguf Q8_0

Fails at tensor `a.conv1d.0.weight` — shape [3,3,1,128] (3D conv1d from the audio encoder). The f32→f16 conversion changes the tensor size, and the split-output writer asserts on the mismatch. Every subsequent 3D tensor fails the same way (a.conv1d.1.weight [3,3,128,32], ...).

Workaround (verified): keep 3D tensors in f32 via tensor-type overrides —
  llama-quantize --allow-requantize \
    --tensor-type "a.conv1d.0.weight=f32" \
    --tensor-type "a.conv1d.1.weight=f32" \
    mmproj-F16.gguf mmproj-F16-q8_0.gguf Q8_0

This works and the resulting Q8_0 mmproj is functionally correct on-device (Android, llama.cpp 4ebdf2c): vision outputs verified same-in-quality as F16 (sign-text reading), encode on a Helio G99 CPU improved 6.4x vs BF16 (37s -> 5.8s for a 91-token image).

Expected behavior: either skip/conversion-preserving handling for N-D tensors whose element count doesn't allow requantization, or a clean error message listing the offending tensors instead of an assert.
